column5: Guide on Producing Fair Maps with Compact Districts
column6:
Thank you for the important work you are doing on redistricting.  I though you might be interested in a Guide on Redistricting that is now available for citizens, and members of redistricting commissions, as well as legislators and judges.  The Guide highlights a new transparent, straightforward procedure for building maps that contain compact districts and are fair.  The approach can be applied by hand.
https://preprints.apsanet.org/engage/apsa/article-details/60132387f0e57e892a97e039       
This work has garnered more than 600 views on the Preprints Page of the American Political Science Association.  As more people become aware of procedures like this, more will ask that such approaches be used to draw fair legislative district maps.  Who draws the maps is important, but what kind of maps they draw is even more important.

column5: Mapping Consultant Selection
column6:
Hello,
Thanks for the chance to give input to your Mapping Consultant selection.  This is a most important decision by the IRC because of the algorithms used by these firms, and their reputations.

Taylor English, and CEO Earl Ehrhart, are greatly concerning.  They are a lobbyist firm, not a mapping firm (look at their website).  Why would a politically well-connected lawyer head a mapping firm if not to influence the outcome politically?  Mr. Ehrhart is a 30 year Georgia state representative and a former Chair of ALEC. That should be enough to immediately disqualify Taylor English.  I fear this firm would run the IRC and not the other way around. 

National Demographics Corp shows to be a quite reputable mapping firm with no extreme political bias noted. Interestingly, CEO Doug Johnson has written several white papers about more competitive districts needed in CA.  NDC served the 2001 AIRC mapping, which withstood AZ court challenges.  However, the drawbacks seem to be that nationally there have been occasional missed deadlines and a history of occasionally not defending well its work in other court challenges.  

HaystaqDNA is a strong contender, though has clear left leaning bias in its political campaign projects. This strong mapping agency successfully helped defend the 2011 AIRC maps all the way to the Supreme Court.  The AIRC project was not a political campaign, but rather a bipartisan mapping exercise. The maps were demonstrated to be balanced, fair and competitive..

Bottom line – Please DO NOT SELECT Taylor English.  Doing so would destroy the balanced and fair bipartisan goals of this Commission. The citizens’ trust in the outcome would be badly compromised at a time when AZ is already suffering from extreme partisanship. 

Thank you,
JMP, Prescott

column5: Selection of Mapping Consultant
column6:
Apparently, the interviews for the Mapping Commission will take place in Executive Session. This is unfortunate, though perhaps it is a consequence of the choice to use the state’s procurement process. Nonetheless, it is my hope that the Commission will make its decision based on the experience of the applicants, and on their demonstrated ability to fulfill the requirements for the position. These criteria might sound obvious, and yet apparently two of the three applicants do not satisfy them.

In the case of Taylor English, as far as I can tell, they have no experience in mapping for redistricting. They have worked on redistricting litigation, but that is not the same thing. This should disqualify them.

While the Timmons Group similarly lacks the relevant experience, they have partnered with the National Demographics Corporation (NDC), who has worked in this area; in fact, I believe that they worked on maps for the 2001 redistricting commission. So it would appear that they pass the “experience test.” However, I do have concerns over their reliability to produce the results that are required. For instance, the Republican Advisory Commission chair for Yuma County has noted that they did not meet deadlines for the county redistricting, not delivering as the contract required. When Doug Johnson of NDC served as an expert witness in several North Carolina redistricting cases, the courts rejected his analysis in each of them.

The third group, HaystaqDNA, appears to be qualified according to both criteria: they are experienced in the specific task, and they produced maps that have withstood court challenges. I understand that at least two of the current Commissioners may have qualms about using them, since they were the mapping consultants for the 2011 IRC. But the other applicants do not satisfy the rather obvious criteria that I have described. I also think that it is important that the Commission not reject out of hand resources just because they were used in 2011 – whatever any Commissioner thinks of the specific district boundaries from that year’s work, they survived numerous court actions, and were competent. 

In summary, please make your hiring decision based on experience and reliability, and suspend any partisan criteria that you might have. You are the INDEPENDENT Redistricting Commission. Please make your choices with this in mind.

column5: HaystaqDNA Proposal
column6:
Commissioners:

As the Vice Chair of the Arizona Independent Redistricting Commission during its last term, I write to counsel you against hiring HaystaqDNA, f/k/a Strategic Telemetry, (“Haystaq”) as the Commission’s mapping consultant.  If the Commission were to retain Haystaq, not only would it again be hiring a highly partisan mapper with deep and exclusive ties to one political party, but it also would be hiring a company that underperformed in executing its duties during the last redistricting.  These failures irreparably harmed public confidence in the redistricting that occurred in 2011.  

As I am sure you are aware, the 2011 Commission hired Haystaq, then known as Strategic Telemetry, after a bizarre and troubling procurement process.  Commissioners purposefully shredded procurement evaluation forms to hide them from later scrutiny, and certain Commissioners collectively discussed hiring Strategic Telemetry through serial telephone calls the Chair initiated, thereby flouting state’s open meeting laws.  Before the Commission voted to hire the mapping consultant, the State Procurement Office withdrew as the Commission’s procurement officer, citing the Commission’s repeated failures to abide by procurement rules.  After a 3-2 vote, and further evidencing a result-oriented, sham process, the Chair read a typed statement that she had drafted before the hearing wherein she attempted to quell the public outcry she had been warned would erupt about a vote that she pre-ordained.    

But the highly partisan nature of Haystaq and its problematic origins as the prior Commission’s mapping consultant are not the only reasons against hiring it again.  Haystaq failed, perhaps purposely so, to discharge fully its most important duties:  (1) recording a detailed and thorough log of the Commission’s directions to “adjust the grid lines” and the constitutional reasons underpinning every mapping change and (2) taking fine-grain and periodic “snapshots” of its changes to the maps as it executed those directions.  

Haystaq’s disappointing failures harmed the Commission because the public had no way to “reverse engineer” the final maps to the original grid maps.  Put another way, the public could not examine a list of detailed and constitutionally based instructions by the Commission and, essentially, watch a time-lapse movie of “snapshots” showing how the mapping consultant implemented those changes, moving from the final maps back in time to the original grid maps.  Consequently, the final maps were unhinged from the Arizona constitution, which requires the Commission to create the grid maps, then “adjust the grid lines” to meet the six redistricting criteria, and then publish draft and final maps.  What the public had, in fact, were maps with districts that the Commission claimed were infused with the values expressed in the six redistricting criteria.  But the public had no way of knowing where those maps came from, how they were derived from constitutional “adjustments” to the grid lines, and whether the maps were influenced by outside sources.

Ultimately, Haystaq’s failure to record adequate snapshots and inability to reverse engineer the final maps forced the Commission to take the position in litigation that it could draw whatever maps it wanted at the end of the day, so long as a Commissioner, at least at some point, grabbed a microphone during a hearing and talked about how the districts met the constitutional criteria.  This argument the Commission’s lawyers advanced was highly expedient in the context of the litigation and never approved, directed, or ratified by the Commission.  Indeed, this argument would read entire provisions out of Arizona constitution, including those related to the creation of “the grid maps” and “adjusting the grid lines,” rendering them of no legal significance, essentially legal nullities or constitutional “fluff.”  If Haystaq had done its job, however, the public could have had confidence that the final maps, whether liked or disliked, were the product of the Commission’s efforts to faithfully discharge the reasonable meaning of every word of the Arizona constitution, a provision that is designed to constrain, at least to some degree, discretion and reduce political interference.  

One thing you might hear from your mapping consultant applicants is none of the foregoing matters because they simply execute the Commission’s instructions and nothing more.  If problems existed with the last set of maps, the last Commission bears responsibility for them, not the mapping consultant.  Indeed, that is the way it should work, with the Commission making all the value judgments and agreeing upon precise instructions, with the mapping consultant using its technical expertise to implement those instructions and nothing more.  As a practical reality, however, you will likely vest your mapping consultant with broad discretion.  With that discretion comes an opening for political mischief.  

As you will quickly find, mapping adjustments are, for the most part, a zero-sum game.  Even a minor adjustment to a grid line on one part of the map can necessitate a cascade of adjustments throughout the map:  populations become unbalanced in districts and must be rebalanced; criteria are caused to be unmet in other parts of the map and must be ameliorated in some way; etc.  These adjustments and readjustments are very tedious and time consuming to implement, often taking hours.  If this Commission intends to direct each concomitant adjustment, my hat is off to you, but you might leave many of these adjustments to your mapping consultant.

For example, you might direct that a grid line be adjusted in one area of the map to make one or more districts more compact, thereby ensuring that you have given voters in that part of the state the constitutional “value” of living in a “compact” district, one of the six constitutional redistricting goals.  But making those districts more compact might cause districts throughout the map to no longer be “equally populated,” another mandatory redistricting value.  Furthermore, your compactness adjustment, and the subsequent effort to rebalance populations throughout the map, might result in voters in another part of the state being draw into districts that are less compact, thereby taking away the value of “compactness” from those voters.  Factors and considerations like these come in to play with virtually every mapping change, and often the mapping consultant is trusted to make them, returning a product that implements your instruction and yet still works as a viable map.

Another way your mapping consultant can be vested with broad discretion is when instructions can be implemented in multiple ways, with the mapping consultant left to determine which way.  For example, returning to the “compactness” criterion, the mapping consultant could be instructed to adjust the grid lines to maximize the compactness of districts throughout the map.  Similarly, using one of the mathematical “measures” of compactness, the mapping consultant could be instructed to adjust the grid lines such that each district is within a certain numerical value of a minimum compactness threshold value the Commission sets.  Either instruction appears reasonable on its face, but these instructions lack precision as to implementation.  Conceivably, several different maps could be drawn that execute these instructions.  If your mapping consultant returns with just one map implementing your instructions rather than, say, five maps, the public might wonder why the mapper chose to present that one map and not alternatives.

Having the mapping consultant keep a running series of fine-grain “snapshots” of its work product is a critical way to address concerns about granting, whether expressly or implicitly, discretion to the mapping consultant.  If a question arises, snapshots allow the public insight into the mapper’s thought processes and efforts to comply with Commission directives.  Snapshots also help preserve the link between the final maps and the grid maps, allowing the public to see that the final maps are grounded in the constitution process the voters approved.  Not having snapshots, or having snapshots that are too “coarse,” i.e., missing the details of many changes, allows the mapper to insert and disguise its own, perhaps politically motivated, judgment.  It also invites litigation, as it did with the last commission.

Haystaq’s failure to generate the record needed to reverse engineer the maps was not its only transgression.  In the aftermath of the Commission hiring Haystaq, the Commission proposed contract addenda, which Haystaq approved, designed in part to mitigate the damage to public confidence caused by its hiring.  As of 2011, Haystaq (then called Strategic Telemetry) was a highly political, Washington, D.C.-based, data mining company with no state-wide redistricting experience.  One contract addendum required Haystaq to perform all its mapping in Arizona, perhaps removing the process to some degree from inside-the-beltway influences.  Years after the mapping was completed, however, a Haystaq employee revealed in litigation that maps had been adjusted outside the state.  This perhaps inadvertent moment of candor, although of no consequence in the litigation, did not go unnoticed.  Haystaq might argue that where the maps are drawn is of little import, but the Commission judged otherwise, viewing it as important to bolster public confidence.  Haystaq should have appreciated this and kept its agreement.  At the very least, Haystaq should have been transparent as to its methods for completing its work.

The primary intent with the foregoing message is to highlight critical duties Haystaq failed to discharge adequately during the 2011 redistricting that perhaps might not have been fully appreciated.  No doubt, others have raised additional concerns with Haystaq’s proposal.  

Thank you for considering this submission.  You are all doing a great job and are in for an intellectually and socially delicious experience as Commissioners.

Scott

Scott Day Freeman
Former Vice Chair of the Arizona Independent Redistricting Commission
Freeman Legal Counsel, PLC
Managing Member
ScottDayFreeman@freemanlegalcounsel.com

column5: Comment on Mapping Consultant NDC.
column6:
Mapping and analysis performed by NDC and Doug Johnson has been rejected and discredited by courts throughout the country.

Hiring a mapping consultant with a record of drawing and defending court-rejected gerrymandered maps would risk the integrity of our maps and the public’s trust in the IRC. The Commission must reject Timmons Group/NDC from consideration.

I.  In North Carolina’s 2019 landmark gerrymandering case Common Cause v Lewis, a three-judge panel tossed out Doug Johnson’s testimony in defense of North Carolina’s gerrymandered map -- testimony which he later admitted was incorrect.
      A.  https://www.newsobserver.com/news/politics-government/article233105817.html
      B.  “The Court finds Dr. Johnson’s analysis unpersuasive and gives his opinions little weight.” https://www.nccourts.gov/assets/inline-files/18-CVS-14001_Final-Judgment.pdf?Bwsegeo1VV20zhJsp9hoClvmoRp3A6AR

II.  The 2018 case Luna vs Kern County is a landmark voting rights victory in which the US District Court Judge ruled that the redistricting plan defended by Doug Johnson unlawfully denied Latinos the ability to elect candidates of their choice.
      A.   https://www.maldef.org/2019/03/kern-country-voting-rights/
      B.  Doug Johnson’s testimony and data were found to be “insufficient.” https://casetext.com/case/luna-v-cnty-of-kern-4

III.  NDC was the mapping consultant for the 2001 Arizona IRC, which produced two legislative maps that were later thrown out. 
      A.  In 2002, the Commission’s first approved map failed to receive preclearance under the Voting Rights Act: https://azredistricting.org/2001/Final/doj_letter.pdf
      B.  In 2004, the Commission's second approved map was ruled unconstitutional: https://azredistricting.org/2001/2004legfinal/2004LegCourtOrder.pdf

IV.  In March of 2019, the West Contra Costa Unified School District (WCCUSD) settled a civil rights lawsuit which claimed that the district's at-large election map "dilutes the voting strength of Latino and African American citizens.
      A.  According to the plaintiff's attorney, "NDC cost the District over $650,000 by spending over a year producing map after map without a Latino majority trustee area."https://www.countyofkings.com/home/showpublisheddocument?id=25778
      B.  In that settlement, WCCUSD conceded that their map was likely in violation of both the California Voting Rights Act (CVRA) and Section 2 of the US Voting Rights Act.
      C. The court adopted the Plaintiff's map -- not NDC's. https://www.wccusd.net/cms/lib/CA01001466/Centricity/Domain/16/Joint%20Ex%20Parte%20Application%20for%20Entry%20of%20Judgment.pdf
V.  In 2018 & 2019, as the demographers for Redwood City's redistricting, NDC claimed that it was not possible to draw two Latino-majority districts in the city. Latino community groups protested after the council passed a map with just one Latino-majority district. Then NDC reversed their position. 
     A.  "After pushback from that community, among others, the city’s demographer announced that it made an error and was in fact able to create maps with two Latino majority districts..."
https://www.smdailyjournal.com/news/local/redwood-city-adopts-district-elections-map/article_29ddd2e8-7127-11e9-9750-c796bd4f69f7.html
     B.  Due to NDC's “error”, the Redwood City Council was forced to start over on their map, adding additional time and cost.
https://www.redwoodcity.org/home/showdocument?id=17969

I see many comments against HaystaqDNA based upon a perception of some political affiliation and some perceived assumption that the maps must be drawn to favor a Republican majority.  However, aside from invoking the perennial bogey-men of Obama and Sanders, none of the comments point to any concrete examples of bias by Haystaq or offer any examples of any unbiased or exemplary work by Timmons Group/NDA.  Please consider then, the following concrete examples of why Timmons should NOT be chosen:
1.  In North Carolina’s 2019 landmark gerrymandering case Common Cause v Lewis, a three-judge panel tossed out Doug Johnson’s testimony in defense of North Carolina’s gerrymandered map -- testimony which he later admitted was incorrect.  The 3-judge panel found that NDC produced gerrymandered maps.  2.  The 2018 case Luna vs Kern County is a landmark voting rights victory in which the US District Court Judge ruled that the redistricting plan defended by Doug Johnson unlawfully denied Latinos the ability to elect candidates of their choice.  3.  In March of 2019, the West Contra Costa Unified School District (WCCUSD) settled a civil rights lawsuit which claimed that the district's at-large election map "dilutes the voting strength of Latino and African American citizens.  According to the plaintiff's attorney, "NDC cost the District over $650,000 by spending over a year producing map after map without a Latino majority trustee area."  The WCCUSD later admitted that NDC’s map was likely in violation of both the California Voting Rights Act (CVRA) and Section 2 of the US Voting Rights Act.  4.  In 2018 & 2019, as the demographers for Redwood City's redistricting, NDC claimed that it was not possible to draw two Latino-majority districts in the city. Latino community groups protested after the council passed a map with just one Latino-majority district. Then NDC reversed their position.   The city later admitted that the map was made in error, forcing the city to start over, adding additional time and cost.
Finally, please don’t forget that NDC was the mapping consultant for the 2001 Arizona IRC, which produced two legislative maps that were later thrown out.   Facts matter, track records matter, hyper-sensitive, highly partisan attacks should not.  Please reject Timmons Group/NDC.

Among the applicants as the IRC's mapping consultant is a firm called National Demographics Corporation (NDC), which has a long history of drawing and defending gerrymandered maps, including several that have been rejected in the court.

The judge deemed Johnson’s testimony and data to be “insufficient.”

The IRC must uphold the trust of Arizonans throughout the redistricting process. Allowing National Demographics Corporation and Doug Johnson anywhere near our maps would immediately undermine that trust.

Please reject NDC as the IRC’s mapping consultant.

Thank you,

Marcia Tingley
Tucson, AZ

column5: Comment on Mapping Consultant NDC
column6:
Mapping and analysis performed by NDC and Doug Johnson has been rejected and discredited by courts throughout the country.

Hiring a mapping consultant with a record of drawing and defending court-rejected gerrymandered maps would risk the integrity of our maps and the public’s trust in the IRC. The Commission must reject Timmons Group/NDC from consideration.
 
I.  In North Carolina’s 2019 landmark gerrymandering case Common Cause v Lewis, a three-judge panel tossed out Doug Johnson’s testimony in defense of North Carolina’s gerrymandered map -- testimony which he later admitted was incorrect.
   A.   https://www.newsobserver.com/news/politics-government/article233105817.html
  B.   “The Court finds Dr. Johnson’s analysis unpersuasive and gives his opinions little weight.” https://www.nccourts.gov/assets/inline-files/18-CVS-14001_Final-Judgment.pdf?Bwsegeo1VV20zhJsp9hoClvmoRp3A6AR

II.  The 2018 case Luna vs Kern County is a landmark voting rights victory in which the US District Court Judge ruled that the redistricting plan defended by Doug Johnson unlawfully denied Latinos the ability to elect candidates of their choice.
  A.    https://www.maldef.org/2019/03/kern-country-voting-rights/
  B.   Doug Johnson’s testimony and data were found to be “insufficient.” https://casetext.com/case/luna-v-cnty-of-kern-4

III.  NDC was the mapping consultant for the 2001 Arizona IRC, which produced two legislative maps that were later thrown out. 
      A.  In 2002, the Commission’s first approved map failed to receive preclearance under the Voting Rights Act: https://azredistricting.org/2001/Final/doj_letter.pdf
      B.  In 2004, the Commission's second approved map was ruled unconstitutional:  https://azredistricting.org/2001/2004legfinal/2004LegCourtOrder.pdf

IV.  In March of 2019, the West Contra Costa Unified School District ( WCCUSD) settled a civil rights lawsuit which claimed that the district's at-large election map "dilutes the voting strength of Latino and African American citizens.

column5: Public Comment on Mapping Firm Choice
column6:
Many commenters have suggested that Haystaq should be disqualified because the firm has worked for and been praised by prominent Democrats or Independents and because some Haystaq employees are, or may be, Democrats themselves.  On its face this argument is specious because: (1) consultants from every firm are likely to have political preferences and (2) consultants are hired by clients, not the reverse.  

What these commenters fail to understand is that such factors are irrelevant because the mapping process is transparent.  Fairness is ensured because the process uses fully public data and is completely open.  Republican members of the California IRC clearly understood this because they recently hired Haystaq as their mapping consultant.  But any Arizonan who remains doubtful has an added safeguard against bias.  We can use publicly available mapping software to draw our own maps, compare them with those proposed by whatever firm is hired, and offer public comment online or at one of the many meetings to be scheduled around the State. 

So what are the criteria for selecting a mapping consultant firm?   Two are the general ones at the top of any hiring list:  superb qualifications and relevant experience.  The third, specific to this Commission’s task and their condensed timeline, is a track record of avoiding and/or overcoming court challenges.  I hope all commissioners will focus on these three criteria and not be distracted by side issues or smokescreens.

column5: Selection of Mapping Consultant
column6:
This is the first of four posts on this topic.

I’m concerned about how the choice of a mapping consultant will impact the public perception of your work output. The public wants a redistricting map that has been drawn independent of political influence (that’s why they set up an Independent Redistricting Commission in the first place). That’s the only way they will consider them to be fair. Given the highly charged partisan atmosphere surrounding the Commission’s processes, it will be important to choose a mapping consultant that will create the kinds of maps the public expects. Ideally, such a consultant would be non-partisan with significant experience in redistricting and related laws as well as an understanding of the many communities that make up the people who live and work in the state. With that in mind, I did some checking into the three companies that are under consideration. I’m alarmed by what I found. Unfortunately other more qualified and less controversial consultants did not step forward, but it means the Commission is in the position of selecting the least objectionable provider. In three additional posts, I will provide my notes and comments on what I found about these firms – and what reporters and the public will find out as well.

William Bowlus-Root
A concerned citizen

column5: Selection of Mapping Consultant
column6:
This is the second of four posts on this topic.

Timmons Group/National Demographics Corporation This firm has very bad history of creating maps that don’t pass muster: * The public in Kings County, CA, weighed in on the work of Doug Johnson and NDC. According to the League of Women Voters of Santa Barbara, "The behavior of Johnson and NDC has become so predictable in regards to these voting rights violations that when the City of Alhambra entered a settlement agreement after facing a lawsuit over the creation of districts, that agreement specifically stated ‘Parties recognize that the City will require the services of a qualified demographer to assist that process; and that demographer will not be National Demographics Corporation or its principals, officers or employees.’ The other public comments against NDC are just as concerning: https://www.countyofkings.com/home/showpublisheddocument?id=25894. * NDC was so unfamiliar with the California voting rights laws and the demographics of West Contra Costa County (or possibly just careless of them) that they created a school board district map that left Latino communities under-represented, an error they were unable to defend when challenged in court (https://richmondconfidential.org/2019/03/07/a-final-trustee-area-map-emerges-as-lawsuit-resolves/) * In a North Carolina redistricting case, NDC’s data was found to be inadequate and unreliable. The judge wrote “The Court finds Dr. Johnson’s analysis unpersuasive and gives his opinions little weight. Dr. Johnson has testified as a live expert witness in four cases previously, and the courts in all four cases have rejected his analysis.” * Even here in Yuma County, where I reside, NDC failed to meet deadlines to provide draft maps. “Two Yuma County Redistricting Advisory Commissioners, Republican Phil Townsend (Advisory Commission chair) and Democrat Alicia Aguirre told the Arizona Eagletarian that they are dissatisfied that National Demographics has failed to meet deadlines and provide the draft maps on a timely basis.” (https://stevemuratore.blogspot.com/2011/06/redistricting-potential-mapping.html) Given the compressed time frame we will have the census data, the people and the commission cannot afford delays or the potential for maps that are of questionable legality or fairness. This firm should not be selected if the Commission expects the public to be satisfied with the new maps.

William Bowlus-Root
A concerned citizen

column5: Selection of Mapping Consultant
column6:
This is the third of four posts on this topic.

Taylor English Decisions I checked out this firm’s website and could find no indication that they’re mapping consultants or have had any experience with redistricting at all. They seem almost more of a marketing organization. It seems they were responsible, at least in part, for the hire of a number of Republican operatives that worked to influence the redistricting process in Georgia in 2011 and to gain Federal approval for the legislative plans in that state. Of course the most recent elections there have made the public keenly aware of how grossly biased and skewed to favor Republicans those districts are. The Arizona IRC cannot risk having their consultants behave in a similar way if they want to keep the public’s faith in them. The people are hiring mapping consultants, not lobbyists. Perhaps most disturbing, the head of the company, the person who directs its work and mission and view of the world, is CEO Earl Ehrhart. Mr. Ehrhart served for 30 years in the Georgia State House as a Republican. According to his bio, he was also the National Chairman of the American Legislative Exchange Council (ALEC) and served on its board for more than 20 years (https://tedecisions.com/about-us/our-team/earl-ehrhart). Clearly he has a very strong Republican bias. That’s not to mention his use of homophobic language (https://www.republicreport.org/2012/former-alec-chairman-homophobic-slur) and his self-proclaimed advocacy for students who are accused of sexual assault (https://www.buzzfeednews.com/article/tylerkingkade/meet-the-republican-lawmaker-whos-taken-up-the-cause-of), both of which call into question his fairness and whether a firm he runs is suitable for our purposes. Can we expect this company to produce maps that are unbiased if their work is under the influence and direction of this man? And will the employees and consultants doing that work be more interested in keeping their jobs by making the boss happy or in serving the people of Arizona? The public will find it hard to believe the latter. If the Commission wants to keep their confidence, it would do well not to select this firm.

William Bowlus-Root
A concerned citizen

column5: IRC (Arizona’s Independent Redistricting Committee)
column6:
Dear Members of Arizona’s Independent Redistricting Commission (IRC),
You will soon hire the IRC's mapping consultant. Among the applicants is a firm called National Demographics Corporation (NDC), which has a long history of drawing and defending gerrymandered maps, including several that have been rejected in the court. 

This isn't a Democrat vs Republican issue. This is about protecting the integrity of our maps and elections for the next decade.

NDC should have NOTHING TO DO WITH DRAWING ARIZONA’s MAPS because of their track record, which includes the following:

In the landmark 2018 California voting rights case Luna v Kern County, a US District Court Judge ruled that the redistricting plan defended by the NDC President unlawfully denied Latinos the ability to elect candidates of their choice. The Judge deemed Johnson’s testimony and data to be “insufficient.”  

As the mapping consultant to the first Arizona IRC in 2001, NDC produced two legislative maps that were later thrown out. The '02 map was rejected for failing to comply with the US Voting Rights Act, and the '04 map was thrown out after it was ruled unconstitutional. The 2001 IRC Vice-Chair Andi Minkoff later testified that the Commission was “manipulated” by NDC into drawing non-competitive maps.

The IRC must uphold the trust of Arizonans throughout the redistricting process. Allowing National Demographics Corporation and Doug Johnson anywhere near our maps would immediately undermine that trust. 

Please do your due diligence to assure that the maps are drawn fairly, without manipulation for political purposes and without gerrymandering. In selecting mapping consultants, their prior tract record is very important. Therefore, NDC and Doug Johnson should NOT be considered.

Respectfully, 

Rita Day, Prescott, AZ 86301

column5: Comment on Mapping Consultant NDC
column6:
I strongly urge you to reject both Taylor English Decisions and Timmons Group/NDC as the IRC’s mapping consultant. Taylor English Decisions has no experience, and NDC has a terrible track record.

Mapping and analysis performed by NDC and Doug Johnson have been rejected and discredited by courts throughout the country.

Hiring a mapping consultant with a record of drawing and defending court-rejected gerrymandered maps would risk the integrity of our maps and destroy the public’s trust in the IRC. The Commission must reject Timmons Group/NDC from consideration.

Here are the reasons, based on NDC’s past performance:

I.	In North Carolina’s 2019 landmark gerrymandering case Common Cause v Lewis, a three-judge panel tossed out Doug Johnson’s testimony in defense of North Carolina’s gerrymandered map—testimony that he later admitted was incorrect.

A.	https://www.newsobserver.com/news/politics-government/article233105817.html

B.	“The Court finds Dr. Johnson’s analysis unpersuasive and gives his opinions little weight.” (https://www.nccourts.gov/assets/inline-files/18-CVS-14001_Final-Judgment.pdf?Bwsegeo1VV20zhJsp9hoClvmoRp3A6AR)

II.	The 2018 case Luna vs Kern County is a landmark voting rights victory in which the US District Court Judge ruled that the redistricting plan defended by Doug Johnson unlawfully denied Latinos the ability to elect candidates of their choice.

A.	https://www.maldef.org/2019/03/kern-country-voting-rights/

B.	Doug Johnson’s testimony and data were found to be “insufficient.” (https://casetext.com/case/luna-v-cnty-of-kern-4)


III.	NDC was the mapping consultant for the 2001 Arizona IRC, which produced two legislative maps that were later thrown out.

A.	In 2002, the Commission’s first approved map failed to receive preclearance under the Voting Rights Act (https://azredistricting.org/2001/Final/doj_letter.pdf)

B.	In 2004, the Commission's second approved map was ruled unconstitutional, (https://azredistricting.org/2001/2004legfinal/2004LegCourtOrder.pdf)

IV.	In March of 2019, the West Contra Costa Unified School District (WCCUSD) settled a civil rights lawsuit that claimed that the district's at-large election map “dilutes the voting strength of Latino and African American citizens.

A.	According to the plaintiff's attorney, "NDC cost the District over $650,000 by spending over a year producing map after map without a Latino majority trustee area." (https://www.countyofkings.com/home/showpublisheddocument?id=25778)

B.	In that settlement, WCCUSD conceded that their map was likely in violation of both the California Voting Rights Act (CVRA) and Section 2 of the US Voting Rights Act.

C.	The court adopted the Plaintiff's map -- not NDC's. (https://www.wccusd.net/cms/lib/CA01001466/Centricity/Domain/16/Joint%20Ex%20Parte%20Application%20for%20Entry%20of%20Judgment.pdf)

V.	In 2018 & 2019, as the demographers for Redwood City's redistricting, NDC claimed that it was not possible to draw two Latino-majority districts in the city. Latino community groups protested after the council passed a map with just one Latino-majority district. Then NDC reversed their position.

A.	After pushback from that community, among others, the city’s demographer announced that it made an error and was in fact able to create maps with two Latino majority districts... (https://www.smdailyjournal.com/news/local/redwood-city-adopts-district-elections-map/article_29ddd2e8-7127-11e9-9750-c796bd4f69f7.html)

B.	Due to NDC's “error,” the Redwood City Council was forced to start over on their map, adding additional time and cost. (https://www.redwoodcity.org/home/showdocument?id=17969)


I strongly urge you NOT to hire NDC for Arizona’s IRC.

Sincerely,

M. W. M. Tingley

column5: Selecting a Mapping Consultant
column6:
Selecting a mapping consultant should be an absolutely transparent process and the selected firm should be absolutely transparent, too.

To be considered, a firm should have shown no interest or inclination toward partisanship.  They need to be experienced and they need to have a demonstrable track record of success.

If the commission is interested in the selected firm "hitting the ground running from day one," why consider any firm without redistricting experience?  And, why would you consider any firm whose previously-drawn maps did not withstand legal challenge?

Why would you consider any firm that has a prior relationship with the American Legislative Exchange Council (ALEC)?  And, why would you consider a firm that is otherwise in the business of lobbying or political campaigning?

If the IRC is serious about applying "the provisions in an honest, independent and impartial fashion to uphold public confidence in the integrity of the redistricting process", it must address the above questions and answer them with an eye to its own independence in this matter.

column5: Mapping consultant choice: focus on competence
column6:
These are contentious times. Most people have pretty strong opinions about which political team is right (about just about everything). Consequently, given that all three mapping firms have partisan connections, there is no applicant that can be chosen without controversy. Haystaq can fairly be associated with the Democrats, and the other two can fairly be associated with the Republicans. We have a fairly evenly divided voting population, and roughly a third are independents who certainly would like to see a fair and aboveboard process.

I believe that in this circumstance, you should make your choice based on competence and reliability. This is the only approach that can minimize (though clearly, not eliminate) contentious litigation that will end in rejected maps.

Using these criteria, I believe that Taylor English must be eliminated from consideration. While they have participated in redistricting litigation, they have never worked on developing the maps themselves.

Choosing between the other two applicants is a bit harder; Haystaq worked on the 2011 maps, and NDC (the key part of the Timmons team) worked on the 2001 maps, so both are experienced. However, the NDC maps did poorly in court challenges, while the Haystaq maps succeeded. There are also questions about more recent performance issues for NDC, since their clients in Yuma were unhappy about their timeliness. I think that you should look more deeply into this aspect of these firms – how did they perform on related tasks?

From my vantage point, the safest approach for the IRC would be to choose the firm that has ample relevant experience and has been most successful in the courts. This would be Haystaq. I am fully aware that this will be unpopular among many Republicans. On the other hand, choosing Timmons/NDC will be unpopular among many Democrats. To do the best job for all Arizonans, you should ignore both slants, and choose the firm that will be the best at the job. Choosing Taylor English clearly doesn’t satisfy that criterion.

In full disclosure, I am a Democrat. But I am doing my best to view this in terms of what I think is best for the state.

Thank you for your efforts in this difficult task. You are in a tough position!

column5: Arizona’s Independent Redistricting Committee: Select HayStaq; REJECT: NDC
column6:
Dear Members of the Arizona Independent Redistricting Commission:

Mapping and analysis performed by NDC and Doug Johnson has been rejected and discredited by courts throughout the country. [See 5 lawsuits below.]

Hiring a mapping consultant with a record of drawing and defending court-rejected gerrymandered maps would risk the integrity of our maps and the public trust in IRC. Not to mention the additional cost of have to redraw court rejected maps. Therefore, the Commission must reject Timmons Group/NDC from consideration.

In addition, the following concerns must be brought to the attention of the Commissioners:
The IRC Commission process is flawed: Many comments have been submitted via the website and there is no confidence that these comments have been read or received. This does not inspire confidence. 

Comments are treated differently based on where they are received. This is not open, transparent or fair. 

Biggest difference between Haystaq and NDC is competence, timeliness, defensibility.  Haystag has a proven record of competence, timeliness & defensibility. NDC has a long record of court rejected maps! See list of 5 of these rejected cases.

Anti-Haystaq comments are mostly generated by two extremely partisan members of the state legislature and the comments seem to be cut and pasted. 

Choose the mapping consultant that has the track record of not having maps overturned in court (Haystaq) 
HayStaq is vilified by the Right and NDC by the Left. TaylorEnglish is unqualified. The Commissioners must ignore all that and pick the candidate who will do the job that will hold up in the courts. 
All the mapping consultants should be required to agree that they should not engage in any campaign work of lobbying work in Arizona during the contract period. 
Any lobbying, campaigns or efforts on a federal, state or local level should be disclosed by the mapping consultant during the contract period.
The choice will be contentious either way, but the Commissioners must focus on the best candidate for the job. 
5 lawsuits concerning NDC & Doug Johnson:
 1.  In North Carolina’s 2019 landmark gerrymandering case Common Cause v Lewis, a three-judge panel tossed out Doug Johnson’s testimony in defense of North Carolina’s gerrymandered map -- testimony which he later admitted was incorrect.
    2.  The 2018 case Luna vs Kern County is a landmark voting rights victory in which the US District Court Judge ruled that the redistricting plan defended by Doug Johnson unlawfully denied Latinos the ability to elect candidates of their choice.

  3.  NDC was the mapping consultant for the 2001 Arizona IRC, which produced two legislative maps that were later thrown out. ( A)  In 2002, the Commission’s first approved map failed to receive preclearance under the Voting Rights Act.  (B)  In 2004, the Commission's 2nd approved map was ruled unconstitutional.)

  4.   In March of 2019, the West Contra Costa Unified School District (WCCUSD) settled a civil rights lawsuit which claimed that the district's at-large election map "dilutes the voting strength of Latino and African American citizens.  ( A) According to the plaintiff's attorney, "NDC cost the District over $650,000 by spending over a year producing map after map without a Latino majority trustee area.  (B) In that settlement, WCCUSD conceded that their map was likely in violation of both the California Voting Rights Act (CVRA) and Section 2 of the US Voting Rights Act.  (C)The court adopted the Plaintiff's map -- not NDC's.)
   5. In 2018 & 2019, as the demographers for Redwood City's redistricting, NDC claimed that it was not possible to draw two Latino-majority districts in the city. Latino community groups protested after the council passed a map with just one Latino-majority district. Then NDC reversed their position. Due to NDC's “error”, the Redwood City Council was forced to start over on their map, adding additional time and cost.

Please choose HayStaq who has a proven record of successful maps not rejected by the courts. The integrity of our maps is critical for the public trust in our elections.

Respectfully, 
Rita Day, 
Prescott, Az 86301

column5: Comment on Mapping Consultant NDC.
column6:
Comment on Mapping Consultant NDC

I have been an Arizona and Pima County Resident and voter for more than twenty-seven years who has admired the work of The Arizona Independent Redistricting Commission (IRC) over past years because it has assured me that our voting districts have been fairly determined and have been free of the distortions of gerrymandering.  The IRC must take care to assure that it does not lose the confidence of the Arizona electorate by engaging the services of a consultant which sports a disreputable track record in the courts.  I will include below further documentation of that record of rejections in gerrymandering court cases.

While I complement the IRC for seeking recognized expertise in mapping technology to give IRC reliable and accurate mapping services, I urge it to reject consideration of the Timmons Group/National Demographics Corporation in part because: (1) it has been reported that they have earned a  poor reputation over the years; and (2) their areas of expertise, according to Dun & Bradstreet, includes: engineering services; the professional services sector; civil engineering; and surveying services with no mention of mapping services.  Additionally, the Richmond Times-Dispatch reported that Timmons Group “specializes in civil engineering, surveying and landscape architecture” but makes no mention of mapping services in its article.

A Timmons document states:  Timmons Group has a business partner agreement with Trimble to resell and distribute selected Mapping & Geographic Information System (GIS) products, including the GPS Pathfinder® Pro series receivers, GeoExplorer® series of rugged GPS handhelds, rugged Trimble® Recon™ handhelds, and Trimble Recon GPS series systems. Timmons Group also provides Trimble hardware and software as part of a complete enterprise data management solution for the firm’s TG LoGIStics product line of solutions, including field-based data management solutions for land records, E-911 addressing, utility inventory and our ArcGIS Server based mobile applications for Land Management agencies serving the Forestry, Natural Resources, Transportation and other State and Local Government applications.

That description of how Timmons Group uses Trimble computer products fails to describe uses that we might expect to be of value to the IRC.

Furthermore, that same document describes the sort of projects which Timmons conducts but none of them includes the kind of mapping services one would expect to be of value to the IRC.  The itemization of projects from that Timmons Group document does not mention mapping but include:  

(1) Engineering - Colleges/Universities; Commercial/Retail; Design-Build/PPEA/PPP; Energy and Renewables; Government; Healthcare; K-12 Schools; Parks/Sports/Recreation; Residential/Multi-Family;   Transportation/Traffic; Water Resources; Water/Wastewater Utilities; and (2) Technology - Local Government; State Government; Federal Government; Utilities; Transportation; Wildland Fire; Fish & Wildlife; Forestry.

A similar listing of Timmons Group services in that document does not mention mapping services but include:  (1) Engineering -     Civil Engineering & Planning; Infrastructure Design; Environmental Services; Geotechnical & CMT Services; Land Surveying; Landscape Architecture; Economic Development; Structural Engineering; Power Engineering and (2) Technology - Web & Mobile Applications; RoadMap; Asset Management; Cloud and Managed Services; Data Development; Analysis & Modeling; Staff Augmentation; Data Insights.

The apparent lack of any reference to expertise in the kind of mapping services the IRC would need in Timmons’ own publications would lead this voter to question their fitness for the IRC contract.  Therefore, I continue to urge the IRC to drop Timmons Group/National Demographics Corporation from further consideration.

Finally, the record of many adverse court decisions by Timmons Group/National Demographics Corporation set forth below attests to their lack of fitness for the purposes of the IRC:

I.  In North Carolina’s 2019 landmark gerrymandering case Common Cause v Lewis, a three-judge panel tossed out Doug Johnson’s testimony in defense of North Carolina’s gerrymandered map -- testimony which he later admitted was incorrect. A.  https://www.newsobserver.com/news/politics-government/article233105817.html 
B.  “The Court finds Dr. Johnson’s analysis unpersuasive and gives his opinions little weight.” https://www.nccourts.gov/assets/inline-files/18-CVS-14001_Final-Judgment.pdf?Bwsegeo1VV20zhJsp9hoClvmoRp3A6AR 

II.  The 2018 case Luna vs. Kern County is a landmark voting rights victory in which the US District Court Judge ruled that the redistricting plan defended by Doug Johnson unlawfully denied Latinos the ability to elect candidates of their choice. 
A.   https://www.maldef.org/2019/03/kern-country-voting-rights/ 
B.  Doug Johnson’s testimony and data were found to be “insufficient.” https://casetext.com/case/luna-v-cnty-of-kern-4 

III.  NDC was the mapping consultant for the 2001 Arizona IRC, which produced two legislative maps that were later thrown out. 
A.  In 2002, the Commission’s first approved map failed to receive preclearance under the Voting Rights Act: https://azredistricting.org/2001/Final/doj_letter.pdf 
B.  In 2004, the Commission's second approved map was ruled unconstitutional: https://azredistricting.org/2001/2004legfinal/2004LegCourtOrder.pdf 

IV.  In March of 2019, the West Contra Costa Unified School District (WCCUSD) settled a civil rights lawsuit which claimed that the district's at-large election map “dilutes the voting strength of Latino and African American citizens.” 
A.  According to the plaintiff's attorney, "NDC cost the District over $650,000 by spending over a year producing map after map without a Latino majority trustee area."https://www.countyofkings.com/home/showpublisheddocument?id=25778 
B.  In that settlement, WCCUSD conceded that their map was likely in violation of both the California Voting Rights Act (CVRA) and Section 2 of the US Voting Rights Act. 
C. The court adopted the Plaintiff's map -- not NDC's. https://www.wccusd.net/cms/lib/CA01001466/Centricity/Domain/16/Joint%20Ex%20Parte%20Application%20for%20Entry%20of%20Judgment.pdf 

V.  In 2018 & 2019, as the demographers for Redwood City's redistricting, NDC claimed that it was not possible to draw two Latino-majority districts in the city. Latino community groups protested after the council passed a map with just one Latino-majority district. Then NDC reversed their position. 
A.  "After pushback from that community, among others, the city’s demographer announced that it made an error and was in fact able to create maps with two Latino majority districts . . . " https://www.smdailyjournal.com/news/local/redwood-city-adopts-district-elections-map/article_29ddd2e8-7127-11e9-9750-c796bd4f69f7.html 
B.  Due to NDC's “error,” the Redwood City Council was forced to start over on their map, adding additional time and cost. https://www.redwoodcity.org/home/showdocument?id=17969

column5: Mappin Contractor selection
column6:
The issue before the Independent Redistricting Commission right now is the choice of a mapping firm. Three firms have submitted proposals:

HaystaqDNA LLC
Taylor English Decisions LLC
Timmons Group/NDC
It is the opinion of the Arizona Democratic Party that HaystaqDNA is the best-qualified. Indivisible Arizona concurs.

While our strike force has submitted well-reasoned and documented comments on the three proposals, the GQP has flooded the commissioners with cookie-cutter comments opposing the firm favored by Democrats.

NOW is the time to fight fire with fire.
DEADLINE TOMORROW (Thursday) at 5 pm.
Use this link on the IRC website:  Contact Us
Subject Line: Comment on Mapping Consultant Contract

Select “Customer Relations” to send your message

Suggested comments to cut and paste:
Comment One
A firm called Timmons Group is slated to work with National Demographics Corporation (NDC), a consultant with an alarming track record across the country. NDC’s maps have been rejected or re-done by several courts and redistricting bodies. Here are just a two examples:

·  In North Carolina, NDC’s president provided testimony about gerrymandered maps. The judge wrote in the final opinion: “The Court finds Dr. Johnson’s analysis unpersuasive and gives his opinions little weight. Dr. Johnson has testified as a live expert witness in four cases previously, and the courts in all four cases have rejected his analysis.

·  When, in Kern County, California, Latino voters were found to have been deprived of an equal opportunity to elect the representatives of their choice, because of under-representation, Doug Johnson submitted testimony to defend those maps, which were overturned for failure to follow California’s laws and requirements for map drawing.

Comment Two
Please make it a condition of the engagement that the firm chosen forego any political or campaign consulting work in Arizona while the maps are being created and for the entire time they are being challenged in court.

Comment Three
Mappers need to be experienced and successful.  Redistricting is not accomplished by an algorithm. Experience and people matter!  The Commission so far has overlooked experience in hiring an executive director and bypassed the one legal firm that had experience above all others. You should not continue this pattern. Redistricting is always a challenge. 2021 is even more challenging given the delay in receiving census data. Taylor English Decisions LLC and Timmons Group would never be good choices, but this year, with these challenges, they are especially bad choices. Haystaq DNA was the mapper in the 2011 cycle. Their maps were approved by the US Department of Justice for pre-clearance and stood up through multiple lawsuits. In contrast, the maps created by NDC for AZ in the 2000 cycle were not approved and had to be redrawn!

Comment Four
Karin MacDonald is perhaps one of the nation’s true redistricting experts without a legal degree. She also manages the CA Statewide database created by the CA Legislature to house all California related census, voting, registration, and statewide elections data. She would be a tremendous asset to the IRC 2021 team. She is partnering with Haystag. Don’t pass her up!

Comment Five
Timmons Group has ZERO redistricting experience. Timmons is partnering with National Demographics Corporation. Douglas Johnson of the National Demographics Corporation has a terrible track record with previous maps. The maps created in 2001 FAILED the Department of Justice preclearance standards and had to be redrawn. The 2001 Commission failed in its primary task – in large part because of Doug Johnson! Elsewhere in the country, many maps created by NDG/Doug Johnson have been rejected by courts resulting in the need for new maps. With Census data delays, we can’t risk having to re-draw our state’s maps. We need a mapping consultant that has proven they can take on this work successfully.

Comment Six
Taylor English Decisions does not have state-wide or redistricting-specific experience. It has no proven record of taking on the challenges of drafting maps for this crucial process.

Taylor English is a lobbying/campaign firm. They would be in the position of drawing new districts for past, present of future clients. This is unacceptable and flies in the face of and undermines the call to “apply the provisions in an honest, independent and impartial fashion to uphold public confidence in the integrity of the redistricting process.” 

Comment Seven
Former CEO of Taylor English, Earl Earhart, has a history of using homophobic language, has adopted controversial issues to champion, and served as Chairman of the American Legislative Exchange Council (ALEC) – a controversial organization that drafts bills to further an anti-government political agenda in state legislatures – including here in AZ. This is unacceptable and should disqualify Taylor English from being hired.

column5: Comment on Mapping Consultant NDC
column6:
Mapping and analysis performed by NDC and Doug Johnson has been rejected and discredited by courts throughout the country.

Hiring a mapping consultant with a record of drawing and defending court-rejected gerrymandered maps would risk the integrity of our maps and the public’s trust in the IRC. The Commission must reject Timmons Group/NDC from consideration.
 
I.  In North Carolina’s 2019 landmark gerrymandering case Common Cause v Lewis, a three-judge panel tossed out Doug Johnson’s testimony in defense of North Carolina’s gerrymandered map -- testimony which he later admitted was incorrect.
   A.  https://www.newsobserver.com/news/politics-government/article233105817.html
  B.  “The Court finds Dr. Johnson’s analysis unpersuasive and gives his opinions little weight.” https://www.nccourts.gov/assets/inline-files/18-CVS-14001_Final-Judgment.pdf?Bwsegeo1VV20zhJsp9hoClvmoRp3A6AR

II.  The 2018 case Luna vs Kern County is a landmark voting rights victory in which the US District Court Judge ruled that the redistricting plan defended by Doug Johnson unlawfully denied Latinos the ability to elect candidates of their choice.
  A.   https://www.maldef.org/2019/03/kern-country-voting-rights/
  B.  Doug Johnson’s testimony and data were found to be “insufficient.” https://casetext.com/case/luna-v-cnty-of-kern-4

III.  NDC was the mapping consultant for the 2001 Arizona IRC, which produced two legislative maps that were later thrown out. 
      A.  In 2002, the Commission’s first approved map failed to receive preclearance under the Voting Rights Act: https://azredistricting.org/2001/Final/doj_letter.pdf
      B.  In 2004, the Commission's second approved map was ruled unconstitutional: https://azredistricting.org/2001/2004legfinal/2004LegCourtOrder.pdf

IV.  In March of 2019, the West Contra Costa Unified School District (WCCUSD) settled a civil rights lawsuit which claimed that the district's at-large election map "dilutes the voting strength of Latino and African American citizens.
      A.  According to the plaintiff's attorney, "NDC cost the District over $650,000 by spending over a year producing map after map without a Latino majority trustee area."https://www.countyofkings.com/home/showpublisheddocument?id=25778
      B.  In that settlement, WCCUSD conceded that their map was likely in violation of both the California Voting Rights Act (CVRA) and Section 2 of the US Voting Rights Act.
      C. The court adopted the Plaintiff's map -- not NDC's. https://www.wccusd.net/cms/lib/CA01001466/Centricity/Domain/16/Joint%20Ex%20Parte%20Application%20for%20Entry%20of%20Judgment.pdf
V.  In 2018 & 2019, as the demographers for Redwood City's redistricting, NDC claimed that it was not possible to draw two Latino-majority districts in the city. Latino community groups protested after the council passed a map with just one Latino-majority district. Then NDC reversed their position. 
     A.  "After pushback from that community, among others, the city’s demographer announced that it made an error and was in fact able to create maps with two Latino majority districts..."
https://www.smdailyjournal.com/news/local/redwood-city-adopts-district-elections-map/article_29ddd2e8-7127-11e9-9750-c796bd4f69f7.html
     B.  Due to NDC's “error”, the Redwood City Council was forced to start over on their map, adding additional time and cost.
https://www.redwoodcity.org/home/showdocument?id=17969

column5: Comment on Mapping Consultant NDC
column6:
Mapping and analysis performed by NDC and Doug Johnson has been rejected and discredited by courts throughout the country.

Hiring a mapping consultant with a record of drawing and defending court-rejected gerrymandered maps would risk the integrity of our maps and the public’s trust in the IRC. The Commission must reject Timmons Group/NDC from consideration. 

More specifically the following facts are presented:
I.  In North Carolina’s 2019 landmark gerrymandering case Common Cause v Lewis, a three-judge panel tossed out Doug Johnson’s testimony in defense of North Carolina’s gerrymandered map -- testimony which he later admitted was incorrect.
   A.  https://www.newsobserver.com/news/politics-government/article233105817.html
  B.  “The Court finds Dr. Johnson’s analysis unpersuasive and gives his opinions little weight.” https://www.nccourts.gov/assets/inline-files/18-CVS-14001_Final-Judgment.pdf?Bwsegeo1VV20zhJsp9hoClvmoRp3A6AR

II.  The 2018 case Luna vs Kern County is a landmark voting rights victory in which the US District Court Judge ruled that the redistricting plan defended by Doug Johnson unlawfully denied Latinos the ability to elect candidates of their choice.
  A.   https://www.maldef.org/2019/03/kern-country-voting-rights/
  B.  Doug Johnson’s testimony and data were found to be “insufficient.” https://casetext.com/case/luna-v-cnty-of-kern-4

III.  NDC was the mapping consultant for the 2001 Arizona IRC, which produced two legislative maps that were later thrown out. 
      A.  In 2002, the Commission’s first approved map failed to receive preclearance under the Voting Rights Act: https://azredistricting.org/2001/Final/doj_letter.pdf
      B.  In 2004, the Commission's second approved map was ruled unconstitutional: https://azredistricting.org/2001/2004legfinal/2004LegCourtOrder.pdf

IV.  In March of 2019, the West Contra Costa Unified School District (WCCUSD) settled a civil rights lawsuit which claimed that the district's at-large election map "dilutes the voting strength of Latino and African American citizens.
      A.  According to the plaintiff's attorney, "NDC cost the District over $650,000 by spending over a year producing map after map without a Latino majority trustee area."https://www.countyofkings.com/home/showpublisheddocument?id=25778
      B.  In that settlement, WCCUSD conceded that their map was likely in violation of both the California Voting Rights Act (CVRA) and Section 2 of the US Voting Rights Act.
      C. The court adopted the Plaintiff's map -- not NDC's. https://www.wccusd.net/cms/lib/CA01001466/Centricity/Domain/16/Joint%20Ex%20Parte%20Application%20for%20Entry%20of%20Judgment.pdf
V.  In 2018 & 2019, as the demographers for Redwood City's redistricting, NDC claimed that it was not possible to draw two Latino-majority districts in the city. Latino community groups protested after the council passed a map with just one Latino-majority district. Then NDC reversed their position. 
     A.  "After pushback from that community, among others, the city’s demographer announced that it made an error and was in fact able to create maps with two Latino majority districts..."
https://www.smdailyjournal.com/news/local/redwood-city-adopts-district-elections-map/article_29ddd2e8-7127-11e9-9750-c796bd4f69f7.html
     B.  Due to NDC's “error”, the Redwood City Council was forced to start over on their map, adding additional time and cost.
https://www.redwoodcity.org/home/showdocument?id=17969

The trial challenging North Carolina’s legislative lines as unconstitutional partisan gerrymanders took a dramatic turn Thursday when an expert witness for Republican lawmakers admitted some of his testimony on their behalf was incorrect.

The challengers used that admission to ask that testimony by Claremont McKenna College political scientist Douglas Johnson be struck from the record.

Wake County Superior Court Judge Paul Ridgeway, who is leading the panel, said North Carolina’s rules for expert witnesses say that “his opinions must be the product of reliable methods and principles ... and the principles used by Dr. Johnson were not reliable.”

I.  In North Carolina’s 2019 landmark gerrymandering case Common Cause v Lewis, a three-judge panel tossed out Doug Johnson’s testimony in defense of North Carolina’s gerrymandered map -- testimony which he later admitted was incorrect.
      A.  https://www.newsobserver.com/news/politics-government/article233105817.html
      B.  “The Court finds Dr. Johnson’s analysis unpersuasive and gives his opinions little weight.” https://www.nccourts.gov/assets/inline-files/18-CVS-14001_Final-Judgment.pdf?Bwsegeo1VV20zhJsp9hoClvmoRp3A6AR

      B.  Doug Johnson’s testimony and data were found to be “insufficient.” https://casetext.com/case/luna-v-cnty-of-kern-4

https://www.smdailyjournal.com/news/local/redwood-city-adopts-district-elections-map/article_29ddd2e8-7127-11e9-9750-c796bd4f69f7.html

https://stevemuratore.blogspot.com/2021/04/what-is-az-redistricting-commission-up.html

What is the AZ redistricting commission up to with it's latest subterfuge?
The first and maybe the most important question is why Arizona's newest iteration of the Independent Redistricting Commission LIMITS public comment AT ALL. I have posed that question to this IRC in time sanctioned comments, but never received any response. Could that have been because Andy Tobin, Ducey's "fixer" (and current director of the Dept of Administration) was overseeing things when I posed the question the first several times?

Tobin has served (been appointed by Ducey) to head other Arizona executive branch agencies as well as (also appointed by Ducey) to fill a Corporation Commission seat when an elected member resigned to work in the Trump administration. Tobin was also Speaker of the Arizona House of Representatives when the legislature sued the 2011 IRC (all the way to the US Supreme Court) because he didn't like that the voters had taken the power to gerrymander legislative and Congressional districts away from him. Review my blog posts from March 2015 and earlier on that very topic.

Because Tobin was now in a position to influence how the 2021 IRC established itself and decided to operate, he could be like The Great Oz. Pay no attention to the man behind the curtain.

Nevertheless, the commission is ALL about, according to the initiative voters approved to pioneer citizen driven independent redistricting, HEARING what the citizens/voters want to tell them about what they are charged by the Arizona Constitution to do. But the IRC under Dr. Erika Neuberg has been nothing at all like that.

Under the direction of Gov. Doug Ducey, the Commission on Appellate Court Appointments, charged with vetting candidates for the commission, eliminated some of the most qualified candidates for the most frivolous of reasons, like that some had worked with--God-forbid--former Democratic Governor Janet Napolitano.

Erika Neuberg presented a (very) strong personality and had donated money to Ducey's campaigns for governor. She's a trained psychologist. Beside being quite confident at conducting meetings (thus far all of the IRC meetings have been on ZOOM or YouTube), Erika seems to be a competent manipulator.

Where Colleen was open and vulnerable, which signaled willingness to consider the views of the four other commissioners AND Arizona citizens who showed up for meetings and hearings, I don't see that at all from Erika. Erika presents a tough façade. Presenting as vulnerable is an indicator of strength of character. Tough façades can mask character weaknesses.

Moving on, the IRC is now trying to figure out which mapping consultant to hire. Two of the contenders have serious history with Arizona's redistricting process. But what is being discussed or written about publicly does NOT match the details of that history.

First, as reported this week by Jeremy Duda of the Arizona Mirror,

Last week’s presentations and interviews were held behind closed doors, in executive session, a requirement of Arizona’s procurement laws. The commissioners are barred from publicly discussing anything that occurs in executive session. Republican Commissioner David Mehl said all three firms interviewed well and provided a lot of details.

“I’m sorry the public was not able to observe that,” he said.
Opposition to the Timmons Group largely revolves around its partnership with National Demographics Corporation, which served as the mapping consultant for Arizona’s first redistricting commission in 2001, and the company’s president, Doug Johnson. Democratic organizations and individuals objected to the company’s Republican ties and its history drawing maps that they allege disenfranchised Latino voters.
What Jeremy left out of that report is that Doug Johnson wasn't fired. He redrew the maps after DOJ rejected the first attempt. That second effort ended up producing for Republicans a legislative supermajority that in 2011 flexed its muscle, along with then Gov. Brewer, to try to decapitate the IRC by firing then chair Colleen Mathis. It succeeded... for about a month. 

The AZ Supreme Court reinstated Mathis after oral arguments presented by former Chief Justice Thomas Zlaket. Among the chief complaints against Mathis, at the time, were related to selection of Strategic Telemetry as mapping consultant. Strategic Telemetry principals later formed HaystaqDNA, which is one of the firms now bidding for the mapping consultant job with the  2021 IRC.

Now, about David Mehl's overtly disingenuous expression of regret that the public was unable to observe the interviews with mapping consultant bidders. In 2011, because the IRC chose to NOT participate in the state procurement process for selection of that consultant, the interviews were ALL observed by the public.

A decision Mehl and his colleagues made this time is THE SOLE reason the public was excluded from observing the interviews. Mehl, Nueberg and company chose to comply with the state procurement process, which--beside excluding the public--again gave Tobin clandestine influence over the selection.

Begging for the public to weigh in on the bidders really almost certainly had hidden purpose.

After Doug Johnson's team drew rightful pushback in the media and from citizens, the only way they could justify hiring him would be if they got copious public comments demanding it and trashing Haystaq. They do NOT have to be allowed to get away with it. It's up to you.

I leave you with this thought.

The legislative maps drawn by the 2011 IRC are most fairly and appropriately characterized as maps favoring which political party? Consider that the only fundamental difference between the 2001 and 2011 maps is that GOP control was NOT a supermajority from 2012-present, like it had been in the previous decade.

The 2011 maps STILL favored the Arizona Republican Party. That party has been in control of the legislature EVERY year in the last TWO decades, the decades with maps drawn by Independent Redistricting Commissions.

Why would Arizona citizens cede the legislature to Doug Johnson's and Andy Tobin's efforts to restore supermajority, and hence ONE PARTY politics to our state?

Submit public comments early and often. And perhaps ask why the current commission is so afraid to let citizens and voters have a say in how this IRC does it's business?

Are we still a democracy, or do we accede to autocracy?

Submit comments (again, early and often) at: https://irc.az.gov/contact-us

And if you ever get an error message saying your comment is not accepted because of time constraints, send me an email with the details or contact me on Twitter @AzEagletarian.

      A.  In 2002, the Commission’s first approved map failed to receive preclearance under the Voting Rights Act: https://azredistricting.org/2001/Final/doj_letter.pdf
      B.  In 2004, the Commission's 2nd approved map was ruled unconstitutional:https://azredistricting.org/2001/2004legfinal/2004LegCourtOrder.pdf

      C. The court adopted the Plaintiff's map -- not NDC's. https://www.wccusd.net/cms/lib/CA01001466/Centricity/Domain/16/Joint%20Ex%20Parte%20Application%20for%20Entry%20of%20Judgment.pdf

     A.  "After pushback from that community, among others, the city’s demographer announced that it made an error and was in fact able to create maps with two Latino majority districts..."

column6:
As you likely know, mapping and analyses performed by NDC and Doug Johnson have been rejected and discredited by courts throughout the country.

Doug Johnson's testimony in NC gerrymandering case, Common Cause v Lewis, was tossed.  He even admitted his testimony was incorrect. 
   
The 2018 case Luna vs Kern County is a landmark voting rights victory in which the US District Court Judge ruled that the redistricting plan defended by Doug Johnson unlawfully denied Latinos the ability to elect candidates of their choice.
His data and testimony were found to be "insufficient."

In March of 2019, the West Contra Costa Unified School District (WCCUSD) settled a civil rights lawsuit which claimed that the district's at-large election map "dilutes the voting strength of Latino and African American citizens."

      B.  In that settlement, WCCUSD conceded that their map was likely in violation of both the California Voting Rights Act (CVRA) and Section 2 of the US Voting Rights Act.

The NDC reversed its position when it claimed that it was not possible to draw two Latino-majority districts in the 2018 & 2019 Redwood City redistricting matter. Latino community groups protested after the council passed a map with just one Latino-majority district. 
     A.  "After pushback from that community, among others, the city’s demographer announced that it made an error and was in fact able to create maps with two Latino majority districts..."
     B.  Due to NDC's “error”, the Redwood City Council was forced to start over on their map, adding additional time and cost.

Please select a firm with good credentials and no reversals on its record.  Clearly that firm should be HaystaqDNA LLC!

column5: Mapping
column6:
Mapping and analysis performed by NDC and Doug Johnson has been rejected and discredited by courts throughout the country.

Hiring a mapping consultant with a record of drawing and defending court-rejected gerrymandered maps would risk the integrity of our maps and the public’s trust in the IRC. The Commission must reject Timmons Group/NDC from consideration.
 
I.  In North Carolina’s 2019 landmark gerrymandering case Common Cause v Lewis, a three-judge panel tossed out Doug Johnson’s testimony in defense of North Carolina’s gerrymandered map -- testimony which he later admitted was incorrect.
   A.  https://www.newsobserver.com/news/politics-government/article233105817.html
  B.  “The Court finds Dr. Johnson’s analysis unpersuasive and gives his opinions little weight.” https://www.nccourts.gov/assets/inline-files/18-CVS-14001_Final-Judgment.pdf?Bwsegeo1VV20zhJsp9hoClvmoRp3A6AR

II.  The 2018 case Luna vs Kern County is a landmark voting rights victory in which the US District Court Judge ruled that the redistricting plan defended by Doug Johnson unlawfully denied Latinos the ability to elect candidates of their choice.
  A.   https://www.maldef.org/2019/03/kern-country-voting-rights/
  B.  Doug Johnson’s testimony and data were found to be “insufficient.” https://casetext.com/case/luna-v-cnty-of-kern-4

III.  NDC was the mapping consultant for the 2001 Arizona IRC, which produced two legislative maps that were later thrown out. 
      A.  In 2002, the Commission’s first approved map failed to receive preclearance under the Voting Rights Act: https://azredistricting.org/2001/Final/doj_letter.pdf
      B.  In 2004, the Commission's second approved map was ruled unconstitutional: https://azredistricting.org/2001/2004legfinal/2004LegCourtOrder.pdf

IV.  In March of 2019, the West Contra Costa Unified School District (WCCUSD) settled a civil rights lawsuit which claimed that the district's at-large election map "dilutes the voting strength of Latino and African American citizens.
      A.  According to the plaintiff's attorney, "NDC cost the District over $650,000 by spending over a year producing map after map without a Latino majority trustee area."https://www.countyofkings.com/home/showpublisheddocument?id=25778
      B.  In that settlement, WCCUSD conceded that their map was likely in violation of both the California Voting Rights Act (CVRA) and Section 2 of the US Voting Rights Act.
      C. The court adopted the Plaintiff's map -- not NDC's. https://www.wccusd.net/cms/lib/CA01001466/Centricity/Domain/16/Joint%20Ex%20Parte%20Application%20for%20Entry%20of%20Judgment.pdf
V.  In 2018 & 2019, as the demographers for Redwood City's redistricting, NDC claimed that it was not possible to draw two Latino-majority districts in the city. Latino community groups protested after the council passed a map with just one Latino-majority district. Then NDC reversed their position. 
     A.  "After pushback from that community, among others, the city’s demographer announced that it made an error and was in fact able to create maps with two Latino majority districts..."
https://www.smdailyjournal.com/news/local/redwood-city-adopts-district-elections-map/article_29ddd2e8-7127-11e9-9750-c796bd4f69f7.html
     B.  Due to NDC's “error”, the Redwood City Council was forced to start over on their map, adding additional time and cost.
https://www.redwoodcity.org/home/showdocument?id=17969
 
I thank you for your prompt attention to this request.
