column5: Mapping
column6:
I.  In North Carolina’s 2019 landmark gerrymandering case Common Cause v Lewis, a three-judge panel tossed out Doug Johnson’s testimony in defense of North Carolina’s gerrymandered map -- testimony which he later admitted was incorrect.
      A.  https://www.newsobserver.com/news/politics-government/article233105817.html
      B.  “The Court finds Dr. Johnson’s analysis unpersuasive and gives his opinions little weight.” https://www.nccourts.gov/assets/inline-files/18-CVS-14001_Final-Judgment.pdf?Bwsegeo1VV20zhJsp9hoClvmoRp3A6AR

II.  The 2018 case Luna vs Kern County is a landmark voting rights victory in which the US District Court Judge ruled that the redistricting plan defended by Doug Johnson unlawfully denied Latinos the ability to elect candidates of their choice.
      A.   https://www.maldef.org/2019/03/kern-country-voting-rights/
      B.  Doug Johnson’s testimony and data were found to be “insufficient.” https://casetext.com/case/luna-v-cnty-of-kern-4

III.  NDC was the mapping consultant for the 2001 Arizona IRC, which produced two legislative maps that were later thrown out. 
      A.  In 2002, the Commission’s first approved map failed to receive preclearance under the Voting Rights Act: https://azredistricting.org/2001/Final/doj_letter.pdf
      B.  In 2004, the Commission's second approved map was ruled unconstitutional: https://azredistricting.org/2001/2004legfinal/2004LegCourtOrder.pdf

IV.  In March of 2019, the West Contra Costa Unified School District (WCCUSD) settled a civil rights lawsuit which claimed that the district's at-large election map "dilutes the voting strength of Latino and African American citizens.
      A.  According to the plaintiff's attorney, "NDC cost the District over $650,000 by spending over a year producing map after map without a Latino majority trustee area."https://www.countyofkings.com/home/showpublisheddocument?id=25778
      B.  In that settlement, WCCUSD conceded that their map was likely in violation of both the California Voting Rights Act (CVRA) and Section 2 of the US Voting Rights Act.
      C. The court adopted the Plaintiff's map -- not NDC's. https://www.wccusd.net/cms/lib/CA01001466/Centricity/Domain/16/Joint%20Ex%20Parte%20Application%20for%20Entry%20of%20Judgment.pdf
V.  In 2018 & 2019, as the demographers for Redwood City's redistricting, NDC claimed that it was not possible to draw two Latino-majority districts in the city. Latino community groups protested after the council passed a map with just one Latino-majority district. Then NDC reversed their position. 
     A.  "After pushback from that community, among others, the city’s demographer announced that it made an error and was in fact able to create maps with two Latino majority districts..."
https://www.smdailyjournal.com/news/local/redwood-city-adopts-district-elections-map/article_29ddd2e8-7127-11e9-9750-c796bd4f69f7.html
     B.  Due to NDC's “error”, the Redwood City Council was forced to start over on their map, adding additional time and cost.
https://www.redwoodcity.org/home/showdocument?id=17969
 
I thank you for your attention to this request.

Annette Petit

column5: AZ Redistricting Commission
column6:
Commissioners, 

Redistricting is supposed to be a nonpartisan process so the resulting maps reflect the make up of the community. However, several major decisions of this Redistricting Commission have not resulted in nonpartisan selections. 
1. The executive director is a partisan selection and the person selected didn’t even meet minimum qualifications.
2.  The law firm selected was a partisan selection.
3.  The Mapping team selected was the most obvious partisan selection. The selection of the mapping team was for Timmons/NDC. The selection totally overlooked the long history of drawing severely gerrymandered maps. In numerous cases, the maps drawn didn’t represent Hispanic and Black populations fairly. These missteps caused delays and additional costs to the districts. There are numerous court cases to support this extensive history of gerrymandered Redistricting maps. These are just a few of the affected districts: West Contra Costa Unified School District: March, 2019;Redwood City Redistricting: 2018 & 2019; Yuma County Redistricting; Luna vs. Kern County-2018; Arizona IRC-2001. 

With this extensive history of drawing gerrymandered maps and losing these court cases, how can this Independent Redistricting Commission sincerely claim the selection of Timmons/NDC is non partisan and selection of the best mapping company?

One of the comments to support this selection was that Timmons/ NDC would be solely focused on Arizona’s mapping while the other better qualified mapping firm, HayStaq/DNA, has been hired by California’s Redistricting. Insinuating that HayStaq will be spread too thin to spend adequate time on Arizona’s maps. However, they have a better track record of producing maps that don’t end up in court.Furthermore, they don’t have a reputation of delays. Where several of the maps drawn by Doug Johnson of Timmons/ NDC had long delays due to having to redraw maps again and again. 
Instead, because of HayStaq’s good reputation, they are in demand for their positive results, as opposed to Timmon’s reputation of having to redraw maps due to court disputes.

So, how can anyone consider this commission is anything but blatantly partisan? 

Respectfully, 

Rita Day
5320 Rainbow Cliff Place
Prescott, AZ 86301

column5: Chair's comments about public comments
column6:
I was surprised and a bit alarmed when I thought I heard Commissioner Neuberg say the commissioners were under no legal obligation to hear public opinion.  I went back and listened to her comments several times to be sure.  What she said, in the context of Commissioner Lerner's concern that some of the public comments were harsh and disrespectful, was that the commissioners were "committed to provide access" but she wanted to remind the public that they (the commissioners) were "under no legal obligation to open ourselves up to this level of public comment".   By "this level" Commissioner Neuberg may have been referring to the accusations and attacks in some of the comments, not that the commissioners were under no obligation to hear comments submitted by the public or that they would ignore public comments.  I'm not sure what role 'legal obligation' plays in this one way or another.  Unfortunately attacks and misinformation are (sadly) part of the landscape when you're open to hearing from the public.  The commissioners are free to handle those (and all) comments in whatever way they feel is appropriate, whether they ignore them or look for value or new ideas in them or gain a sense of the public's consensus.

From Commissioner Neuberg's comments, it would be easy for someone watching the meeting to get the idea that the commissioners don't feel they need to pay attention to what the public thinks.  She may want to go back and clarify her comments so there is no misunderstanding about how the commissioners will treat public comments.

Regarding the 3-2 vs. unanimous decisions, commissioner Neuberg's assertion that the majority of the commission's decisions were unanimous seemed disingenuous.  While it may be correct if you count in the votes to accept the minutes, go into Executive Session, etc., the really important decisions - those that will shape the Commission and its work - were split 3-2 - certainly in the choice of an Executive Director and the mapping consultant.  The decision to hire the two legal counsel firms was unanimous, but that seems to have been the case simply because everybody got something they wanted with that vote (except the people of Arizona who will wind up having to pay the bills).  It's pretty clear that if the commissioners had decided that only one firm could be selected, then the vote would surely have been 3-2.

William Bowlus-Root
A concerned citizen

column5: IRC Executive Session
column6:
Since the IRC has selected legal counsel the meetings have used executive session far more extensively. This is ironic. A fundamental element of an independent commission is to take the back-room dealing out of redistricting and conduct business in public. Of the roughly 12 hours of meetings since April 27, it is not an exaggeration to say that more than 50% of your meetings have been conducted in executive session. 

If the commission is using executive session for legal briefings that do not require privilege, I ask that you reconsider. What really does an executive session  briefing on the open meeting law, ethics, or conflicts of interest achieve? Upon reflection, was it necessary for these trainings to be conducted in executive session? Conducting such trainings in public would both inform the public so that public participation would be, possibly, more meaningful. And secondly, doing so would establish confidence that when the commission does use executive session it is for a discussion that absolutely does requires confidential legal advice. 

While calling out what I believe to be excessive and unnecessary use of executive session, clearly the IRC will require time for private discussion with legal counsel - as was the case with the recent mapping procurement.  To that end, please consider adopting an agenda similar to the one below for an upcoming meeting for the Arizona Fish and Game Commission. It agendizes all possible executive session activity in one block - at the end of the meeting. And there are some items that are noted as time certain. Integrating similar practices for the IRC agendas would provide value to the public that is engaged in your efforts making it easier to follow the discussion and I imagine to the commissioners themselves so that they are not jumping from one item back to another. 

https://publicmeetings.az.gov/sites/default/files/2021.05.14%20Agenda.pdf

Thank you for your consideration of these suggestions.

column5: Leadership, Transparency and Fairness

Since it appears  that there is political pressure being exerted, I ask that all "Contact Us" comments be posted on the website so they are easily viewable by the public. We the people want to see what goes into your consideration, and we deserve the same insight that you have.   

If you could please not use acronyms in your discussions, particularity done during the Executive Director reporting. Most of these are meaningless to the general public. This could be a learning experience if actual words were used. Last, thank you for posting the written meeting minutes. 

The people in this state want fair and balanced maps. With more competitive districts there could be some moderation in what has become too many safe districts. Now the hard work starts. Please be there for all of us.

thank you!

column5: Causus attendence at future meeting(s)
column6:
To the Commissioners, 
I noted with some concern the Commission's apparent intention to invite legislative caucus members to attend its next (and possibly future?) meetings. 
Legislative presence and potential input into the redistricting process, even at this early stage, is problematic for several reasons: 
- First, the Independent Redistricting Commission was created by voters to remove politicians from the redistricting process. Caucus leaders have direct stakes in the outcome of IRC proceedings, which means that their very attendance creates potential conflicts of interest.
- Giving politicians meeting access encourages them to provide opinion, guidance or recommendations about redistricting, which is counter to the independence of the Commission
- And some caucus members are working to pass legislation that would create certain barriers to voting in Arizona, so giving special IRC meeting access to them, would risk sending the wrong message to underrepresented Arizona voters, communities of color and others. 
Please do not invite caucus members to attend Commission meetings, now or in the future.

column5: Inviting Legislative Leaders to
column6:
Dear Commissioners, 

At the May 25 meeting Chairwoman Neuberg raised the issue, explored in a conversation with legal counsel, to invite the legislative minority and majority leaders to an IRC meeting. In response to a question posed by Commissioner Lerner, the Chairwoman explained the intent was "to have those who have been critically involved share with us their vision of our responsibility and have a comfort level with us."  Legal counsel added that in addition to appointing the four partisan members of the IRC, the legislature has the right to review and comment on the district maps created by the IRC. This review is an opportunity shared with every resident of the state. It is not a special authority; nor should it be treated as one.   

The purpose of Prop. 106 was to explicitly remove the personal self-interest of the legislature from the redistricting process. Engaging legislative leadership in your process would be an extraordinarily risky action. It  would undermine public trust that the IRC is acting in an a-partisan manner with integrity and the highest ethical standards. 

I believe the tolerance of your legal counsel, Snell and Wilmer, to continue to advise candidates, consultants, lobbyists, political action committees (PACs), ballot measure and independent expenditure committees, political parties, municipalities, corporations, election-related vendors, trade associations and other tax-exempt organizations, and individual donors and political contributors - is in and of itself risky. Does Snell and Wilmer advise any member of the legislative leadership? I hope you see the legitimacy of such questions and concerns. 

As to the question of vision - it is answered fully in the intent and language of Prop. 106. With the appointment of the four partisan IRC members the responsibility of the legislature was fundamentally completed. Inviting them to engage further only complicates and already complex and challenging agenda.  
 
I appreciate your consideration of these comments.

column5: Invitation to legislators
column6:
Dear Commissioners,

I am writing to express my opposition to inviting legislative caucus leaders to address the Commission at this time. 

First, introducing more partisan politics into the independent redistricting process defeats the very purpose of the IRC, which is to minimize politics in the redistricting process.  Since the November 2020 election, Arizona Republican leaders have introduced various voter suppression bills and embroiled the state in a ridiculous and dangerous “audit” of election results in Maricopa County.  They have done this in the complete absence of evidence of fraud or irregularities in the election; they are simply unhappy that their candidate for President lost.  They ignore facts, including their own electoral victories that allowed them to maintain control of the Arizona Senate and House, and worse, they foster the very lack of confidence in the election process about which they claim to be so concerned.  Far from needing information on Republican leaders’ “vision,” which is clear, the IRC should avoid giving them another forum.  Inviting them to address the IRC now would send a very bad message to Arizona voters regarding the integrity of the IRC process.

Second, the Arizona Constitution, which created the IRC, specifically provides for input from the legislature after the draft maps are drawn.  Inviting legislators to address the IRC before the maps are drawn introduces the potential for serious conflict of interest because state legislative representatives all have a very specific stake in the outcome of redistricting.  And the entire redistricting process is complicated enough without introducing potential partisanship.

Third, the IRC concerns regarding transparency are, frankly, suspect because so much of the IRC’s business has been done in Executive Committee, including the crucial choice of selecting the mapping firm —one with a poor record of map drawing.  This was done without explanation to the public.

In sum, the IRC should not invite state legislators to address the IRC until the draft maps are completed.

ON OPEN MEETINGS 
During discussion Chairwoman Neuberg exclaimed the sentiment that now "the public knows what we've been talking about in executive session. It's not as sexy as you might think." The point is not whether it is sexy or not. The point is none of these state policy trainings were required to be convened in executive session. However, the IRC default to take any non-routine conversation into executive session is troubling. It reflects a discomfort for doing the hard work of the IRC in public; a misreading of basic open meeting framework; and a false dependence of "advice of counsel." The proposed polices have not yet been posted so I can not make any more specific comments other than to say no matter what you put on paper. the proof will be in the pudding. Or in this case the hopefully open meetings of the IRC.  

ON ETHICS - Commissioner York suggested the IRC adopt the House ethic rules as "they are more onerous." Chairwoman Neuberg agreed that the approach of "whatever holds us to the highest standards." I truly can not fathom your tolerance of legal counsel that continues to advise advise candidates, consultants, lobbyists, political action committees (PACs), ballot measure and independent expenditure committees, political parties, municipalities, corporations, election-related vendors, trade associations and other tax-exempt organizations, and individual donors and political contributors.  At the very least there must be PUBLIC disclose of the candidates, political parties, municipalities and other redistricting stakeholders that are being advised by the firm and the assigned lawyers. 

ON PUBLIC RECORDS - The sound was not clear so i am not certain I heard the proposal correctly that the IRC would adopt policies that would commit a 30 day response to public records requests - after a 1 -3 day acknowledgment of the request. If a 30 days response window was proposed I ask that you seriously consider modifications. I appreciate your consideration of these comments.

column5: IRC Process going forward
column6:
A longstanding pattern of gerrymandering prior to 2000 prompted Arizonans to invest considerable time, effort and expense in developing and passing Prop 106, the ballot initiative that created the Independent Redistricting Commission (IRC) in 2000.  Since then, this explicitly bipartisan group of citizen volunteers has replaced the State Legislature as the group responsible for establishing the boundaries of Arizona’s legislative and U.S. congressional districts. The goal of this change was to restore the core principle that elected representatives should be chosen by the voters, not by the political party in power.  

The 2000 and 2010 commissions were not without issues, but they fulfilled their mission.  The current commission is likely to face even more challenges given the current partisan climate and heightened levels of suspicion.  Every effort should be made to demonstrate both independence and transparency.  

Regarding independence: I believe it would be a serious mistake to invite input from any legislators prior to the time specified in the law.  They already had a role in selecting the partisan commissioners and the list of independents that might be chosen to lead the commission.  And they will have an opportunity later to react to your initial maps, at a time when you will be better prepared to put their comments in perspective. Remember this is your job, not theirs.  And it is your job for good reasons.  The roadmap for how to proceed is specified in the legislation.  You can’t be criticized for following it, but you can be criticized for not following it.  

Regarding transparency:  As several have suggested, attendees at every stop on your tour should receive the same introductory presentation.  The Q and A”s that follow will obviously vary based on audience feedback. Since commissioners and staff are all new, I wonder if your preparation might be aided by minutes or other recorded documents from the past commission that could provide some guidance.   I hope you will make time during subsequent public meetings to share key things you have learned along the way. 

I am glad that commissioners have opted to include public comments submitted both during and between meetings.  I think you are getting some very helpful feedback, and most contributors have heeded Commissioner Lerner’s request to be more civil and positive.  I remain concerned with the pace at which key support positions are being filled.  This seems especially critical given your truncated time frame.  I would imagine that the technical glitches we have observed thus far would be reduced substantially once your IT person is on board. (On June 1st, the sound was poor or missing when I watched live, but the recording was audible when I listened later.)  I hope the Executive Director will have your tour itinerary ready very soon, not only so you can learn from constituents but also so that constituents can plan their time as well.  

I appreciate your willingness to serve and the effort you continue to bring to this very important task.

     2) In order to ensure that ALL people can participate, public hearings must be held at various times - not just during normal working hours -- to include evenings, weekends etc.
     3) There must be plenty of advance notice (see 1 above) so those wishing to attend can arrange for child care, elder care & transportation; and the IRC should reach out to non profits to see if some of those will assist in providing child/elder care and transportation at no or reduced cost.
    4) Public hearing locations must be ADA compliant, and to include closed captioning, translation service and interpretation services offered, wherever possible.
    5) And where such exists, locations should be convenient to public transportation.
    6) Public hearings should be geographically diverse to ensure that ALL Arizonans, wherever they live, can participate.
    7) Hearing locations should be selected with input from local organizations/non profits (that work with often marginalized communities) to ensure they are as convenient as possible -- and as 'welcoming' as possible for everyone.

column5: public comments
column6:
My thanks to each of you for your service to the people of Arizona. Thank you for the opportunity to share my comments via this public forum. 

I am a 4th generation Arizona native and I well remember learning the history of Arizona in a publicly funded school system. My grandparents were public school teachers and my grandfather served in the capacity of superintendent in a small but successful school district in southern Arizona.

Work took me away from Arizona for a number of years but I was fortunate to be able to return and ultimately retire here. Living in many different places always reinforced why I was so fortunate to have grown up in Arizona. 

Having a well-rounded education with emphasis every year on Arizona and United States civics is one benefit that I will always treasure. Even though I didn’t reside in Arizona for many years, I remembered that voting was always my duty as a citizen of our democracy.

That being said, you can appreciate that I take redistricting and the process of assuring fair and balanced maps very seriously. Voters in Arizona overwhelmingly approved the formation of the Independent Redistricting Commission to remove politicians from the redistricting process. Because political party leaders in the legislature have direct stakes in the final maps, allowing legislators to provide input prior to draft maps is contrary to the people’s wish and to the Arizona Constitution. I encourage you vote no on this suggestion.

In the spirit of serving all the people of Arizona, I suggest that you give great consideration to accessibility during the upcoming public hearings. 

During the last redistricting effort, I was living in a remote area of Arizona. Nevertheless, I did make certain that I could drive to and from the hearings because I felt that my opinion was important. This made for a few very late nights but I was fortunate because I was retired, I had good health and my schedule was my own.

Please consider scheduling public hearings so that all who wish to offer public comments have access to these meetings. Scheduling accessible meetings includes the following: meeting scheduled for outside of normal working hours; advance notice so that transportation, possible work coverage and child-care can be arranged; locations that give the public relatively easy access especially in areas outside of major metropolitan areas; and the assurance that these sites be safe, secure and ADA-accessible.

To better understand the perspective of the participant commenting at public meeting, participants should identify what town or region they live.

Ensure that those in the hopper to speak know their place in line so as not to miss chance to addresscommittee.

Presentation or invite to IRC meeting
To avoid perspective of discrimination and to keep the legislature separate from IRC, don’t invite legislature to an IRC audience. They can comment in a public meeting.

Policies
Because the IRC has a particular scope of work, do not adopt policies but craft or change to reflect IRC. For example, Conflict of interest/Ethics would be to vote for criteria and federal voting rights law established not to advance partisan interests.

Training for map software
Provide links for training and practice data to public as soon as possible.

Access to draft maps
To accommodate multiple capacities of residents and community, access to draft maps should be available electronically and in hard copy in public spaces.

column5: Agenda item V.5
column6:
﻿

This should be very clear beforehand. So I am very concerned that the Commission hasn’t done the necessary planning & organization to make certain these in person presentations will be effective.

Coconino County is the 2nd largest county in the UNITED STATES! Residents will be coming from great distances. The county covers Grand Canyon Village, Flagstaff, parts of Sedona, Page, Supai, Tuba City, Williams, & Winslow. The residents need to be notified and in sufficient time for them to make travel plans to attend. Given that you are planning two sessions in Maricopa County - I would respectfully suggest that maybe you have one of those sessions be your initial effort, so you are able to prepare and test many of the aspects of your session (background presentation, rules for submitting comment, signing or other ADA services, security, etc.) without the added complications of travel and remote community locations. Very hard for most normal people to take time off work on Tuesday mornings to call in for such a session. I strongly urge you to schedule at least a couple of such sessions in the evenings so that hard-working citizens of Arizona have a chance to be heard.

column5: IRC: Public notice of meeting
column6:
Thank you for coming to Northern Arizona on your listening tour to hear about our Communities of Interest.  I know you are only required to notify us 48 hours in advance of public meetings, so I appreciate you publishing a proposed schedule two weeks before an in-person public meeting in Coconino County, however, I do have some concerns.  Coconino County is the second largest county in the United States.  Depending on where you hold the public hearing, residents here might be driving for a couple of hours to attend.  Grand Canyon Village, Supai, Williams, Flagstaff, Winslow, Page, Tuba City, and parts of Sedona are all in Coconino County.  How will you be notifying these different communities?  Newspaper and radio ads?  Social media?  Notifications to the tribal and county governments, town councils, and city councils?  Some of these areas do not have consistent internet services.  Will you be mailing notices? Can you effectively notify all these communities within two weeks?  Assuming you want to hear about Communities of Interest, will your notifications give a definition of COI and explain the mission of the IRC?
 
Here are some suggestions:
•	Start the meeting with a presentation of the IRC and the redistricting process in Arizona.
•	Determine how much time each presenter will be given and enforce that time limit.
•	Require each presenter to register.   Require home zip code and subject matter, and have someone responsible for organizing the order of presenters.   Please allow those who have traveled the farthest to speak first.  Please ensure that no one side prevents others from speaking.
•	Run the meeting in an organized and respectful manner.
•	Start the meeting during normal business hours, but extend it to beyond 5:00 pm.
•	Follow COVID-19 protocols.
•	Do not allow guns.
*       Anyone that is disrespectful, or disruptive, and doesn't allow others to speak should be escorted out.

column5: IRC Process going forward
column6:
Thank you all for reaffirming the AZ law passed in 2020 that specifies the times when input from State legislators is to be provided.  At last week’s meeting Commissioner Learner raised the issue of putting procedures in place to ensure that local/area voters at each stop along your statewide tour are given speaking priority.  I believe this is an issue worthy of discussion at a public meeting, and I hope you will put it on your agenda.

The purpose of your tour is to get a sense of what matters to voters in different parts of the state.  For this reason, it would be inappropriate if the representative views of voters in any region are overpowered by bands of partisans of either political party who might follow you around the state and make sure that their views are heard over and over at each stop.

I was not a resident of Arizona until 2015, so I am unaware of what procedures were in place to address this concern in prior cycles.  One possible strategy that occurred to me is requiring persons who want to speak to write the town where they vote at the top of the request to speak card that I’m imagining you will ask them to fill out.  It would be easy, then, for staff to grant speaking privileges first to locals.  In addition, all persons who speak should state their hometown before beginning their remarks. The cards of all speakers could be preserved and serve as a record of who participated.  I think this level of documentation and transparency would be useful given the current partisan political climate.

Thank you again for your willingness to serve and support representative democracy.

column5: Redistricting hearings
column6:
During the last redistricting efforts in 2011, 23 public hearings were held prior to grid maps being drawn with multiple meetings being held in remote parts of the state. This allowed for critical early input from often underrepresented Arizona communities. However, this cycle, the tentative schedule only has 9 in-person meetings scheduled. This is unacceptable and the standard set by the previous commission should at the least be met, if not exceeded.
The proposed public hearing schedule currently does not have dedicated dates for Pinal County, the third largest county in our state, and adding dates in counties that have no hearings scheduled was not discussed during today's IRC meeting. All the communities of Arizona should be able to weigh in on redistricting plans.
Pinal County is the third largest county in the state with over half a million people yet we’re being left out of the conversation and ignored. I am from, raised, and work in Pinal county as well as the rest of my family. so please put an emphasis on the fact that we should be included in the redistricting process just like it was in the previous commission and should be able to have access to provide early public input. Pinal County had one early public hearing last cycle which should easily be met if not exceeded due to our high population in the state.
If the current schedule is adopted, it would not give enough time for community outreach before the first hearing to insure the public can have their voices heard. Why is it necessary to complete the hearings by August? The Commission should first engage in significant public outreach to encourage community members to attend and at the very least inform them of the opportunity to attend.

We deserve to be included in this phase of input so the commission can create fair and equitable maps for Arizona. Please include Pinal County in this process.

column5: Please expand public hearings for redistricting!
column6:
Hello,

My name is Kate Boettcher and I am writing to you today to please urge you to increase the amount of public hearings with our communities for redistricting. I live in Maricopa county but have several close friends and family members who live in counties where there are no public hearings scheduled for this cycle. It is unacceptable that only 9 in-person public hearings are scheduled for this cycle, when in 2011 we had 23 public hearings. We should be exceeding this amount by directly talking to our community members. 

I am very passionate about building sustainable and resilient communities, especially in the face of protecting our voting rights and in the presence of anthropogenic climate change. Empowerment among communities starts with their ability to be heard. This process cannot happen without public hearings that are inclusive and equitable across the state, for decisions that will directly impact these communities.

column5: Legal Counsel Political Consulting
column6:
Dear Commissioners,

I repeat my request that the IRC reconsider its tolerance of the continued political consulting of one of your selected law firms, Snell and Wilmer. I went back and listened to their interview and caught that they have agreed to stop consulting for political parties. This indicates they recognize the potential for conflicts of interest – real or perceived. The remainder of their answer was essentially – “trust us – we’ve got this covered.” They named an internal ethics and compliance process for Snell and Wilmer. Again this recognizes the prospect of real and perceived conflicts of interest, but does not address the concern of the public for impartiality or transparency. The firm’s process is in place to protect the firm – not the IRC or the public.  Neither the IRC, nor the public, should be asked to accept at face value the internal processes of the firm. The IRC and the public deserve more. 

I ask that you either 1) request the firm suspend its political consulting for the duration of their contract with the IRC or 2) establish PUBLIC policies, procedures and protocols for standardized and regular disclosers of the work Snell and Wilmer is conducting that intersects with the interests of redistricting. 

As an example, the Snell and Wilmer website states the individual lawyer: 
regularly advises candidates, consultants, lobbyists, political action committees (PACs), ballot measure and independent expenditure committees, political parties, municipalities, corporations, election-related vendors, trade associations and other tax-exempt organizations, and individual donors and political contributors.

I emphasize five specific categories – candidates, consultants, municipalities, individual donors and political contributors. These entities are primary stakeholders – where you draw the lines directly impacts their individual political futures and fortunes. 

To draw this out further: I don’t know which municipalities Snell and Wilmer represent – but suppose they represent Glendale where I live, 2010 population of 191,719. Despite having a population that would easily be contained in just one state legislative district, Glendale is currently divided among seven state legislative districts 13, 15, 20, 21, 22, 29, and 30. If Snell and Wilmer is now representing Glendale, will our city be more fairly treated in 2021? If they are not representing Glendale, will we be sliced and diced again? 

This question highlights just one example of the direct intersection between the political work of Snell and Wilmer and the redistricting work of the IRC. 

This creates a substantial threat to the IRC as it quite easily draws into question the integrity of the core of your work – drawing districts for fair and equal representation for all Arizonans. So many IRC actions taken “in an abundance of caution” to establish public trust and diminish risk for litigation seem performative in comparison. (Such as not posting meeting transcripts that may not exactly match the video – even with a disclaimer.) By taking one of the two actions noted above, this very real and serious threat to the ideals, integrity, and transparency could be mitigated. 

This report by the Pew Research Center (https://www.pewresearch.org/politics/2021/05/17/public-trust-in-government-1958-2021/) reflects the low level of public trust in American government and institutions. Fair, or not, the IRC is part of this universe where an overwhelming majority (76%) do not think they can trust the government to do what is right even most of the time. The work of the 2021 IRC commission can serve as a counterbalance to this mistrust and lay a foundation for a more engaged citizenry to solve the problems most of us agree on. If you choose to. 

I appreciate your attention to this serious and very real ethical conflict.

column5: bburstein@cox.net
column6:
Dear Commissioners:


I am writing because I am concerned about the public hearings that the Independent Redistricting Commission will be holding, and what measures the Commission will take to ensure the the hearings are conducted in an orderly fashion and safely.

One vital step for safety is prohibiting firearms and other weapons from the public hearings

Further, as Commissioner Lerner expressed, I share concerns about the recent takeovers of local school board meetings around the State. While the public should have the opportunity to communicate with the Commission, the hearings should not be overtaken by political extremists, and those whose goals are the taking control of or shutting down the public hearing.  Instead, the the public should be able to participate, as long as it is with respect,  established norms, and a decorum of civility.  
Before the meeting it would be beneficial to adopt and follow commission rules of procedure, including Robert’s Rules of Order.  Where ground rules are understood going in, it can certainly aid in maintaining order and civility.  Consider the option of remote meeting attendance for individuals who cannot attend the meeting in person.  Also, for those who may not be comfortable commenting at the meeting in person, by allowing comments by email or handwritten letters that can be made part of the record. Further, utilizing a sign-up sheet for those who wish to address the Commission that includes the person’s name, address, phone number would help understand who and how many intend to speak, and may facilitate determining the order in which speakers will be called.

Determining ground rules for how the meeting will be run and letting the public know those in advance may also assist the meeting to be orderly. These would include having a reasonable time limit for comments, for example, 3 to 5 minutes, and enforcing that consistently. Also, stating the values and behavior that the public will be expected to demonstrate during the hearing, such as treating others and their opinions respectfully, refraining from personal attacks, not interrupting, and other norms of decorum.   

Also, it would be beneficial to put the public on notice before the hearing, for example, in the notice of hearing or the agenda.  For example, informing the public in advance that the Chair reserves the right to ensure that all comments are appropriate and abide by rules of civility, which applies to the audience as well as to the speakers. Individuals who refuse to abide by these ground rules may not be permitted to continue speaking. Certain individuals who are disruptive and uncivil should not be allowed to intimidate or silence Arizonans who want to make their voices heard at the public hearings.

I urge the Commissioners to consider adopting these measures to aid in conducting safe and orderly public hearings.

column5: Mapping
column6:
Dear Commissioners,

I am writing regarding the need to protect the upcoming mapping process from the spread of disinformation by political organizations and to insure that testimony considered by the IRC is that of real Arizona citizens. 

As you know, disinformation was used extensively in the last election; it’s effect was to confuse voters, discourage and intimidate voters from going to the polls, and ultimately to needlessly cause some voters to lose confidence in the voting process.  The AZ Republican state leadership has continued this process of disinformation by its insistence on an “audit” of votes in Maricopa County although the election results have already been confirmed and certified.  Add to this the potential for gerrymandering and the proliferation of do-it-yourself online redistricting tools, and its plain that the IRC faces a daunting problem to maintain the integrity and transparency of its process.  Use of political disinformation, including bad mapping from political operatives would undermine the entire redistricting process. 

It does not appear to me from the IRC website that anyone other than the IRC can use the IRC mapping tool to draw maps; anyone else would use one of the do-it-yourself tools.  The Commission must give consideration to and outline means to protect the process by, at a minimum, requiring accurate and complete identification of any organization that posts maps, including disclosure of any political affiliation, and banning of fake accounts. Any map posted should disclose the software used to draw the map.  For any such software used, the code or algorithms used to score districts must be disclosed, users must have the ability to obtain data and redistricting plans in machine-analyzable format, and any organizations providing financial backing must be disclosed.  (See The Dawn of Do-It-Yourself Redistricting, Micah Altman, Ph. D. and Michael P. McDonald, Ph. D. , Non-Resident Senior Fellow at the Brookings Institution. https://www.campaignsandelections.com/campaign-insider/the-dawn-of-do-it-yourself-redistricting-online-software-puts-redistricting-tools-in-the-hands-of-the-public )

Many people are likely to post public comments regarding the IRC maps. Again, the IRC should ban fake accounts and require identification of organizations that post comments.  It should also develop its own methods for fact checking and rules under which false statements by political operatives can be removed or at least identified as false statements from a political operative.  Links to fact-checking sites should be included for use by the public.  Disinformation regarding threats to safety at public hearing sites must be promptly removed and reported to the proper authorities.  

Because disinformation from any person or organization can be harmful, it is important that Arizona voters who access the online mapping tool have information on how to recognize disinformation—such as excessive typographical errors, over use of capitalization, punctuation that includes many exclamation marks, an over-the-top message, and lack of identified reliable sources for the information—and to be reminded not to cause the further spread of disinformation by sharing it.  There should be a way for users to report disinformation to the platform.

column5: Public hearing safety and order
column6:
Dear Commissioners:
 
 
I am writing because I am concerned about the public hearings that the Independent Redistricting Commission will be holding and what measures the Commission will take to ensure the the hearings are conducted in an orderly fashion and safely.
 
One vital step for safety is prohibiting firearms and other weapons from the public hearings.
 
Further, as Commissioner Lerner expressed, I share concerns about the recent takeovers of local school board meetings around the State. While the public should have the opportunity to communicate with the Commission, the hearings should not be overtaken by political extremists, and those whose goals are the taking control of or shutting down the public hearing.  Instead, the public should be able to participate, as long as it is done with respect,  established norms, and a decorum of civility.  
 
Before the meeting it would be beneficial to adopt and follow are the commission’s rules of procedure, including Robert’s Rules of Order. When ground rules are understood going in, it can certainly aid in maintaining order and civility.  Consider the option of remote meeting attendance for individuals who cannot attend the meeting in person.  Also, for those who may not be comfortable commenting at the meeting in person, by allowing comments by email or handwritten letters that can be made part of the record. Further, utilizing a sign-up sheet for those who wish to address the Commission that includes the person’s name, address, phone number would help understand who and how many intend to speak, and may facilitate determining the order in which speakers may be called.
 
Determining ground rules for how the meeting will be run and letting the public know those in advance may also assist the meeting to be orderly. These would include having a reasonable time limit for comments, for example, 3 to 5 minutes, and enforcing that consistently. Also, stating the values and behavior that the public will be expected to demonstrate during the hearing, such as treating others and their opinions respectfully, refraining from personal attacks, not interrupting, and other norms of decorum.  
 
Also, it would be beneficial to put the public on notice before the hearing of certain ground rules.  For instance, letting the public know in advance, say in the notice of the hearing or agenda, that the Chair reserves the right to ensure that all comments are appropriate and abide by rules of civility, which applies to the audience as well as to the speakers. Individuals who refuse to abide by these ground rules may not be permitted to continue speaking. Certain individuals who are disruptive and uncivil should not be allowed to intimidate or silence Arizonans who want to make their voices heard at the public hearings.
 
I urge the Commissioners to consider adopting these measures to aid in conducting safe and orderly public hearings.

column5: Hearing Process
column6: Arizona’s Independent Redistricting Commission was established in 2000 by Arizona voters who approved the initiative by more than 150,000 votes. It created a process that removed the redistricting decision-making from the hands of politicians who had a conflict of interest in the outcome.  Inherent in that voter approval was a desire to create an open, transparent process that maximizes the opportunity for Arizona’s diverse population to have input.  The community hearings that may start in two weeks are essential to obtaining that input.  Two weeks is not a lot of time to publicize as widely as possible the times, places, and dates of these hearings.  There should be a saturation of notices in a wide variety of media and languages.  The actual hearing procedures should include the selection of sites that are accessible for the disabled and the provision of translation/captioning services.  In short, the IRC needs a plan.  I hope that it will have a detailed one at its July 13th meeting.

column5: IRC Process going forward
column6:
DIFFERENTIAL PRIVACY PRESENTATIONS:  I appreciated the IRC scheduling presentations by experts with alternative perspectives on differential privacy.  Both were interesting and informative, but I am having some difficulty reconciling their differences.  My takeaways include: (1) Mr. Bryan did not dismiss the value of privacy, but he focused much more on accuracy.  Dr. Moon pointed out that the Census Bureau is mandated by law to use methods that address both concerns.  (2) Mr. Bryan provided examples of data he found especially alarming, e.g., households with children but no adults and households with 15 or more persons, but it was not clear to me from his remarks if and/or how such data would be used to draw maps.  If I understand correctly, Dr. Moon addressed that concern by acknowledging that such anomalies would be present initially when noise was introduced to protect privacy, but these anomalies would disappear through the process of fine tuning required by the differential privacy method.  This conclusion seemed to be supported strongly by her research findings.  (3) If anomalous data such as households with no adults are the basis for drawing maps, then I am concerned.  But if maps are drawn using the finely tuned data discussed by Dr. Moon, then I am persuaded that the Census Bureau has made a sound choice in changing its procedures. (4) This choice was further reinforced by Dr. Moon’s brief description of how individual data could be used for potentially damaging purposes, should they get in the hands unauthorized users.  I question how effectively our privacy can be protected in today’s world, but I support the Census Bureau’s efforts to do so.

LISTENING TOUR:  Like other commenters, I am concerned that the IRC has not yet adopted, let alone publicized, a stock presentation and operating procedures The IRC procedures (1) should be publicized in advance of the first tour stop AND (2) state in writing that at each stop on the tour, all citizens from that area will be allowed to speak before any citizens from outside the area will be allowed to speak.  To do otherwise would give commissioners a false impression of the needs and wishes of citizens from different parts of the State.  That is, after all, the goal of the listening tour.  In the interest of transparency, might I suggest that speakers begin by stating their names and their residences.  And might I suggest further that the Commission collect and retain the request to speak cards as a record.  (Such procedures may have been used in the past, but I doubt I am the only interested person who was not a resident of AZ at the time of the two previous commissions.)

On a different topic entirely, I note that technology issues continue to be a problem.  What I thought was going to be a 5-minute recess turned out to be the end of today’s meeting, at least at my end of the connection.  There were several other important items on the agenda, so I’m hoping followers will be able to watch the rest of today’s meeting on a recording.

column5: Testing the claims about differential privacy
column6:
I appreciate you lining up the two speakers on differential privacy at the last commission meeting. I thought they offered valuable perspectives. I would encourage you to build on the insights and recommendations they offered. 

One line of inquiry that I think would be worth pursuing is an estimation of the Citizen Voting Age Population (CVAP) by Race and Ethnicity for Arizona in 2020. In 2016, the U.S. Census Bureau reported the CVAP for Arizona was 65.6% non-Hispanic white and 33.4% minority. The American Community Survey (ACS) average for 2017-2019 indicated that the state’s CVAP was 37.0% minority and 63.0% non-Hispanic white (+-0.2%). Nailing down these numbers for 2020 might prove important for your redistricting work.

The state demographer’s recent presentation to the commission showed that only two of the current congressional districts for Arizona are minority-majority. The commission might want to explore whether the distribution of the minority CVAP population would support a total of three minority-majority districts. The ACS data could support an exploration of this hypothesis for Arizona. Once an initial feasibility study is conducted, the results could then be profitably compared to the decennial census redistricting data that will be released in mid-August. 

At your recent commission meeting, one of the speakers warned that minority-majority districts could drop below 50% minority because of differential privacy. The other speaker was confident that minority enumerations would be largely unaffected once tabulation blocks were aggregated up to the district level. The experiment I suggested above could give the commission a way to 1) test the competing claims of the speakers and 2) validate the 2020 census data with recent ACS data. That way the commission could be in a better position to demonstrate whether or not it was possible to draw minority-majority CVAP districts as well as how many of these districts the data could support.

column5: Direct Data Download
column6:
There are several hundred Geographic Information Systems (GIS) analysts in Arizona who would like to work with the datasets you will be using. These include the original counts using Census geography, the version of these data by voting precinct used for the draft maps, the district boundary files for CDs and LDs in each of their iterations, and even the initial grid maps (for those interested in educational exposition of your entire process).

I suggest you provide a link to download these datasets as zipped Shapefiles. This is an industry standard format that can be used in virtually all commercial and free open-source GIS systems. I have examined your public information request form and see no problem in asking users to complete this form, but a direct link to the data would expedite the download process and relieve your staff from further involvement.

It would also be helpful if the public could upload similar files for any proposed Communities of Interest, or to illustrate any potential issues they perceive. This would simplify the process of reviewing these items for your mapping consultants when they will be under considerable time constraints.

column5: data recentness and scale
column6:
I appreciated the presentations on July 19th from the mapping consultants. I was impressed with the socioeconomic data report and hope to see it soon on the commission’s web site. The competitiveness presentation provided a nice overview of options available to the commission. But it occurred to me there were some tensions between those presentations. 

One tension is data recentness. The mapping of the socioeconomic data presents the latest data from the American Community Survey (ACS). The competitiveness report will likely examine Arizona election data over the last decade. Perhaps one way to align these two datasets would be to place more weight on the most recent elections and less weight on the older elections.

Another tension is data scale. The smallest geography reported by the ACS is at the block group level. It appears your mapping consultants have parsed those block groups into individual blocks for the socioeconomic mapping that was demonstrated today. The election results they are getting from the Secretary of State are likely at the precinct level, which is an “off-spine” geography. One method for aligning these two datasets would be to decompose the precinct votes into votes at the block level.

This raises a few questions. At what geographic level would you like your mapping consultants to draw your redistricting maps? If it is at the block level, would that give you more control over the composition and competitiveness of the districts? If the maps are drawn at the precinct level, would that help you to preserve communities of interest and minimize precinct splits?

column5: Listening Tour - Round 1
column6:
I'm writing to share feedback on last Thursday night’s Independent Redistricting Commission Listening Tour stop in Pinal County.  I'm a fairly new resident of Arizona, and so I haven't had much exposure to the IRC and its important work.  I attended not to offer testimony but rather to learn about and gain insight into the redistricting process.  What transpired, though, was a maddening disappointment.  The meeting logistics were ill conceived and amateurish in A/V execution.  All the socially distanced chairs in the main presentation room were already occupied, so I was shuffled into an overflow room where the attendees numbered at least as many those in the main room and all of whom were seated in close proximity next to each other at conference room tables.  The proceeding from the main room was presented on TV monitors in a Zoom-like manner.  An understandable A/V approach given the attendee dispersion, but here’s where the wheels fell off.  Initially the presenter microphone in the main room was inoperable, the delay to resolve suggesting the cause to be more than simply an on/off switch.  That got sorted out, but then the audio was barely audible in the overflow room.  Visually, the TV screens were a mess.  The speaker was not visible in the presenter's window, superfluous windows took up valuable screen real estate, the PowerPoint slides of the IRC presentation were too small to read.  The execution suggested the planning decisions for logistical details and A/V set up were based on assumptions rather than on thoughtful discernment and testing done in advance.  I was unable to follow the proceedings, and left after 15 minutes with regrets for having made the drive to attend.  On my way out the door, I shared my annoyance with a couple of Pinal County employees who informed that the County had offered to support the hearing with their public meeting equipment and experience.  They indicated the IRC eschewed this offer and chose instead to rely on the desire of their consultants to manage the meeting logistics.  If accurate, the black eye for failed execution is an unintended consequence that accrues to the IRC, not their consultants.  I understand the proceedings were recorded, so I may yet be able to gain some knowledge and learning.  I offer these comments as constructive criticism, and hope they and similar feedback will prompt the IRC to revisit its processes and methods and ensure a better organization and presentation at the remaining public hearings.

Regards,

Dal Norris
Eloy, AZ

column5: Summary of comments to the Commission on Sunday, July 25th
column6:
Dear Commission Members,

From 2010 through Jan, 2021, I represented LD28 , in the Arizona House and Senate.  LD28 encompasses communities of interest North Central Phoenix, Sunnyslope, Biltmore, Arcadia, Shea Corridor and Paradise Valley The district has many active neighborhood leaders and organizations with whom I worked closely for over 10 years.

Over time, LD28 became a tale of two districts - west and east. The bifurcation between east side and west side related to quality-of-life issues my neighborhood leaders were addressing. For example, on the east side, we battled out of control Short Term Rentals and high-rise, high-density zoning requests. On the west side, we fought crime, blight, homelessness, and poorly regulated drug treatment centers.

THE GEOGRAPHICAL DIVIDING LINES FOR THESE DIFFERENCES ARE I-17 AND 19TH AVENUE. MOVING EAST FROM 19TH AVENUE TOWARDS 7TH AVENUE AND 7TH STREET, THE WEST SIDE DISTRICT PROBLEMS BEGAN TO CHANGE TO THE EAST SIDE PROBLEMS. Examples include a City of Phoenix Task Force, named the Violence Impact Project, which is focused on identifying and solving the problems adjacent to the I-17 including crime, prostitution and drug sales. 19th Avenue, a major thoroughfare, includes the Light Rail up to Dunlap and has imported crime to the adjacent neighborhoods, including drugs and gangs. On the other hand, SR51, as it runs through LD28 is flanked primarily by the Phoenix Preserve and prime residential areas. These neighborhoods are a magnet for short term rental companies, buying up residential properties throughout the area, and the area's prime real estate attracts national and international development attention.

I ask that you take this bifurcation into consideration when redrawing district lines. I Please let me know if you have any questions, I would be pleased to respond. And thank you for your work. Arizona appreciates your service!

Sincerely,

Kate Brophy McGee

I attended the meeting on public comments in Sedona at the Yavapai College campus.  I did make a three minute statement and submitted my text to the commentator. 1. Sedona and the Village of Oak Creek (VOC) lie in both Coconino and Yavapai county.  However the MAJORITY of our residents are in Yavapai and therefore the majority of our property tax dollars goes to Prescott, not Coconino. 
  
2. We have huge infrastructure issues in the Verde Valley, all our small towns are working together on this serious issue along with Yavapai County and our County Commissioners.  Flagstaff and Coconino are not involved what happens in the VV.
  
3. Our Yavapai Community College campus is always getting the short end of the funding for our Sedona campus by Prescott, therefore we work with Prescott to fix this,  Flagstaff is not involved. 
 
4. There is a MAJOR fiber optic line that is coming up I17 to specifically provide internet infrastructure to the VERDE VALLEY, not Flagstaff. This is through a multi-million grant from the feds. Flagstaff is NOT involved.

5. Our airport which is part of the national infrastructure is owned and controlled by Prescott, and has ZERO to do with Coconino OR Flagstaff.

6. Our jails are on Highway 260 in Camp Verde and in Prescott,  NOT Coconino or Flagstaff.

7. Our COURTS, superior and others are located on Highway 260 in Camp Verde and in Prescott,  not Flagstaff or Coconino. 

8. Our law enforcement is YAVAPAI County Sheriff, with offices in the Village of Oak Creek, not Coconino or Flagstaff. 

9. Our regional development in housing and transportation is between the rural Verde Valley towns like Camp Verde, Cottonwood, Cornville etc. Yavapai County and Prescott, not Coconino or Flagstaff are partners in these issues.

10. Our water use and planning,  which I learned a lot more about yesterday flying 8 members of the Friends of the Verde River conservation group,  including several of our Vineyard owners, has NOTHING to do with Flagstaff OR Coconino County.
 
11. The cultural and music programs at the Yavapai College auditorium in Prescott are not available in Flagstaff unless you like college kids Rock  concerts.  

12. Over half of the service companies I use, appliance repair, DISH Network, deck sealing, gate repair etc originate in Prescott, OR in Sedona. NOT in Flagstaff or Coconino.

13. The Sedona Fire District covers areas outside of Sedona, including the Village of Oak Creek and part of the forest area between Sedona and Cottonwood, not Flagstaff.

These 13 points and more show that rural Arizona should stay RURAL Arizona and not be associated with a city that has no ties or relationship with anything going on in the Verde Valley.  With all due respect to the city of Flagstaff, and we do use Northern Arizona Healthcare there, AND their Cottonwood Campus, they are not rural and they do not participate in much of anything that happens in Sedona, Village of Oak Creek or the Verde Valley as a whole.

When I attended and participated in the listening session in Sedona on July 27th I didn't hear any of this. We should have political representation where our money goes and with the partners we use for infrastructure and future development, not a disinterested major city and Country that we barley interface with.

The  Commission has a very difficult responsibility and your work is appreciated.  Please take these very important points into consideration when you start drawing your maps. 

Thank you,
Michael and Christine Schroeder
100 N Primrose Pt
Sedona AZ 86336

column5: Redistricting of Southern Navajo County and communities of interest
column6:
Hello, 
My name is Cari Lindquist. I am currently part of district 7 and reside in Lakeside, Arizona. Today I urge you to put southern Navajo County back with our neighbors and other communities of interest.

The current districts are confusing and in no way competitive for or representative of the residents in rural Eastern Arizona. The current districting cuts through City limits and County lines. We are in the same town, the same schools, the same churches, the same everything… except districts. In this case, we are not just communities of interest, we are ONE community separated.

In prior elections, district 7 has overwhelmingly been represented by one political party. This is not competitive or representative of the diverse population we have. Those candidates do not speak for or care about the issue important to Eastern Arizona because we do not share the same interests or resources. They are focused on what is best for Northern Arizona. 

We are asking for the same consideration and representation for the issues unique to our communities. Allow Eastern Arizona to be a competitive district again. Allow Eastern Arizona to have a Representative that will speak for our people and our interests again. In 2010, 15 Cities and Towns within Eastern Arizona unanimously adopted a resolution to keep us united (Town of Pinetop-Lakeside Resolution No. 11-1204). These towns included the City of Globe, Town of Miami, Town of Superior, Town of Winkelman, Town of Duncan, Town of Hayden, City of Show Low, Town of Eagar, Town of Springerville, Town of Pinetop-Lakeside, City of Winslow, Town of Snowflake, Town of Camp Verde, City of St. Johns and Town of Pima. We are one united voice asking to be one district.  Those in charge of redistricting ignored the resolution last time, going against what was best for our communities. Please, do not ignore us again. 

Finally, we are communities of interest. Our communities have strong ties to one another, many common interests, and a history of being one Legislative District. These communities are focused on natural resources, including the mining of copper and minerals, ranching, farming, and timber. We are a tourism and recreational hotspot for hiking, camping, skiing, fishing, hunting, and more. Because we consist of large amounts of National Forest and limited private land our issues of education, water, power, and federal land management are unique and require representation focused on our needs. 

Please reunite the rural 5+ Eastern Counites (Southern Navajo, Southern Apache, Gila, Graham, and Greenlee. Give us a voice that focuses on our interests.

Thank you.

column5: Redistricting Southern Tier of Western NY
column6:
Dear New York State IRC:
The Southern Tier is a distinct community of interest that is different from Buffalo, Rochester and Syracuse, with much different issues and concerns.

The counties along the Southern Tier are connected by the I-86 corridor and have their own regional economy and way of life. The I-86 corridor also impacts the Southern Tier in a manner which is also unique. This corridor is the preferred route of travel in an easterly and westerly direction between major commerce centers such as New York City and Chicago and points west. As such, this commerce impacts the Souther Tier in many ways such as interstate commerce, law enforcement issues and tourism. We need proper representation in local, State and Federal government to assure that these issues in our jurisdiction are properly addressed. 

From the special challenges facing rural healthcare providers and school districts to a lack of broadband access and the financial challenges facing our small cities, the Southern Tier needs its own voice in Washington to ensure we are heard.

Historically, the differences between the Southern Tier and both Western and Central New York have been reflected in the drawing of congressional and state legislative district boundaries.

That’s helped ensure that government in Washington and Albany pays attention to our area and is focused on the unique challenges we currently face in our area. 

Unlike Central and Western New York, Southern Tier counties share a common border with Pennsylvania. When dealing with interstate issues, it’s criticality important that our region has its own representative in Congress. We are a unique geographical and geopolitical entity within New York State because of our agricultural influences upon the State of New York as a whole. 

Unlike the regions centered around the larger metropolitan areas of Buffalo, Syracuse and Rochester, the structure of our economy and the delivery of social and community services is drastically different in a rural area like the Southern Tier of Western NY State. As a result, the role of state and federal government and the way it engages the people who live here is different.  The same approach and solutions that work in other parts of Upstate are ill suited to the Southern Tier.

For generations, the Southern Tier has had a dedicated member of Congress, even as the state has lost congressional districts to other states.  It’s critically important that the Southern Tier continues to have a seat in the House of Representatives.

New York’s Independent Redistricting Commission was designed to take politics out of the redistricting process and ensure that each region of the state was treated fairly.  The Southern Tier is unquestionably a community of interest and I ask the commission to ensure the Southern Tier keeps its voice in the House of Representatives.
Respectfully submitted,

column5: Fair Maps Arizona - problematic org pushing public testimony
column6:
I am concerned about the organization Fair Maps Arizona and the information on their website titled “How to Write Effective Testimony”.  It gives explicit talking points (which contain some misinformation) and instructs supporters to email their comments to the Fair Maps State Director, who will then “finish them up.” This seems counter to the purpose of public testimony.  The founder and president of this organization is Steve Gaynor, a current Republican candidate for Governor, and vocal supporter of the AZ Senates problematic “audit” of the 2020 election in Maricopa County. He clearly has a partisan purpose in providing these instructions.  Some of the Fair Maps recommended talking points include:

“Explain that the previous commission was too focused on competitiveness. When districts are too competitive, nearly half of the population is bound to feel unrepresented.”

And 

“Inform the commission that the previous maps that were drawn did not have equal population. Some districts had 12% more population than others.”

The “12%” statistic is false. In 2011, the difference between the lowest populated district and the highest was less than 9%. More importantly, these population variations were challenged in court, and ultimately upheld by the US Supreme Court in a rare unanimous decision. 

Here is the full text from the Fair Maps Arizona website https://fairmapsarizona.org/how-to-write-effective-testimony/, as it appeared on 8/1/2021:
How to Write Effective Testimony
by Fair Maps Arizona in News. Posted July 13, 2021
The Arizona State Constitution requires the Independent Redistricting Commission to “respect communities of interest” when they draw congressional and legislative district boundaries. To learn about potential communities of interest, the Commission has announced that they will conduct a round of Public Hearings. Click here for the schedule.

The commission will be listening to public testimony at these hearings. Individuals will be limited to three minutes. We recommend preparing your testimony in advance, and reading it to the commission at the hearing in your area.

When writing your testimony focus on these points:

Introduction
Tell the commission who you are, where you live, where you work, where your children go to school, where you spend your free time, etc.
Body
Inform the commission of your communities of interest. Examples include your local school district, your zip code, your children’s sports teams, your local church, where you work, and where you live. Your neighborhood, your area, and your town are all communities of interest and they should remain whole.
Tell the commission to follow the constitution. Stress the importance of adhering to all six of the criteria laid out in the Constitution.
Explain that the previous commission was too focused on competitiveness. When districts are too competitive, nearly half of the population is bound to feel unrepresented.
If there was a problem, explain what went wrong 10 years ago with your current legislative and congressional district.
Inform the commission that the previous maps that were drawn did not have equal population. Some districts had 12% more population than others.
Districts should be compact to accurately represent communities of interest who live and work together.
Conclusion
Convincing the commission you belong to a community of interest is the goal of your testimony.
Combine arguments about the other points with arguments about communities of interest.
The commission has specifically called these hearings on communities of interest. That is what they are most interested in hearing about.
Try to write no more than 300 words. You will be limited to three minutes and it is important to be to the point. Once you have a draft, send it to our Statewide Director Jay Wilson at jay@fairmapsarizona.org and he will help you finish it up. If you need more help writing your draft, review the below example of community of interest testimony:

Hello, my name is [insert your name here], I live in Cochise County, and I am here today to give you information about my communities of interest.

My community works in agriculture, tourism, mining and small businesses across the southern border. Many people work at government border agencies and others in produce and shipping at ports with Mexico. We are a proud lower income community that supports each other through family, churches and other local resources. We have a mining industry in Patagonia which is partnered with local Provisional colleges to train mining jobs.

My community gathers in Nogales, and socializes at churches and schools in that community. We also gather with others in churches and schools in Sonoita. We shop in Nogales and Sierra Vista and access healthcare at clinics and hospitals in those towns. Our food banks are also in those towns. We are rural and use mainly our own transportation to get around. There are many lakes at which we recreate: Parker lake, Patagonia lake and Pena Blanca lake, and we have our county fair in Sonoita. We travel to Mexico frequently.

Last time around my community was split into two different legislative districts. Santa Cruz and Cochise County were split when they should not have been. The districts the previous commission drew were not compact, did not have equal population, and were too focused on competitiveness. I do not want that to happen to us again. Please follow the Arizona Constitution when you are drawing districts this time.

Please do not include us in a legislative district with Tucson. My Hispanic community needs to be with other rural border communities. My rural border town has concerns about border security same as Cochise county. We need strong rural law enforcement. We do not share religious and cultural characteristics with “Latinos” in Tucson. We need to be able to develop plans with other border towns with our same job training and employment issues, utilizing our community colleges and small businesses.

column5: Where to start the Grid Map
column6:
As an Arizonan who lives in Yuma, I'm flattered by Commissioner York's proposal to start the drawing of the Grid Map here in Yuma (although I would point out that Yuma is not really in the farthest southwest corner of the state and also that water and immigration are just two of the significant issues facing us today - although you have heard many others that communities around the state are sharing with you during your public hearings in the past weeks.)

One of the disadvantages of starting the process at a corner (or side) of the state is that such a method results in more erratic results the as you move farther from the chosen starting point.  And it's a long, long, way from any corner of this state to the opposite corner.

But there may be another approach that will work as well.

Proposal:  Once the census data is available, it will be possible to determine the exact center of population in the state.  Start in the township or census block that is there.

Of course, you'll still have the same additional choices to make that you would have with whatever starting point you decide on.  How you move around the map to assemble the districts after choosing the starting point will have to be decided.

Starting somewhere in the middle of the state would have the added benefit of being less erratic the farther you get from the starting point than if you start in one of the corners or sides of the state.

Just a suggestion,


William Bowlus-Root
A concerned citizen
