column5: My testimony before the IRC at the Public Hearing in Yuma 8/4/21
column6:
For the record, here is the text of the Public Hearing testimony I delivered at Yuma this evening:
---------------------

My name is William Bowlus-Root.  I’m a retired software engineer in Yuma, 85365, CD4 and LD13.

Chair Neuberg and Commissioners, thank you for the opportunity to present my views to the Commission tonight.  It’s a pleasure to finally see you in person!  I greatly appreciate the personal sacrifices each of you has made to help us with this consequential civic work.  We all need to help you do that work conscientiously, so you can draw maps that result in fair and good representation and promote good governance.

And so my comments tonight are intended in the spirit of constructive criticism – a reminder that I hope will help you do your work well.

I’m here tonight as a concerned citizen and an Independent, like roughly a third of Arizonans (about the same as for each of the major political parties).  We cast our ballots based not on a candidate’s political party, but if the person has a good grasp of the challenges facing our communities as well as their connection to the people who struggle every day to live, work, and play in them.  We ask how a candidate will tap into the rich set of talents and skills and ideas that Arizonans have for solving those challenges, for making life better for us – ALL of us, not just Democrats or Republicans, but ALL Arizonans.

But we can’t make those kinds of evaluations between candidates if the best candidates each party has to offer are not on the ballot.

At the end of the last century, Arizonans became sick of the political parties vying for power rather than effectively governing.  We became apathetic about voting, and candidates with new ideas were reluctant to enter a race that was stacked against them from the start.

And, as our Framers fully anticipated in The Federalist Papers, The People took the steps necessary to take back the power they had entrusted to their representatives.  They passed Proposition 106.

It pays to remember what those voters read at the top of their ballots that day:

“…RELATING TO ENDING THE PRACTICE OF GERRYMANDERING AND IMPROVING VOTER AND CANDIDATE PARTICIPATION IN ELECTIONS BY CREATING AN INDEPENDENT COMMISSION OF BALANCED APPOINTMENTS TO OVERSEE THE MAPPING OF FAIR AND COMPETITIVE CONGRESSIONAL AND LEGISLATIVE DISTRICTS.”

Fair and competitive districts – districts that are responsive to the voters, to the will of The People.  That’s the vison the voters had and that you’re tasked with making a reality.

To do your duty, it’s necessary for each of you to set aside your political bias and work together, not as competitors but as collaborators to draw districts that are fair and competitive.  Doing so will bring out the best in both of the major parties, encourage new candidates with fresh ideas to come forward, and give ALL Arizonans meaningful choices at the polls.

Once again, I thank you for your time and efforts on behalf of ALL The People of Arizona.  I hope my comments will serve to assist you in your mission to make that vision a reality.

column5: A Side-Benefit of the Listening Tour Sessions
column6:
Thank you for conducting your Public Hearing in Yuma this evening.  I felt it was a successful meeting.  Of course it's a good opportunity for the public to get to know the members of the commission and to familiarize them with the process you're going through to arrive at the new district maps.

But thinking a bit more about it, there's another benefit that you may not have been aware.

As a participant, I learned a great deal about the wide range of perceptions my neighbors have of the efficacy of the current boundaries - what they find beneficial and/or dysfunctional about them as they relate to the ability of their representatives to effect good governance or not.  I heard more satisfaction with the situation than I expected and was encouraged that members of my own community had thoughtful and potentially useful ideas for how to make small, or occasionally large, improvements.  Granted we were seeing a somewhat select and probably not very representative cross-section of residents (it was pointed out to me that it was virtually impossible for most workers who live in San Luis to have knocked off work at 3:00 in order to have made it in time for the 5:00pm start), but even among the group that was in the room there were similar sentiments.

I was also struck but the number of people who were surprised to have to admit that having Yuma split into three legislative districts had turned out to be favorable to the region because we have more representatives working to resolve our resource and funding issues.  But then to have many of those very same people contradict their own argument and advocate for the creation of a single 'river counties' or full-western-AZ district that would have just one Congressman to represent us instead of the three that (should be) working in our combined interests under the current situation.  It was surprising to see that people seemed to be taking up talking points they'd received instead of applying the same logic to both situations.

In any case, the additional benefit I mention in the subject line refers to the fact that the participants are provided a unique window on the thinking of their neighbors, something they may have been unaware of before, and hopefully one that will provide avenues of civic collaboration for the future.

Thanks again for stopping in Yuma,


William Bowlus-Root
A concerned citizen

As a bi- or non-partisan Commission, each of you are mandated to be clear of partisanship as you take comments and move on to developing new congressional and legislative district lines.  As such, and as you deliberate on new maps, you are set to be an exemplary Commission to, and for, all Arizonans, and possibly the entire USA.  In compliance with mandates in the Arizona Constitution, please pay particular attention to the “compactness and contiguousness” pertaining to our specific “communities of interest.”  
The current CDs, 1 and 2, meet these representation criteria in sharing Arizona/Mexico border that includes Cochise, Santa Cruz and Pima Counties. column5: Participation
column6:
While I thank all of you for your service, I want to thank Commissioner Watchman in particular for two things.  First, for being sure that fellow Commissioners, staff and the listening public become more familiar with the history of voting rights and abuses experienced by residents of Arizona's 23 tribal communities.  And second, for requesting that the Executive Director provide all Commissioners and the public with at least monthly budget reports.  Transparency is always important, but especially in our current political environment, where suspicion abounds.   

An example: I am wondering why both Tucson sites are being held in private hotel/resort locations rather than at one of the Pima Community College campuses or other public venues.  If these commercial businesses offered their facilities gratis as a service to the community, we all owe them our thanks and this should be acknowledged publiclv.  If public facilities were unavailable and/or more expensive, that should be acknowledged as well.  But even if the choices were made for sound business reasons,  I urge the Commissioners and staff to be sensitive going forward to the message we may be sending unwittingly, i.e., the locations chosen might be considered by some voters to be an indicator of who is expected to come, whose opinions are being solicited, and/or even worse, who is welcome to come.  Commissioners are guests in these communities, and it is important that the meetings be held where all voters feel comfortable.  

Another example:  Why did we not nail down the locations of the Tucson listening tour stops until just a few days before the events?  One explanation I've heard is to depress the turnout because Tucson is a Democratic stronghold.  I'm not saying this explanation is accurate, but I am saying that in the absence of an explanation for the Commission's decisions, Arizonans will supply their own.  So while I recognize and appreciate that Commissioners have been sensitive to the emotionally charged and partisan environment in which they are doing their work, I request that they go the extra mile necessary to share with the public not only their decisions but the reasons underlying their decisions.  I also request that they direct their staff to do the same. 

And lastly, why was an outreach coordinator not hired months ago--rather than halfway into the current listening tour?  Given how remote and sparsely populated several areas in AZ are and given the long history of discrimination against our tribal communities, we could and should have anticipated that community outreach would be especially important to elicit input from residents of these areas--input that the Commissioners want and need to do their job effectively.  It is clear from participation data reported on 8.3.21 that outreach efforts are sorely needed before the next round of listening tours. 

My goal in sharing my thoughts is not to criticize, but rather to provide information and ideas that may help you in the months ahead. Those of us who have attended your public meetings value and admire your efforts and commitment, and we are grateful.

column5: Community of Interest
column6:
Dear Commissioners,

Thank you for the opportunity to address the Independent Redistricting Commission regarding the initial phase of the mapping process. I would have testified in person, but I am concerned about rising COVID numbers and the number of unmasked hearing participants.

I am a retired attorney who moved to Tucson from NYC about 24 years ago.  I was drawn to Tucson because of its natural beauty, its small-town feel in a large city, and its remarkable diversity. I was impressed by the presence of the University of Arizona and the availability of higher education at the many campuses of Pima Community College. In the midst of incredible wildlife and natural beauty, such as Sabino Canyon and Saguaro National Forest,Tucson offers so many of the amenities of a large city —the Arizona Theater Company, the Fox Theater, the Loft, the Tucson Museum of Art, the Desert Museum.  We are now a UNESCO-designated Capital of Gastronomy— a tribute to our multi-cultural heritage.  We live near luxury resorts and the extraordinary San Javier Del Bac, which is not just an historic site but a functioning church for the people of the Tohono O’odham nation.  Unfortunately, we also have incredible economic disparities; I am fortunate to live in the foothills near Sabino Canyon, but I deliver mobile meals in Picture Rock and have visited people living in mobile homes with card board covered windows and almost no furniture. Numerous community- based organizations such as Primavera, the Community Food Bank, Iskashitaa Refugee Network, and Youth on Their Own provide services to residents in need and define us as a community.

Arizona voters overwhelmingly passed the proposition creating the IRC.  We wanted an end to gerrymandering; we wanted competitive districts that represent the increasingly diverse population of our voters.  Tucson is the second largest city in Arizona.  Tucson is not just for retirees; we have military personnel, academics, employees in the tourism industry, employees of companies like Raytheon,  employees at the forefront of the solar energy development, and many unemployed and underemployed.  We are Latino, Native American, African American, and White.

We currently have two Congressional Districts, which are fairly drawn and competitive; these CDs provide representation to these different constituencies.  I live in LD9, which is also competitive, being nearly equally populated by Republicans, Democrats, and Independents.

Because of its diversity, Tucson and Pima County require, at a minimum, two CDs to provide fair and competitive representation.  LD9 is well drawn and any changes must keep it fair and competitive. We will be closely watching the mapping process and the results to ensure that the IRC fulfills its obligations to us under the Arizona Constitution and the Voting Rights Act.

Thank you,
Suzanne King

column5: Redistricting for CD1 and LD6&7
column6:
August 8, 2021

To: 	Independent Redistricting Commission
	Commission Chair Neuberg and Redistricting Commission Members

My name is Vickie Parks, and I’m a fourth generation Arizonan, and my husband’s heritage goes back to when Arizona was barely a territory.   Our roots run deep.  First, to thank you for this opportunity to express concerns to redraw Arizona Congressional and Legislative districts in suitable maps according to the census as well as following the Federal Voting Rights Act, including especially geographical, communities of interest and potential competiveness and to follow criteria described in the Arizona Constitution.  It does not appear these guidelines were followed ten years ago. 

I am concerned specifically with CD1 and LD6&7.  First, CD1 is too large to manage extending too far south.  Pinal County and Graham County should, in no way, be included in CD1.  Also southern Arizona has completely different communities of interest with border issues, unique water issues as well as even ranching issues differ widely in northern Arizona from southern Arizona. CD1 might be better served to include Yavapai County with the exception of Sedona, since that community really doesn’t have a community of interest with rural Arizona.  Please leave CD1 rural.  This current massive area is unthinkable for a Congressman to cover efficiently and effectively.  

My other concern lies with LD6 and LD7.  I live at the east end of Flagstaff in LD7, which currently attaches to the tribal lands.  Respectfully, the tribal lands have their own councils independent from Flagstaff, Page or Williams for example.  While we enjoy and respect the culture and traditions of our tribal neighbors, the community of interests are vastly different between the tribal lands and non-tribal lands They have Federal oversight and answer to the Bureau of Indian Affairs. As it is, LD7 is unconscionably too large for any legislator to represent effectively or efficiently.  If population does not prove large enough for the tribal lands, could I suggest communities of interest and geographical considerations are given serious attention.   Flagstaff is a hub for northern Arizona and surrounding small towns, which fall into communities of interest and to keep Arizona rural.  LD7 is, in some areas, recklessly drawn.  To divide neighborhoods from one side of the street in LD6 and the other side of the street in LD7 seem unconscionable.  Having been in LD7 for the past ten years, experience has proven lack of response from LD7 legislators on issues and can assume this is due to the extreme difference in communities of interest.  

Thank you for consideration to work on such an important task that has existed for the past ten years and for your time.  As noted in the Arizona Constitution, districts should be compact to accurately represent communities of interest who live and work together.  This was clearly not followed ten years ago.  I would like to say that Rural Arizonans want to stay RURAL and also be able to have a Voice.  I appreciate your hard work and time to create the best map for all Arizonans for the next ten years.

Highest Regards,

Vickie Parks
11160 Townsend Winona Road
Flagstaff, AZ  86004

column5: community  of interest meeting 8/8/21 Tucson
column6:
Madam Chairwoman and Commissioners:
   I am an 85 year old retired California civil servant and mostly retired Episcopal priest, resident in Tucson (85749; LD10; CD2).
   I appeared before you at your 2nd Tucson meeting in order to state that my community of interest is the people of the State of Arizona, specifically any and all who, when pricked with a needle, bleed.  As I sat and listened to public comments yesterday it became clear that they fell generally into two categories in roughly equal numbers.  Some described their communities of interest and asked for districts that mirrored those communities.  Those in this category who found themselves in an electoral minority were most insistent on the need to change this situation.  Others said little or nothing of communities of interest and focussed their comments on a desire for competitive districts.  Taking both positions seriously, you have a problem or two.  First, for everyone who sought a district that mirrors their community of interest to be satisfied would require closer to 300 LDs than 30.  Second, convinced as I am that your predecessor IRC did its best in 2011 to give us competitive districts, it's a nearly impossible undertaking.
   I don't know exactly how many  current LDs can objectively be considered copeititve, but a majority are not.  I consider LDs 2, 9 and 10 competitive because they have elected to theHouse members of both major parties.   I've been active in campaigns in LD30 from 2004 to 2010 and LD10 to the present.  Without fear of contradiction I'll say that no Republican could conceivably lose a legislative race in LD30.  And the results in LD10, mostly Democratic wins, have been relatively close when the candidates have been well qualified.  And I'll say the same for LDs 2 with a modicum of confidence and 9 with great confidence.
   CDs fall into 3 categories: 3 are competitive (1,2, 9); 2 are safe Democratic due to the minority majority requirement (3 & 7). Of the competitive ones, 2 has elected women and men from both parties; 1 & 9 have been Democratic through the decade.  I think will every difficult to improve on the 2011 work.  However, if the minority majority requirement were eliminated and the Commission committed to seek first to create competitive districts, we might be able to improve on 2011.
   In retrospect it seems to me unfortunate that Proposition 106 was worded in a way that makes competitiveness depend on satisfaction of other requirements.  The success of democratic government and indeed of any element of a complex society depends on people working together even in spite of all their very real differences.  Lack of competitiveness encourages folks on the fringes to seek office and to legislate with no concern for opposing views.  
   I have no idea of how I may be of service to the commission and its daunting task beyond sharing my opinions and insights, and keeping you in my prayers.
   Thank you all for undertaking this work.

I applaud the previous work of the IRC and I recognize that perfection is unattainable. My voting experience indicates that the current IRC can improve on it's past efforts.

I have been unable to post public comments for the August 9, 2021 Independent Redistricting Commision public hearing. Please accept the following comments due the barrier to post comments.
 
ACCESSIBILITY + COMMUNITY OUTREACH

●	Extend the deadline for the community of interest survey. The Commission shouldn’t cap the deadline for COI survey when Census data won’t be coming in until a couple of days after. The more opportunities the Commission can provide for public input, the better.

●	Several hearing locations were cancelled or scheduled at the last minute. This makes it harder for community members to plan to attend and make arrangements.

●	There have been inconsistencies with the hearing agenda and COI survey being available in Spanish or other languages at public hearings.

●	There hasn’t been considerable community outreach to ensure wider attendance at the public hearings.
●	The Commission still has no Community Outreach Coordinator dedicated to this work.
●	There was no press in Spanish-language media outlets announcing the hearings.
●	The hearings were only announced via media alerts and on the IRC website. There didn’t seem to be attempts to increase public engagement by alerting other community organizations or community outlets.

DISTRICTS

●	Arizona’s Constitution requires the Independent Redistricting Commission to comply with the Voting Rights Act.
●	The Commission needs to, at minimum, maintain or expand the number of districts where communities of color have the ability to elect the candidate of their own choosing.
●	That right for communities of color to elect a member of their own choosing is protected in the Voting Rights Act, and the Commission must uphold those protections in the maps that they draft for the next ten years of Arizona's electoral representation. That voting strength should not be diluted.

●	Uphold 2 Arizona Congressional districts with primarily non-white, Latino populations:
●	One in Tucson, encompassing Southern AZ, the western part of the US/Mex border, and Latino communities in Yuma.
●	One in the Phoenix metro area that runs through the West Valley that is primarily Latino. It should run from southern Glendale, through the West Valley, and down to Avondale and Tolleson.

●	For Legislative Districts:
○	PHOENIX METRO: The Phoenix metro area has a large Latino population, particularly in the West Valley, that have the right to choose who represents them in the legislature. Protect 4 “minority-majority” districts in the Phoenix metro area. These are represented by the current Legislative Districts 19, 27, 29, 30.
○	SOUTHERN AZ: There is a large Latino population in border communities and across Southern AZ, and they also have rights to choose who represents them in the legislature. Protect 3 “minority-majority” districts in Southern Arizona. These are represented by the current Legislative Districts 2, 3 and 4.

The power for the Latino community to elect those leaders means that there are legislators that we can hold accountable to our communities, calling on them to specifically represent regional interests and the interests of our communities at the legislature, where our voices must be heard.

Respectfully submitted by,
John Mireles

column5: Competitiveness
column6:
The IRC agenda for tomorrow's meeting includes the topic of competitiveness. 

The first and most important thing for the IRC to do is to affirm its strong commitment to draw as many competitive districts as practical given the limitations of the Voting Rights Act and geography (the big sort). The measure of competitiveness is less important than a clear direction to the mapping consultant that the goal of competitive districts should not be an after thought. 

As for the measures presented in Mr. Johnson's 39 page powerpoint presentation, it is not at all clear that it is necessary for the IRC to limit itself to one method at this point. The experts were very clear on one point. Even though they might come at the issue from slightly different perspectives, their overall message to the IRC was that this is not complicated and that all of their methods would work to help the IRC evaluate its draft maps. Mr. McGhee even demonstrated Plan Score in real time. Dr. Duchin seemed willing to remain involved and give her team's feedback on draft maps. Dr. Wang brought up a template that his team had created and he offered to share. Here is the question you should ask: Why is there a need to narrow the information that could be provided to the IRC at the draft map stage? If I were a serving commissioner, I would want to see the varied evaluations. The public will also be interested in seeing multiple evaluations of draft maps. As an aside, it would have been useful if Mr. Johnson had posted the letters he received last week from Dr. McGhee and Dr. Wang rather than just cite to them in his powerpoint presentation. These letters should be posted on the IRC website immediately so that the public has access to them before the meeting tomorrow.

Mr. Johnson's powerpoint presentation makes this seem like a difficult if not impossible task. This is the opposite of what the experts were each telling you. He also uses the word "complicated" to describe several of the methods under consideration which is a pejorative that is not useful in comparing methods. You want to have a communications strategy that makes it clear to the public which methods were employed in evaluating the maps; that does not mean that the public needs to be able to perform the mathematics used in the evaluation. It is enough to be able to say to the public that the IRC used several widely respected metrics and then identify the metric(s) employed. 

I understand that there is a need to do data entry for past election results at the census tract level in order to evaluate the maps for competitiveness. Given the recent growth and demographic changes in the state, it makes sense to limit the historic data to two or at most three election cycles. If the IRC goes back any farther, you run the risk of including data that provides a false positive. As far as specific elections are concerned, there seemed to be consensus that the Presidential election Data was quite useful and that several other state wide races such as secretary of state or treasurer could be helpful. There was also a consensus that using the gubernatorial races could skew the data set so those should probably be excluded. 

In sum, the experts were quite clear that evaluating maps for competitiveness is fairly easily achievable using the tools that are readily available to the IRC. From a policy standpoint the critical thing is for the IRC to state publicly that it is committed to drawing competitive maps wherever possible and directing the mapping consultant to ensure that it is considered from the outset.

column5: Competitive Districts
column6:
NOW is a nonprofit 501(c)(4) corporation incorporated and headquartered in Washington, D.C.  and is the largest organization of feminist grassroots activists in the United States. AZ NOW is a unit of the national organization, has been in existence for over fifty years, and has members statewide.

Since its founding in 1966, NOW’s purpose has been to take action through intersectional grassroots activism to promote feminist ideals, lead societal change, eliminate discrimination, and achieve and protect the equal rights of all women and girls in all aspects of social, political, and economic life. AZ NOW uses a variety of strategies, including public education and legislative advocacy, to advance women’s rights and address NOW’s six key issues important to our members and women in general: (1) reproductive rights and justice; (2) economic justice; (3) ending violence against women; (4) racial justice; (5) LGBTQIA+ rights; and (6) constitutional equality. 

The political action work has been focused on election of candidates from local to federal levels that will work to achieve the six key issues.  One of the problems that has surfaced every single election cycle is the lack of competitive districts.  Arizona is very closely divided with nearly equal numbers of independents, Democrats and Republicans.  That should mean that our state electoral districts are competitive so that the voices of all are heard and have an equal opportunity to prevail.  That is not the case.  In fact, very few of the districts are competitive.

This has hampered the representation of those who live there as required by both the national and state constitution. Their voices are silenced and even when a majority of people in the district desire a certain outcome, the elected representatives who know they have a lock on the district, ignore them.

Our members live throughout the state so naturally some live in what are now considered Democratic districts, some live in what are considered Republican districts and some live in the few competitive districts.  Those who live in what are now considered Democratic districts have reported that they are often precinct captains and work very hard to maintain representatives who actually listen and respond to constituent needs.

Those who live in Republican districts have mostly lost their right of representation completely because the current party platform is antagonistic to the six key goals of NOW.  Even when the majority of the people in that district try to be heard, even when they want the elected representative to be held accountable for violating the law, they cannot overcome the financial and numerical advantage structured into the district e.g. LD11.  The last two years, COVID has severally constrained political work with constituents on the ground and will continue to do so as our state refuses to respond adequately and scientifically to the virus. We can expect another campaign season where people who care about public health and their neighbors cannot go door to door to campaign. 

Independents don’t have it any better because they don’t get serious competitive debates among candidates, or realistic platforms, or in-depth information on the persons experience or abilities.  So they have limited and one-sided, information on which to make their decisions.  

To maintain uncompetitive districts simply increases the divisions already existing in the country and being fanned into violent flames.  It means that people do not have to speak to each other or hear each other but can continue to live in bubbles of their own creation.  If there was a fair contest, candidates would have to put forth an actual platform with concrete steps so people can evaluate them, not rely on empty slogans and emotional memes.  They would have to list their actual credentials and past deeds showing they have the knowledge and ability to make good decisions and to take appropriate action.  They would have to meet with the constituents, listen to their concerns and address them.  They would have to compromise – the glue missing from our political posturing today.

So while we do have to ensure that communities of interest are allowed to elect someone that represents them we also have to ensure that all constituents in our closely divided state have an equal voice.

My name is Priscilla and I live in Teec Nos Pos, AZ 86514, a good development potential along a major tourist highway, and a Census-designated place in Apache County.
My community is in the northeast state of Arizona that is pronounced T’iis Názbąs in Diné bizaad (Navajo language) and translates as “cottonwoods in a circle.”
I live 3.75 hours from St. Johns, AZ, two hours from Window Rock, AZ, 90 miles from Chinle, AZ, and 1.25 hours (77 miles) from Kayenta, AZ.
We have one store in Teec Nos Pos that supplies our community with general supplies and local people shop for basic daily needs. The trading post sell rugs, turquoise jewelry, and livestock supplies.
T’iis Názbąs has some gorgeous hiking trails with an astonishing waterfall, “Twin Falls” and Tsé ́Da’shii’jaai (Three Monkeys Mesa). Tourists can stop at the Four Corners Tribal Park to take a picture in all four states in one snapshot. Within an hour, visitors can be in Monument Valley and another hour they can be in Grand Canyon.

Teec Nos Pos is a rural community that needs a larger post office and rural addressing for all the residents. The United States Postal Service is our lifeline to many essential needs. We need more clean water, better internet services, a radio broadcasting service, a waste management system or transfer stations, recycling centers, a library, more playgrounds, improved classrooms for our students, laundromats, a recreational sports center with baseball field/ basketball court, and a healthy restaurant with a coffee bar. The local tribal university campus is an extension center/ instructional site of Navajo Technical University that can provide additional innovative higher educational opportunities from Red Mesa High School dual credit students and graduates. NTU is affordable and local for students interested in computers, healthcare profession, carpentry, Navajo/ Diné studies, teaching, and more disciplines. We need more general public education and most importantly communications in our languages.

Our cultural bonds in our community consists of internationally renowned artisans, spiritual leaders from all faiths, Navajo/ Diné hataali (medicinal healers & chanters), and livestock owners. We all share the beauty of living around the Carizzo Mountain and the San Juan River. We love our land and all our environment.

T’iis Názbąs has a strong history where our elders shared food and coffee together, not just for the tourists. They worked together with community leaders who advocated for education. They were able to have a Bureau Indian Affairs/ Educational facilities built in the community. The BIA and Red Mesa school districts put up dormitories, a cafeteria, a gymnasium, and housing units (apartments & homes) for staff, faculty, and administrators for Teec Nos Pos and Red Mesa. Despite the circumstances of being in an isolated Arizona location, our families have persevered and maintained residencies in Arizona. I worry about the Census data in our communities because we might have been undercounted during 2020, the pandemic/ COVID crisis. We have to deal with many boundaries and do not add another line to our Navajo Nation in Apache County. I want fair representation and fair mapping.

column5: Confusing motion about where to start the grid map
column6:
At your meeting on Tuesday, 08/10/21, you had a discussion about where to start drawing the grid map (as well as whether to go clockwise or counter-clockwise from that point).  However, if you'll review the meeting video of that segment (starting at ~58:00 into the meeting), you discover that there is considerable confusion about the exact wording of the motion that you voted on.  It's not clear whether you voted to start in the median (or, as the Chair calls it, the 'township medium') of the township in the geographic center of the state or the township in the population center of the state.  After everyone apparently agreeing that they wanted it in the population center of the state, the Chair re-stated the motion as being in the geographic center of the state.  What was the real motion and was that what the commissioners really agreed they were voting on or not?  (I wonder what the minutes show was passed.)

Much of this sort of confusion could be avoided if the conduct of the meetings were to follow normal (and good) practices for taking up a topic.  That means stating a motion and requiring a second BEFORE debate begins on it.  If, during the debate, there are proposed modifications to the original motion (as there almost inevitably are), they can be debated and/or the person making the original motion can simply accept them.  However, there should ALWAYS be a written record of the exact motion (however altered) that is before the group at any given time.  Furthermore, it should ALWAYS be read verbatim when debate ends.  If there is further debate or clarification needed, that should be undertaken and when finished the full motion should be read again and a vote IMMEDIATELY taken.  That way, there are no questions about exactly what the commissioners are voting on and that it covers everything that's expected to be in it (and that nothing is in it that was thought to be out of it).  That's just good Roberts Rules.

It will be interesting to find out which interpretation NDC implements and also whether that maps (pun intended) to what the commissioners thought they were going to see.

William Bowlus-Root
A concerned citizen

column5: IRC Process going forward
column6:
Thank you for being accessible to voters wishing to share their views about redistricting. I consider myself a Tucsonan, although I live north of the city limits and adjacent to the Catalina Foothills. I attended both Tucson sessions via Zoom.  On Saturday, several speakers who reside in exurban communities like Oro Valley and Marana spoke passionately that they wanted to be in districts with “like-minded” voters.  Addressing their communities of interest, they described what they valued about their geographical areas --good schools, safe neighborhoods, access to quality health care, air and water, recreational venues, and more. Interestingly, these are things Tucsonans value as well, though the similarities were overlooked by the folks from Oro Valley and Marana. Their common theme was “We don’t want to be in the same district as them because we have absolutely nothing in common.”  Their focus was not on what unites us.  They seemed to want to build silos, not bridges. 

So let’s state the obvious here. Tucson is more diverse, racially, ethnically, and economically.  Tucson has its share of wealthy people, but it has a larger percentage of poorer folks as well.  Residents of both geographical areas want safe neighborhoods, but crime rates are higher in poorer areas where residents have a harder time meeting their basic needs. The desire of folks from affluent areas to preserve what they have is understandable and should be respected.  Less privileged citizens should be understood and respected as well, but many need more than that. They need government assistance to promote their general welfare, something guaranteed under the Constitution.  I continue to believe the majority of Arizonans support that.  And I suspect that when citizens from different socioeconomic backgrounds sit down together to discuss the problems faced by poor folks (whether that be in urban, rural or tribal areas), they can find solutions that benefit everyone.   For example, they might reach consensus that all Arizonans would be better off if a larger share of the AZ corrections budget (reportedly $1.3 billion last year) was spent in local communities on diversion and drug treatment programs and on reducing the caseloads of probation officers so they could provide more support to help their clients stay out of prison. 

Here’s one more example. All Arizona residents want good schools, but schools in poorer areas are not as well funded as those in affluent areas because poorer communities lack the means to supplement State school funding with local tax dollars. As a result, children with the greatest needs have the fewest resources.  In most states, lawmakers acknowledge this and allocate additional funding for low-income students.  Arizona does not.  Arizona also has trouble attracting and retaining good teachers because our teacher salaries are not competitive. The governor talks often about the progress we have made in this area, but the fact is that recent hikes in teacher salaries have barely moved the needle.  Studies document that Arizona now ranks 48th rather than 49th place among the 50 states.  

The most troubling thing to say about Arizona education funding is that the disparities are by design, planned and enacted on a party line vote by our Arizona Legislature. The most encouraging thing to say about Arizona’s current education policies is that they are not endorsed by the majority of Arizona voters.  The majority know good schools benefit all of us, producing employable graduates who pay taxes, raise families, and stay out of trouble.  The majority know good schools and a reliable workforce grow the economy by attracting new businesses to Arizona.  

The most promising thing to say regarding educational inequities in Arizona is that the majority of voters were so fed up with the Legislature’s failure to draft and pass educational reform that they took matters into their own hands.  They drafted their own bill, Prop 208, that addressed the problems and passed the measure on a bipartisan basis in 2020. This is reminiscent, of course, of Prop 106, the citizen’s ballot initiative that created the Independent Redistricting Commission in 2000.  The success of both initiatives demonstrates the majority of Arizonans want fairness and can and will work together to pass legislation that benefits all of us. 

The success of these citizen initiatives also begs the question: Why was the Arizona Legislature not responsive to this voting majority?  One possible answer is that our legislators are not hearing the voices of enough Arizonans when they visit their districts.  The task before us is to be sure they hear our voices going forward so we don’t have to do their work for them.  

A key takeaway from the success of Propositions 106 and 208 is that the collaboration necessary to pass legislation that benefits all Arizonans does not occur in silos inhabited only by “like-minded” folks.  It happens when people with different ideas and perspectives meet, when their paths cross, when they must explain and justify their positions to each other. One way to make paths cross is to create voting districts that have somewhat equal representation.  (Arizonans who want to see this kind of collaboration at work need only watch public meetings of the Arizona Independent Redistricting Commission.)  An added benefit of drawing more inclusive voting districts is that potential candidates (and eventual winners) will be more aware of and accountable to their constituents’ diverse views.  

In closing, let me address the concern partisans from both political parties are likely to raise, i.e., competitive districts will cause party control to flip more often.  This might well happen,  but if and when it does, it is likely to be because voters considered many ideas and many candidates and the best prevailed.  I believe good solutions should always take priority over party control.  Arizona is fairly evenly divided among Republicans, Democrats, and Independents.  It is time we unite to support good ideas.

Since the goal is Fair and Competitive districts, we need to make sure that the map does not lose track of Competitiveness.  Some wish to minimize this criteria but it goes to the heart of Prop 106.  As you balance the Voting Rights Act, communities of interest, and compactness - please remember to make Arizona a fair and competitive state that can be a roll model for others.

Maybe it is not a "Sufficient Detriment" to the other criteria when a district contributes to the state's overall competitiveness.  BALANCE.
Thank you for your sincere care with this project.

And as Americans, we are bound by the same Constitution, which requires us to promote not only liberty, but justice, peace, prosperity and the general welfare as well.  

Promoting the general welfare is expensive.  The cost must be shared by all, but it cannot be shared equally because Americans do not have equal economic resources. The gap between the rich and the poor has been growing steadily for more than fifty years, and it is most pronounced in cities. Tucson is no different.  It has its share of wealthy people, but it has a far larger percentage of poor folks, many of whom are unable to provide for their basic needs. Such poverty leads to a host of social problems--substandard housing, food insecurity, poor schools, inadequate social services and infrastructure, as well crime, depression and other psychological problems, and substance abuse.  I believe the majority of Arizonans understand these linkages.  I believe citizens of good will from different socioeconomic backgrounds can sit down together to discuss the problems faced by poor folks in urban, rural and tribal areas and find solutions that benefit everyone.   Two detailed examples are provided below.  The details matter because this is no time for unfunded mandates.

Criminal Justice Reform:  All Arizonans are concerned about safety.  A strong case can be made that all Arizonans would be safer if a larger share of the AZ corrections budget (reportedly $1.3 billion last year) was spent in local communities on education, diversion and drug treatment programs, and hiring more probation officers to reduce caseloads, thereby providing more support to help clients avoid violations that send them back to prison. Research indicates that such innovations could be funded without budget increases (and possibly budget savings) by reducing the prison population using strategies such as shortening mandatory minimum sentences and allowing deserving inmates to apply for probation before serving 85% of their terms.    

Education:  All Arizona residents want good schools, but schools in poorer areas are not as well funded as those in affluent areas because poorer communities lack the means to supplement State school funding with local tax dollars. As a result, children with the greatest needs have the fewest resources.  In most states, lawmakers acknowledge this and allocate additional funding for low-income students.  Arizona does not.  Arizona also has trouble attracting and retaining good teachers because our teacher salaries are not competitive. The governor talks often about the progress we have made in this area, but the fact is that recent hikes in teacher salaries have barely moved the needle.  Studies document that Arizona now ranks 48th rather than 49th place among the 50 states.  

The most troubling thing to say about Arizona education funding is that the disparities are by design, planned and enacted on a party line vote by our Arizona Legislature. The most encouraging thing to say about these inequities in education is that they are not endorsed by the majority of Arizona voters.  The majority know good schools benefit all of us by producing employable graduates who pay taxes, raise families, and stay out of trouble.  The majority know good schools and a reliable workforce grow the economy by attracting new businesses to Arizona.  

The most hopeful thing to say regarding educational inequities in Arizona is that the majority of voters were so fed up with the Legislature’s failure to draft and pass educational reform that they took matters into their own hands.  They drafted their own bill, Prop 208, that addressed the problems and passed the measure on a bipartisan basis in 2020. This is reminiscent, of course, of Prop 106, the citizen’s ballot initiative that created the Independent Redistricting Commission in 2000.  The success of both initiatives demonstrates the majority of Arizonans want fairness and can and will work together to pass legislation that benefits all of us. 

The success of these citizen initiatives begs the question: Why was the Arizona Legislature not responsive to this voting majority?  Why, in fact, did they attempt to ignore the will of the majority by going to court to overturn parts of Prop 106 and by enacting legislation to offset parts of Prop 208?  One possible answer is that our legislators are not hearing the voices of the majority of Arizonans when they visit their districts.  The task before us is to be sure they hear all our voices going forward so we don’t have to do their work for them.  

Our experiences with Propositions 106 and 208 demonstrate that the collaboration necessary to pass legislation that benefits all Arizonans does not occur in silos inhabited only by “like-minded” folks.  It happens when people with different ideas and perspectives meet, when their paths cross, when they must explain and justify their positions to each other. One way to make paths cross is to create voting districts that have somewhat equal representation.  An added benefit of drawing more competitive (i.e., inclusive voting districts) is that potential candidates will be more aware of where constituents of every political persuasion can agree and find consensus.   (Arizonans who want to see this kind of collaboration at work need only watch public meetings of the Arizona Independent Redistricting Commission.)

This could happen, but when it does, it is likely to be because voters considered many ideas and many candidates and the best prevailed. It is time we unite to support the best ideas.

Importantly, she noted that there really aren't any particular boundaries or communities of interest that she would recommend, because everyone in AZ has water concerns and even differing concerns within regional communities. 
It is interesting that the Arizona Farm Bureau (the agricultural industry lobbyists) were given such a privileged amount of time to present and advocate for their specified communities of interests.

For example, the smaller "legacy" farmers who are seeing their wells dry up from the new large agricultural activities that come in and drill deeper wells (and which AFB represents).

I believe that the commission should consider hearing from other important interests, not just industries. For example, as Sarah Porter mentioned, the environment is an important water user that doesn't have many people speaking for it. The IRC could/should broaden the voices they hear from to include such constituencies. 
I suggest that you reach out to The Nature Conservancy, especially the Malpai Borderlands of southern Arizona. This link will give you an idea of their interests.  I suggest that you ask Bill McDonald to speak to the commission as a representative of this group.

column5: Process Considerations
column6:
Dear Commissioners,

I’ve spent nearly 40 years working to make Arizona a better place, so I wanted to first thank you for your service to the state. Your work on the Independent Redistricting Commission (IRC) will influence policy and impact Arizonans for decades to come. 

Because of that fact, there are a lot of special interests and partisan activists who want to influence the IRC process for their own gain. That’s one of the fundamental reasons the voters created the IRC: to reduce the influence of partisan politics and the possibility of gerrymandering. By passing the ballot measure in 2000, voters agreed that Arizona should use an impartial system to create fair maps, rather than the political games we see in many other states that don’t use independent commissions for redistricting. 

In my role at the Center for the Future of Arizona and as chair of the Arizona Town Hall Board, I work with Arizonans from all walks of life and one thing is clear: for the most part, Arizonans want the same things. We want quality schools for our children, accessible healthcare, sound infrastructure, good jobs, and a sustainable future. Perhaps most importantly, we want civic leaders who will work together to solve the problems facing the state. The decisions you make will have a significant impact on who these future leaders will be.

This is why it’s so important the final maps you adopt reflect the demographics of our state. We are growing more ethnically diverse and will continue to do so moving forward. The maps should mirror this diversity. We are also becoming more politically diverse. The proportions of Republican, Democratic, and Independent voters are almost equally divided at this point. Therefore, the final maps shouldn’t give one Party an inherently greater advantage over another. 

This might be easier said than done, as I know you are going to be pulled in many different directions as the Commission continues its work. You’re going to hear from all kinds of people and groups claiming they know best. Through it all I ask that you focus on serving only one interest: the long-term future of Arizona. 

I love my state and I am thrilled that we have an independent commission in charge of the redistricting process. It reflects the independent spirit of Arizona, and it sets us apart from many other states that are dominated by partisan politics throughout the redistricting process. The work you are doing is of the utmost importance, and I commend each and every one of you for serving on the Independent Redistricting Commission.

column5: Letter from the Arizona Faith Network
column6:
Dear Commissioners,

The Arizona Faith Network is an interfaith organization focused on bringing people of faith together to promote civil dialogue and positive change for the common good. The independent redistricting process represents an opportunity to utilize that same approach in creating fair and representative maps for Arizonans of all walks of life.

Active civic participation is a fundamental goal of our organization. We believe it is a moral obligation for all people, regardless of faith, to actively participate in their communities. But the moral obligation of allowing and opening the doors to that participation often lies within the hands of leaders such as yourselves. The work you are doing on the Independent Redistricting Commission will have an impact on Arizonans for decades to come.

Why do we say decades? Because the legislative and congressional delegations that will be elected as a result of the approved maps will make policy choices that go well beyond the 10-year shelf life of these maps. And those policies will be a direct reflection of the values of the leaders elected to represent their constituents. Therefore it is incumbent on this Commission to create maps that accurately reflect the diverse and shared values of all Arizonans, as opposed to maps that give a particular advantage to one particular Party or ideology.

As recent census data shows, Arizona continues to become more diverse. This is reflected in the composition of our faith-based communities. We are a state of numerous faiths - all of whom should have a fair opportunity to have their voices heard in our state’s political process. As an interfaith leadership organization, we respectfully implore you to remember this in every decision you make. 

Finally, please know that we appreciate and understand the challenges of the job before you because, much like the Commission, we are an organization that is responsible for representing the voices of diverse groups of people. We understand how hard it is to balance out the needs and goals of various interests, and we are proof that it can be achieved. So, if we can be of further assistance or serve as a resource in any way, please don’t hesitate to reach out to us. 

Thank you for your service to the people of Arizona. 

Sincerely,


Reverend Katie Sexton-Wood
Executive Director
Arizona Faith Network

column5: Failure to Respond in a Timely Manner to Public Record Act Requests
column6:
I have submitted several public records requests for a non-commercial purpose to the IRC  dating back to June. To date the IRC has not responded to even one of them. Nor offered me a reason for the lack of a response.  Arizona’s public records law requires the custodian of records to “promptly furnish such copies, printouts or photographs. . .”  Arizona Revised Statutes Section 39-121.01-D-1.  The Arizona Agency Handbook quotes from a 2007 Court of Appeals decision stating that “ ‘[p]rompt .  .  .mean[s] ‘quick to act or to do what is required,’ or ‘done, spoken, etc. at once or without delay.’”  Section 6.5.1 of the handbook. In any litigation relating to a public records request, the Arizona State agency to which a public record has been made must demonstrate to the court that it acted promptly.  
None of my requests seeks a voluminous amount of records and, in any event, the IRC has not been in existence long enough to have produced truckloads of records.  So I am perplexed and disappointed that the IRC, which is supposed to act transparently during its short existence, seems to have ignored its responsibility under the public records law.  I can’t fathom any legitimate reason for this delay.  If the delay relates to an incompatibility between the IRC’s technology and that of outside counsel, the public records law does not establish an exception to the promptness mandate for legal review, which could be done in any event in person at the IRC’s offices. 
Upon submitting duplicate requests in August I received these numbers: 
•	#975 - seeking copies of monthly invoices submitted by Timmons Group; NDC; Ballard Spahr; and Snell and Wilmer  (certain months) 
•	#981 - CSV files for 910 community of interest submissions  
•	#982 - documents (call records, emails, etc.) related to the planning and selection of sites for the Round 1 listening tour
•	#983 - seeking copies of monthly invoices submitted by Timmons Group; NDC; Ballard Spahr; and Snell and Wilmer  (certain months) 
•	#984 - list of all public record act requests received to date (submitted June 21 and again Aug 25) 
•	#985 - transcripts of business meetings (All dates - these could be posted!) 
•	#986 - Expense records for five commisisoners (Certain months) 
•	#988 - seeking calendars of commissioners and executive staff reflecting all meetings with third parties related to the business of redistricting 
•	#990 - seeking communications between Ex. Director Brian Schmitt and staff in the Governor's office regarding budget planning 2021 and beyond. 
I ask that you redress this failure immediately and comply with Arizona law as required by all public agencies.

column5: Input on Community of Interest
column6:
Dear Commission Members,

I voted for Proposition 106 in 2000. Like thousands of Arizonans, I sought to reduce political partisanship and improve our electoral system for the good of all Arizonans. The Arizona Independent Redistricting Commission process has proven to be a positive step from my perspective. 

As you lead the third redistricting process, I know you are thinking about how your work will shape the election of legislators and Congressional members now and policy and political outcomes far beyond 2030. You are certainly considering how the 2021 maps will help or hinder Arizonans’ efforts to serve a state where the electorate is divided roughly into thirds among Republicans, Democrats, and independents. You know well that your work will affect decisions about critical issues from health disparities to water, jobs, education, and much more. This is particularly true at the legislative level, where the actions taken by an individual legislator rarely impact only their district. 

You are certainly considering how your maps soon will touch Arizona’s some 1.6 million youth, 1.3 million seniors, and 4.4 million working-age adults. The nearly 500,000 students in public community colleges and universities must be in your thoughts, as are the quarter of Arizonans in rural areas. 

The U.S.Census has made you acutely aware of Arizona’s growing diversity and the critical part our Latino, African American, Asian American, Native American, and other groups play in our communities and economy now and in the future. You are obviously thinking too about tribal communities in reservation areas and in cities.

You have asked Arizonans to tell you about how they see their communities of interest, and have heard from many groups that are trying to further their own agendas. I submit that the most important community of interest is the entire state. More than 7 million Arizonans, from Window Rock to Somerton, Kingman to Safford—and everywhere in between—together comprise the most important community of interest. I ask you, as you discuss the minutiae of redistricting and your numerous goals and constraints, to keep fairness and ensuring all Arizonans an opportunity to be well represented squarely in front of you. I know you must think about individual districts but you must look at the same time at the state as a whole. Your result should be more than the sum of its parts.

Arizonans took the dramatic step of creating the Arizona Independent Redistricting Commission, in part, to reduce party-serving decisions. Your products need to accurately reflect the breadth and depth of Arizona diversity so that no party ends up with an unfair advantage.

Those elected on your commission’s maps will make long-term decisions. Your legacy should be not just fair maps for the next decade but also a catalyst for wise long-term decisions by elected leaders acting in Arizona’s best interests, regardless of party.

You have one of the most difficult jobs in governance. However, success is both possible and more critical even than 20 years ago. I know you are thinking deeply about doing the best you can for our state.

column5: Avoiding prison gerrymandering during redistricting
column6: Thank you for the opportunity to submit testimony. We at the Prison Policy Initiative have been working to quantify the harm to our democracy caused by the Census Bureau’s practice of counting incarcerated people as residents of the prison location. This practice, known as prison gerrymandering, distorts democracy. To ensure equal representation, we suggest that the Commission take the prison populations in to account and use allowable deviations and try to minimize the impact of the Census Bureau’s prison miscount. In fact, this year, the Census Bureau published data, the P5 table, for the express purpose of making it easier for jurisdictions to adjust for correctional populations. We have also compiled a list of each state facility in Arizona, the corresponding census block number, and the incarcerated population counted there by the Census Bureau. For more information, please see our full comments at https://www.prisonersofthecensus.org/testimony/AZ_testimony_september2021.pdf.

column5: Grid Map Hearings
column6:
I appreciate the fact that the IRC has added 5 public hearings at 14 sites over the next two weeks.  I am confused that the IRC seeks public comments on its grid maps, which do not play a substantive role in the overall effort to draw new districts.  I hope that this scheduling of hearings will ramp up vigorously and with better notice when the IRC publishes its draft maps.

My concern with the hearing schedule is threefold. First, it appears that very few - perhaps only three - of the 14 sites are located in communities of color.  Given the data from the Census showing a significant growth in Arizona's minority population, that seems to be an inadequate allocation of the opportunity to be heard.

Additionally, the satellite locations at Window Rock and Kayenta are restricted to 25 persons.  I understand that the Navajo Nation has a 25-person limit in place for gatherings as part of its covid plan.  I am not sure that I understand why there is a limit for the township of Kayenta.  Perhaps it has instituted a gathering  due to its proximity to the Nation.  But these limits, coupled with the limited number of hearings in minority-populated parts of the State, suggest, fairly or not, that the IRC is being cavalier about its obligation to hear minority voices.

Finally, the IRC has scheduled these 5 hearings to last only one hour - from 4 to 5.   For each of the 5 main hearing locations, there are 1 to 4 satellite locations.  The 1 hour time limit along with the fact that folks from multiple sites will compete for that limited time makes the chances of hearing a broad spectrum of opinions unlikely, particularly from minority voices.

column5: Competitiveness
column6:
Comments from many voters on the listening tour indicate they believe their interests would be better served in a district of “likeminded persons.”  But isn’t that another label for a non-competitive or safe district?  And haven’t we seen often enough that it is elected officials from such districts that argue for partisan positions that place the wishes of the few ahead of the needs of the many and contribute to power struggles and gridlock?  

To avoid a dysfunctional system that produces winners and losers rather than progress, we should focus on problems and solutions, not political Parties and power.  This needs to happen at every level of government, but it should start at the local level.  The best way to ensure that voters are exposed to different ideas and solutions, as well as to the candidates who espouse them, is to have diverse districts where good ideas and good candidates can be heard and prevail.  It is unfortunate that such districts have been labeled “competitive,” because when the best qualified candidates are elected, there are no losers.  

Independent redistricting commissions are a constructive tool for eliminating, or at least significantly reducing, the partisan gerrymandering that has produced the current dysfunction and replacing it with a legislative system that focuses on what benefits the entire community, not a smaller but more powerful minority.  It is clear most voters understand and value the concept of communities of interest, but I am not as sure they understand and appreciate the concept of competitive, or better stated, more balanced, districts.  This is a topic I would like to see our Arizona IRC members address more fully during public meetings.

column5: My testimony before the IRC at the Public Hearing in Yuma 9/21/21
column6:
Here is the testimony I gave to the IRC regarding the Grid Map at the Public Hearing in Yuma on 9/21/21:

My name is William Bowlus-Root. I’m a retired software developer in Yuma, 85365, CD4 and LD13.
Chair Neuberg and Commissioners, thank you for the opportunity to share my views with the Commission tonight regarding the Grid Map that was generated as the starting point for drawing the Draft Maps and eventually the Final Maps for Congressional and Legislative District boundaries.  According to the Arizona Constitution, the process to arrive at these maps is expected to be transparent, carried out in public so we can feel confident it’s as free of political bias and tampering as possible.
I have several concerns about this process already that I feel are important to raise and give voice to.
First, it’s not clear that the mapping consultants actually carried out the wishes of the Commissioners when they produced the original Grid Map.  The instructions agreed on by the Commissioners stated that the starting point would be the “Township Median” of the state, and rotate clockwise, gathering voters in neighboring census blocks until the target number for a district was reached.  However, the commission omitted the other important instruction, namely which direction from census block containing the township median should be the next one.  Should it be the one directly above it?  Or to the right?  Or perhaps below it?  The question is really which block is clockwise from the one in the center?  That choice would have affected the boundaries of the resulting Grid Map in subtle ways.  But because the Commission failed to specify it, that choice was left to the mapping consultants, who had to act on an assumption in order to generate the map on time.  We also don’t know how neighboring blocks were combined to grow each district, but they appear to have been added radiating from the starting point.  The published diagram on the website doesn’t tell us much.  In any case, the choices they made have never been shared with the public, leading us to question the process they used to create the Grid Map.
My second concern has to do with the mapping software that’s been offered to help adjust the boundaries of the Grid Map when proposing new districts.  It’s just plain too difficult to use.  I’m an experienced software developer and I’ve tinkered with it for hours without finishing a single map.  Even with the training that’s been offered, if I struggle with it how do you expect the public at large to use it?  I doubt that 1% of them would have any success trying to figure out how to change boundaries or deal with the consequent ripple effects, much less how to get their proposed map to the point it’s worth submitting, assuming they can figure out how to accomplish that.  The Commission must be willing to accept maps submitted by other means and make sure they are input into the system so we can see them and so that they are not perceived to be disregarded or considered of lesser importance than those submitted through the current tool that are proposed by extremely savvy individuals or by powerful organizations that can afford to hire mapping professionals to promote their own agendas.  It’s the only way to get public input.
Finally, during the public training on the software, much was made about how individuals could share their maps with others so they could collaborate.  But, that functionality is not enabled for the average user.  According to Esri Tech Support, that must be configured by someone in the role of Administrator.  Although I submitted that information through your Contact Us form, but there’s been no response yet.  Given that Timmons has stated they will NOT provide technical support for their product to the public – the people who are footing the bill for their services – I suspect it will continue to be ignored.  In the meantime, there are people who would like to collaborate on maps as a Group.  Please ask Timmons to ensure this capability is enabled as soon as possible so we don’t waste more time waiting.

Thank you for your time this evening.


William Bowlus-Root
A concerned citizen

column5: Public Comment
column6:
Dear IRC Commissioners:

Thank you for your service on the Independent Redistricting Commission. As a former member of the Arizona Legislature, I know how important your work is for the future of our state. In fact, it will have a bigger impact on Arizona’s political environment than most anything else. 

That is important because our political environment continues to become increasingly polarized. Since my time in the legislature, the ideological divide between the two parties has expanded at a faster rate than any other time I can remember in our state’s, and perhaps nation’s, history. This has led to a breakdown in civic discourse and the ability for legislators to effectively work together across partisan lines to address Arizona’s biggest concerns. More importantly, it has led to an even higher level of societal mistrust and disdain for those entrusted to legislate and govern. Unless something changes now, that mistrust and disdain will lead to a further breakdown of the very norms that make our state and nation great. 

At the state level, I believe one of the biggest contributors to this trend is that most of our legislative districts are not competitive, but are instead, dominated by either the Democrat or Republican Parties. Unfortunately, this means the vast majority of these races are decided in the primary election, which, as you know, has very low overall voter participation and favors extreme and polarizing candidates in both Parties. With a lopsided percent of voters from either Party in a single district, the votes cast in the general election are essentially irrelevant and candidates can cater to their Party’s base while disenfranchising all others. Redistricting offers us a chance to rectify this and chart a new course. 

I know that competitiveness isn’t the only factor you must consider when creating the new maps, but competitive districts should be a natural outcome of all other considered factors. As Arizona has continued to grow in size, our political affiliations have become more diverse as well. The final maps need to take this diversity into account and accurately reflect the population of our great state, incentivize each candidate to represent all voters in the district, and empower each voter in each district, regardless of Party affiliation, with a voice in how they’ll be governed.

I am a lifelong Republican who, because of the disproportionate number of registered Democrats in my district (LD26), have switched to a “No Party“ affiliation to ensure that I have a voice in the primary, which, because of that disproportionality, makes it nearly impossible, for even a moderate Republican to win in the general. I firmly believe gerrymandering for either Party is detrimental to the long-term interests of our state. The voters created the Independent Redistricting Commission to reduce the influence of partisan politics….I pray that you will have the courage to honor those voters.

Thank you again for your service on the Independent Redistricting Commission. 

Sincerely,

Former Senator Jerry Lewis

column5: Lack of responsiveness to public record requests
column6:
I have filed public records requests via the form on the IRC’s website and through the "contact us" link when the public records request form was not working. I summarize those requests below. If the request received a pro-forma acknowledgment and public records act request number from the IRC, I have noted it. If no such number is noted, no acknowledgment was received. 
* June 21 - seeking the list of all public record requests to date (#984 - in response to repeated request on 8/25) 
* July 12 - emails between Erica Neuberg and Brian Schmitt for the dates 4/1- 6/30 
* August 4 - seeking meeting transcripts for the dates June 22 - August 3
* August 4 - calendars of all five commissioners and Brian Schmitt 
* August 4 -expense reports of all five commissioners for the month of July (#986) 
* August 4 - Invoices for the months of April, May, June, and July for 1) Timmons Group, 2) NDC Doug Johnson; 3) Ballard Spahr and 4) Snell and Wilmer (#983)
* August 25 - copies of all paper map submissions received during the Round 1 Listening Tour (July 9 - August 10) 
Some speakers handed the IRC staff their presentation and talking points. I believe these documents should fall under the framework of minutes and should have been made publicly available within 3 working days of the meeting. Given that these documents were not yet publicly available I submitted this request. 
* August 25 - The contact list, and contacts made by Outreach Coordinator Marie Chapel-Camacho of local elected officials, governments, government officials, and civic engagement groups - for period of August 1 - 25. 
* August 25 - a copy of the excel spreadsheet with comments from the 910 COI submissions (not a pdf version which does not provide a full record of all comments.) Time period July 1 - August 11. (#981) 
* August 25 - notes, emails and other documents used to inform the selection of specific locales and sites for the Round 1 listening tour. Time Period June 1 - July 31. (#982)
*August 25 - REPEAT of August 4 request of monthly invoices for mapping and legal consultants. (#975) 
* August 25 - AMENDED request for meeting transcripts to include all dates - January 21 - August 24. (#985) 
* August 25 - Calendars of all commissioners and staff members Schmitt, Van Haren, Neumann, Crank, Chapel-Camacho, and Pena reflecting all meetings and discussions with interested third parties related to the business of redistricting. This request included a suggested broad definition of "interested third parties" to indicate the request was for the most expansive definition. (#988)
* August 25 - copies of emails, phone logs and other documentation of communications between executive director Brian Schmitt and the Arizona Governor's office pertaining to IRC 2022 budget negotiations. (#990) 
* September 18 - copies of the sign-in sheets for each of the Round 1 Listening tour hearings. 
September 18 - REPEAT request for excel spreadsheet of 910 COI submissions. 
* September 18 - REPEAT request for calendars of all five commissioners reflecting meetings and conversations with interested third party stakeholders related to redistricting. Time frame: August 26- September 17. 
* September 18 - REPEAT: requesting transcripts of IRC business meetings 8/24 - 9/14) (#995) 
* September 18 - REPEAT - request for invoices of mapping and legal consultants for August. (#996) 
* September 18 - REPEAT - request for list of all public record act requests. Time period: January 21 - September 18 
* September 18 - requesting copies of August expense statements for each of the five commissioners and staff members Brian Schmitt and Lori Van Halen. 
* September 18 - a request for a record of all IRC expenditures for the month of August. 
Note: For records requested on September 18 I received email responses noting that the request was received, and numbers were assigned, but the response did not include the request itself, so I am uncertain which number goes with which request. These include numbers 994, 999, 993, 992, 997, and 998.) 

These records are not voluminous. Responding to them should not be an arduous task. To date I have not received any of the records requested. None. 

At its September 21 meeting, Chair Neuberg announced that the IRC staff is working on processing public records requests and hopes to be ready to respond in three to six weeks. She gave no reason for the delays.  Under established case law, the IRC must provide a written notice of the delay along with a “legally sufficient” reason for it in order to prove that the IRC is attempting in good faith to comply with the law’s “promptness” requirement.  The Chair’s casual comment does not constitute any legally sufficient reason for the delays. 

Since the IRC provided a place on its website for public records requests to be made, it is reasonable to conclude that the IRC anticipated requests to be made.  It is also reasonable to conclude that, given the high visibility of its work, the IRC expected the number of requests to be significant. The fact that the Chair acknowledged general delays in processing records requests – presumably even the easy ones – suggests that the IRC didn’t have a processing plan in place at the outset of its work and places a low priority on compliance. 

This is in stark contrast to the responsiveness of ADOA prior to the IRC adopting the public records act policy constructed by legal counsel. Prior to that policy, it was common for ADOA to respond within two or three days with the requested records - or rationale as to why requested records would not be made available. Not one request was left pending more than a week. 

Access to records is wrongfully denied when an agency delays in providing the requested documents and fails to offer a legally sufficient reason for the delay. Phoenix Newspapers, Inc. v. Ellis (App. 2007); Lunney v. State of Arizona (App. 2017) (Because the State did not provide a legally sufficient reason for a 150-day delay, the State’s response to the request was not prompt.) If a legally sufficient delay occurs, the person requesting the records should be advised, in writing, of the delay and the reason for it. Phoenix Newspapers, Inc. v. Ellis (App. 2007). 

All requests listed above (except for those made in September) are beyond the 30 day window. Some go back more than 50 or 90 days. These delays reflect a blatant disregard for the intent of public transparency and disclosure. Even worse it reflects internal operations that are inadequate and/or incompetent, and which are unambiguously unacceptable. Due to the IRC’s delay and complete lack of candor or understanding of its legal obligations, I request the opportunity to inspect the records physically and to obtain an index of records specified in A.R.S. § 39-121.01(D)(2). In doing this, I am not withdrawing my public records requests.   

I appreciate your timely response to this request.
