column5: South Phoenix and Laveen
column6:
Dear IRC,
Hello Commissioners! Thank you for all the hard work you are doing to draw out maps for our great State of Arizona. I’ve spoken publicly twice and am a native resident and currently residing in South Phoenix. I’ve seen some drafts recently on the maps that show South Phoenix is still being split and Laveen is separated from South Phoenix. South Phoenix goes as far East as 48th St. We go as far south to where the last homes meet the Northern part of South Mountain. The Southern edges of the mountains are Ahwatukee and has a completely different culture and basically shares little community of interest. South Phoenix goes up to the Salt River bed. North of the riverbed is Downtown Phoenix. This area is also very different from South Phoenix. Laveen is a community that shares a strong similarity in culture and demographics. I always recommend that if more population is needed, connect South Phoenix and Laveen. Between the two areas, we have a very dense black voting block. Splitting this community would weaken their voices in Arizona. Please keep them United and stronger. There’s also a strong Southside Latino Community between South Phoenix and Laveen. Within latino voters, you often hear about Southsiders and Westsiders. There’s a strong Lowrider culture but we like to distinguish South Phoenix and Laveen as Southsiders. The Westsiders are further West of us. We have our differences. These terms are simply for communities based on geographical location and we take pride in our communities. The terms Southsiders and Westsiders is not necessarily based on any illegal activity. It’s very common for our people to say they are proud Southsiders. 
Downtown Phoenix is not very similar in culture. Most of the developments and people are not native to the area since these developments are still fairly new since downtown used to almost have no housing. It used to be more business focused. 
Thank you for your consideration.
Sincerely, 
Tatiana Peña

column5: Mapping Process
column6:
I was concerned today by Commissioner Mehl's haste to make a motion to adopt his preferred Congressional District map and cut off discussion.  He did cede the floor long enough for Commissioners Lerner and Watchman to state what were clear and specific reasons for their preference for 4.0 and their concerns about 4.2  But rather than responding to their points, he abruptly shut off the discussion by making a motion to adopt his choice, a motion promptly supported by Commissioner York. 
 
 In my experience as a White female administrator myself, I am all too familiar with this tactic, and I ram compelled to point out that White male privilege is no substitute for honest debate.  I am, therefore, requesting that Chairperson Neuberg ensure this does not happen again. 

I would also remind all interested parties that earlier in this process when Republicans and Democrats had different preferences, the decision was made to pursue both starting points for a period of time until it became clear that one was more workable than the other.  I believe this approach will be most productive in the long run.  While time is a concern, getting the best solution is more important than "moving along", something Doug Johnson has emphasized on several occasions.

column5: Keep Verde Valley, including Sedona as in region with Flagstaff
column6:
I am a resident of Sedona and Verde Valley, and I urge you to keep my community of interest, as described in the following, together in one legislative district in the Arizona redistricting process.  

My Community of Interest includes Sedona, Verde Valley, Cottonwood and Flagstaff.  Scenic Oak Creek Canyon connects Sedona with Flagstaff, and Oak Creek continues downstream through Page Springs wine growing region, Cornville and Cottonwood to the Verde River.  Tourism brings up a large group of visitors from the I-17 corridor through Sedona, Oak Creek Canyon, Flagstaff to Grand Canyon.  Mayors and City Managers of Verde Valley, including Sedona, meet monthly to work together on issues of mutual interest.  Basic shopping needs are met by stores in Flagstaff and the region; only a few times during the past 5 years have I crossed over Mingus Mountain to go to Prescott to shop at Costco and other big box stores not available here.

As part of the Northern AZ Healthcare system, I have had one heart procedure at Flagstaff Medical Center and am scheduled for a follow-up procedure in December.  My wife and I have used physician and medical practices with offices in Flagstaff, Sedona and Cottonwood.  Our neighbor is now recovering from a complex bone fracture that could only be treated in Flagstaff.  

We in the Verde Valley have many cultural ties with Flagstaff – the Northern AZ watercolor society has primarily members from Flagstaff, Sedona and Cottonwood.  I will attend one of the Sedona - Fall Open Studios in a few weeks held by an artist in Cornville, part of the Verde Valley.  The Verde Valley Sinfionetta includes musicians from Flagstaff, Sedona, Verde Valley and Cottonwood; Sedona/Verde Valley residents attend Flagstaff Symphony concerts as well as other film and theater venues in Flagstaff.  The Sedona International Film Festival has outlets in Flagstaff in addition to its home.  

Although Sedona is physically split between Coconino and Yavapai counties, all residents need to belong to the same legislative district along with Cottonwood, Verde Valley and most of Flagstaff. 

This is our Community of Interest.  I urge you to keep this community of interest whole in the new Redistricting Map.

Sincerely,
Dieter Knecht
65 Sandstone Dr
Sedona, AZ 86336

column5: Gila River Indian Reservation Comments
column6:
October 20, 2021

Dear Commissioners,

The Commission holds a constitutional responsibility to the Voter Rights Act. As such, it must
consider a series of 6 factors when looking at each of these districts and at each change made
to our boundaries. We request that the GRIC continue to be with neighboring communities like
the city of Coolidge and Casa Grande. The cities of Coolidge and Casa Grande and the GRlC sit
on the l-10 corridor into Phoenix, and many of our community members have historically
resided in these communities. our neighboring communities have faced similar issues and
would be best represented together. We do not want our challenges to potentially overshadow
or be overshadowed by communities that face vastly different challenges than our voters.
The most recent map showing LD 16, 4.0/4.1map, regroups the GRlC with these communities,
and we would like to express our support of these maps. As it relates to the 4.2 congressional
map most recently discussed the morning of October 19th, it does not consider the Community
of interest described above. We would ask that you consider moving the GRlC into CD 2
outlined in the 4.2 version. This request would ensure our community voice is not potentially
marginalized or has reduced focused representation proposed in recent maps.
we are willing to discuss this further as your process moves forward. As Governor of the Gila
River Indian community, it is of extreme importance that I express our community's support
and concern related to the most recent maps to preserve our Community's balance and
constitutional criteria needed in this process. we ask you to consider this proposal and allow
the Gila River Indian Community to offer solutions in laying the foundation for Arizona voters
over the next decade.

I want to thank you for your time and work on the independent Redistricting Commission for
Arizona voters. The work and decisions you make this year will indeed be a bedrock for Arizona
voters over the next decade. The amount of dialogue and meetings to solicit feedback from the
public only help to strengthen that bedrock. As the Governor of the Gila River Indian
Community (GRIC), I would like to offer our perspective on our Community as you continue the
important work you are all doing. We know there will be many changes to the Congressional
and Legislative Districts and would request to keep the balance we have had over the past
decade in any maps approved by the Commission and encourage the Commission to continue
to listen to our native voice.

Sincerely,
Stephen Roe Lewis
Governor

column5: The need for competitive maps
column6:
Dear Commissioners,

Let me begin by thanking you for your service to our state. The role of the Independent Redistricting Commission is one of the most important in the state, and I know it can be an often thankless and demanding job, so please know that many of us appreciate your commitment to Arizona. 

As the Mayor of Casa Grande during the time of the last redistricting, I paid close attention to the process and worked with other leaders in Pinal County to make sure our concerns were heard and considered. I was very pleased with the last commission’s willingness to listen and work with us, and to this point I have been very pleased with your work to engage people across the state. 

A lot has changed in Pinal county since the last redistricting. Our population growth has exploded and we have new industry coming into the area. But one thing hasn’t changed - we are not Maricopa or Pima county. We are still a very different region than either of the two big urban areas of the state, and I hope you won’t forget this fact while making the new congressional and legislative maps. 

Overall, I was happy with the outcome of the last redistricting process for two reasons. 

First, the commission did a good job of recognizing the above fact and not allowing our political power to be wrapped into Maricopa or Pima counties. At both the congressional and legislative level, Pinal county was allowed to have elected officials who weren’t coming from the two big metro areas. This is still immensely important to us.

Second, the overall maps did a fairly good job of reflecting the population of the state. It fairly balanced out partisan interests, protected many communities of interest, and made sure rural Arizona had adequate representation. I hope you will pursue these same goals once again.

The only suggestion I would add is directed at the legislative maps, and that would be to encourage you to create more districts with competitive general elections. Right now, too many legislative races are decided in the primary election. It is giving partisan extremists way too much power over who serves in the legislature and what policy agendas are going to be pursued. That is not good for the future of our state. 

Whether it’s water, job creation, or education, the big issues facing our state shouldn’t be partisan. We need elected officials who are willing to work together to tackle the problems. Creating more competitive maps will be a huge step in the right direction.

Sincerely,
Bob Jackson

column5: Addressing Competitivess
column6:
Arizona is quite evenly divided among Republicans, Democrats and Independents, so partisanship is inevitable.  But gridlock is not inevitable-- provided both parties support candidates who (1) are more interested in solutions than power, and (2) are committed to working across party lines to find common ground and enact legislation that benefits all Arizonans.  

There are legislators from both parties in the Arizona Legislature who exhibit these qualities, but we need many more.  Unfortunately, candidates with these qualities are less likely to run, let alone get elected, in districts that are overwhelmingly Democrat or Republican, what are referred to as uncompetitive districts or “safe seats.” In such districts, the winning strategy is to say as little as possible, keep it simple, and avoid alienating the most extreme members of your party.  This discourages civic engagement and limits opportunities to better inform and educate voters.  

THE DILEMMA:  What it takes to get elected is not what it takes to be an effective legislator. 
THE SOLUTION:  Competitiveness must be addressed WITHIN districts so that tolerance for differing perspectives and disposition to compromise are reinforced within parties.  The best way to do that is to draw as many competitive districts “as is practicable.” If we can elect more legislators committed to working together, then maybe other legislators will become more inclined to do so as well.  

A POSSIBLE STRATEGY: Since we know many areas of Arizona are so red or so blue that drawing competitive districts is impossible, the IRC might use voting history data to pinpoint geographical areas where it is at least possible, draw those districts, and then draw the rest focusing on the other criteria--COIs, compact and contiguous, etc.

column6:
Thank you for your efforts in creating districts.  I understand that there are many requirements pulling you in various directions as you create these maps.  I will leave to your sound judgment the creation of the various districts, but I did want to share my thoughts in regards to some of the discussions around the Mesa districts that I live in.

I have watched with interest as the commission has considered various maps related to central Mesa over the last few weeks.  I currently live in legislative district 26 or the districts 9 and 10 being considered now.  During the past ten years I have been represented by individuals almost exclusively from Tempe and focused on Tempe interests.  I do not want to see that again.  

West and central Mesa has its own concerns and interests.  While I am a proud alumn of ASU, since graduating I almost never find myself in the Tempe area.  My family, friends, and even coworkers are dispersed primarily throughout Mesa with a sprinkling of Gilbert addresses as well.  Church congregations, food, and entertainment are primarily found in different areas of Mesa.  We simply are not Tempe, and our interests don’t align with those of Tempe whether you look at religious, educational, socioeconomic, racial, work, or any other way of comparing them.  None of my neighbors work in Tempe, have family in Tempe, go to church in Tempe, rarely eat in Tempe, or visit Tempe.

There just isn’t much that my neighbors have in common with Tempe; which is why I was surprised to see consideration of connecting my neighborhood in Mesa with a Tempe district again.  It was even more surprising to see very gerrymandered districts with boundaries shaped more like the famous salamander than any tight circle or square I have ever seen, spread across Mesa, Chandler, Tempe, Gilbert, and Phoenix.  This seems to be in clear violation of the Constitutional requirements for compact districts, respecting city boundaries and communities of interest.

Again, I understand the process is complicated, but I just want someone representing me who cares about my community.  Who is considering the interests and needs of central Mesa.  Please include us with a district from Mesa. 

Thank you for your consideration.

column5: Competitiveness
column6:
Arizona is quite evenly divided among Republicans, Democrats and Independents, so partisanship is inevitable.  But gridlock is not inevitable-- provided both parties support candidates who (1) are more interested in solutions than power, and (2) are committed to working across party lines to find common ground and enact legislation that benefits all Arizonans.  

There are legislators from both parties in the Arizona Legislature who exhibit these qualities, but we need many more.  Unfortunately, candidates with these qualities are less likely to run, let alone get elected, in districts that are overwhelmingly Democrat or Republican, what are referred to as uncompetitive districts or “safe seats.” In such districts, the winning strategy is to say as little as possible, keep it simple, and avoid alienating the most extreme members of your party.  This discourages civic engagement and limits opportunities to better inform and educate voters.  

THE DILEMMA:  What it takes to get elected is not what it takes to be an effective legislator. 
THE SOLUTION:  Competitiveness must be addressed WITHIN districts so that tolerance for differing perspectives and disposition to compromise are reinforced within parties.  The best way to do that is to draw as many competitive district “as is practicable.” If we can elect more legislators committed to working together, then maybe other legislators will become more inclined to do so as well.  

A POSSIBLE STRATEGY: Since we know many areas of Arizona are so red or so blue that drawing competitive districts is impossible, the IRC might use voting history data to pinpoint geographical areas where it is at least possible, draw those districts, and then draw the rest focusing on the other criteria--COIs, compact and contiguous, etc.

column5: Comments on First LD Draft Map - Phil Goode City of Prescott
column6:
IRC Commissioners, 

I am currently a City Councilman and the Mayor elect of Prescott who testified at the original public hearing at Yavapai College in Prescott and did not comment or testify on the grid maps because based on the LD map presented, Yavapai was shown to be its own LD.  The first issuance of your draft maps changed my concerns about LD1 significantly.

As you may know, Prescott was the first territorial capitol and Yavapai County is known as the mother of many other counties in Arizona.  The counties of Apache, Navajo, Coconino, Gila, and Maricopa were formed from the original Yavapai County,.  By state statue, Yavapai County is given the distinction of being recognized as LD-1.  This historical distinction of LD-1 should remain.

In addition, Yavapai County should be composed as its own LD for several reasons:

•	In the recent census, Yavapai county was found to have a population of over 236,600, and at our county’s current growth rate, the county most likely has exceeded the LD minimum number of 238,384 this year. Yavapai county’s new home permits in 2020 were 715, and so far in 2021 (end of September), 662 permits have been issued (estimating 2.5 persons per household).  This doesn't take into consideration the new home permits issued by cities and towns throughout the county.  Again, it's very likely the county has already exceeded the required minimum population number to qualify as its own LD.  
•	Yavapai County has a long history of Western heritage and culture involving ranching, mining, and forestry industries.  Our Western heritage is a major element of our community of interest.  People claiming Mingus mountain is a barrier to community interest and common economic and social concerns are clearly not widely connected to the wider cities and towns. I frequently visit and meet with community leaders in the Verde Valley and have found that we agree upon issues important to our communities and identify as rural Yavapai communities.  Many of the people who I heard testify against being aligned with Yavapai County because of the "mountain barrier", also indicated that they come to Prescott to shop at our Costco and Trader Joes retailers and attend many of our Prescott held events, parades and holiday celebrations.    
•	It is important to the constituents of the county to remain whole as a county for the services provided to them that are funded by their property and TPT taxes.  Government is more effective when issues arise that can be addressed from a central rather than defused authority and where their elected representatives have direct accountability.
•	Water is becoming a major issue of concern in rural areas and particularly in the Prescott Active Management Area. The management of the aquifer in this area is intimately connected to the Verde River and its continued perennial flow. Since the City of Prescott is the only designated assured water provider in the PrAMA we must consider downstream impacts of our decisions related to the lower reaches of the Verde River .It is important that Yavapai County and other rural counties protect their water resources to sustain their industries and their way of life, and we can only do that if we are of one mind.    
•	In my view, the current draft map and continued efforts to split Yavapai County is highly likely to create a safe democrat LD for the next 10-years.  Since the redistricting statute requires competitiveness in our elections, there is greater competition in keeping Yavapai County as its own LD.

I respectfully request that the next IRC draft map keep Yavapai County whole and not be split across other LDs.  For many of the reasons (excluding water resource PrAMA issues) North Wickenburg should remain in the Yavapai County LD, and in an effort not to split the Town of Sedona, it should be incorporated entirely in LD-1 (Yavapai County).

I respectfully ask that my concerns be seriously considered.

Phil Goode
Prescott Mayor elect
Prescott City Councilman
Phil.Goode@prescott-az.gov

column5: Oro Valley Community of Interest
column6: Significant IRC discussion has centered on Marana and Oro Valley being a community of interest.  They are not.  Oro Valley continues to annex into the Casas Adobes and Catalina Foothills communities.  Oro Valley and Casas Adobes share a school district (Amphitheater Unified), shopping centers, parks, recreation areas, etc.  Marana is distinct with a separate school district, and a strong agricultural presence.  Oro Valley, Casas Adobes, and Catalina Foothills lack any agricultural industry and are more traditional suburbs of Tucson.  Oro Valley is actually an outgrowth of Casas Adobes over the past 70 years.  Marana has long been distinct and historically west of Interstate-10.  Marana only recently annexed farther east of I-10.  The acrobatics necessary to combine Oro Valley and Marana in one district at the expense of other communities of interest should not be pursued.  A general survey of Oro Valley residents regarding a shared link with Marana would inevitably show that such a link is highly attenuated, at best.  Keep up the good work, IRC, and please review ALL viewpoints when making decisions regarding communities of interest.

column5: Draft maps for Verde Valley area
column6: I am writing to express objection to the current draft maps for the Verde Valley.  One of the specific requirements of redistricting is to respect communities of interest, where practicable. Another is to use visible geographic features, city, town and county boundaries.  Of these criteria, the commission has chosen only to use county boundaries in my area.  It would certainly appear practicable to make the choice to respect the consistent, strong and public wishes of the Sedona, Verde Valley and Flagstaff areas to be included as a community of interest.  We share common natural resources, a tourism economy, a shared employment base, and shared medical services.  We are on the north side of a large visible geographic feature - Mingus Mountain.  You have chosen to split a vibrant long established town at arbitrary road boundaries around County borders that simply do not make sense to every day life.  You have split Sedona and the Village of Oak Creek apart though we share common schools and fire department.  The insistence on splitting at a county line does not appear to be applied equally across the state, but has been used here to split an established community.  I urge you, with respect, in the strongest possible terms, please make practicable adjustments as expressly described in the Arizona constitution to meet our community of interest, geographic, city and town boundaries.

column5: Redistricting Process
column6:
Dear Sirs and Madams of the IRC:

I am a physician practicing in Scottsdale, serving patients from all over the Valley since 2006, including Phoenix.

My goal is to continue to provide public comment to you regarding any concerns I see regarding your challenging process of redistricting fairly. Your mandate, as described clearly in the AZ Constitution, and that I am sure you are very aware, is quite clear and I look forward to this process reflecting all six (6) aspects including:

1. Comply with the US Constitution and US Voting Rights Act

2. Congressional & Legislative Districts divided into equal populations

3. Districts should be geographically compact & connected

4. District boundaries must respect communities of interest

5. Use geographic features such as city and town boundaries and undivided census tracks

6. Competitive Districts as long as the other five requirements are prioritized

This comment refers to Uptown Phoenix and the fact that it is an urban area that should be included in the same district as central Phoenix, as this is reflective of the AZ Constitutional requirement that Districts should be geographically compact & connected and District boundaries must respect communities of interest, at the very least.

Voters in Uptown Phoenix will be deprived of proper and balanced representation by being drawn into a suburban district. Uptown Phoenix is NOT suburban. 

I also believe that by properly including Uptown Phoenix with Central Phoenix helps to strengthen Phoenix proper as a growing metropolitan area with a diverse yet consistent set of values, earning its place as one of the most important cities in the US. 

Thank you for your balanced consideration of these facts.

Dr. John A. Robinson

column5: The Independent Redistricting Commission is Deferring to the Priorities of Republican Commissioner Mehl at the Expense of Tucson

This week's Independent Redistricting Commission meetings have shown that the IRC is prioritizing the partisan agenda of Republican Commissioner Mehl by joining Marana and Oro Valley in a Legislative District that wraps around Tucson to create an artificially homogenous suburban Republican district. By deliberately skirting the edges of the city of Tucson, the proposed district not only ignores the interests and concerns of Tucson residents, but creates an electoral divide that does not in any way reflect how citizens in these areas truly interact.

 

Prioritizing Commissioner Mehl's repeatedly stated goal of keeping Marana and Oro Valley together has resulted in IRC LD Test Map v8.0, proposed by Commissioner Mehl, that uses tendrils from rural and semi-rural districts to split the heart of metro Tucson into five Legislative Districts.

The Arizona redistricting process should not revolve around one Commissioner's vision for what his home district should look like, especially when that vision fragments nearby areas with a much larger population. The IRC should discard Mehl's vision for Southern Arizona and draw Legislative District Maps that give all Arizonans equal priority.

The topography of this long county is very different which makes the concerns at times opposite.  Northern Gila County is surrounded by and/or part of the Kaibab National Forest.  Recreational activities like boating, hunting, fishing, hiking, biking at the Payson elevation of 5000' are very different from the Globe area. Globe's elevation is only 1500' lower is

The northern and southern areas of Gila County are too different to continue as one.  Payson should, in my opinion, perhaps be part of Coconino and/or Navajo.  I'm not sure where eastern Gila County would go...

column5: The Verde Valley
column6: SInce moving to Arizona 20 years ago, we have rarely had representation in the Arizona Legislature. For a while, Tom O'Halleran (R) was our Legislator and then our Senator in Phoenix. Then he was pushed out by extreme right-wingers from Prescott. Since then, we've not be represented. None of the current people from LD-6 live in the Verde Valley, nor do they know or understand our issues. None of the legislation in the last session dealt with issues important to us in the Verde Valley. Rogers, Blackman and Barton consistently proposed meaningless or hostile legislation that either did not serve our interests or actually threatened our safety and well-being. Now, your maps propose to break Sedona apart and throw part of the Verde Valley under the rule of the people of Prescott. Please don't do this to us. We need the entire Verde Valley and Sedona to be in one legislative district with communities that share our concerns and values. If the current map stands, we will again be denied representation in the Arizona Legislature. And that's a crime.

This is contrary to the interests of the citizens of the Tucson community, contrary to the spirit of competitiveness, reflects a republican agenda, and does not reflect the community and its interactions.

The redistricting process for Arizona should not revolve around one commissioner's vision is for his home district, which fragments the entire population of Tucson. column5: Draft map 8.0
column6:
I share Commissioner Lerner’s concerns about the inclusion of the Southern Arizona Leadership Council Districts.
Those districts were submitted to the Commission late Wednesday, and there is no information on the process that SALC - a special interest group from Tucson - used to draw them.
I echo Commissioner Lerner’s question: Did they consult the southern Arizona Latino communities when drafting these districts? This is a question that must be addressed.
The Commission must draw districts that adhere to the U.S. Voting Rights Act, which was written to ensure that the voting power of historically marginalized communities of color are protected under law. The voting power of Native American, Latino and other communities of color should be protected by the Independent Redistricting Commission. To dismiss the proposals from the Navajo Nation without serious consideration and analysis, and to completely reject the legislative districts submitted by the Latino Coalition with little justification, were decisions completely counter to this duty. 
The immediate embrace of a map submitted late in the process by a special interest group, and the Republican Commissioners’ attempt to immediately force those district configurations into the official draft maps, was alarming and completely counter to the intent of independent redistricting. 
By approving Commissioner Mehl's preferred Southern Arizona map in order to keep Marana and Oro Valley together, the IRC has chopped the heart of Tucson up into little pieces. This effectively packs Democrats into one district.
I am asking you to reject the LD draft map 8.0 version. As a resident of unincorporated Tucson, I am familiar with the proposed LD17 area. 
Draft map LD 8.0 ignores natural boundaries by including two mountain ranges in LD17. This would make outreach to communities in this LD virtually impossible. 
Draft map LD 8.0 ignores county boundaries by including a large chunk of distant places in Pinal County with distant places in Pima County. 
Draft map LD 8.0 ignores Oro Valley's larger community of interest of Casas Adobes and Tucson. Oro Valley is diverse by every measure. Tucson is our hub. 
Oro Valley doesn't belong in a primarily rural homogeneous district. Oro Valley is urban-suburban and diverse

column5: Tucson Area Maps
column6:
As a Tucson resident for 37 years, I’m very concerned about the LD Test Map v8.0 proposed by Republican Commissioner Mehl. I strongly support the formation of an alternative map that ensures boundaries that serve the people of Arizona and the residents of Tucson, not the partisan interests of politicians.

Commissioner Mehl has created a Legislative District--joining Marana and Oro Valley and skirting the edges of Tucson—that is deliberately and artificially suburban, homogenous, and Republican. It creates an electoral divide that does not reflect how citizens in these areas truly interact and ignores the interests and concerns of Tucson’s residents.

I am also opposed to the way Commissioner Mehl’s map fragments the Tucson area—an area with a far larger population than the Commissioner’s home district--under the Southern Arizona Leadership Council’s (SALC) preferred legislative districts. I share Commissioner Lerner’s concerns that these districts were submitted to the Commission late Wednesday with no information on the process that SALC—a special interest group—used to draw them.

The above indicates that the IRC is falling far short of its stated goals to be fair and non-partisan and to ensure that all Arizona residents have equal priority in the process of redistricting. I strongly support a much-improved alternative to LD Test Map v8.0.

column5: Southern Arizona LDs
column6:
Commissioner Mehl has been focused on keeping Marana and Oro Valley together as a community of interest and he attempts to do that by including vast quantities of uninhabited land in the Coronado National Forest and a significant chunk of Pinal County. This is simply an attempt to grant the wish of Major General Ted Maxwell, President & CEO of the Southern Arizona Leadership Council for a Republican Legislative District that represents the business interests of Southern Arizona. They currently have that voice with LD14 which includes Cochise County and a significant part of East Central Pima County as well as LD11 which includes most of Oro Valley and Marana as well as much of Pinal County. Both of those districts have been solidly Republican for most if not all of the last ten years. All Commissioner Mehl is doing is swapping one portion of Pinal County for another and sweeping over to eastern Pima County creating a district that is divided in half by the Catalina Mountains and the Coronado National Forest. If this isn’t a blatant gerrymander, then I don’t know what is.
I can assure you that the citizens of Marana and Oro Valley have no more in common with San Manual and Mammoth than they currently have with Casa Grande and Maricopa City and even less in common with the residents of eastern Pima County.
I have placed a proposed map in the “Everyone” folder called “Southern AZ Legislative Districts” which places virtually all of Marana and Oro Valley along with Casas Adobes and the Catalina Foothills into one legislative district, with a much stronger community of interest than Marana and Oro Valley have with San Manuel, Mammoth and the Tanque Verde area of eastern Pima County.
The map also keeps Graham and Greenlee Counties whole and out of the southern LDs providing an opportunity to include them with the Navajo Nation and also includes Vail, Rita Ranch, Corona de Tucson, Sahuarita, Green Valley and Davis Monthan AFB which they want to form a military corridor which includes Ft. Huachuca.
If the goal is to  keep Marana and Oro Valley in the same district, there are better ways to accomplish that goal than Commissioner Mehl has proposed. But if the goal is to create another Republican legislative district, well we all know what that’s called.

This disparity can be equalized by making both LD 3 and LD 8 competitive.  Moving the Pima/Salt River Reservation and parts of northern Tempe into LD 3 would accomplish this.  It would also combine the Pima/Salt River and Fort McDowell Reservations under the same LD.

I am also concerned with the lack of true competitiveness of all LDs in the 8.0 version.  Eleven districts are drawn to favor Democrats, 14 to favor Republicans and only 5 fall within the adopted competitive range.  This too does not meet the intent of Prop 106. Best decisions cannot be a rushed. It is obvious that the State Legislature is projected in favor of one party with the current drawing of the LDs.

column5: Fair and Balanced Map for D3 in LD Version 8.0
column6:
I have lived in Carefree for 10 years and have never been able to elect the candidates of my choice for the state legislature or U.S. Congress. My current legislative district is non-competitive with a 26.5% disadvantage for one party. 

Fairly balanced maps will benefit citizens of all parties since they will help guard against extremist ideology and require candidates and legislators to be more responsive to the interests and needs of all their constituents. 

I thank the Commission for separating our current district from Yavapai County, but urge you to understand that our community of interest not only extends south from Carefree Highway, but also seeks more political balance within Maricopa County. 

One way to achieve this is by incorporating parts of the adjoining new Legislative D8 which has an uncompetitive vote spread of 64.19 D to 35.81 R into new LD 3 which has a non-competitive vote spread of 39.79 D to 60.21 R. These spreads do not compare favorably with the maximum targeted 46.5 to 53 range that the Commission initially agreed on. In particular, I suggest adding the Salt River Pima Reservation in its entirety and portions of northern Tempe into LD3 with the intent of balancing competitiveness for the two districts.

Thank you.

column5: LD Maps - Tucson, Pima County
column6:

I share Commissioner Lerner’s concerns in this regard, particularly inclusion of the map drawn by SALC, a special interest group.  Did SALC consult with the Latino communities in Southern Arizona?  The districts must comply with the VRA to ensure that historically marginalized communities are protected, including Native American and Latino.  It appears the Navajo Nation and Latino Coalition proposals have been disregarded. 

Compliance with the VRA is but one of the independent redistricting criteria this proposed map would violate. The LDs in Test Map v8.0 clearly fail to comply with two other Redistricting criteria:  Compactness and Competitiveness.  As drafted, LDs 18, 20, 21, and 23 would be “safe” Democratic districts, and LDs 17 and 19 would be “safe” Republican districts.  All five of these districts include oddly shaped squiggles, bulges and tails; classic hallmarks of gerrymandering.  It is obvious that these tortured shapes have been drawn in order to keep Marana and Oro Valley together, while chopping the heart of Tucson into tiny, separate pieces. There would be no Competitive Districts in the Tucson & Pima County area!

The sudden embrace of a map submitted so late in the process by a special interest group, and the Republican Commissioners’ attempt to force those non-compliant district configurations into the official draft maps, is counter to the meaning of independent redistricting.

Please redraw the maps to more fully capture and comply with the Redistricting Criteria established in our laws.
Thank you.

column5: SALC: Special Interest Group Shouldn’t Draw IRC Maps
column6: The voters of Arizona created the Independent Redistricting Commission to be independent. We wanted the IRC to deliver the state of Arizona Legislative and Congressional Districts that were not gerrymandered to favor one political party or another. Arizona is a purple state. It is almost evenly divided between Democrats, Independents and Republicans. The majority of voters are not registered Republicans. column5: Tucson Community of Interest and version 8
column6:
The district map of Southern AZ must recognize the essential unity of Tucson as a community of interest by placing as much of the metro population in as few compact districts as possible. Cracking the metro area into parts of 4 or 5 districts is deeply violative of Tucson's community. 

The proposed version 8 map seems to demonstrate an intent to dilute and divide the Tucson community of interest in order to create a single district of the two separate communities of Oro Valley and Marana. Those towns have distinct geographic separations, different growth histories, land use, and economic foundations. The real aim of SALC in drafting this propsed map seems to be to pack a congressional district in Pima County with Republicans. As such, the proposed map is also very likely violative of the core legal requirements of the Constitution and Voting Rights Act, and likely to be challenged and struck down in court.

Adopting the version 8 map, which was drafted behind closed doors by a special interest organization (SALC) with close ties of one of the Republican commissioners, would be also a deeply troubling abdication of the intent of Arizona's citizens in creating the IRC as a non-partisan body and violates the integrity of the IRC process. 

In addition to these concerns, the adoption of version 8 would completely ignore the input and interests of our minority racial, ethnic, cultural, and language populations here in southern AZ. Specifically, version 8 would ignore the input and interests of our Latino and Native American communities in favor of a map drafted in secret and adopted in haste without sufficient consideration of the principles the IRC was established to protect.

I am frankly outraged that the IRC would even consider the adoption of the version 8 map.

column6:
Chair Neuberg, you have allowed Commissioner Mehl to ride roughshod over other Commissioners in the latest changes to the draft maps, and you must undo these changes and stop overly deferring to him in order for the IRC to regain its independence. Mehl's directed changes have particularly skewed the LD maps and created multiple imbalances in both population and competitiveness. Commissioner Mehl has had too much authority over the latest test map changes, which have incorporated the desires of his pet interest group SALC and his false assertion that Marana and Oro Valley must be kept together as a "community of interest" (they are no more a community of interest than any other neighborhood or suburb of Tucson is with each other). As a Tucsonan who grew up in the Catalina Foothills area, I do not appreciate the way Tucson's voting power has been minimized. Meanwhile, the IRC is required to follow the Constitution and the Voting Rights Act. This is the only criterion that is non-negotiable, as every other criterion is to be followed "to the extent practicable." Yet the IRC has so far given short shrift to the input of the important VRA constituencies engaging in the mapping process. The IRC has not considered the maps submitted by the Latino Coalition or the Navajo Nation. And the IRC appears to have ignored the Latino Coalition's recommendation of creating an additional minority-majority district, despite the fact that Arizona's growth in the last decade has been driven by minority populations, especially the Latino population. The IRC must give appropriate consideration to these suggestions, especially when interest groups like the SALC have already had significant sway in the mapping process. Please incorporate the suggestions of the VRA constituencies when you meet on Tuesday.

column5: Include Verde Valley with Flagstafff in Redistricting maps
column6:
I am deeply concerned that several Commissioners are stating that “the Verde Valley is divided in its desire to be connected with either Prescott or Flagstaff.” Being divided between these two connection is an inaccurate description. Instead it should be made clear that the majority of residents of Verde Valley and the residents of Prescott are clear in their desire that Verde Valley should be included with Flagstaff and NOT Prescott. Those saying they want Verde Valley included with Prescott rather than Flagstaff and a very small minority. 

It was quite clear at the Prescott and Sedona Community of Interest Hearing in July that the “split” was approximately 85% in favor of the Verde Valley/Sedona area being part of what is know LD6, remaining with Flagstaff. In Flagstaff, of the 20 or more people who spoke, only 1 preferred to be included with Prescott. So commissioner’s comments that Verde Valley is divided in its desire to be connected with either Flagstaff or Prescott, is a huge distortion of the fact that the vast majority, 85% of more, of those speaking at the community of interest hearings clearly preferred Verde Valley to be included with Flagstaff.

These are some of the reasons that Verde Valley, Cottonwood & Sedona should NOT be connected with Prescott, but included with Flagstaff:

They are separated geographically, economically, agriculturally, and socially by the virtue of the Mingus Mountains. 

  There is a separate county administration building in Cottonwood where the County Supervisor from that area, District 3, has her office.

     The YC Sheriff’s Office has an eastern Yavapai County command(Cornville, Lake Montezuma, Oak Creek, Rim Rock, Beaver Creek, Verde Village and the Village of Oak Creek), with stations in Camp Verde and the Village of Oak Creek. 

     There is a separate detention center in Camp Verde.

     They also have their own school districts, newspaper, radio station, etc.

So please listen to the majority if 85% or more who spoke at the Community of Interest Hearings and the many comments made on the IRC website supporting the fact that the majority want Verde Valley, Cottonwood and Sedona included with Flagstaff and NOT Prescott.

Respectfully, 
Rita Day

It helps to have a starting point, right? There are experts in the field of redistricting that provide guidelines and standards to follow. Because this process can be so easily manipulated – history proves that gerrymandering is contrary to the goals of fair maps but, is done all the time; It is imperative that the AZ IRC incorporate the standards consistently and I am currently unsure if that is happening right now.

The concept of ‘separating’ yourself from the rest of the community breeds mistrust and hate and not only is harmful in the redistricting process but, does damage to our society as a whole in perpetuity…and we don’t want Arizona to add to this division in our country. At the same time, we are asked to provide you “communities of interest”. 
For example: Oro Valley shares many more economic and social ties to Tucson than Marana but, as of yesterday, there appeared to be more weight given the S AZ Leadership council founded by Commissioner Mehl. What about the Latino Coalition or the Navajo Nation?

column5: Opposition to LD Test Map v.8
column6:
In Nov. 2000, Prop. 106, a citizen's initiative, passed by a 12% margin amending the AZ Constitution to create the IRC. The IRC's task is to oversee the mapping of Fair and Competitive Districts in a "grid-like pattern".  
State LDs shall ( to the extent practicable) : be "equal in population", be "geographically compact and contiguous", have " boundaries" that "respect communities of interest", and have "lines" that "use visible geographic features, city, town, and county boundaries, and undivided census tracts."  The Current LD 10 map does just that; it complies with the AZ Constitution.    The LD Test Map v.8 has LD 10 Replaced with LD 21.  LD 21 is NOT "Geographically Compact and Contiguous" at all; it stretches from Central Tucson South to the Mexican Border, then West to Sasabe and East to Elgin.  This ridiculously shaped district is appalling!  It is the very definition of "gerrymandering"; This is the very reason why AZ citizens definitively passed Prop.106, so that AZ would NOT allow such redistricting to occur.   "LD 21's  boundaries do NOT Respect "Communities of Interest" in any way, shape, or form!.  Central Tucson is nothing like the much smaller towns in the the large expanse of Southern Arizona.  LD 21 does NOT" follow visible geographic features, city, town, or county boundaries".  The LD 21 map is unacceptable, and needs to be redrawn!  I suggest keeping LD 10 just as it is now; it meets all of the criteria set forth by the AZ Constitution, and it truly represents our neighborhoods and the community at large. 
The LDs in Southern Arizona are vastly different from those in the Phoenix region which are " Geographically Compact and Contiguous.  The LD maps that were submitted late Wednesday (10/20) by the Southern Arizona Leadership Council (SALC), a civic and advocacy group founded by Commissioner Mehl should not be considered. The SALC does not represent a "Community of Interest"; it represents a special interest group.  The adoption of maps submitted by an organization (SALC) with personal ties to one of the Commissioners is troublesome and raises concerns about the independence, fairness and the integrity of the redistricting process.

column5: Verde Valley Together with Flagstaff
column6:
Chairman Neuberg and Committee members,

I am Ernie Strauch, 23-year resident of the Coconino County portion of Sedona.  I have been President of Keep Sedona Beautiful, Inc. and Vice-Mayor of the City of Sedona.  I am actively involved in the redistricting process, and was an applicant to serve on the IRC as a Democrat.  

I am personally shocked that I have heard several Commission Members state that "the Verde Valley is divided in its desire to be either connected with Prescott or Flagstaff".  This statement is significantly INCORRECT.  I have attended both the Prescott listening session and the Flagstaff satellite listening session.  In the former, the “split” was approximately 85% in favor of the connection to Flagstaff. At Flagstaff, of the 20+ people who spoke, only 1 was in favor of a connection to Prescott.  Further, no one at either meeting believed that 35% of our residents should continue to vote in Coconino County, and 65% vote in Yavapai County.  We are in the same school district, the same fire district, and obviously the same small 10,000-person city.  Please do not continue to split us apart!

Please DO NOT continue to characterize the Verde Valley as divided in our interest!

A Final Report just released from the recent Verde Valley Town Hall (which I also attended), contained these particular statements:

WHAT I WOULD TELL ARIZONA’S ELECTED LEADERS
	The Verde Valley needs to continue to work together including the redistricting process.

	I will visit with Arizona state legislators (representatives and senators) and Congressman Tom O’Halleran regarding the importance of “Keeping the Verde Valley Together” as well as major themes from Verde Valley Community Town Hall.

The 83 attendees at the Verde Valley Town Hall on October 8, 2021 representing a myriad of public and private entities were unanimous in their desire that the Verde Valley Remain Together and the Vastly greater numbers related the Verde Valley to Flagstaff.  The list of attendees to confirm my statements is found here:

https://aztownhall.org/resources/Documents/113%20Creating%20Vibrant%20Communities/113%20Verde%20Valley%20Community%20Town%20Hall%20Participant%20List.pdf

I’m sorry, but if even an 80-20 split is considered “divided”, I need to turn in my degree in Political Science from Beloit College, because I know nothing about the concept of democracy or democratic policy making!

Thank you for your complex and difficult service - I will remain “tuned-in”.

 Ernie Strauch
148 Cathedral Lane, Sedona, AZ 86336
Hm: 928.282.6666    Cell: 928.300.2307
Email: erniestrauch@mac.com

column6: Hello. I am writing on behalf of my community, which spans down the I-17 including New River, Anthem, Tramonto, Sonoran Foothills, Stetson Hills, Norterra, and Deer Valley. Our community is currently included in D28 with rural northwest Maricopa County out to Wickenburg. Not only do we have nothing in common with those areas, but it creates a 65R/35D split, removing any chance of competition in the district. Additionally, it makes representation and community-building almost impossible when our district is that large. A large district makes sense for rural areas, but there is no reason for Maricopa County districts to cover that much distance. We are all suburbs of Phoenix, and belong with our community of interest down the I-17. To increase competitiveness, the district can be pulled as far south as necessary to get within the 7 point recommended spread. It is very important when measuring competitiveness that we not only try to balance the number of R and D districts, but that we create every district as competitively as possible so that all citizens in that district can have their voices heard. I am asking you to please keep our north Phoenix community together, and to work on ensuring that we are in a competitive district. I appreciate the work you are doing. Thank you.

column5: Proposed Congressional District 9
column6:
Chairman Neuberg and Commissioners Watchman, Mehl, Lerner and York:
I am a member of the Lake Havasu City business community and I respectfully submit these comments today in opposition of the proposed Congressional District 9. 
While our current congressional district isn’t perfect, and includes portions of metropolitan Phoenix and Maricopa County, it primarily encompasses more rural geography. The proposed new district however, highly favors the populated areas of western Maricopa County.
The proposed District 9 does include most of Arizona’s west coast, which is appropriate; however, it dovetails into the west valley communities including Sun City West, Surprise, Luke Air Force Base, Goodyear and Buckeye, where at least 70 percent of the proposed district’s population reside. This is clearly not representative of the 57,000 residents of Lake Havasu City, nor the residents of greater Mohave, La Paz and Yuma Counties. In a district with these demographics, the chances of representation from and for rural communities would be unlikely.
Even the IRC’s mapping consultant Doug Johnson wonders if it’s appropriate, and was quoted saying: “Even though it looks like a rural district…it’s actually a West Valley seat.” (Today’s News-Herald, Oct. 22, 2021)
All Arizonans matter and all voices should have equal opportunities to be heard. We should not be punished with the potential of under-representation for choosing to live and work in “greater” Arizona. I urge you to reconsider the proposed alignment of Congressional District 9 in an effort that more fairly represents the rural voice of western Arizona.

I live in the Broadmoor subdivision of Tucson, just south of Broadway, between Tucson Blvd and Country Club Rd. column5: congressional district maps and the VRA
column6: As a resident of northern Arizona, I am greatly concerned about the nature of CD 2 in V 6.0 and several preceding maps. The northern and eastern portions of our state contain many of our tribal nations, including those with significant interests in federal relations, state and regional water rights, and other areas of economic and political relevance to Arizona. The state would benefit greatly from these tribes being able to elect a candidate of their choice, who would develop expertise in their issues and would serve both them and the state in a well-informed, attentive manner. Yet the proposed congressional district erases any hint of competitiveness or of the ability of these Native Americans to elect a candidate of their choice. I don’t see how this proposed district can be interpreted in any way other than the abandonment of a VRA-relevant district. It also moves many, many communities from currently belonging to a VERY competitive district (Representative O’Halleran’s) to a decidedly NON-competitive, GOP-dominated district. (I would guess this is from adding Prescott to the Flagstaff – Navajo Nation district.) I understand it may be difficult to find enough population, especially given what is perhaps undercounting on the Navajo Nation by the Census, but this proposed CD 2 would be a terrible – and, it would appear, non-VRA-compliant – solution. Do not forget your obligation to maintain districts in which communities of color are able to elect the candidates of their choice. And, though I am not Native American and have no official tie to the tribal nations, as a resident of this region I too object to being moved from a highly competitive to a grossly non-competitive district.

column5: Reactions to proposed redistricting map for Tucson area
column6:
Comments on the AIRC Adoption of SALC proposed State Legislative Districts for Tucson
 I was born and raised in Tucson Arizona and have returned to take care of my mother in the house I grew up in and have been living here again since 2004.  I have the following concerns about the proposed redistricting maps.

Last Wednesday afternoon, near the end of its fifth day of mapping deliberations, Commissioner Mehl proposed that the AIRC adopt a proposed map of state legislative districts in Tucson and southern Arizona submitted by the Southern Arizona Leadership Council (“SALC”), a non-profit advocacy group that he founded. This map was actually published on the IRC website as map number 6.3 despite the fact that it had no audit trail tying it to the original grid map. The AIRC’s lawyers intervened, apparently asking the AIRC to take down map 6.3 from the official website but Commissioner Mehl simply made a motion to adopt the southern Arizona districts proposed by SALC. The AIRC decided to “look at” this proposal, abandoning the previous four and a half days of mapping decisions in favor a partisan map which violates all six of the required constitutional criteria. 

A.	The first criterion which must be followed by the AIRC is the United States Constitution and the Voting Rights Act (“VRA”). 

Commissioner York announced, without any analysis, that the proposed SALC LD maps strengthened the proposed VRA LDs in southern Arizona. Actually, the opposite is true. The mapping consultants should be requested to compare the southern Arizona VRA LDs in map 4.0 (containing the Latino Coalition proposed districts) to the SALC LDs. When that comparison is made it will be evident that the SALC map weakened the VRA districts. For example, map 4.0 had eight districts with a Hispanic citizen voting population over 43%; map 8.0 only has six such districts. Evidently these maps were drawn without any input from the Latino community so perhaps this is no surprise. Nevertheless, adopting the SALC proposal creates significant litigation risk for the AIRC because it weakens the southern Arizona VRA districts. 

B.	The second constitutional criterion which must be followed by the AIRC is Equal Population

Commissioner Mehl is especially fond of this specific constitutional criterion but the SALC maps fail to meet it. Ironically, Commissioner Mehl mused in passing on the record that a population deviation might be justified in order to sustain SALC’s partisan maps. Legislative District 16 is under population by 11,029 or 4.6%; LD 17 is under population by 6839 or 2.87%; LD 18 is over population by 4668 or 1.96% and LD 19 is over population by 4935 or 2.07%. 

C.	The third constitutional criterion is that districts must be Compact and Contiguous. 

The SALC proposed Legislative Districts may be contiguous but they are plainly not compact, especially district 17. For a senator or representative (or candidate) to drive from the Tanque Verde section of east Tucson to Marana could take over an hour even in light to moderate traffic. And the driver would not even be in his/her own legislative district during the trip. 

D.	The fourth constitutional criterion is that proposed maps should respect Communities of Interest.

District 17 fails to respect Communities of Interest. With all due respect to Commissioner Mehl and SALC, there is nothing that ties together the east Tucson/Tanque Verde region with Marana and Oro Valley. They do not share the same schools. In fact, there are at least two and maybe three school districts in between the Tanque Verde area and Oro Valley. These communities do not worship together. Residents of Oro Valley/Marana do not share the same economy or employers with east Tucson. No one in east Tucson regularly shops in Oro Valley or Marana. In fact, the only time east Tucsonans would visit Marana would be driving through on the way to Phoenix. Similarly, no one in Oro Valley or Marana visits or shops in east Tucson/Tanque Verde unless they are taking a day trip to Mount Lemmon. 

The SALC map has naturally created a spillover effect in other districts around Tucson.  Portions of midtown Tucson neighborhoods have been joined into Districts 21 and 19 which seem incredibly forced, and certainly not in the interests of those communities.



E.	The fifth constitutional criterion is that proposed maps should use “VISIBLE GEOGRAPHIC FEATURES, CITY, TOWN AND COUNTY BOUNDARIES, AND UNDIVIDED CENSUS TRACTS”
District 17 is a spectacular failure on this criterion. First, Commissioner Mehl has emphasized that his most important priority was to combine the cities of Marana and Oro Valley. Setting aside the fact that these are two very different communities that share little in common that would justify joining them in a single legislative district, the SALC map excludes a substantial portion of Marana and it excludes a substantial portion of Oro Valley. SALC excluded these portions of the two cities for purely partisan purposes. The northern parts of Marana and Oro Valley, which tend to be Republican, are combined in proposed LD 17 and the southern parts, which tend to be more Democratic, are excluded. This is gerrymandering pure and simple. To achieve its gerrymander, city boundaries are disrespected; both Marana and Oro Valley are split into two districts. Moreover, there is a mountain range, the Catalina Mountains, which separates east Tucson/Tanque Verde from Oro Valley and Marana. Consequently, the map also fails to account for “visible geographic features.” Finally, District 17 also includes rural parts of Pinal County that share nothing in common with suburban Tucson.


F.	The sixth criterion in the Arizona constitution is that maps should favor competitive districts. 

The SALC maps appear to have been drawn in order to gerrymander a Tucson based district for the republican party. District 17 went from a partisan split slightly in favor of Democrats to a partisan split strongly in favor of Republicans. Moreover, the change dramatically impacted the partisan balance in the rest of the state. Solid Democratic districts were reduced from 13 to ten (competitive analysis pdf for Map 6.0 vs. Map 8.0); solid Republic districts were increased from 13 to 15 (id). And, all of this was done under the rubric of uniting the cities of Marana and Oro Valley even though it did no such thing.

In sum, this was not about uniting the cities of Marana and Oro Valley. It was about abandoning four days of mapping where the commissioners were trying to draw fair maps in favor of an unvetted partisan map designed to achieve partisan goals. In doing so, this turns the purpose of the AIRC—which is to put a stop to gerrymandering—on its head. 

Even worse, if the SALC maps are accepted, it could create a road map for partisan groups in the future to corrupt the AIRC mapping process. The game plan could be used by either side. First, organize partisans to present community of interest testimony that is made up of purely partisan talking points when there is no real community of interest, only a desire to pack a district to elect a candidate of their partisan leaning. Next, ask one of their partisan commissioners use that testimony to contend that a real community of interest exists even though groups are separated by multiple school districts and a mountain range. Finally, arrange for a non-profit affiliate to submit an unvetted, gerrymandered map late in the process with a claim that it advances the supposed communities of interest. This style of partisan gambit could effectively put an end to independent redistricting in Arizona. 

Thanks you for considering my major concerns. 

Jennifer Sue Bond 3143 East Lester Street Tucson, AZ 85716

column5: Commission's 15-15 state Senate "goal," proportionality, and competitiveness
column6:
The stated goal of a 15-15 state Senate through redistricting, as reiterated during your October 21 hearing, is very troubling.  This goal overtly injects partisan politics into a redistricting process that was sold to voters as "talking the politics out of redistricting."  

Arizona's constitution establishes six mandatory redistricting goals.  Not five, seven, or eleven -- six.  Commissioners of the Arizona Independent Redistricting Commission are required to effectuate each of those six goals, not their own "high-minded" goals, and particularly not their own partisan objectives.  

The notion that Arizona is a 50-50 state when it comes to redistricting is utterly false and entirely irrelevant.  Arizona could have made "proporational representation" an overall goal of its maps.  It did not.  Indeed, each of the six goals Arizona did adopt work to thwart and frustrate partisan proportionality.  When districts need to be compact and contiguous, equally populated, follow county or municipal lines, follow geographic features or whole census tracks, respect communities of interest, etc., proportionality goes by the wayside.  

Even the competitiveness criterion, when applied fairly to all voters and evenhandedly across the map, drives the map away from proportionality.  A "more competitive district" (using the language from the Arizona Supreme Court's 2009 decision in Minority Coalition vs. AIRC) is a value each voter gets to have in his or her district, no matter where that voter lives in the state.  The competitiveness criterion yields to the OTHER five redistricting goals per the constitution, but it does not yield to itself.  Accordingly, the AIRC cannot refuse to make a district more competitive if to do so causes another "perfect" district to be slightly less competitive, but not less competitive than the district sought to be improved.  

Finally, application of the Voting Rights Act has a profound effect that works against partisan proportionality on the map as a whole.  A political party that might benefit from VRA compliance, using up a disproportionate number of its voters in the process, does not also get an artificial boost toward overall proportionality elsewhere on the map.

Arizona has a district system.  The district system upholds values different than proportionality.  Some of those values are set forth in Arizona's six constitutional redistricting goals.  Arizona is like every other state since the founding of the United State:  the district system prevails.

People can disagree about what goal is more important, but Arizona's constitution is the law and decides what is "fair."  Failure of a Commissioner to follow the law is unfair and undermines public confidence in Arizona's redistricting system.  

Please focus on a fair, evenhanded, application of all six mandatory redistricting goals with respect to each district.  Please also work equally hard to make EACH DISTRICT "more competitive" and do not affirmatively give up on districts that are lopsided or even lean strongly in one direction.  Everyone is entitled to the constitutional value of a “more competitive” district, and even incremental changes in a district's make-up can enhance the voice of the minority party, encourage candidates to run, encourage better candidates to run, and foster fundraising and party building.  

Thank you,

Scott
Scott Day Freeman

column5: Tucson's urban core should not be put in rural districts
column6:
Central Tucson should not be carved up into multiple legislative districts, as proposed in the Version 8 maps of LDs 21, 18, 20 and 19. These maps have divided up Tucson’s urban core and put these neighborhoods into largely rural districts. These urban and rural communities are not similar and have different needs. Furthermore, the LD21, LD20, LD19 and LD17 maps ignore the natural boundary of Interstate 10.

Midtown Tucson is a cohesive, multicultural, economically diverse urban community of older homes. People in these neighborhoods, which make up Tucson’s core, face the common problems of traffic enforcement, noise, crime, blight, gentrification, housing speculation, short-term rentals, slumlords, homelessness, refugee resettlement, public transportation, urban poverty, old infrastructure, urban flooding, substandard housing stock, and more. 
The Midtown neighborhoods of Catalina Vista, Blenman-Elm, Palo Verde, Grant and Alvernon, Dodge-Flower, Sam Hughes, Broadmoor, Miramonte and others have much in common with each other and with other older neighborhoods outside of the proposed Version 8 map of LD21. These dense urban neighborhoods have nothing in common with rural Pima and Santa Cruz Counties, which are also on this map. Version 8 of the LD21 map shows the gerrymandered head of a dragon reaching up into Midtown and grouping half of it with the border region and rural Arizona. Version 8 of LD21 is not compact, these communities are not similar, and it ignores the natural boundary of Interstate 10.

The northern half of Midtown has been cut off from the neighborhoods listed above and are in the Version 8 map of LD18. Midtown’s dense, diverse, poor-to-middle income neighborhoods have been lumped with mansions and resorts on the LD18(V8) map. Version 8 of LD18 is not compact, and these communities are not similar. 

In addition, sections of Tucson on the east side of Interstate 10 should be included in LD18(V8) not in LD20(V8) and certainly not in LD17(V8). Interstate 10 should be respected as a natural boundary. Version 8 of LD17 is not compact, these communities are not similar, and it ignores the natural boundary of Interstate 10 in multiple places.

Version 8 of LD20 also puts another piece of Tucson’s urban core in a district that is more rural. In addition, lumping the Flowing Wells area into this west side district ignores the natural dividing line of Interstate 10. Version 8 of LD20 is not compact, and these communities are not similar. 

Version 8 of LD 19 puts a chunk of Tucson’s urban south side into a very large rural district. The south side of Tucson has little in common with Thatcher, Sierra Vista or Douglas, but LD19(V8) ignores the dissimilarity of these urban and rural communities. Version 8 of LD19 is not compact, these communities are not similar, and it ignores the natural boundary of Interstate 10.

In its 2020 Maternal and Child Health Needs Report, the Arizona Department of Health Services reported that Central Tucson is an at-risk area for primary care. In fact, most of Tucson proper is at a risk level 3 or 4. The report also says that racial and ethnic disparities exist in access and outcomes to maternal and child health. This is yet another example of the unique issues facing Tucson’s urban core. If these communities are split up and shoved into rural districts, their urban needs will be ignored.

column5: Legislative Maps Lack of Competitiveness
column6:
Competitiveness deserves equal weight with the other five redistricting factors found in Article IV of the Arizona Constitution.  Competitiveness leads to good government since districts that can be won by either party produce representatives who are more responsive to their constituents. LD Test Map 8.0 fails the competitiveness test with its huge vote spreads for many districts.

When Arizona voters amended the Constitution to create an Independent Redistricting Commission, the only purpose stated at the top of Prop 106 was to create a Commission to “oversee the mapping of fair and competitive districts.” Only later, buried in section 14, did the proposition lay out the six criteria to be used in creating “fair and competitive districts.” The will of the voters and the clear and plain purpose of the constitutional amendment creating the IRC was to create competitive districts. There are infinite ways to draw legislative districts with today’s modern mapping tools so the mapping consultants should be able to do a much better job of fulfilling the constitutional obligation to “favor” competitive legislative districts as required by Paragraph 14)E of Article IV, Part 1, Section 2. This battle has been fought in the courts and the courts agree with this interpretation.

column5: Legislative District Mapping
column6:
Good Evening - 

I have concerns about the AIRC Adoption of SALC proposed State Legislative Districts for Tucson.  Specifically:  

            The fifth constitutional criterion is that proposed maps should use “VISIBLE GEOGRAPHIC FEATURES, CITY, TOWN AND COUNTY BOUNDARIES, AND UNDIVIDED CENSUS TRACTS”

District 17 is a spectacular failure on this criteria. First, Commissioner Mehl has emphasized that his most important priority was to combine the cities of Marana and Oro Valley. Setting aside the fact that these are two very different communities that share little in common that would justify joining them in a single legislative district, the SALC map excludes a substantial portion of Marana and it excludes a substantial portion of Oro Valley. SALC excluded these portions of the two cities for purely partisan purposes. The northern parts of Marana and Oro Valley, which tend to be Republican, are combined in proposed LD 17 and the southern parts, which tend to be more Democratic, are excluded. This is gerrymandering pure and simple. To achieve its gerrymander, city boundaries are disrespected; both Marana and Oro Valley are split into two districts. Moreover, there is a mountain range, the Catalina Mountains, which separates east Tucson/Tanque Verde from Oro Valley and Marana. Consequently, the map also fails to account for “visible geographic features.” Finally, District 17 also includes rural parts of Pinal County that share nothing in common with suburban Tucson.

 

 

        The sixth criterion in the Arizona constitution is that maps should favor competitive districts.

 

The SALC maps appear to have been drawn in order to gerrymander a Tucson based district for the republican party. District 17 went from a partisan split slightly in favor of Democrats to a partisan split strongly in favor of Republicans. Moreover, the change dramatically impacted the partisan balance in the rest of the state. Solid Democratic districts were reduced from 13 to ten (competitive analysis pdf for Map 6.0 vs. Map 8.0); solid Republic districts were increased from 13 to 15 (id). And, all of this was done under the rubric of uniting the cities of Marana and Oro Valley even though it did no such thing.

 

In sum, this was not about uniting the cities of Marana and Oro Valley. It was about abandoning four days of mapping where the commissioners were trying to draw fair maps in favor of an unvetted partisan map designed to achieve partisan goals. In doing so, this turns the purpose of the AIRC—which is to put a stop to gerrymandering—on its head.

 

Even worse, if the SALC maps are accepted, it could create a road map for partisan groups in the future to corrupt the AIRC mapping process. The game plan could be used by either side. First, organize partisans to present community of interest testimony that is made up of purely partisan talking points when there is no real community of interest, only a desire to pack a district to elect a candidate of their partisan leaning. Next, ask one of their partisan commissioners use that testimony to contend that a real community of interest exists even though groups are separated by multiple school districts and a mountain range. Finally, arrange for a non-profit affiliate to submit an unvetted, gerrymandered map late in the process with a claim that it advances the supposed communities of interest. This style of partisan gambit could effectively put an end to independent redistricting in Arizona.

 Thank you for considering this objections to this important issue - in making sure we have fair legislative districts.

Stephen Caster
Oro Valley

column5: Draft Maps
column6:
The Independent Redistricting Committee is deliberating the next 10 years of political representation of Arizona. Decisions they make will affect our entire state for 10 years. So, these decisions shouldn’t be based on the particular Commissioner’s preferences, but on the people of Arizona. However, this last week’s meeting has shown that Republican commissioners are prioritizing the input of a land developer association (Southern Arizona Leadership Council-SALC) over the voices of citizens of the Navajo Nation and Latinos in Southern Arizona. Republican Commissioner David Mehl is a founder and influential member of SALC. He introduced a draft map prepared by SALC and has repeatedly promoted that map over all others. He even attempted to get it published on the IRC website as the official draft map without discussion or debate.  If it wasn’t for public outcry against this preferential treatment, he would’ve succeeded in getting this map published without debate.

The SALC MAP VIOLATES SEVERAL OF THE IRC’s CONSTITUTIONAL  REQUIREMENTS:

- consideration of real Communities of Interest (COI),

- compactness, 

-geography and

-weakening of the Voting Rights Act.

The SALC map was catapulted to the top of the heap while maps submitted by Communities of Interest representing Navajo and Latinos were dismissed without debate or discussion. This is preferential treatment given to a special interest group of ONE of the Commissioner’s. This is not fair and impartial treatment. This can not be tolerated. The Commissioners shouldn’t be prioritizing groups that they are personally affiliated with and giving these groups special treatment.

Decisions should be made consistently, with consistent treatment given to the various maps submitted by all groups. Rural communities should be treated equally to Urban communities.Also, paper maps should be given equal consideration to maps created on the IRC mapping tool.

Also, some commissioners are making “so-called” factual statements that are NOT supported by any facts. Statements like: “The Verde Valley is divided in its desire to be included with either Prescott or Flagstaff.” This statement is NOT ACCURATE. At the Prescott and Sedona COI hearing in July, 85% favored having the Verde Valley/Sedona area being included with Flagstaff, which is currently LD 6. Also of those in Flagstaff who commented during these COI hearings only one out of over 20 preferred to NOT have Verde Valley/ Sedona included with Flagstaff. So the statement of Commissioners that Verde Valley is divided in its desire to be included with either Prescott or Flagstaff is misleading or just plain FALSE.  20 For included with Flagstaff vs. 1 Against being included with Flagstaff. This is divided, But DEFINITELY NO WHERE NEAR EVENLY DIVIDED.

Respectfully, 
Rita Day

District 17 went from a partisan split slightly in favor of Democrats to a partisan split strongly in favor of Republicans. Moreover, the change dramatically impacted the partisan balance in the rest of the state. Solid Democratic districts were reduced from 13 to ten (competitive analysis pdf for Map 6.0 vs. Map 8.0); solid Republic districts were increased from 13 to 15 (id). And, all of this was done under the rubric of uniting the cities of Marana and Oro Valley even though it did no such thing.
