column5: Comments on CD 6.0 and LD 8.0 Maps
column6:
I ask the Commission to address  a BIG-PICTURE point absent from the current overwhelm focus on details, and to do so before submitting maps for 30-day public review.  This to eliminate current egregious aspects in 8.0 from that review and reduce legal challenges after final maps are released.
Specifically, please review ALL districts in all maps regarding their conformity with all six criteria and inform which criteria in each individual LD and CD districts are NOT met, and, if the Commission is not going to change the non-conformity, please explain clearly and fully why not.

  The following are a few non-compliance examples,  and are not by any means complete.

EXAMPLES OF CURRENT BIG-TIME NON-COMPLIANCE WITH INDIVIDUAL CRITERIA.

RESPECT FOR POLITICAL AND GEOGRAPHICAL BOUNDARIES

-- Kudos for acknowledging in LD 8.0 the mountains on/near the Maricopa and Yavapai boundary as a significant factor in separating Yavapai from Maricopa in the current LD1.

-- But have you acknowledged the east-west mountain range dividing the southern half of LD17 from its northern half?  

COMPACTNESS AND CONTIGUITY

-- How does CD2 6.0 rate on compactness and contiguity?

COMMUNITY OF INTERESTS

-- How does CD2 6.0 rate on COI?

VOTING RIGHTS ACT

-- Why has the Commission, as of last week, dismissed protests of the Hispanic and Native American Community in contrast to the immediate processing of a last-minute submission by the GOP commissioners attempting to immediately configuring those GOP SALC-submitted maps into official draft maps?

COMPETITIVENESS

-- The Commission has five CD's with a competitive spread of 7.4% spread.   How does the Commission justify packing a super-safe 48.4% Dem vote spread into CD3 6.0, which is 21.2% greater than the second highest spread, CD9's super-safe 27.2% GOP spread?  CD3 has the effect, if not a deliberate attempt to dilute Dems in other CDs and diminishing competitiveness. 

-- The same phenomena occurs in LD 8.0 with all three LDs with a 50+% Dem spread, in effect if not deliberately packing Dems there, diluting their presence elsewhere which dilutes competitiveness.  How justified?

-- The general issue is NOT guaranteeing Cave Creek and Carefree, my area, its first Dem state senator since 1982 if not earlier, nor guaranteeing Tucson area Republicans (SALC) a continued GOP representative.  NOT the Commission's job.  It is making each area FAR MORE competitive to the extent possible to give hope to all minority-party voters in current lopsided single-party safe districts that their candidates have a competitive chance of winning. 

-- In 2020 general elections, 3 of 30 or 10% of the LD's state senate races were won by 5% or less.  This Commission can do better than that.  LD 8.0 has 4 LDs of 30 or 13% in the 5% or less spread.  The LD 8.0  map has 6 of 30 LDs or 20% in the 7% or less range.  The LD 8.0, under the 5% spread or 7% spread has 13 Dem LDs and the GOP with FOUR MORE or 17 GOP LDs.  The Commission under the independent, nonpartisan chair can do better than that.

 EQUAL POPULATION. OK on CD and LD Districts.  Yay!

column5: IRC Draft Map
column6:
To Whom It May Concern:

Please consider the following regarding the IRC Draft Map:

CD Test Map Version 6.0: D1

This map version meets a level of competitiveness that is fair and balanced. I commend the Commission on creating this fair and competitive map.

LD Test Map Version 8.0: D3

Currently this map @ 39.79 D to 60.21 R is completely uncompetitive. This is compared to the targeted 46.5 to 53 competitive range that the Commission approved.

I propose incorporating parts of Legislative D8 (64.19 D to 35.81 R) into D3. In particular, I propose adding the Salt River Pima Reservation in its entirety and portions of northern Tempe into LD3 with the intent of balancing competitiveness for the two districts.

I thank the Commission for separating the district from Yavapai County, but urge you to understand the community of interest and draw maps that create a better balance between D3 and D8.

Statewide Competitiveness

In LD Test Map 8.0, there are 11 legislative districts that favor Democrats, 14 that favor Republicans and five that fall within a competitive range. This does not fulfill the intent of fair and competitive districts as established in Prop 106. This limits the possibility of a fair and balanced legislature.

Thank you very much for your time in this matter.

For me personally, in your most recent proposed map, my community of friends and close acquaintances are split into four districts. The proposed map might nevertheless make sense if it served some other more important goals. But it doesn’t. The districts are not “geographically compact.” The proposed districts don’t use “city, town, and county boundaries” In midtown Tucson they do the opposite. The districts aren’t “competitive” either. Assuming the independent vote will split evenly, only District 16 seems competitive. The rest appear to be safe for either democrats or republicans. If somehow you had managed to make make two or more latino majority (or close to majority) districts in the Tucson area, maybe this would be justifiable. But your proposed map doesn’t do that either. The only thing it arguably does is to protect the community of interest in Marana, Oro Valley, Saddlebrook, and parts of Pinal county. Why is that more important than anything else?

column5: Buckeye Farming Communities - LD 16
column6:
My name is Loren Ratlief and I have lived and or farmed in Liberty, which is an area of the Buckeye Valley, for my entire life. I appreciate all of the work that the Independent Redistricting Commission has been doing to ensure redistricting is done in a way that honors communities of interest.

One thing that I have noticed, that should be improved, is the inclusion of the Buckeye farming community in a district that shares similar agriculture interests. It would seem clear to me that the proposed Legislative District 16 would be the best fit for us as it would include the similar communities of Stanfield, Eloy and Casa Grande. Those of us in these communities know each other, work with each other and have ties that run generations deep.

The Liberty community of Buckeye has historically been in the area between Watson and Perryville Roads (going east to west) and Broadway to Lower Buckeye Roads (going from north to south). I would request that this area be placed in the proposed District 16.

Our residents share a common sense of community and devotion to agriculture, an industry reliant on the water policy discussions at the state legislature, with the residents of Maricopa, Stanfield, Casa Grande, Eloy and their surrounding farming areas in Pinal County. As an industry, agriculture has become more and more underrepresented at the Capitol as Arizona has diversified its economy. By grouping our farming community with the urban areas of west Phoenix, Tolleson and Avondale, our collective voice in legislative discussions will be even further diluted.

In the current legislative district 13, our farming community has been aligned with other farming communities in western Maricopa County and Yuma County. This has worked well as our communities are certainly communities of interest. We request similar representation by unifying our community of interest with the farming communities in Pinal County.

Thank you,

Loren Ratlief

column5: IRC Process going forward
column6:
Arizona is no stranger to divisive and coercive hyper-partisanship. It is, after all, what catalyzed the citizens ballot initiative that prompted Arizona voters to create the Independent Redistricting Commission in 2000.  But partisanship need not be nasty, in your face, or even conscious. In fact, unconscious bias has been researched extensively. It often manifests as a rush to judgment that short-circuits the time needed to process information fully and engage in collaborative problem solving.  I believe that is what we saw last week.

It began with Commissioner Mehl preempting control by making a motion almost before the discussion had even begun.  When that tactic met with criticism, it was followed by a period of relatively collaborative give and take.  The Commissioners welcomed input from minority groups and even adopted the Latino Coalition maps.  But this return to what I would characterize as normal procedure was short lived.  Late Wednesday afternoon Commissioner Mehl introduced a totally new map provided to him by the Southern AZ Leadership Council, a group he founded.  That map was accepted, but then removed from consideration the next morning after consultation with the legal team.  But it, or a close facsimile, resurface the same afternoon, this time with Mehl as submitter.  At that point my head was spinning.

As a consistent attendee at IRC meetings, the redistricting process is starting to resemble a chess match, a boxing match, or a debate.  None of these is appropriate because the goal is not for one side or the other to win.  The goal is for the commission to produce fair maps.  In my view, the best way to do that is to for everyone to keep laser focused on the six Constitutional criteria.   

Bias, both conscious and unconscious, are real.  For this reason, personalities and parties should not be center stage.  Let the data speak.  Have the mapping team prepare two reports, one showing how the Southern AZ Legislative map proposed last week by Commissioner Mehl would impact the six criteria and the other report showing how Commissioner Lerner’s proposed changes would impact the six criteria.  These results provide a clear, transparent, and unbiased basis for decision making.  (And should Commissioner Mehl propose yet another LD map for Southern Arizona on Thursday, the mapping team could do the same analyses, though obviously this could delay a decision.)

I have lived here all my life and it’s where my husband and I raise our two daughters. We are heavily involved in our school and community organizations like 4-H.

After looking at the latest legislative draft map, I think it would make most sense to place the farming communities of Buckeye with the proposed Legislative District 16. The reason for this is because our interests and community ties run deeper with the communities of Casa Grande and Eloy than they do with Goodyear and Avondale. This would also help provide for representation at the Capitol that better understand the issues we face on water, agriculture and many other rural issues.

Honoring communities of interest is a critical component of redistricting and I humbly ask that our community can be placed in a district, such as District 16, that reflects our interests, community ties and rural focus.

Thank you,
Morgan Ohlin

column5: Redistricting
column6:
1. The first criterion which must be followed by the AIRC is the United States Constitution and the Voting Rights Act (“VRA”).
Commissioner York announced, without any analysis, that the proposed SALC LD maps strengthened the proposed VRA LDs in southern Arizona. Actually, the opposite is true. The mapping consultants should be requested to compare the southern Arizona VRA LDs in map 4.0 (containing the Latino Coalition proposed districts) to the SALC LDs. When that comparison is made it will be evident that the SALC map weakened the VRA districts. For example, map 4.0 had eight districts with a Hispanic citizen voting population over 43%; map 8.0 only has six such districts. Evidently these maps were drawn without any input from the Latino community so perhaps this is no surprise. Nevertheless, adopting the SALC proposal creates significant litigation risk for the AIRC because it weakens the southern Arizona VRA districts.
 
2. The second constitutional criterion which must be followed by the AIRC is Equal Population
Commissioner Mehl is especially fond of this specific constitutional criterion but the SALC maps fail to meet it. Ironically, Commissioner Mehl mused in passing on the record that a population deviation might be justified in order to sustain SALC’s partisan maps. Legislative District 16 is under population by 11,029 or 4.6%; LD 17 is under population by 6839 or 2.87%; LD 18 is over population by 4668 or 1.96% and LD 19 is over population by 4935 or 2.07%.
 
3. The third constitutional criterion is that districts must be Compact and Contiguous. 
The SALC proposed Legislative Districts may be contiguous but they are plainly not compact, especially district 17. For a senator or representative (or candidate) to drive from the Tanque Verde section of east Tucson to Marana could take over an hour even in light to moderate traffic. And the driver would not even be in his/her own legislative district during the trip. 
 
4. The fourth constitutional criterion is that proposed maps should respect Communities of Interest.
District 17 fails to respect Communities of Interest. With all due respect to Commissioner Mehl and SALC, there is nothing that ties together the east Tucson/Tanque Verde region with Marana and Oro Valley. They do not share the same schools. In fact, there are at least two and maybe three school districts in between the Tanque Verde area and Oro Valley. These communities do not worship together. Residents of Oro Valley/Marana do not share the same economy or employers with east Tucson. No one in east Tucson regularly shops in Oro Valley or Marana. In fact, the only time east Tucsonans would visit Marana would be driving through on the way to Phoenix. Similarly, no one in Oro Valley or Marana visits or shops in east Tucson/Tanque Verde unless they are taking a day trip to Mount Lemmon. 
The SALC map has naturally created a spillover effect in other districts around Tucson.  Portions of midtown Tucson neighborhoods have been joined into Districts 21 and 19 which seem incredibly forced, and certainly not in the interests of those communities.
 

5. The sixth criterion in the Arizona constitution is that maps should favor competitive districts. 
The SALC maps appear to have been drawn in order to gerrymander a Tucson based district for the republican party. District 17 went from a partisan split slightly in favor of Democrats to a partisan split strongly in favor of Republicans. Moreover, the change dramatically impacted the partisan balance in the rest of the state. Solid Democratic districts were reduced from 13 to ten (competitive analysis pdf for Map 6.0 vs. Map 8.0); solid Republic districts were increased from 13 to 15 (id). And, all of this was done under the rubric of uniting the cities of Marana and Oro Valley even though it did no such thing.
 
In sum, this was not about uniting the cities of Marana and Oro Valley. It was about abandoning four days of mapping where the commissioners were trying to draw fair maps in favor of an unvetted partisan map designed to achieve partisan goals. In doing so, this turns the purpose of the AIRC—which is to put a stop to gerrymandering—on its head. 
 
Even worse, if the SALC maps are accepted, it could create a road map for partisan groups in the future to corrupt the AIRC mapping process. The game plan could be used by either side. First, organize partisans to present community of interest testimony that is made up of purely partisan talking points when there is no real community of interest, only a desire to pack a district to elect a candidate of their partisan leaning. Next, ask one of their partisan commissioners use that testimony to contend that a real community of interest exists even though groups are separated by multiple school districts and a mountain range. Finally, arrange for a non-profit affiliate to submit an unvetted, gerrymandered map late in the process with a claim that it advances the supposed communities of interest. This style of partisan gambit could effectively put an end to independent redistricting in Arizona.

column5: defining communities of interest
column6:
Of all the criteria the IRC is tasked with considering as it redraws AZ's voting maps, the one that is the most difficult to define is "communities of interest," and I'm worried it has become a vulnerability in the process.  Could the commission take steps to define what this means more clearly in the interest of institutionalizing a more robust redistricting system?  What qualifies as a "community of interest" in the eyes of the IRC? 

A community of interest could be based on a school district, municipal borders, tribal affiliation, or the much more loosely defined "like-minded people," among so many others.  It is this last definition that most concerns me - in much of the early public comment, it seemed people were defining their community of interest as "the people who vote like me," and I see this approach continuing to influence the process.  Defining a community of interest in this way has the potential to derail every other intention and requirement behind our exemplary independent redistricting process.

However, when we look at the origin of the voter-adopted amendment that created the IRC, it is clear that the intent was to increase citizen engagement and participation by ensuring that districts were competitive to the extent possible (not "safe" for any party) and that representatives were responsive to their constituents.  If we allow "communities of interest" to be defined in a way that violates that intent, we've failed AZ voters.

column5: Objection to Draft Map 9.0
column6:
I object to the legislative boundaries shown on draft map 9.0. As it would apply in Pima County, that draft is not materially different from the districting with which we have live for the past decade. It ignore the dictates of the Arizona Constitution by exalting competitiveness over representation of communities of interest. Basically it requires the suburban parts of Pima County to compete against the densely populated urban areas, and it virtually guarantees that the densely urban interests will prevail. That has been the huge problem with the current maps. As an example, there is a provision of Title 9 ARS that was clearly meant to prohibit the City of Tucson's charging higher water rates for customers outside the city limits. Minor tweaking of the language of that statute would clarify that, but contacting our state legislators about this problem is like banging one's head against a wall. 

The boundaries shown in Drafts 9.1 and 9.2 are much more consistent with the intent of our constitutional scheme. It would basically provide a chance for the suburban, unincorporated, and small town parts of the county to elect representation to advocate for and protect their interests. 

The 2011 maps were upheld by the Supreme Court ONLY because the Commission contended that it had drawn those boundaries to ensure satisfaction of Sec. 5 of the Voting Rights Act. That provision of the VRA has been invalidated by the Court, and can no longer justify establishment of boundaries that violate the one man one vote rule.

First, organize partisans to present community of interest testimony that is made up of purely partisan talking points when there is no real community of interest, only a desire to pack a district to elect a candidate of their partisan leaning. Next, ask one of their partisan commissioners use that testimony to contend that a real community of interest exists even though groups are separated by multiple school districts and a mountain range. Finally, arrange for a non-profit affiliate to submit an unvetted, gerrymandered map late in the process with a claim that it advances the supposed communities of interest. This style of partisan gambit could effectively put an end to independent redistricting in Arizona.

> I am very concerned about the southern Arizona legislative map that the IRC adopted last week. Would they think that the voters of Arizona would be confident that the process they put in place to ensure that the creation of legislative and Congressional districts was fair had been followed? column5: Tucson area redistricting
column6:
I strongly urge the commission to reject Commissioner Mehl's district D17 in LD Test Maps v9.1 & v9.2 and adopt Commissioner Lerner's v9.0 map for the following reasons:

They create a district D17 that is really two geographically separate areas divided by an unpopulated and roadless portion of Catalina Mountains. The map creates 7 competitive seats, defined as being within an 8 point vote margin.  In contrast, Commissioner Mehl's LD Test Maps v9.1 & 9.2 purposely make District 17 a safe Republican district, and only have 6 competitive seats using the 8-point criteria.  The statewide balance under Mehl’s maps would tilt the state totals even further toward the Republicans (13 Democratic seats and 17 Republican seats).

4. As described in the Oct 27 Arizona Daily Star article, Commissioner Mehl and the Southern Arizona Leadership Council have proposed LD Test Maps v9.1 & v9.2 for the partisan goal of creating a safe Republican district in the Tucson area. The Arizona Constitution does not have that goal as a legitimate redistricting goal.

column5: Proposed Map concerns
column6:
Hello,

I share Commissioner Lerner’s concerns about the inclusion of the Southern Arizona Leadership Council Districts.
Those districts were submitted to the Commission late Wednesday, and there is no information on the process that SALC - a special interest group - used to draw them.
I echo Commissioner Lerner’s question: Did they consult the southern Arizona Latino communities when drafting these districts? This is a question that must be addressed.
The Commission must draw districts that adhere to the U.S. Voting Rights Act, which was written to ensure that the voting power of historically marginalized communities of color are protected under law.
The voting power of Native American, Latino and other communities of color should be protected by the Independent Redistricting Commission. To dismiss the proposals from the Navajo Nation without serious consideration and analysis, and to completely reject the legislative districts submitted by the Latino Coalition with little justification, were decisions completely counter to this duty.
The immediate embrace of a map submitted late in the process by a special interest group, and the Republican Commissioners’ attempt to immediately force those district configurations into the official draft maps, was alarming and completely counter to the intent of independent redistricting.
Voters in Pima County strongly condemn Republicans’ attempts to define Arizona voting districts according to the wishes of powerful single-interest entities. As citizens of our proudly multicultural, multiethnic county, we in Pima stand firmly with our Indigenous neighbors as they assert their Constitutional right to fair representation and unfettered access to the vote.

column5: Deep concerns about the inequity of Map 8.0
column6:
Dear IRC members:

As an Arizona resident, I always felt confident that the state's redistricting would be equitable. After all, it has an Independent Redistricting Commission.

I have been following the IRC process. Your most recent map — 8.0 — is neither independent nor equitable.

Statewide

Map 8.0 creates 15 firm Republican districts (up two) while reducing solid Democratic districts to 10 (down three). 
   **According to figures from the Arizona Secretary of State’s office, the July 2021 breakdown of party affiliation was 34.72 percent Republican, 31.82 percent Democratic, and 32.60 percent independent. These figures would not justify the large shift in districts toward the Republican party.

In addition, Map 8.0 has created 17 districts whose racial makeup are from between 57.2 percent to 80.6 percent white. According to the US Census Department (https://www.census.gov/library/stories/state-by-state/arizona-population-change-between-census-decade.html):
   **Arizona’s diversity index rose from 54.9 percent to 61.1 percent. 
   **Non-white racial makeup was: Black alone — 12.4 percent, Hispanic —18.7 percent, Asian alone — 6 percent, American Indian/Alaska Native alone — 1.1 percent, Native Hawaiian/other Pacific Islander alone — 0.2 percent, some other race alone — 8. 4 percent. Arizonans of two or more races were 10.2 percent. 
   **Despite those who are white alone only being 61.6 percent of the population, it is unlikely that 17 districts out of 25 would have between 57.2 percent to 80.6 percent white population — unless they were drawn to achieve that end. 

Pima County

I am a resident of Pima County.

Currently, the county has four legislative districts. Map 8.0 creates seven districts that are combined with six other counties: Cochise, Graham, Greenlee, Pinal, Santa Cruz, and Yuma. In addition, the map creates two safe Republican districts. Why?
   **The county’s registration makeup is 40.3 percent Democratic, 28.7 Republican, and 31.0 independent.

The only conclusion that can be drawn is that these districts were created to diminish the Pima County’s Democratic majority.
    **Example: District 18 — This district has been drawn to dilute the Tucson Foothills, which is strongly Democratic by putting it with Republican areas. Map 8.0 puts the Foothills in a political concoction with Tucson National Estates in Oro Valley, the area south of Grant, and Rolling Hills Country Club.

I am asking you to revisit Map 8.0 and create independent, equitable districts that provide voting power to all Arizonans — not just white and Republican voters.

Thank you.

leslie j yerman

I am hoping that the commission will use CD draft map version 6.0 and LD draft map version 9.0 as starting points for discussion on Thursday, October 28th. I am also hopeful that the commission with keep in mind all the constitutional requirement while adjusting these draft map versions including:
* community of interest - Oro Valley's larger community of interest is Casas Adobes and Tucson. Oro Valley shouldn't be split into separate LDs. Oro Valley should be in a Pima County legislative district. 
* respect for natural and city/county boundaries - Oro Valley should be in a Pima County LD and shouldn't extend into Pinal County. Mountains are natural barriers and Oro Valley's LD should end at the Catalina Mountains.
* compactness - Oro Valley shouldn't be in a sprawling district. It is suburban- urban. The proposed Legislative District 17 in LD draft map version 9.1 and 9.2 give outsized representation to rural places with which Oro Valley has little in common.
* competitiveness - no party should be given a competitive advantage in the purple state of AZ. LD draft map version 9.1 and 9.2 give Republicans an unfair advantage due to packing Democrats into districts. 
* equal in population - districts should stay within the 1% variance of the target population.

column5: LD Test Maps comparison
column6:
THE ARIZONA CONSTITUTION STATES:

• "Districts shall be geographically compact and contiguous to the extent practicable"

Yet, in Mehl's LD Test Maps v9.1 & v9.2 it is clear that in an attempt to create a non-competitive district for Republicans, D17 includes voters living in a community on the northeast side of Tucson with 2 communities on the northwest side of Tucson, which in reality are SEPARATED by the CATALINA MOUNTAIN RANGE! 

By comparison, Lerner’s D17 in map LDv9.0 keeps all of the suburban residents in a compact, contiguous area.

•"District boundaries shall respect communities of interest to the extent practicable"

The communities of Oro Valley and Marana share almost nothing with the Tanque Verde area of residents, and in fact, Mehl’s maps intentionally cut Tanque Verde off from the Tucson area where Tanque Verde residents are employed, attend school, shop, socialize, and attend religious services. 

By comparison, Lerner's districts D17 and D18 in LD Test Map v9.0 keep local communities together.

•"To the extent practicable, district lines shall use visible geographic features, city, town and county boundaries, and undivided census tracts”

Yet Mehl's district D17 as shown in LD Test Maps v9.1 & 9.2 creates a district D17 that tries to include 2 geographically areas separated by an UNPOPULATED ROADLESS portion of the Catalina MOUNTAINS! One would have to drive more than 45 minutes OUTSIDE THE DISTRICT to get from the Tanque Verde community to the Oro Valley-Marana area.

•"To the extent practicable, competitive districts should be favored where to do so would create no significant detriment to the other goals."

Yet Mehl's LD Test Maps v9.1 & 9.2 purposely make District 17 a NON-COMPETITIVE Republican district, and only have 6 competitive seats using the 8-point criteria. The statewide balance under Mehl’s maps would tilt the state totals even further toward the Republicans (13 Democratic seats and 17 Republican seats).

By comparison, Lerner's LD Test Map v9.0 makes District 17 a VERY COMPETITIVE district, and balances the statewide totals of predicted party seats relatively evenly (14 Democratic seats & 16 Republican seats).  The map creates 7 competitive seats, defined as being within an 8 point vote margin.

Despite the fact that the Arizona Constitution clearly states that "competitive districts should be favored where to do so would create no significant detriment to the other goals”… Mehl and the SALC are blatantly disregarding the AZ Constitution by doing everything possible to create a “safe” Republican district in the Tucson area!

.to four horses who will then be driven at once toward the four corners of the plaza, pulling the arms and legs from his body. column5: Reallocating Populations in Districts 12, 13, and 14 to lower the overall levels ot deviation to be close to 2%
column6:
I support the Commission’s goal of trying to keep each Legislative District in the state as near as possible to being equal in population. I reside near the corner of Lindsay Road and Riggs Road in Chandler. As of the time of this writing, this would be in the new District 13. Its population is 2.02% over the target population you aspire each district to have. The district to the west of my district, Legislative District 12, has a population deviation that is 3.55% over the target population goal. The district to the east of mine, District 14, has a population that is close to the target population, but still is 0.66% over the target population goal. 

It is the Commission’s goal to have each district with a percentage of population deviation from the target population goal to be as close to zero as possible. There are no districts abutting Districts 12 which have significantly lower levels of population deviation. There is only one district that abuts District 13 that has a lower level of population deviation: District 14

May I respectfully suggest that the three districts that comprise portions of the Town of Gilbert and the City of Chandler, south of the 202, Districts 12, 13, and 14, might be able to get to a lower level of deviation in each District if seen together as a block. What would happen if the levels of deviation from the population goal in those three districts were to be added together, and then divided by 3. That would come to an average deviation level for each District of 2.08%.

Proposed District 13 is now very near that level of deviation. I believe that reducing some of the population in District 12, adding it to District 13, and removing a similar level of population in District 13 and adding it to District 14. Here is how I would suggest how this could be accomplished:

Four square miles of District 12, bounded by Ray Road, Price Road, the 202 alignment, and Rural Road could be added to District 13. All of this area is part of the City of Chandler. Simultaneously, about six square miles in District 13 could be subtracted and moved to District 14. The area I am suggesting would be the one-mile wide strip between the 202 freeway, Greenfield, the County line/Hunt Highway, and Val Vista Road.  All of this is in the Town of Gilbert. Almost half of it presently is rural and agricultural. Val Vista Road is a major highway, some of which is the boundary between Chandler and Gilbert. This would leave the majority of the Town of Gilbert intact in one District. I believe that those two moves would make each of the three Districts, 12, 13, and 14, each very close to the deviation from the population goal very near 2.08%.

Thank you again for your consideration of this respectful suggestion.

Especially when other viable submitted maps from other communities were essentially dismissed without a serious look.  The fact that the openly-admitted motivation of these maps is to create a safe Republican district flies in the face of the constitutional goal of creating  competitive districts wherever possible.   The process and the intent behind these maps I believe are a violation of the public trust, and would undermine that trust.

column5: The moral basis for fair maps
column6:
To quote  a recent article published in “The Bulwark” by noted Conservative William Kristol and others,
“democracy depends on free and fair elections, respect for the rights of others, the rule of law, [and] a commitment to truth …All of these are now in serious danger.”

He then discusses the recent false accusations against  elections in Arizona by many in the Republican Party… and other efforts  “to discredit the very practice of free and fair elections.”

This is why the work that you commissioners are doing is so important.  The work you do underpins the moral basis for our democracy.  The principle that all men (ard women)  are created equal and endowed by their creator with unalienable rights.

If  the  commissioners can put aside the idea that this is just another contest to be won, just another chance to move the football a little closer to your own political goalpost, and instead realize that you are architects of  democracy - then  you will be bolstering the future of our country.

Your legacy will be based on how much you were able to step back from your short term goals  and look at the bigger picture of what future you are creating. In your hearts, are you working from a commitment to truth, a desire to make the fairest possible maps?

I understand that Commissioner Mehl is working with SALC to create a safe Republican district in Pima county  and this will make it easier to promote Pima County business interests in the state legislature. I understand that the commission will vote on a map which incorporates districts created for this purpose.  And I can see from statistical analysis of partisanship  and wasted votes that this map (8.0), is not “free and fair” but favors Republicans in 80% or more scenarios.  9.1 and 9.2 are even less fair. 

In normal times, perhaps a little unfairness would not be a big deal. We all know that the choice of who would fill the Independent slot was likely to be someone more favorable to Republicans, given the fact that Ducey controlled the board who selected the candidates.

But these are not normal times.  Again as Kristol writes, speaking about ensuring that elections are fair.

“democracy itself is in serious danger. “We need to join together to defend [It]”
…
Now is the time for leaders in all walks of life—for citizens of all political backgrounds and persuasions—to come to the aid of the Republic.”

A map with a 3.4 % partisan bias towards Republicans is not good enough.  It is not fair. It is also not fair to adopt a map for Pima county based wholesale on suggestions from a business league, while ignoring scores of other maps submitted, including the Latino Coalition's.

The commission has a sacred duty to our state and country to put the principle of democracy 
above the economic interest of a group of Pima county businesses and to do the absolute best you can to closely adhere to all of your constitutional requirements... And make the fairest least partisan map you can that respects the needs of all of Arizona.  If you do this, your legacy  will  be that  of a protector of democracy, that you came to the aid of the state of Arizona and of the country when it needed you most.

Thank you all for the long hours and  hard work you have given to this purpose.

column5: Redistricting CD9
column6:
Chairman Neuberg and Commissioners Watchman, Mehl, Lerner and York: 
I live in Kingman and frequently support businesses in Bullhead and Lake Havasu City. I respectfully submit these comments today in opposition of the proposed Congressional District 9.  
 
While our current congressional district isn’t perfect, and includes portions of metropolitan Phoenix and Maricopa County, it primarily encompasses more rural geography. The proposed new district however, highly favors the populated areas of western Maricopa County. 
 
The proposed District 9 does include most of Arizona’s west coast, which is appropriate; however, it dovetails into the west valley communities including Sun City West, Surprise, Luke Air Force Base, Goodyear and Buckeye, where at least 70 percent of the proposed district’s population reside.
This is clearly not representative of the residents of Kingman, Bullhead and Lake Havasu City, nor the residents of greater Mohave, La Paz and Yuma Counties.
In a district with these demographics, the chances of representation from and for rural communities would be unlikely. 
 
All Arizonans matter and all voices should have equal opportunities to be heard. We should not be punished with the potential of under-representation
for choosing to live and work in rural Arizona. I urge you to reconsider the proposed alignment of Congressional District 9 in an effort that more fairly
 represents the rural voice of western Arizona.
 
Thank you for your action!

column5: Keep Greater Scottsdale Together
column6:
The current draft maps and previous iterations have, in varying ways, split Scottsdale into two or three legislative districts.  As much as is practicable, greater Scottsdale should be kept together.

Keeping greater Scottsdale together is wholly consistent with all six of the constitutional criteria for drawing a district.  At roughly 240,000 people, it is within the margin of error for equal population. 

Keeping greater Scottsdale together achieves compactness and contiguousness.  It incorporates visible geographic features.  The geographic footprint of Scottsdale remains virtually in tact as does the Salt River Pima-Maricopa community.  It includes all of the unique features of both: urban, suburban and rural.  

Further, it creates competitiveness that the previous draft iterations do not.  It comes very close to creating parity between the two major political parties with the advantage slightly favoring Republicans.  Keeping greater Scottsdale together offers the opportunity for legislative candidates to run and govern from the middle, thereby serving the majority of voters in the proposed greater Scottsdale district.  

We already know that this level of party parity works.  Two examples in the city of Scottsdale are the City Council and the Scottsdale Unified School District Governing Board.  Both are composed of centrist candidates from both parties and both govern as citizen-centric. 

This greater Scottsdale district also complies with the Voting Rights Act in ways that the current LD23 does not. 

The proposed greater Scottsdale district has a compelling economic community of interest that includes tourism, local business interests on the 101 corridor south of 90th Street, along with Scottsdale Community College - all of which are on tribal lands.  

Putting these two communities together also preserves their mutual interest in sustainable land use, respect for the individual character of diverse and distinct neighborhoods, a culture of citizen involvement, environmental stewardship & open space preservation, along with a citizen-centric focus on planning, community building & decision-making.

Both communities - Scottsdale and the Salt River Pima-Maricopa Indian community value their unique sense of place.  The IRC should value that as well by keeping greater Scottsdale together.

You are invited to refer to map #CDF009.  While this map has a CD designation, it is a legislative district map that implements the forgoing.  It was developed and submitted by Scottsdale resident, Emily Wilson.

Thank you for your time and consideration

Victoria Kauzlarich
Scottsdale Resident

column5: Redistricting: Draft Map Series 9

Hi, I live at Grand Avenue and Taylor Street and I just wanted to highlight my support for including a legislative district centered around the light rail which connects communities from Uptown to Downtown Phoenix. 

Additionally, I am in general support of the Latino Coalition maps. While I prefer keeping Central City Village as close together as possible, there certainly is a strong connection between Central City South and South Phoenix. There are also very strong communities that are correctly grouped together in the Latino Coalition maps in the western side of Phoenix.

When it comes to the broader maps, I do defer to the Navajo Nation's comments on those that affect tribal impacts. I think it is very important to respect communities such as the tribes and others protected by the Voting Rights Act. 

After that, I think it is possible to add as much competitiveness as possible to congressional and legislative districts. Most Arizonans are not the dedicated partisans that are so engaged in these processes. As someone who has knocked many a door and convinced folks to vote with candidates not of their own party, Arizonans care a lot more about getting pragmatic things done to help their local communities have great education, safe transportation and a strong network of jobs in their neighborhoods. We can't get there without working together and we don't work together when we don't talk to people who have different opinions from us. Packing more voters into "safe" districts prevents this. If you only have to talk to the most extremely opinionated voters to win and there is no true competition, we won't work together and we won't achieve these major goals. Maps should represent Arizonans' diverse opinions, not whether given two choices they prefer red or blue.

Thank you for your hard work and I hope you come out to more communities in Phoenix as the draft maps are approved.

column5: Redistributing maps
column6:
Why is it that everything residents from Maricopa southward get what they want and not a single commissioner has registered the valid points made by the continually overlooked residents of Northern Arizona. Why do you not listen?

You want communities of interest. The maps you have presented are an outrage. They skew heavily to Republican interests  and totally ignore common sense. Splitting Sedona disadvantages some of our residents by making it impossible for the city to vote as a whole. 

Sedona belongs with the entire Verde Valley and Flagstaff. We have proven over and over that we have nothing in common with the Quad Cities (Prescott) and do not want to be lumped in with them. Politically, you then essentially deliver political control to Prescott. Do not take away the Yavapai-Apache Nation. They are a part of the Verde Valley. Your total disregard of the Navajo points of view is simply disrespectful. They should be entitled to handle their own decisions in this area and presented very reasonable maps. Please tell me which group is most entitled to make their own points. If you do not say Navajo, that’s insulting to our Native American neighbors. 

Please stop caving in to business and political pressure and do what’s right. If you don’t, you are basically taking away our ability to elect the people we want to serve. There will be no fair contests when you place Sedona (purple) with flaming red Prescott-area towns. Be fair to us please.

So far very little seems fair or reasonable. This is our future for the next ten years and right now we are not being treated fairly. How is it that Tucson gets whatever it wants. All but one of you live out of our area. Try to understand that we are different from the rest of the state and deserve fairness.

Thank you.

column5: Redistricting of Scottsdale's boundaries
column6:
To the IRC: 
I am a current resident in Scottsdale, AZ and I have been watching the hard task of redistricting our legislative districts. I am concerned with spreading the current LD 23 so far to the west and into urban areas. I cannot imagine trying to find a facility that would be large enough and not creating a significant amount of time for travel. This would lessen the participation in this crucial legislative process. This is what I would like to propose:
Remove the far western parts of new LD3 into another adjacent district in that vicinity and have new LD3 regain Scottsdale precincts to the city's current western border near Scottsdale Road and further to the south (from LD4 & LD8). This may also include removing Cave Creek and Carefree from LD 3 and having those communities join another LD to the north. This would essentially largely preserve what is currently LD23, resist much of Scottsdale being "lost" to Tempe, and allow beneficial changes in adjacent districts to our west and northwest (the current LD15).
Thank you for your consideration,
Jeff Goracke

column5: Adopt CD6
column6:
I live in Oro Valley.  I request that the committee adopt CD6, for the following reasons:
* community of interest - Oro Valley shouldn't be split into separate LDs.

* compactness - Oro Valley shouldn't be in a sprawling district. It is suburban- urban. The proposed Legislative District 17 in LD draft map version 9.1 and 9.2 give outsized representation to rural places with which Oro Valley has little in common.
* competitiveness - no party should be given a competitive advantage in the purple state of AZ. LD draft map version 9.1 and 9.2 give Republicans an unfair advantage due to packing Democrats into districts. Only 9.0 comes close to being representative of AZ's competitiveness.
* equal in population - districts should stay within the 1% variance of the target population.

I believe the proposed d3 should be adjusted not to include Care Free, Cave Creek, or North Phoenix, and instead should include the areas of Scottsdale in proposed D8.  The areas of Tempe currently proposed to be included in D8 should be included in D11 or D12.  This would make more logical sense and would be a less dramatic shift from the current districts.

For Congressional districts, again District 1 seems to combine communities that have little in common.  District 1 sweeps into Phoenix and extends all the way to Lake Roosevelt.  This makes little sense.  It seems more logical to combine district 3 and district 8 and divide district 1 into two separate districts.  This will provide a better representation in congress for ALL constituents of Arizona.  There is no reason the interests of those voters living east of the 87 should be lumped in with the interests of those voters near downtown phoenix.

Thank you,

column5: Drafts maps Sedona, Verde Valley, Flagstaff
column6: Community is what binds us together.  It is what helps to make civil society more civil.  We may not always agree, but if we share a common set of needs, access to shared resources, and proximity, we are more likely to focus on solutions.  Actions such as those taken for the draft maps of LD5, LD6 and LD7 are tearing established communities apart.  As we have consistently advocated, community of interest, city boundaries, town boundaries and geographic boundaries all act to bring out area together.  Breaking Sedona within the city is blow against the community.  Failure to link the Village of Oak Creek to Sedona separates shared services (school, fire, library).  Breaking Sedona from Flagstaff with an intervening district fails to support and honor our shared land resources, and services.  Failure to link the Verde Valley disavows our shared economies and facilities.  Linking to Prescott across Mingus Mountain does not make sense to how we shop, access medical facilities or support our tourist resources.  Community works best when respected by a shared effort to keep it whole.  Please step forward as the Independent Redistricting Commission and correct these grievous oversights.

column5: Redistricting
column6:
I have lived in Arizona for over 35 years. The proposed redistricting map again, as in 2011, seems to favor Democrats over Republicans.  I can only speak for the area that I have lived in these past 35 years, which is North Phoenix, first south of the 101, and presently north of the 101.  

The area from the 101 to around Cactus (north to south) and from Scottsdale Rd. to I-17 (east to west) is predominately Republican (presently part of LD15, and previously part of LD7.  The new map proposes to  have this district include all the way to Osborn.  According to the percentages shown on the proposed redistricting map, this is now going to be tilted Democratic.  More importantly, there is a huge difference in social-economic lifestyles, shopping, income, etc. between the north and south.  It makes no sense to combine them.

Also, combining the present LD15 with LD23 makes no sense unless the goal of the commission is to reduce one Republican senator and two Republican representatives in the legislature. They are deleting the southern portion and western portion of LD15 and combining it within a much larger LD23.  This proposed area is now huge, and still includes rural areas east and north of Fountain Hills, which should be lumped in with Payson.  You are proposing to divide Scottsdale into 3 sections which makes no sense as again north Scottsdale from south Scottsdale are two different entities.  Scottsdale Rd. has always been, and should remain, the dividing line between LD15 and LD23.  It makes more sense to have LD15 have boundaries along the 101 on the south, Scottsdale Rd on the east, Carefree/Cave Creek or up to Anthem on the north, and the I-17 on the west.  These are common sense boundaries.  Please reconsider.  Thank you.

column5: More compact Tucson LDs in the draft map
column6:
The geometry of proposed Legislative District 21 has become progressively more tortured between Version 5 and the current approved draft maps. A long, relatively thin tendril of this district now reaches past I10 into Tucson. 

As a resident of the neighboring proposed LD 18, this has consequences for my representation in the state government. In Version 5, LD18 covered my home, my partner's employer, our doctors, the public high school a few minutes away, another local school where I volunteer, and the majority of businesses that we visit on a weekly basis. In the present draft maps, the incursion of LD21 and resulting shifts in LD18 and LD20 have resulted in these community resources being split across the domains of three different state representatives. 

When facing issues related to employment, healthcare, education, and business in my community, I will  infrequently be in the constituency of the politicians representing the areas where these issues arise.

There will always be some fraction of the state population that straddles LD borders, especially in urban areas where the population must be divided to ensure proportional representation. However, maps that needlessly increase the number of boundary intersections in densely populated areas like Tucson also needlessly inflate the fraction of people facing this situation.

Please consider revising the LD boundaries in and around Tucson to more closely resemble those in Version 5 in order to provide a more compact and coherent districts for residents like me. Thank you for your time serving Arizona in this important work.

column5: Legislative Redistricting
column6:
Article 4 Part 2 Section 1 of the Arizona Constitution
(14)
C. Districts shall be geographically compact and contiguous to the extent practicable – Creating a gerrymandered district that starts at Marana, runs through Oro Valley, leaving out Casas Adobes,  and around Tucson’s northern and eastern edge to take in Tanque Verde and Vail solely for the purpose of creating a Republican leaning district violates this requirement
.D. District boundaries shall respect communities of interest to the extent practicable;
E. To the extent practicable, district lines shall use visible geographic features, city, town and county boundaries, and undivided census tracts;
F. To the extent practicable, competitive districts should be favored where to do so would create no significant detriment to the other goals. – David Mehl has stated (Arizona Daily Star, Oct 28 2021) that there needs to be at least one district with a Republican edge.  This map clearly does not create a competitive district.  By Mr. Mehl’s own admission, it specifically creates a Republican district.

Casas Adobe, along with the Flowing Wells area, should be included in LD17, keeping Amphi and Catalina Foothills school districts in the same political district.

Vail and the Tanque Verde valley should be included in LD21 to make that district more competitive.

Voter registrations in Pima County are about 40% Democrats, 28.5% Republicans and 30.4% independents, plus a handful of Libertarians, so the legislative districts would naturally tend to lean Democratic.

Follow the Arizona Constitution and create competitive districts as much as possible.  

If Ms. Neuberg is truly an independent, she should strive to fairly create legislative districts that do not favor a specific party.  Agreeing to create a district to give accountability to the right of center folks, as she has stated, is not an independent point of view.

Thank you,

William Read

After many many weeks of asking for and explaining why there should be at least one competitive district in Northern Arizona, our requests have LARGELY FALLEN ON DEAF EARS. Competition at the ballot box is what this state wants and needs.

LD5 could make up for the Verde Valley population by going into Mohave County where rural and conservative sentiments better align.  They get their representation without compromising a competitive district next door.  

The adjacent LD6 version submitted by Coconino County BOS as LDF051 is also a great improvement.  It fixes the current problem of packing 71.22% of Democrats into LD6, with the new boundaries showing at 57.9%.  This version of LD6 keeps Navajo and Apache counties whole (where they are now split in your current LD6 version) and puts Winslow in with the Native lands. All of us make up a cohesive community with cultural, educational, and geographic ties to each other and we should be grouped together. Additionally, as communities that border the First Nations, we best understand their needs and problems and should therefore remain together. Please do not separate us! We belong together!

column5: Keep Scottsdale Separate - No Redistricting!
column6:
I am a resident of North Scottsdale (zip code 85255). In learning recently about the propsed redistricting ideas, I was shocked to hear that there is an attempt to merge Scottsdale with areas such as Desert Ridge and Deer Valley. it absolutely makes NO sense for Desert Ridge and Deer Valley airport to be in my district. I live, shop and conduct all of my personal business in the Scottsdale area. The Western Boundary for Scottsdale, Fountain Hills and the Rio Verde district should be the city line which is Scottsdale Road, not the I-17!!!

Scottsdale, Fountain Hills and Rio Verde are quite different areas and populations age wise than Desert Ridge and near the I-17. I do not support this change nor see value in the merge. Our communities have different needs and therefore need to be separated, not paired into the same district.

Thank you.

column5: Maps 7.1 and 10.0
column6:
I am a Sun City West resident and believe both the CD 9 and LD29 maps as drawn do not meet the standards for competitiveness nor for community interest. CD9 is almost entirely rural except for the Sun City West/Surprise portion. LD22 is not a competitive District and needs additional Democratic voters added. 
I believe by trying to keep Yavapai County complete has resulted in a map, which effects the Northern, Western and Northwest Valley sections on the State as completely non competitive.

column5: Fair Voting Districts
column6:
The proposed redistricting map has split our town of Sedona into separate legislative districts. Our sense of community is important to us here and dividing us up like this risks pulling our community apart. I strongly feel that it would benefit us all to be represented by a single set of legislators. I ask you to please restore our unity. 
I appreciate this opportunity to express my thoughts and thank you all for your dedication and for the hard work you have already put in on this critical issue of redistricting our state. 
With sincere thanks,
Fredi Olster

column5: LD8
column6:
I reside in the southern end of Tempe near Guadalupe and Price roads. My community of interest for church, shopping, medical care, exercise, recreation, restaurants, etc. (same for many people in my neighborhood) is south Tempe, west Mesa, and west Chandler. The current draft map has my neighborhood part of LD8 with north Tempe, Salt River Indian Community, and northeast Scottsdale including Gainey Ranch, all of which we have zero common interest. 

LD8 has 8978 fewer voters relative to the target voter count. Just south of us is LD12, which has 8452 excess voters relative to the target vote count. My neighborhood should be part of the south Tempe LD.

column5: Redistricting Northern AZ
column6:
Dear Commissioners,
It is absurd to keep Yavapai County whole, by sacrificing communities of interest, contiguity, and competitiveness in LDs 5, 6 and 7. You can easily correct all this issues by adopting them maps proposed by the Coconino County Board of Supervisors and supported by the City of Sedona. Please do so!.

column5: Redistricting Map
column6:
Dear Commissioners,
Please adopt the maps proposed by the Coconino County Board of Supervisors and supported by the City of Sedona. Splitting up Sedona will cause irreparable harm.

column5: Redistricting
column6:
Flowing downhill northward from Nogales, the Santa Cruz River, I-19 teeming with produce and maquila trucks, and the BNSFRR nourish our smallest county.  From the east, it's joined by the tributary from Elgin, Sonoita and Patagonia; north again through Rio Rico, Tumacacori, Carmen and Tubac, joined at Amado by Arivaca from the west.  On to Green Vally, Sahuarita and finally, Tucson.
We who live here depend on this lifeline for our food, shelter, transportation.  For our education, safety, health care; for our representation in government; our entertainment, relaxation.  We are alive and united by the arteries of this corridor.
And now, the smooth continuation of all this is in your hands.  We implore you, please do not derail the efficient functioning of this lifeline.  Please, do not chop off pieces here and there, tossing them randomly into unwanted oblivion with unaccepting recipients.  Allow the current calm and equitable operations to continue.
Please.  Thank you.

column5: Congressional Draft Map
column6:
The Draft Congressional Map turns CD2 which has been Arizona’s most competitive district into a strong Republican district with no apparent justification. Prescott has been happily co-existing with the Colorado River district and should stay there. That helps Mohave County which doesn’t want to be with urban Maricopa. Graham and Greenlee counties have more in common with northeastern and north central Arizona than those areas have with the Colorado River communities. There is no good reason to mix up the historical alignment of CD2 and two very bad reasons to use the Draft Map configuration: Reducing competitiveness and reducing the voices of our Native American communities. 

The Navajo Nation has submitted a proposed revision to CD 2 which I support. It is CDF010. The draft map of CD 2 does not honor the constitutional criteria of competitiveness or communities of interest. The map submitted by the Navajo Nation does so and gives our Native American Arizonans a stronger voice in Congress.

column5: Redistricting
column6:
Why are you trying to destroy the scottsdale that I know by changing the lines?? I dont live, eat, drive or even interact with people on the I-17 or that far away. I simply dont want my tax money/ school money to be spended on areas that I really dont have any gain or interest. 
The western boundary for the scottsdale, fountain hills, rio verde district should be the city line, which is SCOTTSDALE RD.  not I-17. 
What is is the purpose of these??

column5: LD Map 10.2 and CD Map 7.1
column6:
My name is Bernard Miller and I live in Gilbert. 
In reviewing the Legislative District map I have many concerns. I have lived in NW Gilbert for over 27 years. The proposed LD Map 10.2 does not respect Gilbert’s community of interest or town boundaries. It separates Gilbert into five different districts. The Heritage District of Gilbert is the heart and soul of the community with shops, restaurants, a farmer’s market and many parades and special events throughout the year. Yet it is placed in a district with Ahwatukee which is on the other side of the county and shares no community of interest with Gilbert.
I strongly encourage you to respect the city boundaries and keep Gilbert whole. The northern boundary should be Baseline and the western boundary should be Arizona Ave.
I would also like to request that a Draft Map Hearing be scheduled in the East Valley. Not a single hearing is scheduled in the East Valley and I can see no good reason why that is so.
In reviewing CD Map 7.1 I also have concerns. It again groups Gilbert together with areas that share no community of interest. I ask that you keep Gilbert together with Queen Creek and Mesa. The district needs to stay within Maricopa County and not include parts of Pinal County.

column5: Comment on the most recent maps
column6: As a 35-year resident of Northern Arizona (both in Coconino County and Yavapai County) I am sorely disappointed and very upset about the latest maps that take Sedona and the Verde Valley out of the same districts as Flagstaff.  This decision by Chairs Neuberg and Commissioners York and Mehl truly reeks of partisanship and gerrymandering.  Chair Neuberg can proclaim all she wants that she is an Independent, but she is only fooling herself because no one else believes it based on her voting record and siding with the Republican Commissioners on just about everything from the hiring of Brian Schmidt to these latest so-called "approved" maps.  For Chair Neuberg and Commissioners York and Mehl to say that there is no consensus on keeping the Verde Valley separate from Prescott means that they are either completely ignoring the public comments from voters and local public officials who understand that keeping Sedona and the Verde Valley with Flagstaff is based on sound reasoning (economic, commercial, healthcare, geographic, infrastructure) or they really just don't want to hear about sound reasoning and instead are listening to their partisan buddies or are listening to members of the public who have no concept of the constitutional criteria or redistricting and think the commission is going to be redrawing County lines, or they too are looking to see these districts gerrymandered and not competitive because of their partisanship.  This needs to stop for the good of the State.  The commissioners need to start listening to all sides of the fence and stop with the gerrymandered districts.

column5: Redistricting of Scottsdale
column6: Hi, I'm an investment professional and mom of 5 in Scottsdale. We stay within Scottsdale for church, business and shopping. Deer Valley and Desert Ridge make no sense being part of the district. I'm against it. Scottsdale Rd not Hwy 17 should be the western boundary.

column5: Splitting Sedona and the Verde Valley from Flagstaff
column6: I just read the public comment submitted on 11/3 by Yavapai County Supervisor James Gregory.  He states that "I strongly disagree with the Coconino proposal to split the county in half. This proposal is being pushed from a group in Sedona. This does not reflect the opinion in the rest of Yavapai County or the rest of the Verde Valley."  The commission needs to ignore this comment because James Gregory is not speaking for the "rest" of Yavapai County or the "rest" of the Verde Valley.  This is his partisan opinion. I live in Dewey (not part of what he calls a group in Sedona) and I do not agree that Sedona should be split in districts and that the Verde Valley should be in the same districts are Prescott and the rest of Yavapai County.  If you read the public comments submitted, you will see that most of the people from these areas (who have submitted comments) feel the same way I do.  Verde Valley Medical Center and Sedona Medical Center are part of Northern Arizona Healthcare (which includes Flagstaff Medical Center).  These two hospitals are not associated with any of the medical centers in Prescott.  It's presumptive of Mr. Gregory to insinuate that people in the Verde Valley only shop in Prescott Valley.  That is not true.  With the horrific traffic in Prescott Valley, it is actually easier for residents in the Verde Valley to go to Flagstaff to shop. With or without traffic, it takes less time to drive to Flagstaff from Cottonwood than it does to drive to Prescott Valley from Cottonwood.  Again, read the comments of the people from these areas and you will see that the majority of these folks do not want the Verde Valley lumped in with the Prescott Quad-City area.  They want to be with Sedona and Flagstaff because that is where their community of interest lies.  Read the public comments.

column5: legislative district draft map
column6: I'm distressed that the draft legislative map ignores natural geographic and municipal boundaries and a preponderance of evidence related to economic, social, and environmental communities of interest in the northern part of the state. I know from watching/listening to most of your meetings and hearings that you have heard from MANY more people about interests uniting the Flagstaff/Oak Creek/Sedona/Cottonwood/Verde Valley corridor, than from those favoring keeping Yavapai County whole. I am enthusiastic about the proposal from the Coconino County Board of Supervisors to keep this corridor intact in a single district (subsequently keeping Flagstaff connected to most of its outlying areas, keeping Sedona intact, and also keeping the Yavapai - Apache tribal lands whole and connected with the Verde Valley. This plan reflects the wishes of the majority (including local government leaders in these communities), creates a very competitive district, AND makes more sense than keeping Yavapai County whole while ignoring all these other geographic, natural, and social connections. Please incorporate this proposal from the Coconino County BoS into your northern Arizona map for legislative districts.

column5: LD 17
column6:
The inclusion of Tanque Verde and Vail in LD 17 creates a significant barrier to participation in the democratic process. The geographic distances will prohibit participation for in-person events. 

In addition, Vail and Tanque Verde are not that similar to Oro Valley, in that both are more rural. 

This is not a map that provides good representation for these areas.

Leslie Clark

column5: Future district 7
column6:
The best communities of interest are, on AZ Draft 1.0 Legislative District 7. That being said the communities of Winslow, Holbrook, Snowflake, Taylor, are not the same communities of interest.
These Communities are High Desert with Ranching and farming. They should be excluded from AZ Draft 1.0. With the communities of Lakeside/Pinetop, Payson, Heber/Overgaard, Forest Lakes, Doney Park, Grand Canyon Staples, Parks are Communities within AZ Draft 1.0 Legislative District 7, they need to be added. These areas who have unique individual requirements, different from those of metro/urban High Desert areas, including recreation, ranching, rivers and lakes, forest maintenance etc. which all have the same Communities of interests.

column5: Redistricting
column6: We oppose the redistricting which would combine Paradise Valley with Tempe.  Our family lives in Paradise Valley, and frequents many types of businesses in Phoenix and Scottsdale. This move is non-sensical.
