the current maps seem to fracture established communities into districts that dilute common values...
this doesn't make civic sense.
what is happening??
a

column5: Arizona Redistricting
column6: I am against redistricting which would include Paradise Valley with Tempe.   Tempe is a college town, while PV is residential. This makes no sense!

column5: Redistricting
column6: Please reconsider and find to merge us with an area that has at least SOME thing in common with our area or with whom we can meet with to discuss our similarities/differences.  There must be a means to do this.

column5: Redistricting
column6: I see nothing in common with the area drafted to merge with the Picture Rocks area. In addition it would be very difficult to meet with the area drafted so we can discuss differences or things in common.  The area so far defined with our area really needs some attention and, I imagine, the other areas feel the same.

column5: LD 17 and CD 7
column6:
I hope enough people have commented on how bad the proposed LD 17 is. I thought the chair was particularly interested in creating competitive districts, which the proposed LD 17 is not. Competitive districts are so good for the electorate. If Commissioner Mehl wants it to be a Republican district, then he can create a better district and get out there and campaign for his chosen candidates. 
As for the proposed CD 7, I do not agree that the line should be pushed further east. Doing that will just pack the district with more Democrats than it needs. 
Again, thank you all for your terrific service to the state. It is a huge job.

column5: I do not support the current draft map
column6: I do not support the current district 17 as outlined in the draft map. It makes no sense to have such a large geographic district in an urban area. The people in these areas don't have much in common. The issues in Oro Valley are different than those in Vail. This map creates a solidly republican district. This is gerrymandering and unacceptable. Please fix this problem in the draft map. Thank you.

column5: Redistricting maps
column6: As a retired nurse I live and play in the family friendly Desert Ridge area. High Street specifically is home with it catering to urban, vibrant, young professionals. In stark contrast are the areas of Rio Verde, a rural, active adult golfing community as well as North Scottsdale and Fountain Hills, both elderly, quiet, retirement communities. The Representatives for each of these areas know their unique constituents and what each community needs; lumping areas together with such contrasting cultures and certainly contrasting needs is not in anyone's best interest. Referencing the proposed district map, please consider smaller, more manageable, more cohesive areas ensuring We The People are fully and properly represented. Thank you for your consideration.

column5: Redistributing Green Valley and Sahuarita
column6: Please reconsider the redistributing putting Green Valley and Sahuarita in different districts.  We are one community, even though Green Valley is a retirement community.  Shopping and community involvement happens within both of these communities.  People live in one and work in the other and the decisions made by one affect the other;  it makes no sense to divide them up and put them in a district with Sierra Vista!

column5: Redistricting In southern AZ
column6:
I am completely disgusted with how this so-called independent redistricting commission got bamboozled by Pima County Republican David Mehl to gerrymander the new proposed districts!
Not only does it geographically don’t make any sense it’s clearly intended to dilute any Democratic stronghold and build up Republican ones!! some of the rules that were not follow within the bylaws in the IDC clearly benefits commissioner David Mehls intentions.

It’s clear that he wants to create a dominant Republican stronghold by insisting on keeping Oro Valley, Marana, Saddlebrook, and neighboring communities north of Tucson together in a single legislative district.

Not to mention by taking away the Latino vote in Santa Cruz County by cutting it in half and combining the Republican stronghold of Cochise County together.

It’s clear as day on how much this is such a conflict of interest with him that he lobbied for legislative maps that were drawn by the Southern Arizona leadership council where he is a founding member!!!!!

Well I know that this is not easy and such a hot button issue for this council especially in today’s political climate, but to clearly let somebody control it in a manner that is surgically designed to disenfranchise certain segments of the population because they can’t clearly win any other way is disgusting and disappointing and not with this commission was intended to do!!!!

I ask you to go back to the drawing board and figure something out because this is clearly not the answer.

column5: Problem with dividing Interstate 19 into two Legislative districts
column6:
AZ REDISTRICTING INPUT 11/6/21

I am Analizabeth Doan.  My greatgrandfather was the first territorial judge who presided over all the courthouses from Nogales to the NM border before Arizona became a State.  I disagree with the way AZ Legislative District 21 has been outlined on your approved draft map.  One of the most important indicators of a fair and cohesive Legislative voting area is respecting ‘Community of Interest’.  Interstate 19 runs from Nogales to South Tucson, this ‘Community of Interest’ brings in BILLIONS of dollars in revenue to the State of Arizona through tourism, trade and the produce industry.  This Community of Interest needs decisions made, at the State level by the same State Senators and Representatives, people interested in our economic strength who benefit from a positive cross-border relationship.  The area north of Rio Rico and south of Tucson has been moved into District 19 which covers most of Cochise County.  The goals in the south east of the State are quite different from this part of the State.  (I have worked in and driven through the south eastern part of the State where there are militia at the US/Mexico border, where the Hannigans were accused of torturing undocumented men walking through their property, where you see signs disparaging Mexicans (whether documented or not, from entering Arizona).  Those opposite perspectives will come to nothing good for Arizona, if I19 is divided between Santa Cruz County and Cochise County.

Another criteria for a balanced Az Legislative voting district is ‘incorporation of visible geographic areas and I19 is one of three major highways in Arizona, it should not be split between two voting districts. Another criteria of ‘compactness and contiguousness’ is totally destroyed if you pull the middle of I19 into Cochise County, when the communities along I19 attend to their health care issues, business, recreation, the Arts mostly in Tucson, few people in this area use Sierra Vista as their main hub for economic and personal growth.

The criteria of an ‘equal population’ is non-existent by pulling out the middle communities of I19 from District 21, you cause a great disparity in socioeconomic income and also demographics, which are two other key criteria in redistricting voting areas so they can have a balance of ethnicities and incomes.  The present map creates an issue with socioeconomic and demographic equality.

An example of representation in the AZ Legislation is Gail Griffin who in 2019 proposed a bill to fund a US-Mexican border wall by levying a tax on Arizonans.  I19 will have representation from people align with Joe Arpayo and the former US President’s who would probably propose to add another US Border Patrol checkpoint north of the Tohono Oʼodham
 reservation, slowing down the trip for car and semi truck travel.  

I19 has to ALL be part of District 21 and not part of Cochise County.

column5: redistricting proposed maps
column6:
As an AZ resident, I understand how important redistricting is for the future of our state and our democracy. I was a history professor and I remember that AZ was the land of Native Americans and Latinx People before it was included in the USA. As a professor, I always reminded my students, "Democracy works best when all voices are heard and compromise prevails". I believe AZ voters spoke that message when they passed Prop106 and its criteria. 

The current proposed map does not fit the criteria. For example, LD 17 is not geographically compat and includes disparate parts of Pinal and Pima Counties. The new map must also consider communities of interest.  Santa Cruz County, with its Lantinx population, must be kept so the population and geographic area makes common sense.

Currently, I live in LD 9 which has included all the criteria as well as being a competitive district with two different parties having had candidates elected to offices. This type of district should be maintained.

Please member democracy fails and authoritarianism wins when different voices fail to have an opportunity to be heard.

column5: maps
column6: It is the job of Independent Redistricting Commission to uphold the criteria set by the voters. For one Commissioner to railroad through LD 17 for his own personal gain and for the independent chair to support an obvious and deliberate partisan map continues to erode public confidence in this redistricting process and in all of our public institutions. Integrity of the process should be the first priority. Personal greed, especially on the part of one of the selected commissioners, should be disregarded immediately in this process. As you have already seen, there are many ways to build an LD 17 that includes Oro Valley and the areas near it into a competitive district that reflects its 30R/30D/30Ind population.

column5: Scottsdale districting
column6:
Being a longtime Scottsdale resident, I appreciate the “one voice” we have for congressional representation. Dividing our community would be a disservice to our unity. As Scottsdale has grown, I have worried a divide between North/South could occur. Splitting the city in to districts would be the beginning of what I have always feared. 

Please consider

Thank you

Brad Saylor

column5: Proposed LD17 in Pima is a PARTISAN GERRYMANDER
column6:
I spoke in a previous hearing about the importance of competitive districts. Let's allow the voters to pick the candidate who connects best with the electorate.

Imagine my horror when the IRC approved District 17 in Map 10.0 which-- LITERALLY-- was conceived of and drawn by the Pima GOP to give the Republicans a safe district. Gotta hand it to them, it wasn't easy. They had to include a mountain range and wrap it around the city like a boa constrictor. You can't drive from one end of it to another without driving through other districts. D17, as drawn, is a PARTISAN GERRYMANDER, plain and simple. It is unconstitutional. 

I urge you to use LD Map 9.0. The county lines are respected. Counties are important communities of interest. The Foothills area of D17 is also more compact and competitive in District 17 on Map 9.0. It could be won by any party who advances a capable candidate.

column5: Sedona redistricting
column6: I continue to be appalled by the various redistricting maps that have been proposed for Sedona, with the exception of the one prepared by Coconino County.     Flagstaff and Coconino County are communities of interest closely allied to Sedona and the Verde Valley; our ties to Prescott and to Payson are tenuous.     Furthermore, splitting Sedona into two districts effectively mutes our voice for the next ten years, which is both divisive to our town and undemocratic.    Please keep us whole!

column5: Keep the Verde Valley WHOLE
column6: I agree with the City of Sedona’s letter supporting Coconino county’s recently submitted district maps. These maps keep Sedona whole, keep the Verde Valley whole, keep the Yavapai-Apache Nation whole and align us with Flagstaff in the same legislative district.

column5: Verde Valley District Maps
column6: Please keep the City of Sedona intact and with our neighboring Verde Valley communities of interest as well as with Flagstaff.  Please do not split Sedona into districts along County lines.  We are one city and we deserve an intact voice in electing our representatives.  We also need to be kept with the rest of the Verde Valley and Flagstaff as our interests are intertwined.  Those interests include: business (retail and service industries) tourism, healthcare (we are in one system), education (NAU is our four year college opportunity), transportation (I-17 corridor and public transportation), history, natural physical features, and natural resources (Oak Creek and the Verde River.) Please do not separate us from the things that make us one community. Thank you.

I write in opposition to the final redistricting proposal as regards splitting Santa Cruz County. We are a small county both in geographic size (1250 square miles) and in population (under 48,000). We share a fascinating, vibrant and cohesive heritage across our territory from the mountain empire in the east to the river valley that carves its path north to the high country on our western boundaries. Our human history is based on this watershed and it continues to shape us today. 

As a population, we may have our differences, but our striking similarities are what bind us together as a community. The current proposal divides critically important local political blocs such as school districts and fire districts. In a small county, these are vital organizing entities and provide community identity. 

The division of the community of Rio Rico in its northern sectors is just plain wrong. This community, though unincorporated, is the largest in the county, even outstripping Nogales in population. Rio Rico should not have its political ascendency cut off just as it begins to find its identity within the county and the state. 

We care for each other in Santa Cruz County and we want to be able to be effective as a political community. Dividing our small county is not in our interest.

column5: IRC - Support Latino Coalition Maps

column5: Redistricting
column6:
Hello, my name is Barbara Jennings, I live in Maricopa County, and I am here today to give you information about my communities of interest.
I live off of 56th Street and Sweetwater. My community is made up of families and elderly couples, young working people who shop, attend church and work in the North corridor from 75th Ave to Tatum Rd, and from Desert Ridge North of the 101 down to Thunderbird Rd
The commission’s proposed CD1 is currently excluding the area between Cave Creek Rd and I-17. Many of my neighbors and friends work and live here. Please extend the Western boundary to include this community. We need to have communities that have similar values and priorities otherwise it would make it very difficult for legislative representatives to be effective in serving its constituents. My friends and I have developed strong relationships with our Representative and we would feel very disenfranchised and bankrupt in all the efforts we have put forth to ensure proper representation of our values. 
I am asking that you please move the western boundary for CD1 beyond Cave Creek Rd to I-17. 
Please follow the Arizona Constitution when you are drawing districts this time. Your current map disrupts the main focus which is community of interest.
Thank you for your time.
Barbara Jennings

column5: Redistricting LD15
column6:
Hello, my name is Barbara Jennings, I live in Maricopa County, and I am here today to give you information about my communities of interest.
I live off of 56th Street and Sweetwater. My community is made up of families, retirees and hard working individuals, who work in the North corridor from 75th Ave to Tatum Rd, and from Desert Ridge North of the 101 down to Thunderbird Rd
I never travel south of Thunderbird into the Sunny Slope area, west of Cave Creek Rd. It is an entirely different community and the crime rate is very high in that area so I try to avoid it altogether. The Sunny Slope community is very different from the suburban single family housing you will find north of Thunderbird. 
The commission’s proposed legislative map for LD2 is mixing communities that have very different values and priorities making it very difficult for legislative representatives to be effective in serving its constituents. I am asking that you please move the line for LD2 UP to Thunderbird and to encompass more population then extend it a bit above the 101 to include Desert Ridge community, then move the Western boundary to 75th Ave.  I work  from home, shop at Desert Ridge and also off Tatum and Cactus and my sons Doctor and Dentist have offices in the Scottsdale/Pinnacle Peak area. I am having a lot of anxiety over the thought that crime rate is going to increase in my neighborhood with the shifting south of my district. 
Please follow the Arizona Constitution when you are drawing districts this time. Your current map not only disrupts the main focus of community of interest but also competitiveness. 
Thank you for your time today.
Barbara Jennings

column5: Map versions 9 and 10
column6: Our new LD - LD16 - will not be competitive, guaranteeing we only have Republican legislators. I live in Picture Rocks ( Pima County) and will have us in the same LD as Coolidge, Arizona City - hours away from  here, This violates the mandate to create competitive districts that are fair and democratic - not gerrymandered for the purpose of securing an outcome in elections. Do we want to remain a democracy - let's start here by fairly drawing the maps. Stop ignoring the mandates.

column5: Pima County District Boundaries
column6:
My name is Ricky Sage. I have lived in Tucson since 2015.
I am retired from the Air Force and also an early retiree from Boeing Military Aircraft in Kansas. I was a Reservist, so I have dual retirements! In fact I moved to Tucson due to the Davis Monthan Air Force Base, and I work at the base as a simulator trainer for aircrews. I live in Northeast Tucson, not far from Udall Park. I love it here and consider myself permanent!
My daughter and Grandson joined me in Tucson a couple of years ago. They are now settled in Vail. 
In reviewing map 9.3 I think it is called, I realized that my daughter and I would be in different legislative districts. I would be in District 18 and she would be in District 17. A closer look at district 17 makes for a big puzzle. Half of district 17 is Northwest of Tucson – The Oro Valley/Marana group, and the other portion of district 17 is Southeast Tucson Vail, etc.  This is a silly combination, to have these two regions tied together, with an intervening district 18 in the middle. My family can’t even get from Vail to Oro Valley without driving for 30 minutes through other districts. The Santa Catalina mountains form a natural “barrier” of sorts. 
When we were making Halloween preparation, no consideration was given to going to Marana for trick or treat, or even to purchase candy. Oro Valley and Marana are OK, but to go there requires preparations similar to a trip to Phoenix – i.e. pack a lunch and if you have pets, make sure they are fed and watered before you go. 
Oro Valley and Marana have as transportation corridors I-10  towards Casa Grande and AZ77 towards Catalina, Oracle Junction and Oracle – to include neighborhoods such as Saddlebrook, Saddlebrook II, Red Rocks, Eloy, etc that form a natural contiguous grouping. By ignoring this natural grouping, and instead hop skipping over mountains and major cities, it is evident that the true agenda of some participants is to “carve up” the voters of Tucson and reduce their representation in the State Legislature. Correct me if I am wrong, but this approach is exactly opposite of the stated goals of this commission, and exactly opposite of the intent of the voters who enacted this bipartisan process two decades ago.
In an earlier version of the legislative district maps, my neighborhood was in an LD that stretched to include Cochise county. I made an online comment about that, and I am happy to see that reason prevailed, and district 18 is an improvement. But it is clear to all observers that some entities are using this redistricting process to attempt to gain partisan advantage. 
My current Congressional District has had both a Republican and a Democrat in the past 10 years  - very competitive. Competitive districts, I believe, draw candidates more closely to the center. The need to appeal to the large number of independent voters requires a candidates to listen closer to the electorate. I believe that gerrymandering districts that are very very safe for one party or another can lead to extreme views and individuals getting into government. I would hope to not have elected officials legislate against aircraft contrails.
I am told that comments have been made by during public discussions about the desire of the commission to create safe districts, and what is considered to be a “safe” district. column5: Objection to District 17 in the Adopted Draft Legislative Map
column6:
I write to object to District 17  in the Adopted Draft Legislative Map.

District 17 in the Adopted Draft Legislative Map is problematic for several reasons.   Its design disregards many important goals of fair redistricting set out in the Arizona Constitution; instead, it promotes the creation of a safe Republican district in a predominantly Democratic county. That goal is not in our Arizona Constitution.

District 17 is not "compact and contiguous to the extent practicable." It is made up of selected Republican-leaning suburbs from opposite ends of the Tucson area that are separated by a mountain range and a long drive.

District 17 does not "respect communities of interest to the extent practicable." The residents of both Tanque Verde and Vail have little to do with the distant suburbs of Marana and Oro Valley, and have much closer ties to eastern and midtown Tucson.

District 17 is designed to create a safe Republican district, but that goal violates the constitutional requirement that "to the extent practicable, competitive districts should be favored where to do so would create no significant detriment to the other goals." Democratic Commissioner Lerner proposed an alternative version of District 17 that was highly competitive, but it was rejected on the grounds that it failed to create a safe Republican district.  The Independent Chair stated she was impressed by a letter from the Marana Mayor and a state Senator favoring the Mehl map and she wanted to make sure that “center right” voters have a chance of electing their candidate.  But Prop. 106 clearly instructs the IRC not to consider the preferences of a given legislator, and center right voters hardly need protecting in Arizona, where Republicans are known for pushing the Big Lie, advancing voter suppression bills, and even attending the January 6 insurrection.  The Independent Chair needs to be reminded that safe partisan districts are the opposite of competitive districts envisioned by the Arizona Constitution and that fair competitive districts promote democracy and politician accountability.

For these reasons, the IRC should use LD Test map v9.0 as proposed by Commissioner Lerner.


Sent from my iPad

column5: Use of Safe Districts in Draft Maps - 1
column6:
In the days before Proposition 106, the legislators drew the boundaries of the legislative districts and they did so to ensure their party had the best chance to retain power.  They created as many ‘safe’ districts as they could – districts where the party bosses could put up a candidate they could rely on to toe the party line, districts they could win time after time without much investment of effort or money, districts that were safe for their party’s interests never mind the voters.

But that led to very poor governance.  People were fed up with a government that failed to address their issues or provide the kinds of services that would help them and their communities prosper.  The ‘safe’ districts weren’t responsive to their needs.  The recognized that the ‘safe’ districts were dysfunctional, that they produced voter apathy or disenchantment with government and low voter participation.  Why bother voting when your vote wasn’t needed to win or wouldn’t make any difference anyway?  Safe districts are the antithesis of Democracy.

In the election of 2000, they took back the power from the legislature and passed Proposition 106, which created a new Independent Redistricting Commission, which they charged with creating “fair and competitive…districts.”  Not safe districts.  Competitive districts.

They knew that competitive districts would have the opposite effect.  To win a district, the parties must put forth their best candidates, those who are familiar with the needs of the district and will put forth innovative ideas and programs to resolve them, those who listen to the voters and respond to them with policies they can defend in debate.  When that happens, the voters become engaged in the political process, their government, their communities, and their elections.  They vote in greater numbers and expect more of their elected officials (who are consequently more capable of delivering).  All of that leads to more effective and responsive governance.  But you only get that when you have districts that are competitive.

I know the commission feels like it’s doing a good job with creating the districts.  But if you look at the Draft Maps you’ve come up with, it’s obvious that they you have failed to carry out what the voters have charged you with – creating fair and competitive districts.

Yes, it’s true that the current Draft Maps are not the final maps and there is work to be done.  But if the current maps are any indication, you seem to be heading in the wrong direction.

Of the 30 districts in the current legislative Draft Map, there are 2 districts by your definition that are “Highly Competitive”, 4 more that are “Competitive”, and the remaining 24 districts are “safe” districts – districts that are safe for one or the other parties – 24 out of 30, that’s 80%.  80% of the districts you’ve drawn are dysfunctional.  That’s exactly the opposite of what the voters said they wanted from you.

You say, ‘Oh but those safe districts are balanced between the Republicans and Democrats so they cancel each other out.’  That may be true when it comes to the political makeup of the legislature, but that’s not the point.  The voters sought to stop the corrosion of democracy that’s the inevitable result of every safe district.  Just because they balance each other out does not justify using them.

Two spoiled apples do not make a good pie.

The commission has a LONG way to go to turn as many of these safe districts into competitive ones as possible.  Failure to do so is a betrayal of the spirit of Proposition 106 and is no better than the legislator-drawn partisan districts that it tried to prevent.

The health of our democracy must be defended and that can only happen by eliminating safe districts – regardless of the party they prop up – and restoring competition, as our Founders and the Arizona voters intended.

William Bowlus-Root
A concerned citizen

column5: skipped to speak at the meeting today

I signed up to speak at the meeting today, and received a confirmation via email.  However, I did not appear on your speaker list.  Here are the comments I wanted to read into the record:

Civility in American politics is at an all-time low, and this has terrible consequences for the tenor of our public discourse and in our ability to tackle our common challenges.  In Arizona, our constitution gives us a tool that can help, but we’re not adequately using it.  That tool is competitiveness.  

In 2008 the AZ Supreme Court ruled that the competitiveness goal cannot be considered less mandatory than the other goals, ignored, or relegated to a secondary role, yet in shifting LD17 from a competitive to non-competitive district, the commission is doing exactly this, and contriving districts like LD21 so we can pretend that Oro Valley and Vail, separated by mountains, are somehow deeply connected to each other.

Competition is good for business, and it’s good for voting – it makes politicians better.  When we make voting districts safe, we disenfranchise minority party voters and independents in those districts.

I live in a competitive district, in the current LD10.  Under these proposed maps, I’m in the head of the weird dragon that is LD21, and I feel like I’ve been gerrymandered.  Not only am I in a neighborhood that’s been unnaturally bisected from my surrounding community, I’m now in a district that’s safely Democratic.  This is a deep disservice to the 50% of voters in my neighborhood who are not Democrats – I say this as a Democrat who believes deeply in the importance of meaningful representation.  

Extreme polarization is counterproductive, and dangerous.  When we make districts safe, we guarantee that our elected officials will speak only to their base, and never to the broad electorate.  Please redraw Pima County’s districts to recognize compactness, my community of interest in midtown Tucson, and the critical importance of competitiveness.  Make my vote count.

column5: Keep Greater Scottsdale Together
column6:
Keep Greater Scottsdale Together

Our family has lived in Scottsdale for over 20 years. We are actively involved in our local community, my wife having served for several years on our HOA board.

We are concerned that the final draft maps split Scottsdale into three legislative districts. It separates Northern Scottsdale from Southern Scottsdale and Eastern Scottsdale from Western Scottsdale. As much as is practicable, greater Scottsdale should be kept together.

The final draft maps would place our community in D3. This district would stretch from the far east valley to Interstate 17, connecting disparate parts of several communities that have little in common. This map would seem to violate at least three of the constitutional criteria for drawing maps:

     (1) The final draft map does not take communities of interest into account.

     (2) The final draft map ignores Scottsdale boundaries.

     (3) The final draft map would create a non-competitive district.

We ask that you keep greater Scottsdale together and consider map #CDF009. While this map has a CD designation, it is a legislative district map that is fully consistent with all six of the constitutional criteria. It was developed and submitted by Scottsdale resident, Emily Wilson. 

The greater Scottsdale district would keep the geographic footprint of Scottsdale nearly in tact. It would also incorporate all of the Salt River Pima-Maricopa community. These communities comprise a compelling economic community of interest that includes tourism, local business interests on the 101 corridor south of 90th Street, along with Scottsdale Community College - all of which are on tribal lands. 

Putting these two communities together also preserves their mutual interest in sustainable land use, respect for the individual character of diverse and distinct neighborhoods, a culture of citizen involvement, environmental stewardship & open space preservation, along with a citizen-centric focus on planning, community building & decision-making.

Further, it creates competitiveness that the previous draft iterations do not. It comes very close to creating parity between the two major political parties with the advantage slightly favoring Republicans. Keeping greater Scottsdale together offers the opportunity for legislative candidates to run and govern from the middle, thereby serving the majority of voters in the proposed greater Scottsdale district.

This greater Scottsdale district also complies with the Voting Rights Act in ways that the current LD23 does not. 

Thank you for consideration of our proposed map.

Your service to our state is greatly appreciated.

George and Joyce Loughmiller
Scottsdale Residents

column6:
Chairman Neuberg and Commissioners,

My name is Marilyn Weissman.  I am a 29 year resident of the City of Flagstaff. Thank you for the work you are doing on this difficult task.  I have watched some of your deliberations and have been surprised by the small amount of time you have spent discussing the maps in Northern Arizona.  I have no idea what the criteria  is that you used to decide the defining lines of our legislative and congressional districts.

I am in the current LD 6. I have written and spoken previously of the importance of keeping the city and the communities that depend on Flagstaff in one legislative district.  I have also asked previously that you consider the I-17 corridor that highlights the tourist communities above and right below the Mogollon Rim as a part of our Community of Interest.  I have also asked that the greater Flagstaff area be put in a competitive district that allows the future possibility of electing someone from our growing town that represents our values and concerns.

Instead you have created, using parts of our LD 6 and 7 district, three districts, LD 5, 6, and 7, that are not politically competitive or defined by communities of interest.  For the City of Flagstaff our competition within your draft district 6 is now with our Native neighbors, a distinct community of interest, who I support in their efforts to be able to elect their own representatives without having the  possibility of Flagstaff diluting their ability to do so.  This is unfair to both the Native vote and the City of Flagstaff. I ask you again to create a legislative district that includes all of greater Flagstaff, including the communities of Kachina and Mountainaire, and join us with the communities below the rim lying East of Mingus Mountain in the Verde Valley - Sedona, Camp Verde, Clarkdale and Cottonwood. The map submitted by the Coconino County Board of Supervisors, LDF050 and LDF051, does just that. It is supported by the City Councils of Flagstaff, Sedona and Clarkdale. Please consider replacing your draft legislative map of Northern Arizona with this submitted one.

I was also disappointed to see that your current draft of Congressional maps puts Flagstaff and it’s native neighbors in a new non-competitive district 2 that will primarily reflect the policy priorities and concerns of the people of the Prescott area, very different from our own.  Currently we are represented here in Flagstaff by a moderate.  This is the result of the district being politically competitive.  Districts that are lopsided in one direction, as the new CD 2 is, have the effect of electing extremists who rarely campaign in,visit or represent the values of the parts of the district that did not vote for them. 

Why have you eliminated the one competitive congressional district in Northern Arizona and added us to a non-competitive congressional district?  The Flagstaff area and our native neighbors will now have no voice in the congress.  Please consider accepting the map submitted by the Navajo Nation, CDF010, which restores congressional competitiveness to our area. 

Thank you,

Marilyn Weissman
Flagstaff, AZ

column5: November 6 Hearing
column6: I have been listening to this hearing and to the speakers from the public all day. If, at this point, it has not become clear to the Commission that the latest maps that the Commission has approved for Northern Arizona and the Tucson area are gerrymandered to give the Republican party an overwhelming advantage, that these maps are a blatant violation of prop 106 and a slap in the face to our State Constitution and to the voters of Arizona, then the Chair and the Commissioners who approved these maps are, frankly, traitors of the State Constitution and traitors to all voters of Arizona (not just certain voters) and obviously are deep in the pockets of the Republican Party.  We need competitive districts all over the state, not gerrymandered districts that will lead to ongoing extremism in politics.  The Commission has a chance to prove that Arizona can move past this divisiveness.  The Commission has the chance to prove that politics and different political parties in Arizona can co-exist and work together despite our differences of political opinion.  If not, then these commission members and their reputations will forever be sullied by being remembered as the commissioners who were bought and paid for by one political party. No amount of saying "we did out best" will overcome that. Please don't let that happen.

column5: You left me out of the presentation
column6:
I have been online with today's virtual hearing since 10:00 am. That's almost six hours of waiting my turn--which somehow never came. Is this because Northern Arizona is united against your unfair and biased maps? 

You left me out even though I was on the list and appropriately registered. I think I deserve an explanation. Also, this will tell me if you ever read the comments we send.

Are you so unable to listen to the very valid criticisms that residents of the North have made?

column5: Northeast Arizona Legislative and Congressional Districts
column6: Please accept the Flagstaff proposals for the LDs and CDs of Northeast Arizona. We need competitive maps, not gerrymandered messes designed to prop up failing politicians. The commission proposal for LD6 and LD7 disenfranchises 321,000 people either because they would be in districts so favorable that their votes would not matter or because they would be automatic losers. The Native Americans of Northeast Arizona should not be split, but should also not be packed into districts where there votes are meaningless in legislative elections. Flagstaff should not be split. The bulk of Yavapai County should be in a different congressional district, leaving the Verde Valley and Sedona with Flagstaff.

column5: Redistricting
column6:
My name is Steve Robinson, and I reside in Oro Valley. The map proposed and endorsed by the Republican Commissioner on behalf of Southern Arizona business interests violates several mandates the Commission is entrusted with adhering to. It does not protect the interests of people of color who are specifically protected under the law. It would not be competitive and balanced, and as a result candidates for office would need only to cater to the most extreme among the electorate.
The map proposed by Republican interests simply repudiates the very fact that those of us in Oro Valley are far more connected to the communities in Tucson around which the proposed map draws a tortuous, artificial boundary line. Connecting Oro Valley to Marana to the west, Tanque Verde to the southeast and Saddlebrooke to the north (and situated in Pinal County) is a blatant gambit to construct a district of affluent suburban whites. This is a disservice to people of color and to those of us in Oro Valley whose "community of interest" is firmly linked to central Tucson, not to homogenous subdivisions flung about the perimeter of the city.
Thank you for considering my remarks and for the difficult work you are doing.

column5: ordering of speakers for the Draft Map Town Halls
column6: Having just watched the webex meeting today, I have a suggestion for both virtual and in-person meetings: please shuffle (i.e., randomize) the ordering of the speakers. The ordering by geographic area as was done today means that some group is inevitably going to feel disadvantaged. For the in-person meetings, the ordering has sometimes been first come first served, and sometimes has been shuffled. The latter is far better, as it precludes gaming by having an organized group dominating early on. While someone will always be first and someone else last, at least if the order is fairly random, there is no appearance of favoritism. And I further suggest that you announce this policy so that people understand what is being done. Thank you.

column5: Legislative redistricting
column6:
I am currently a 20 year resident of Sedona.  After reviewing the proposed State legislative redistricting, I see that Sedona has been completely cut off from the Village of Oak Creek and the rest of the Verde Valley, including Cottonwood, Camp Verde and surrounding towns. Everything that happens in our communities is reflected and influenced among our unique  collective bonds. This is the community that we Sedona residents most closely align ourselves with economically, socially and culturally.  I feel that our State Representative should be the same person as these communities because of this and that we are represented as a community, with common goals that we will want to have represented at the State level.  Sedonans have NOTHING in common with the areas represented in District 7, where the new plan has us placed.  I feel that it would be a disservice to us to be included in District 7 and as we have a close community bond with other District 5 communities we would be much bettered served if included in District 5 with our very close neighbors. 
Thank you for your time,  Kathleen Wege

column5: Thanks for sticking with us
column6:
Just a quick note of thanks to commissioners Lerner and Neuberg.  Kudos to you for staying online the whole time through today's virtual town hall - and especially for keeping your video on the entire time.  (I'm not sure where commissioner York was.  Commissioner Mehl was also in the Participants list all day, but we couldn't tell whether he was really there or what he might have been doing during the testimony.)  It was reassuring to see that you both seemed to be listening and engaged with the public.  It gave me and I'm sure other people who testified at least some reassurance that their time waiting wasn't completely wasted, that at least someone on the commission was paying attention and it gave us hope we might have been heard.

Thanks for sticking it out.  It wasn't easy for any of us.

William Bowlus-Root
A concerned citizen

column5: Fair Voting Districts
column6:
Sedona is composed of various small neighborhoods including West Sedona, Uptown Sedona, the Village of Oak Creek, the Chapel area, Big Park etc....but we are all a COMMUNITY of like minded citizens.
We share common interests and concerns and I think it would be detrimental to our sense of community to be divided into two separate voting districts.
Please to restore our unity. 
I appreciate this opportunity to express my thoughts and thank you all for your dedication and for the hard work you have already put in on this critical issue of redistricting our state.

column5: Approved Speaker/Could not get online/technical problems
column6:
Today I wished to make comments about the proposed redistricting in my area, but technical problems prevented me from doing so.  I would still like to enter my comments into the record.

I live in the Grayhawk Subdivision in North Scottsdale.  My husband and I are retired.  Upon retirement we agreed to move to the Scottsdale area for its friendly amenities for retirees.

We are situated close to the McDowell Mountains where we can all enjoy many outdoor activities such as hiking, nature and wildlife watching.  We also have nearby restaurants, shopping at the Promenade and along the 101 Corridor.  We have good medical facilities at a close distance.  Many retirees live in Scottsdale for the above reasons.

So I am baffled that Desert Ridge, a bustling area of young energetic families with different needs would be included in our same district.  We never go to Desert Ridge or east beyond that area.

Even more baffling is the inclusion of the Deer Valley Airport, the Deer Valley Industrial Park and the extension to I-17.  Much of these areas are fast growing commercial and industrial.  They have little in common with Scottsdale, and are completely unlike the area we chose to live in.

So I am asking you to adjust rhe map to include Scottsdale, Fountain Hills, Rio Verde only.  Our representatives can better focus on like communities of interest.  Hopefully you will take these needs into greater consideration as you debate legislative redistricting.

column5: Summary of 11/6/21 meeting
column6:
After listening to all 6 hours of the public comment meeting on 11/6/21, these are the points made very clear. Citizens were clearly unhappy with Neuberg for allowing Mehl to submit a map made from a political organization and approving it. A map that doesn't uphold Prop 106 and the laws of the AZ Constitution. 

Specifically in Southern AZ three things were addressed that were deemed unacceptable. The following should be fixed.

Legislative Map:
1) District 17 must be redrawn going back to LD 9.0 as the preferred map.
2) Santa Cruz County should not be split up and remaim as part of LD21 as in LD 9.0 map.

Congressional Map:
1) D6 is unacceptable in its currently approved Congressional Map. With D6 snaking its way up I-10 like a finger to include Casa Grande is gerrymandering. Doing so will make D6 compose of 5 different counties (Graham, Greenlee, Cochise, Pima and Pinal) which doesn't adhere to the "communities of interest" or "geographically compact" rule of Prop 106.
2) Reverting to CD Map 1.1 for southern AZ is the most logical and representational option keeping D6 south of Pinal County line.

We hope the entire IRC committee will listen to the communities and follow our requests. There have been MANY, MANY submitted plans that follow the rules of Prop 106 and the AZ Constitution that are being ignored. We dont want political parties having preference to submit gerrymandered districts like Mehl put forth. He should be reprimanded for even allowing it. He even admitted to his partisan proposal of LD17. How that can stand is astonishing.

column5: Final IRC Map Comments for Southern Arizona
column6:
I reside in precinct #84 in an Active Adult Retirement Community just outside Green Valley/Sahuarita.  The community is located in a rural area surrounded by pecan orchards, BLM land, mines, and the Santa Rita Mountains.  We choose to live in this area because of its location, we wanted a small community environment.

Comments regarding the Final Draft Maps for Legislative Districts and Congressional Districts:
1 - The commission has placed our area in LD19 which is a good match and choice.  We have a lot in common with Cochise County which is also rural & semi-rural, with a lot of retirees, veterans, border patrol and law enforcement families.  We need to be kept in LD19, it is a good fit.

2 - The commission has placed our area in CD7 which is a terrible match and a bad choice for our community.   We have nothing in common with the City of Tucson, South Tucson and the Reservation.  We belong in CD6, with Cochise County, and the eastern and northern part of Pima County.  We have small rural and semi-rural community needs that will be overshadowed by “big city” needs in CD7.  We will not have a voice if kept in CD7, we will be silenced.  This is not right.  

Summary: Please remove Green Valley, Sahuarita and precinct #84 from CD7 and place them in CD6.  This can be done by moving Casa Grande out of CD6 and moving it into a CD in Maricopa or Pinal County.  It would be an injustice to our retirees and small communities if they were left in CD7, we belong in CD6.  Leave precinct #84 in LD19 with Cochise County, we have much more in common with this area than we do with LD21 and Tucson.  
Thank you.
Christi Emery

column5: East Valley Redistricting
column6:
Dear Commissioners:  My name is Jeffrey Tucker and write to you from South Tempe.  I have lived here for 8 years, I work in North Chandler and, as an Ahwatukee property owner, I have been a taxpayer in the Kyrene School District for over 15 years.
I first want to thank you for the Approved LD Draft Map recognizing and representing the Kyrene School District so well.  After over 20 years of being excluded, you have finally made the school district whole within a single LD (LD12) by including the Lone Butte precinct from the Gila River Tribal Lands.  Thank you!
I’d like to raise a few major concerns that I see with the Draft Map.  
First, as a Tempe resident, I want to tell you that my city of Tempe is small.  It’s so small that with its 204,000 residents, that it could actually be within a single district of its own.  Yet, the current map splits us up into four new districts when it seems that really only two districts are warranted: an urban North Tempe district and a suburban South Tempe district representing the neighborhoods below Southern Avenue.
My next issue with the Draft Map concerns the area where I work, North Chandler.  This is a highly concentrated Hispanic and Latino area of Chandler that has effectively been split from the new District 13.  This Hispanic community of interest population has now been lumped into LD 12, when instead, it seems to make more sense to extend the new District 13 northward, and effectively remove the LD12 “arm” that was created.
About that LD12 arm, it’s not very compact.  It stretches all the way east to Val Vista Drive, and cuts through the cities of Gilbert and Chandler.  Going westward, LD 12 ends at the base of the western point of the South Mountain area.  This stretch of land is 21 miles long. Even the city of Phoenix at its widest point is no bigger than 20 miles!  Let’s please make this densely populated suburban district far more compact, by removing the LD12 arm at the 101 and simultaneously accomplish the goal of not splitting the Latino district of West Chandler in half.
In summary, please consider these three changes:  
1)	Please split Tempe into only two districts at Southern Avenue. 
2)	Please keep the Latino community of Chandler whole, by moving the north Chandler section of LD12 into LD 13, and 
3)	Combining these 2 points, effectively make LD 12 much more compact by please removing the eastward arm at the 101, and stretch the LD12 district further northward into Tempe instead.
Thank you so much for hearing my suggestions.  Further, thank you so much for the tireless work and the many miles you have each traveled for the past year!  I appreciate your efforts to make these maps fair, balanced, and representative of the Arizona we live in.
Jeff Tucker

column5: Congressional District map submission CDF010
column6: As a long-time resident of northern Arizona, I write to register my strong support for the congressional district map submitted by the Navajo Nation Human Rights Commission (CDF010). This map is highly preferable to the Draft Congressional Map for the northern part of the state for many reasons. It unites many of the northern and eastern tribal nations (from Hualapai and Kaibab through Hopi and Navajo all the way to Fort Apache and San Carlos). It avoids diluting the voting power of these Native Americans (as the draft map does, by incorporating Prescott's population). It keeps this region highly competitive (by your metrics) - which I greatly appreciate - while the draft map consigns us to a highly Republican district and disenfranchises the largely moderate population center of Flagstaff and northeastern towns. I also believe it is very important to have congressional representation with real expertise in tribal issues, given the many key issues where tribes play a major role in federal relations (from water rights to energy development) - this region of the state presents a unique opportunity to elect a representative with close connections to tribal interests. Please maintain competitiveness and the electoral power of the largest Native American population center in the US - adopt the key features of submission CDF010.

column5: Thanks for sticking with us - 2
column6:
I realized that I unintentionally omitted mention of Commissioner Watchman from my earlier email thanking the commissioners who stayed with us all the way through yesterday's Virtual Town Hall.  Thank you, Commissioner Watchman!

William Bowlus-Root
A concerned citizen

column5: support for proposed district changes
column6: We are in Precinct 82, Broadmoor - Broadway Village neighborhood.  This precinct is dominated by far-left voters, many affiliated with the university.  We tend to vote centrist but feel that gamesmanship by the far left has deprived us of any meaningful choice of candidates.  So redistricting that counteracts such gamesmanship is welcome, even if it makes our precinct even more leftist.

column5: Draft Maps for Public Comment- Pima County area
column6:
I moved here from another state seven years ago. One of my first positive impressions of my new community was the vibrant, competitive nature of elections. For example, the party of my congressperson has changed not once, but twice in a short time. 

But now I am very concerned about losing all that during the next 10 years. Why?  Because proposed LD17 would take that away.  LD17 disregards many of the goals of the Arizona Constitution: It is not at all compact or contiguous. Its communities of interest are far-flung and desperate. And it lacks competitiveness. It encircles the outskirts of Tucson in an oddly configured fashion, to create an obviously safe Republican district.

I really fear that this version of LD17, will not only chill voter participation, but it will also encourage extremism.

What can we do?  There is a viable alternative. I urge the Commission to go back to test Map LD 9.0 that Commissioner Lerner proposed.  That test map corrects the Constitutional shortcomings found in the current LD17 and it ensures that all of us voters have an equal voice.

Thank you Commissioners for your commitment and hard work in addressing this important redistricting process.

column5: Redistricting Northern AZ
column6:
Dear Commissioners,
I am most perturbed by the way your proposed LD maps distort competitiveness, community of interest issues and contiguity in northern Arizona proposed LDs 5, 6 and 7 in conflict with the expressed wishes of most of the voters in these areas. You can correct this - easily - by adopting the maps proposed by the Coconino Countey Board of Supervisors and supported by the City of Sedona. We ask only that you meet your obligations to the voters and adhere to the 6 factors required of you.

column5: Redistricting Map
column6:
As proposed the LD map makes a mockery of the concept of "community of interest" as well as stretching the bounds of the interlocking requirements of contiguity and political boundaries. In proposed districts 5 and 7, Sedona is split in two and divided from neighboring Village of Oak Creek. The map places most of the Verde Valley and Sedonawithn the more distant town of Prescott and disassociates it from its close companion of Flagstaff, it splits the Yavapai Apache Nation and generally shatters the existing relationship among all of these entities - in opposition to nearly 85% of the citizen comments made at the Commission's  public hearings.
Please adopt the LD map proposed by the Coconino County Board of Supervisors and supported by the City of Sedona which corrects all of these problems and keeps our area whole.

column5: proposed redistricting
column6:
The proposed redistricting map has split Sedona/VOC into separate legislative districts. We are one community with shared goals....I strongly feel that it would benefit us to be represented by a single set of legislators so our needs are not diluted.
Thank you for your consideration of this issue.

column5: AZ Legistlative Redistricting
column6:
It does not seem appropriate to me to have towns such as Sedona split and put in separate districts or to have the Village of Oak Creek, where I live, separated from Sedona  legislative districts.  We in the Verde Valley, Cottonwood, Cornville, Camp Verde, McGuireville, Rimrock, the VOC and Sedona have common interests that are distinct from say, Flagstaff, the Reservations, or Prescott, Prescott Valley and the Chino Valley.  Please reconsider these divisions and allow the Verde Valley to have a unified voice with our state government.
Thank you for considering my thoughts on redistricting.  Joan Steninger

column5: redistricting
column6: The most important thing to consider with redistricting is that each district should be competitive between Democrats and Republicans.

column5: Redistricting -
column6: My name is Dora Harrison, a 24 year resident of Coconino County.  Having worked for the county, I have been aware of my districting status for many years.  I am in support of the map submitted by the Coconino Board of Supervisors and supported by the City Councils of Sedona and Flagstaff. I urge your adoption of the maps and communities presented in this document.  These past ten years have been years of total aleination from my legislative "representatives".  I would love to have my district be one that understands my views, needs, and culture;  I have not had that in more than 10 years.

column5: Contressional Redistricting
column6: P lease support the proposed revision of CD 2 - CDF010.  This has been proposed by the Navajo Nation and seems most appropriate for the district serving that area.

column5: Redistricting for D19
column6:
I don't understand how the new D6 district on the Congressional map can be allowed. There are plenty of other ways to draw this district to meet the requirements of Prop 106.

Look at these submitted and published plans that are competitively drawn: 
IRC Plan Name: CD0059 (its a 51% to 48%)
IRC Plan Name: CD0058 (its a 51% to 48%)
IRC Plan Name: CD0057 (its a 53% to 46%)
IRC Plan Name: CD0056 (its a 53% to 46%)
IRC Plan Name: CD0032

There are options out there other than having a snake head pop northward just to gain the population of Casa Grande region. The people of SE Arizona has nothing to do with this issues that face Pinal County and this entire center of the state that is really becoming more of a Phx suburb than anything to do with Tucson and SE Arizona. Please dont go north of the Pima County line or close to it.

column5: Scottsdale Redistricting
column6:
I live in north Scottsdale. My family lives, shops, go to schools, go to church and play in Scottsdale.  It is not logical to have Desert Ridge and Deer Valley Airport to be in my district.

Why is there a need to move the western boundary past Scottsdale Road, the city boundary?  What is the compelling urgent need?

The communities are different and the current district boundaries should remain unchanged.

column5: Greenlee County should be included in proposed CD2, not CD6
column6:
I have lived in Greenlee County for the past 38 years.  We have no "community of interest" with the southern counties. We in Graham and Greenlee don't have any part of our boundaries on the southern border; don't have military bases; don't have wineries; don't have any urban or suburban areas. Our rural needs will be overwhelmed by those of larger population areas in the district.
I feel  that because all of Greenlee is rural, we should remain with the rural parts of the state in the proposed CD 2. As primarily a mining and agricultural county, we have more "community of interest' with parts of Gila, Apache and Navajo Counties as well as Graham. Our topography is similar, our water, employment and infrastructure needs are similar. 
  Thank you for your consideration.

column5: Congressional map should have Greenlee with northern counties as it has been this decade
column6:
In my opinion, Greenlee has more in common with northern counties such as Apache, Navajo, and adjoining counties of Graham and Gila (what is being called CD2). We have no "community of interest" with the southern counties. In Greenlee there is no part of our boundary on the southern border. Our economic base doesn't incude military bases or wineries; additionally we don't have any urban or suburban areas. I fear that if we become part of CD 6, our rural needs will be overwhelmed by those of larger population areas in the district.
Greenlee is one of the most rural counties in AZ. It should therefore remain with the other rural parts of the state that have primarily mining and agriculture as the top industries in the proposed CD 2. 
Thank you for considering this.

column5: LD 17
column6:
A large number of citizens from across Pima County testified they do not like the boundary lines drawn for the proposed LD 17. People in Vail and people in Marana agree we do not belong together.  I live near Marana in Pima precinct 40. Here in NW Pima County some Communities of interest that DO belong together are Marana, Picture Rocks, and Avra Valley.  All of these communities are served by Marana Unified School District.  All are within Pima County. All work and play and worship in the same general area. Please put us together in a reasonably compact Legislative District with Oro Valley and Amphitheater School District. If we need to pick up more population, look to the Flowing Wells School District or look to Casas Adobes.

Liberate Vail from this LD because there is actually no good way to get there froAdobe's.

Thank you for reading my comments.

column5: AZ Legislative Districts
column6: I urge the IRC to keep Sedona, Village of Oak Creek and the Verde Valley as a unified “community of interest. My husband and I have owned our home in west Sedona for 20 years, and we believe that the proposed map is divisive and ignores the common interests, concerns an realities of the current map. Sedona should not be split up as a city, nor should it be split from the Village of Oak Creek or Flagstaff or the Verde Valley. As a community of interest, we not only prioritize and hold concerns for the beauty and value of natural environment, we frequently interact with each other for shopping, education, cultural and social events, to name a few. We rarely interact with Prescott in these ways, and therefore we oppose the current proposed map.

column5: Fair and competitive keeps candidates rational
column6: I am writing to urge the commission to keep the maps as fair and competitive as you possibly can. While candidates think their side will win with an advantage, both sides lose: The less competitive the district, the more politicians, either left or right, become more extreme to compete. The centrists will be eliminated in the primaries, and the most extreme candidate will win. That is not in the best interest of anyone in AZ, which has such a strong swing vote. It’s what makes people get disillusioned with politics, and encourages less people to vote. Please keep competitive districts, so that we can have level-headed legislators. Thank you.

column5: redistricting
column6: The districts must comply withy US Constitution, Equal populations as practical in CD's and State LD's.  Districts shall be compact and contiguous.  Boundaries shall respect communities of interest as much as possible.  District lines should use physical features, such as cities and county boundaries. Competitive districts should be favored as much as possible.

column5: 2 maps
column6: I am urging you to support 2 maps: LDF0050 and LDF0051. Thank you. Jane Ryan

column5: strong disagreement with LD17 boundaries
column6: I live in Oro Valley, and the new boundaries of LD17 seem completely inappropriate to me. Why such a sprawling district, when you could make a compact one with shared community interests by including Oro Valley, Casa Adobes, Marana, and northwest Tucson. Adding in distant rural communities on the other side of the mountains just doesn't make any sense - they have nothing in common with us. Why force us into a district with a large, unrelated rural area more than 50 miles away?  This seems like the classic case of a  gerrymandered district, and it is not in the least competitive.  I strongly urge that your follow the mandate of the IRC and update this map to create a more compact and competitive district for those of us in the Northwest Greater Tucson area. Thank you.

column5: Re Districting
column6:
I am a retired resident of Paradise Valley, having lived here for almost 32 years.  We are a predominately residential area where we can live, go to church, send kids to school, in a neighborhood environment. We hold Community functions to instill a close-knit feeling.  IT makes NO sense to break us into 4 legislative districts. Our close neighbor is Scottsdale so it makes no sense to include us with Tempe or Glendale. We are a residential community. 
Please keep communities of interest together as mandated.

column5: map trainings
column6: thank you so much for scheduling mapping tutorials.  however, since all three are scheduled for the same day of the week and at the same time of day, I feel there are people that would want to engage while it is live, and will not be able to do so.

column5: proposed LD 17
column6:
It makes no sense for Marana and Vail to be in the same Legislative District17. There is no way to get from one end of the district to the other without traveling through other proposed districts. I live in Unincorporated Pima County between Marana and Oro Valley. I've lived here 30 years and never even once had occasion to travel to Vail. 

I have followed the IRC proposals and listened to testimony. People from Vail, and people from Marana are in complete agreement we should be in separate LDs.  Please liberate Vail from LD 17. This will enable you to solve another worrisome aspect of the map, namely that Santa Cruz County is split up even though they prefer to remain whole.  Since you'd need to pick up some population elsewhere, it makes sense to add Picture Rocks and Avra Valley on the Marana end of the Map.  Those two communities are part of a wider community of interest, namely Marana Unified School District, Pima County, and the Interstate !0 transportation corridor. They have no desire to be a tiny appendage of an LD that is mainly Pinal County.

Thank you for taking the time to read and consider commentary from AZ citizens.

column5: Redistricting in Sedona
redistricting
column6:
Our community of interest...Sedona/VOC...is being splintered by the proposed redistricting map. I sincerely hope this is due to an oversight on the part of the commission and not an attempt to negate the voices of the citizens of Sedona/VOC.
Please restore the unity of our community.

column5: Proposed maps for Northern Arizona

column5: Mesa/SE Mesa
column6:
Mesa District 6 is split into 3 Legislative Districts (D10, D14, D15).
•	D10
     o	Placed medium income single family neighborhoods into areas with lower income and retirement communities. Values and economic needs are different. Significant differences even exist between D5 (northeast Mesa) and D6 (southeast Mesa) in Mesa.
•	D14
     o	No significant issues. Neighborhoods share commonalities, values, etc.

     o	Placed urban east Mesa in a more rural portion of Pinal County with San Tan Valley, Apache Junction, Queen Creek, and Gila Indian Reservation.  There are very little historical, economical, and cultural commonalities between the communities. 
     o	Took more fundamentally stable, medium to high income, professional, young, family-oriented neighborhoods and put them with retirement communities, lower income, and county islands, none of which share similarities in values and economic needs.
Mesa is still split in 2 CD’s (D4, D6).
•	D4 
     o	North, Central and South Mesa are grouped together with Tempe, Ahwatukee, and Salt River Pima Indian Reservation.  The histories are different, the cultures are different, and the values are different. Mesa should not be combined with Tempe or Salt River Pima.
     o	South Mesa shares more commonalities and values with the residents in Gilbert than they do with Tempe and Ahwatukee.
•	D5
     o	The southern border of Mesa (Germann Rd) is split away from Mesa and placed into D2. This makes zero sense. The entire area from SR24 to Germann is zoned is a light and heavy industrial zoned business corridors by Mesa and should not be split apart, but rather part of the overall encompassing area of PMGA and adjacent businesses.

     o The retirement communities along Southern Ave in east Mesa (including Leisure World) have shared economic and social values that align with other communities like Sun Lakes. If there is an opportunity to include them together, that would be a positive.

Thank you for the opportunity to provide feedback based on my knowledge of my community and the surrounding areas.

Thank you for your consideration.
Kathleen S. Littlefield
Councilwoman, City of Scottsdale

column5: LD17
column6:
I know you've seen this language previously, but the IRC does not seem to be paying attention to the citizens of Oro Valley:
LD17 doesn’t meet the IRC's constitutional criteria:
• Districts shall be geographically compact and contiguous to the extent practicable – LD17 isn’t contiguous when a mountain range sits right in the middle. You would have to cross at least two other legislative districts to go from Oro Valley to Vail. LD17 also isn’t compact. Its perimeter is convoluted and sprawling. The constituents residing in one part of the district are hours away from constituents living in other places.
• District boundaries shall respect communities of interest to the extent practicable. LD17 doesn’t respect communities of interest. Oro Valley has commonalities with Casas Adobes and northern Pima County. They have similar demographics, economies, urbanization, and trajectories. Oro Valley shares a school district with Casas Adobes, as well as water and land concerns and transportation corridors. You can drive from any part of Oro Valley into Casas Adobes and northern Pima county and not notice. Oro Valley is urban-suburban, not rural. LD17 has an almost 10% vote spread which puts the legislative district in the uncompetitive range. Oro Valley’s party affiliation mirrors that of the state, not that of a safe Republican district. LD17 is not representative of the citizens of Oro Valley.
• To the extent practicable, district lines shall use visible geographic features, but LD 17 ignores the Catalina and Rincon Mountains. LD17 also ignores political boundaries by including Pinal County places.
• To the extent practicable, competitive districts should be favored where to do so would create no significant detriment to the other goals. None of the constitutional criteria are negatively impacted by changing LD17, they are only enhanced. Commissioner Lerner's map (9.0) offers an acceptable alternative to the adopted Legislative Draft Map.

column5: SUPPORT FOR PROPOSED MAP #LDF049
column6:
My name is Jann-Michael Greenburg, and I am the current president of Scottsdale Unified School District No. 48’s (“SUSD”) Governing Board, a nonpartisan elected body. I have lived in the City of Scottsdale since 2017 and serve as the vice president of business affairs for Tresóna Multimedia, LLC, my family’s Scottsdale-based company. My grandparents, parents, and younger brother also live in Scottsdale.

As an elected official, I believe elections and the voting process should be fair, neutral, and accessible to all legally eligible United States citizens. A critical component to achieving these goals is ensuring our voting districts are drawn in accordance with the Independent Restriction Commission’s (“IRC”) six criteria, namely, that districts must generally have an equal population, be compact and contiguous, comply with the United States Constitution and the Voting Rights Act, respect communities of interest, incorporate visible geographic features, and be competitive. Based on these criteria, I support the proposed Map #LDF049 (also known as the “Keep Greater Scottsdale Together Map”) because it meets these essential criteria.

Notably, the final draft map splits the following voting precincts: Pine Valley, Mustang, Del Joya, San Simon, McCormick Ranch (in which I, my parents, and my younger brother live), Redwing, Pecos, and Pueblo. Proposed Map #LDF049 addresses this issue, while also offering the IRC the ability to meet all other criteria. Importantly, Map #LDF049 closely achieves my goal of fair and neutral districts by developing a near even split between our nation’s two major political parties, with Republicans having only a slight voter registration advantage.
	
Thank you very much for your service, time, and consideration. As always, it is greatly appreciated.

column5: Greenlee County's Comments on Final Draft Maps.
column6:
November 9, 2021

Arizona Redistricting Commission

	RE: Comments on Final Draft Maps

Commissioners,

	Thank you for your work on the 2020 Census based redistricting maps.  Greenlee County has reviewed them and find that generally speaking, the proposals in Draft Maps CD 7.1 and LD 10.0 are acceptable to Greenlee County.  Greenlee County has been placed in proposed Congressional District 6 and proposed Legislative District 19.  
With respect to Congressional District 6, Greenlee County would suggest that southern Gila County be included in this congressional district and the parts of Pinal and Pima County that currently are part of the proposed district be attached to another congressional district.  We recognize that the population of southern Gila County may not be a one-for-one trade off with the portions of Pinal and Pima Counties and that some of these areas may need to remain with District 6.  But southern Gila County has many common interests with Greenlee, Graham and Cochise counties, chief among them is a strong mining sector in the local economy.  Additionally, there is a commonality of public lands: National Forests, Bureau of Land Management and State lands which is shared with the core of District 6.  The majority of the areas in Pinal and Pima counties that are currently proposed are not as affected by mining and public land policy as is southern Gila County.  For our local economies which are based in mining, agriculture, including ranching, and outdoor recreation, these common issues define much of what is the core of our communities in District 6.  Therefore, Greenlee County asks that these common communities of interest be considered and the maps be redrawn to include southern Gila County with District 6 and make whatever adjustments are necessary in Pinal and Pima Counties to accommodate this adjustment.
As for Legislative District 19, Greenlee County strongly prefers the adopted LD Draft Map, 10.0.  If it were possible to exchange portions of Santa Cruz and Pima for southern Gila County, we would again prefer that as well for the same reasons set forth above regarding CD 6.  Nevertheless, we feel it is imperative to keep LD 19 as set out in Draft LD Map 10.0 and not separate the border from the rest of the district.  The areas along the Arizona-Mexico border share communities of interest with more than one neighboring community, however, to assume that this community has its strongest ties to Latino communities in Pima and Santa Cruz County over the Latino community in the remainder of Cochise, Graham and Greenlee Counties simply attempts to put form over substance while ignoring agricultural and ranching interests and border issues common to the Cochise, Graham, Greenlee communities.  Additionally, having the border represented by three senators and six representatives gives a more effective and broader voice to these issues that are constantly at the forefront of policy issues in Arizona.  More specifically, having state representation specific to the developing port of entry in Douglas is both significant and critical to advocating for state-wide support for an economic driver that will become an increasingly important factor as Arizona competes with other border states for its share of the border economy.  Lastly, southern Cochise is rural, and in many cases remote.  Issues pertinent to rural/remote communities, especially rural Latino communities are not best served by primarily urban legislators who will likely favor urban interests over rural simply by nature of where the majority of their constituents reside.
Thank you for considering our comments.  We hope you will consider our requests regarding southern Gila County but above all, we ask that you respect the communities of interest set forth in CD Draft Map 7.1 and LD Draft Map 10.0.


Sincerely,



Richard Lunt, Chairman
Greenlee County Board of Supervisors

column5: Competitive Distrits
column6: The most important criterion for the new districts, be they federal or state, is that they be competitive.  Our democratic system only works if the districts are competitive.  Districts that are firmly Republican or Democratic result in governance by the minority, the extreme of either party.  Those elected from non-competitive districts answer to their extreme base and not to the electorate as a whole.  When districts are competitive, the majority governs.  Those elected from competitive districts have to answer to the entire electorate.  When districts are competitive, the resulting legislature is less polarized.  The elected representatives are more likely to work across the aisle and compromise.  Please do everything legally permissible to make as many of the districts competitive as possible.

column5: IRC - proposed draft map - " District 17"
column6:
The proposed district 17 does not comply with federal and state law and is Illegal. 
District 17 is not "compact and contiguous..”: it is made up of cherry-picked Republican leaning suburbs from opposite ends of the Tucson area, separated by a mountain range and 45-minute-long drive.

It does not "respect communities of interest to the extent practicable." The residents of Tanque Verde and Vail have much closer ties to Tucson than to Marana and Oro Valley.Why are these 4 areas being crammed together?

In creating a “safe” Republican district, 17 is not competitive, violating the constitutional requirement that "… competitive districts should be favored where to do so would create no significant detriment to the other goals."

Democratic Commissioner Lerner proposed an alternative version of District 17 that was contiguous and highly competitive, but it was rejected on the grounds that it failed to create a “safe” Republican district.

Therefore - to meet federal and state requirements, the IRC needs to go back to LD Test map version 9.0 as proposed by Commissioner Lerner.

A. Districts shall comply with the U.S. Constitution and the U.S. Voting Rights Act

B. Congressional districts shall have equal population to the extent practicable.  Ditto with state legislative districts.

C. Districts shall be geographically compact and contiguous to the extent practicable.  (You can't split them up any old way.)

D. District boundaries shall respect "communities of interest" (the Navajos, your school district, your immediate neighborhood, etc.)

E. District lines shall use visible geographic features (mountains, rivers, etc.)  and city, town and county boundaries.

F. Districts should be competitive ("fair and balanced" in political representation - each party has a roughly equal chance of winning an election.)
