column5: Mapping
column6: I urge the Commission to honor the wishes of Arizona voters and "oversee the mapping of fair and competitive congressional and legislative districts." Arizona voters created the IRC to generate competitive districts. To that end, the Commission MUST maximize competitiveness in as many districts as possible.

column5: mapping
column6:
My name is Linda Chiles and I reside in (currently) LD30 and CD6.  Thank you, Commission, for allowing public input.  I fervently hope you will utilize…and not just listen to… the masses of public comments regarding this redistricting process you are conducting.
My concern is with the apparent gerrymandering that you have shown with this draft of maps.  Proposition 106 charges you to create “fair and balanced” districts.  What you have created are maps that are 80% “safe” and in no way competitive.  “Safe” districts mean the other party has NO chance of ever getting elected in that district.  “Competitive” districts mean both parties have a chance to win and that electorate can believe their candidate at least has a fighting chance to win.  By your own stated measure of range which was 0-7%, this result you have created is way over that mark.  And your argument that this 80% is balanced between Republican and Democrat holds no water whatsoever.  A “safe” district means a deterioration of the quality of candidates, a lack of government’s responsiveness to the people, voter apathy, disenchantment with and low participation in elections.  It results in the general population’s perception and comment…”My vote doesn’t count.”  A “competitive” district, on the other hand, creates quality candidates, voter participation and strengthens…not weakens…our way of governing.
Stop the gerrymandering that you are currently doing.  Adhere to the directives of Proposition 106 and create a final result of “fair and balanced” districts.  Listen to what we are pleading you to do….please!

column6: I don't know if this can be addressed via this commission, but Sky Ranch shouldn't be under Yavapai Jurisdiction, because they have had years of complaints about how they blast loud music usually from 6-10 pm, on weeknights too, from an outdoor tent on Airport Mesa. column5: Redistricting LD3
column6:
Hi - I am an attorney and I live in north Scottsdale with my husband and children. Please do not split Scottsdale into 3 districts. Our city is very special, it's nationally known for how unique it is - we need to be kept together as much as possible.  

Most of us in Central and north Scottsdale stay north of Chaparral Rd, so if you have to divide it, I guess that would be a fair dividing line. South Scottsdale is most like Tempe - ASU grads typically move to South Scottsdale so put south Scottsdale with LD8.

This way, Scottsdale is only split in 2 and our citizens and representatives stand a chance. Thank you.

column5: Legislative District Proposed Boundaries
column6: I have been a Scottsdale businessman for over 50 years and have lived in LD23 Scottsdale/Fountain Hills the entire time. This is where our lives are, church, friends, business partners. Please don't move the boundaries as currently proposed.

column5: Redistricting
column6: I am writing in support of maps BOS LDF 0050 and LDF 0051 that the Elected City Councils of Sedona and Flagstaff and the Coconino County Board of Supervisors have submitted and support for drawing the Legislative Districts.  Keeping Sedona together is critical for shared services including government, school, fire and library.  Also, keeping Sedona together along with Flagstaff and the Verde Valley honors our shared economies and facilities including infrastructure, healthcare, natural resources and culture as a community.  We are collectively an economy that relies on tourism to a much greater extent than Prescott, and we need to recognize that reality. In addition, voters passed Prop 106 to create fair and competitive districts.  Northern Arizona Districts as drawn by the IRC do not meet these standards.  Competitive districts keep voters engaged and turnout high, and all voices are heard, including Independents.  This is critical for the health of our democracy. I strongly urge you to honor the unique character of our community East of Mingus Mountain and support maps BOS LDF 0050 and LDF 0051.

column5: Arizona Redistricting
column6:
Please keep Scottsdale whole! Scottsdale is one town, complete and independent!   I am a resident in North Scottsdale. 
 Our home is in Scottsdale, we shop, seek medical care, attend church, and dine in Scottsdale.  Most of our friends, live in Scottsdale. Our extended family lives in Scottsdale.  We attend cultural events in Scottsdale.  We occassionaly travel to Cave Creek or Fountain Hills for dining and events, but the majority of our time and money is spent right here in Scottsdale. 
I have very little in common with people in North Phoenix, DC Ranch, and certainly nothing related to the Deerfield Airpark area.  I have never even been to this area!  Scottsdale is a unified district and should be kept whole.  There is a natural boundary at Scottsdale Road.   This should be utilized.

There is no possibility that anyone could represent the interests of Scottsdale, North Phoenix, and the Deerpark Airfield.  This is too broad of a district and covers a multitude of diverse interests and needs.

Please reconsider the lines you have drawn...ensure that those lines do not favor one political party over another.... and guarantee fair elections for us all.

column6:

column6: I am 70 years old and have never missed a federal election since I became eligible to vote. I have only missed two local/state elections, both because I was in the process of moving. column5: Redistricting
column6: I have lived in eastern Arizona for over 30 years.  Raised 4 children here.  And 5 plus one coming grandchildren growing up here.  My husband was a logger for many years before that industry was destroyed.  Now we have a backhoe business. I also lived in the valley for many years have a son and his family two more grandkids living there.  It is a great difference in how we live. Rural Az is a very different way of life than urban or metropolitan areas. I personally fought long and hard to save the logging ranching mining farming and recreational industries that we once had thriving here.  Now we are more of a service based economy. 11/19/2021

Chairwoman Schupak Neuberg and Members of the Arizona Redistricting Commission,
Thank you for considering my comments as you consider both the Federal Congressional Districts and our State legislative districts. My name is Bruce Bracker; I was born and raised in Nogales Arizona where my family has been involved in local government, nonprofits and operating businesses since 1924.
I am currently serve on the Santa Cruz County Board of Supervisors representing District #3 which encompasses Tubac, East Rio Rico and all of eastern Santa Cruz County which includes Patagonia, Sonoita and Elgin. 
When I addressed this commission at the meeting in Nogales, I emphasized that it was very important to keep Santa Cruz County whole. And this is the first point I would like to draw you attention to. As a rural county, it is very important that our need as a community be important to our Congressional Representative, if you divide us you weaken that voice.
It is also very important to maintain Santa Cruz County in the current community of interest, north to Tucson, which includes the University of Arizona, and Pima Community College is very important to us. Pima Community College is our partner for our local community college and our partner for our local high school JETD programs. The University of Arizona has had a satellite campus in Santa Cruz County for many years and we benefit from their economic research of our community.
In map 10.0 and 10.2, you have drawn Santa Cruz County into a district that includes the Southern portion of Cochise County. I must emphasize that we do not have the economic, familial, educational nexus to this group of people. 
 I have refrained up to this point, to talk about the political affiliation motive, which you should not be considering, but I can see no other reason to be carving out southern Cochise County for a district that includes Santa Cruz yet taking away Southern Pima County that we share so many common interests just not political ones. I feel compelled to repeat myself, is an economic, educational and familial nexus to Pima County that simply does not exist with Cochise County.
At some point, your commission is charged with maintaining Voting Rights Act districts in Arizona. I believe that Santa Cruz County and Nogales belongs in this type of district because of its profile population as I mentioned before.
In closing, I also mentioned at your meeting in Nogales that it is very important to have two congressional districts that represent the communities on the US-Mexican border. This reasoning also applies to State legislative Districts. Though rural, our proximity to the US – Mexican Border means that we are dealing with issues that require the attention of the State Legislature and the Governor. By creating a long and narrow border district, you dilute the representation for the region. Thanking you in advance for your consideration of my comments
Sincerely,
 
Bruce Bracker
District 3 Supervisor
Santa Cruz County

column6:
Thank you for the opportunity to provide input.  I am a resident of Tubac in Santa Cruz County.  I live in the 2nd Legislative District.  If the current draft maps are approved, I will live in LD 19.

Active Management Areas
There are reasons that the State of Arizona created the Santa Cruz Active Management Area (“SCAMA”) out of the Tucson Active Management Area (“TAMA”) in the mid-’90s to closely monitor and regulate underground water in the SCAMA.  SCAMA covers an area from the border with Mexico through Tubac to the boundary with Pima County around Amado where it interfaces with the TAMA.  State legislative support concerning water regulation is useful when needed.
THERE ARE NO ACTIVE MANAGEMENT AREAS IN COCHISE, GREENLEE, NOR GRAHAM COUNTIES!

International Wastewater Treatment Plant
The U.S. International Boundary and Water Commission (“USIBWC”) operates the Nogales International Wastewater Treatment Plant (“NIWTP”) in Rio Rico, AZ where it treats about 15M gallons/day of effluent from Nogales AZ (~20%) and Nogales Sonora Mexico (~80%).  That treated effluent is released into the Santa Cruz River where it helps to replenish some of the aquifer and the Santa Cruz River then flows above ground to a little bit north of Tubac and then goes underground through the TAMA and the Pinal Active Management Area until it reaches the Phoenix Active Management Area and then meets up with the Gila River on the outskirts of Phoenix.  State legislative support of the NIWTP, and the USIBWC as it deals with rogue effluent discharges from the Sonora side of the border, is critical to ensure continued clean water flow of the Santa Cruz River which helps ensure wildlife that brings tourists.



National Heritage Area
The US Congress had reasons to create the Santa Cruz Valley National Heritage Area in 2019, and determine its boundaries, which follows, generally, the Santa Cruz River from the border with Mexico through Tubac and further north to about Marana.  There will be coordination of various factors in the Area.  This Area is about to submit its Management Plan to the US Secretary of the Interior.
NO PORTION OF COCHISE, GREENLEE NOR GRAHAM COUNTIES ARE WITH THE BOUNDARY OF THE SANTA CRUZ VALLEY NATIONAL HERITAGE AREA!

I ask that you consider the above as you consider in which district it makes sense to include the Tubac, Tumacacori, Carmen and Amado areas.

column5: Observations on the Salt River Public Hearing
column6:
My name is Victoria Kauzlarich.  I have lived in Scottsdale for ten years and have been a property owner here for 20.  

Since becoming a full-time resident, I have served on four of my HOA’s committees, I am a Deputy Registrar, a graduate of the Botanical Garden’s Desert Landscape School and, for 6 years, the author of a sustainability column in my HOA’s monthly magazine.  Volunteer activities, all.

I’ve been following the IRC’s progress toward redistricting for months.  I have submitted several written comments and appeared before you publicly during the last round of public hearings.

I attended the Salt River hearing last Thursday and I would like to make a couple of observations on two lines of reasoning that came through loud and clear during public comments.

The first, and one the IRC has heard routinely, is the litany of people who begin their comments with “I shop at x, I eat at y and my doctor is at z, therefore that’s my community of interest.”  This is nonsense and yet it has been repeatedly expressed, right after each speaker’s opening biographical remarks.

These are not reasoned arguments and, as often as these have been repeated, literally dozens of times across the 3 meetings I’ve attended, it is clear that these are talking points the speakers have been instructed to use.  This observation led me to wonder, has the IRC asked any of these speakers what these comments mean and why they think that ‘where I shop is my community of interest’?

The second set of comments I heard is far more troubling and last night was the first I’ve heard them.   They go something like this, “competitive maps = gerrymandering”.  One of the later speakers was outraged over this, particularly as it relates to the draft CD1 map.

I fear that argument will take hold much as other equally-outraged contemporary messaging has.  I know that these hearings are not intended to be debates and I’m not sure how or if the IRC should address this second observation, but it looks like the basis for a future legal argument in the making. 

Thank you for your time and your service to our state.

Victoria Kauzlarich
Scottsdale Resident

column5: Scottsdale Redistricting
column6:
egislative districts.  As much as is practicable, greater Scottsdale should be kept together. Keeping greater Scottsdale together is wholly consistent with all six of the constitutional criteria for drawing a district.  At roughly 240,000 people, it is within the margin of error for equal population.  Keeping greater Scottsdale together achieves compactness and contiguousness.  It incorporates visible geographic features.  The geographic footprint of Scottsdale remains virtually in tact as does the Salt River Pima-Maricopa community.  It includes all of the unique features of both: urban, suburban and rural.   Further, it creates competitiveness that the previous draft iterations do not. Keeping greater Scottsdale together offers the opportunity for legislative candidates to run and govern from the middle, thereby serving the majority of voters in the proposed greater Scottsdale district.   We already know that this level of party parity works.  Two examples in the city of Scottsdale are the City Council and the Scottsdale Unified School District Governing Board.  Both are composed of centrist candidates from both parties and both govern as citizen-centric.  This greater Scottsdale district also complies with the Voting Rights Act in ways that the current LD23 does not.  The proposed greater Scottsdale district has a compelling economic community of interest that  includes tourism, local business interests on the 101 corridor south of 90th Street, along with Scottsdale Community College - all of which are on tribal lands.   Putting these two communities together also preserves their mutual interest in sustainable land use, respect for the individual character of diverse and distinct neighborhoods, a culture of citizen involvement, environmental stewardship & open space preservation, along with a citizen-centric focus on planning, community building & decision-making. Both communities - Scottsdale and the Salt River Pima-Maricopa Indian community value their unique sense of place.  The IRC should value that as well by keeping greater Scottsdale together. column5: Northern Arizona Districts
column6:
In November 2000, Arizona voters passed Proposition 106 in order to remove power to draw congressional and state legislative districts from the state legislature. Voters approved Prop. 106 by a vote of 56.1% to 43.9% The Commission's mandate is to draw districts according to six criteria. One of these is that districts should be electorally competitive whenever possible.

Currently, none of the Commission's draft districts for northern Arizona are competitive. District 6 leans Democrat by 42 points, District 7 leans Republican by 29 points, and District 5 leans Republican by more than 20 points.

The current draft map does not honor the Arizona voters who overwhelmingly voted for a bipartisan Commission that would create competitive districts so that ALL Arizonans would have a voice.

column5: Redistricting
column6:
I am a resident in the 8th Congressional District and 1st Legislative District. I have been a non-partisan voter during all of my 53 years of voting and have never registered with any political party. As an “independent” voter, I have come to believe that my vote has little to no significance in these districts.  

When one political party has an overwhelming advantage over all others in a district, the system becomes more autocratic and less democratic. The voice of the minority voter is all but silenced. At times, I have had difficulty in getting my representatives to even respond to my inquiries, let alone engage in dialogue. It leaves those, like me, wondering whether to cast a vote at all.

It has been said that the touchstone of a republican form of government is political equality. I understand that in the redistricting process, there will be some districts configured that favor one political party over another. That is likely unavoidable. But what can be avoided is the configuration of districts that gives a decisive advantage to one political party. If there is a lack of competitiveness within a voting district, it leaves many voters, like me, apathetic. When that occurs, our democracy is in jeopardy.

I simply ask that when you consider the redistricting of the 8th Congressional and 1st Legislative districts, that you allow for competition in political races that are truly that - competitive. To do otherwise, promotes extremism, discourages citizen participation and creates political inequality, thereby placing our republic at risk.

Politics is like hardball. Rules are made to make baseball fair. We implore the Commission to keep our elections fair by following the three Cs. Thank you.

column5: Comments on Proposed Maps for Northern AZ
column6:
I am writing concerning the proposed voter maps for Northern Arizona.  I am a resident of Prescott.  First I urge you to adopt CDF 010 as recommended by the Navajo Nation Human Rights Commission.  This would provide a much more competitive district than what the Commission is currently proposing.  CDF 010 would have a 1% voter spread, while the proposed CDF 2 has more than a 7% voter spread, which is outside of the range of competitiveness.  Further, this proposed district does not meet the Voting Rights Act requirements.

Second, I urge you to move Yavapai County back into CD9 and remove the portion of Marciopa County.  Further, I would like to see the Verde Valley and the Sedona area moved into CD2.  Rural Arizona deserves two rural districts.  CD9 as it is now proposed effectively removes one of them with the huge dominance of west valley communities in Maricopa County.  And the proposed CD9 is not competitive.  Additionally putting all of Yavapai County in one district does not address our population growth, our geography, our water management or any other measure.

I realize you are being lobbied heavily by Republican interests in Northern Arizona, but you are charged with making non-partisan decisions that lead to competitive state-wide maps.  Arizona has been a leader in this regard and it would be a travesty if this was the commission that drew maps with a partisan bias.

column5: Keep Greater Scottsdale Together
column6:
Keeping Greater Scottsdale Together

My name is Susan Roth. I have owned land in 85255 since 2001 and moved permanently to Scottsdale 6 years ago. I frequently volunteer with Brandeis University Arizona and National Council of Jewish Women to serve our local population. 

Scottsdale is a city that respects its citizens and has a city council and Scottsdale Unified School District Governing Board who work together for the greater good of its citizens. Both groups have centrist members of both political parties. It is a system that works well and should be reinforced rather than undermined.

The new IRC map divides Scottsdale into 3 legislative districts. It would make it difficult for our mayor and city council to deal with 6 house representatives and 3 senators. It diminishes our citizens’ power and influence. LD 23 would become LD 3 and does not meet the IRC six constitutional criteria for drawing a District. It makes the new plan contrary to the goal of the IRC to assure a fair and competitive breakdown between the two parties that will create maximum openness, dialogue and citizen participation.

 I recommend we follow the Keep Greater Scottsdale Together Map #LDF049 which I am attaching. 
This map creates near parity between the two political parties with R having a slight majority. By including the Salt River Pima Indian Community with the city of Scottsdale we preserve both groups interest in sustainable land use and business interests along the 101 Corridor south of 90th St. to McDowell  which is on reservation land. It would address one of the major goals of the IRC and that is to incorporate and give equal voice to minorities in this situation the indigenous people. 

Please consider using MAP #LDF049 Keep Greater Scottsdale Together. This map would come very close to have an even split between our political parties.

Thank you for all of your hard work to be fair to our residents.

column5: Please consider Maps CDF 10, LDF 50, and LDF 51 to eliminate "safe" districts.
column6:
Good morning.  My name is Jessica Ebel.  I am a teacher with Prescott Unified, and my husband just retired from 20 years of service with the U.S. Navy.  We’ve put down roots in Prescott, where we’ll raise our two young children.  

I am here to voice my concern that the current draft maps do not honor the will of the voters- specifically the constitutional requirement from PROP 106 for fair and competitive districts.  We can do better.  

Yavapai county itself is too large to be a community of interest and does not need to be kept whole, especially when it’s at the expense of slicing and dicing actual communities such as Flagstaff, Sedona, and Wickenburg.  This makes no sense. As an alternative, Maps LDF50 and LDF 51 keep the Verde Valley whole, and are significantly more compact and competitive.

If Yavapai were kept whole we’d only get 1 congressional district and 3 legislators.  This map cuts our representation in half, and that’s not fair.  Yavapai County is growing and we need more representation, not less.  Map CDF 10 recognizes Mingus Mountain as a natural boundary with distinct areas of service and representation on either side. It’s highly competitive, honors the voting rights act, and respects Native voices.

As an independent voter, I want my vote to count.  When districts are too safe, candidates cater to their base and extreme positions.  The primaries will determine the outcome of the general election.  We want more competitive districts in Northern Arizona, with better candidates who focus on the issues that matter in our communities, and must listen to all constituents.

I am deeply concerned about the growing influence of extremism, violence, and corruption.

Look around our state.  We already have elected officials who:
Do not respect the boundaries between church and state
Accept corporate donations from outside interests while obstructing the will of the people
Openly threaten other members of Congress with online violence
Publicly support vigilante justice
Refuse to accept the results of a free and fair election and
Helped to plan a violent insurrection at our nation’s capital

Violent extremism is becoming more prevalent and when it is accepted in our politics, it spreads to our communities. In Prescott, we have people making threats to members of our school board about masks.  We have people coming to the square with weapons to intimidate peaceful protestors. We cannot create districts where violent or extreme candidates will be “safe” and therefore unaccountable.  Over time, “safe” maps will make our state and our democracy less safe.

I agree with all of the Hopi and Navajo speakers regarding CDF 10, and I am also asking you to consider Maps LDF 50 and LDF 51as alternatives. 

THANK YOU for taking the time to listen and for the important work you are doing here today.

column5: The New Maps for AZ
column6:

Citizens in EACH individual district should have a chance at being elected in their districts: Legislative or Congressional!   We want representatives that are highly qualified, that listen to ALL their citizens, who know how to negotiate. Candidates who have opposition.  Candidates who put forth an effort to resolve the problems in their district - not just the ones from their own party.  Having an equal share of "safe districts" is not what Prop 206 had in mind. 

Having said that, having citizens from Maricopa County in with citizens in Mohave, Yuma and La Paz does not comply with the AZ Constitution.  Maricopa County is not in our community of interests.  They are more in line with city or urban interface residents.  70% of our population would therefore be from Maricopa County, drowning out the voice of the people who live in rural Arizona along the western part of the State.  I would much rather have our additional numbers come from Yavapai County.  They are rural residents as well and understand many of the same issues we have in Mohave County.

column5: Redistricting - Scottsdale Community
column6:
2021 Arizona Redistricting
My name is Douglass Ebstyne, I live in northern Scottsdale. My wife and I moved here nearly 6 years ago because we thought Scottsdale was a great community to live in.
From my perspective the key issue in re-districting is community of interest. All other criteria are anchored to community of interest. For example, adherence to city, town and county boundaries and undivided census tracts, districts being compact and contiguous as much as practical all tie into community of interest.
Our Scottsdale home is north of Cave Creek Parkway in the proposed LD3. We live way north of 101, yet we shop in both Scottsdale Quarters and Fashion Square and everywhere in between. Our Church, which we love, is on Shea. We buy our cars and have them serviced in Scottsdale south of 101. We grocery shop at Sprouts, Trader Joes and Whole Foods. Costco is an integral part of our weekly routine. All our medical services are in Scottsdale. We eat in restaurants all over in Scottsdale.
Please do not split up Scottsdale - or include it with Desert Ridge and the I-17 area, since those are not in our community of interest, going to either of them is a “road trip.” That is nonsensical. Scottsdale’s western boundary should define the western edge of our district. If you have to make a change, Camelback south should go to D8. And remove central Phoenix from CD1 – that is a non-starter. It is blatant jerrymandering!
Between sitting for 3 1⁄2 hours at the redistricting meeting Tuesday evening (11/16) and another 2 1⁄2 hours Thursday evening (11/18) I’ve heard a few people say that they want to have competitive districts. They suggest that people will be “more engaged” in the political process if everything is balanced. I find that to be a thin, weak and incorrect rationalization.
To suggest that a detached, governmental body should be empowered to create unwanted and unnatural boundaries to neutralize one mind thought for the benefit of another is nothing short of ridiculous and unacceptable. This is a God-like task.
Why should any government entity be allowed to determine voting lines that fragment existing communities of interest? That is a process built upon prejudice! The government does not know better than a community that has developed over generations what its community of interest is. Nor is the government able to determine that one arbitrary voting configuration is “more fair” than what already exists within a natural community. To suggest otherwise is to say that we do not merit being treated as a free and independent people.
Arizona has been a state for 109 years and today it is exactly the way “we the people” have made it. If that is unsatisfactory or repugnant to some, those individuals are free to either engage in the political process or opt for one of the other 49 states that more fully aligns with their expectations. Thank you.

column5: Proposed maps
column6:
The proposed draft maps have no competitive LD’s in Northern AZ.  This is unnecessary, as the other five criteria mandated by the AZ constitution could be met, and competitive districts created, by the adoption of LDF 50, 51 and CDF 10.  Please note that, pursuant to the AZ Court of Appeals, the criteria of competitiveness is equal in weight to the other criteria mandated by prop 106.

This is important, because a healthy democracy requires that all voices be heard.  Non-competitive districts foster extremism and corruption and disregard the voices of independent, non-partisan voters.  Anyone who is not member of the majority party in the safe district is left feeling like they have no voice, and, in fact, they do not, as representatives from such districts cater to their base voters, at the exclusion of the rest of the population of the district.

Competitive districts create greater interest in the democratic process, better candidates to run for office and produce a government that is responsive to the interests and viewpoints of all constituents.  We all prosper if all ideas are considered on their merits, and not through a partisan lens.

Finally, the adoption of LDF 50, 51 and CDF 10 would create more representation for Yavapai, a large and growing county, than the proposed draft maps.  The county lines for Yavapai were drawn in 1864.  In 2021, Yavapai encompasses multiple communities of interest, not bound by the county lines.  These communities are best represented by the implementation LDF 50, 51 and CDF 10.

column5: Redistricting
column6:
Hello, My name is Corinne Haynes.   I live in Maricopa County and am here today to give you information about my community of interest.

I live off of El Mirage and Vistancia Bld. just north of the 303 and Happy Valley Road in Peoria.  My community of interest is made up of families and retirees.  Because of the proximity of the 303, 101, and the I-17, families can work close to home but also have easy access to work in neighboring towns.  My community offers many activities in which both families and retirees can interact and enhance our quality of life.

In my community, we play together, work together, attend neighborhood churches, and our kids attend schools in like districts.  Many Friday nights, families gather together at CCV (Christ's Church of the Valley) where their children compete in sports events.  On these evenings we encounter all kinds of friends that we have grown up with, gone to school with, and share common values and goals.  It's like living in a small town within a big city.  We choose to live here because we share so much in common with those in our community and it is important that we have representation who understands and shares our values.

During the last redistricting, our community was literally split right down the middle.  If you lived on one side of the street you were in a different congressional district than the other side of the street.  It was confusing and didn't make sense.  The West Valley needs to be whole again.  In the draft map, Congressional District 8 has been split but this can be corrected simply by moving some of the boundary lines to the left or west uniting Surprise, Sun City West, Sun City, Peoria, and Autumn Ridge into the same district. column5: Redistricting
column6:
To: Independent Redistricting Commission
From: Kevin Janssen
Subject: Arizona Congressional and Legislative District Maps
Date: November 22nd, 2021

My first home was purchased in old town Scottsdale with my brother in 1984. I sold my interest in that house in 1986 to my brother, who still lives there, after I was transferred out of state for work. In 2010 I bought the house next door to my brother.  We use that house for family and friends who visited Scottsdale.  In 2015, we moved back to Scottsdale to retire.  We bought our home in McCormick Ranch and have loved the area.

Our lives revolve around activities in Old Town, McCormick Ranch and Kierland,  Fountain Hills and Pinnacle Peak Thompson Peak and TPC areas. We golf at McCormick Ranch,  Desert Canyon, Continental, Kierland, Silverado, Starfire, Talking Stick, etc.  We eat out in our communities restaurants from the Isabel, Coopers Hawk, State 48 and Fates in the North to Craft 64 FnB, Montauk, Braut Haus in the South of Scottsdale.
My Doctors are in Fountain Hills and Scottsdale, we shop in Scottsdale and we use the bike trails and enjoy the parks like Railroad park and the summer concerts there and in old town.
Since I left Arizona and came back our state has grown significantly and recognizing the demographic shifts and emergence of new communities is important for having a truly representative democracy.
After attending the meeting last week I wanted to echo Tom Anderson who said it perfectly on the night of the 18th.  Tom stated:
“The criteria you have been asked to use are important … but not of equal importance! Having similar populations and having physical continuity are obvious requirements …
Preserving existing districts where possible is also important because it minimizes disruption for current representation and citizen engagement.
The most important objective is grouping communities of interest so that elected officials understand and represent their constituents … this is the essence of our representative democracy.
Per the National Conference of State Legislatures, the “competitiveness” of a district is only to be considered if it does not come at the expense of all other attributes. Trying to predetermine the outcome of a district's election by creating unnatural boundaries is “Gerrymandering”. Just look at a boundary map and you see where it is happening.”
It would be wrong to break Scottsdale up into two different districts that would have different representation.  
This is a unique town and I moved back to Scottsdale, (not Tempe, Phoenix or Anthem) because of all that has become Scottsdale. The only goal of splitting representation in Scottsdale is to weaken our representation.  Government is to work for its citizens, not for us to be at the mercy of any Political party’s desired gerrymandering. 
Scottsdale is diverse with over 30% of registered voters self-identified as Independents or Party Not Declared.  So no one party is dominant.   It is hubris to suggest anyone knows how a district is going to vote. It should be the candidates and voters that determine elections … not unnatural “gerrymandered” district boundaries.  
Thank You

column5: Competitive Districts
column6:
My name is Leah Donell, and I am an independent voter and resident of the Verde Valley, a place that feels like home to me. But the last couple of years have fueled extremist activities that threaten the peace of the community that I call home. I think the legislative and congressional district maps are a crucial tool in reducing hostility locally and throughout the state.

The purpose of the IRC is to help Arizona achieve a heathy democracy where all feel served, and where the voters are empowered. And when done properly these maps help our neighbors find common ground. The beauty of having opposing viewpoints is that when governed well the outcome allows communities to thrive, and for everyone to feel that their voice has been represented. Without competitive maps the prudent checks and balances of our system are overwhelmed by extremist viewpoints that are a toxic threat to our democracy. 

The draft maps proposed by the IRC fail to make competitive legislative and congressional districts for the people of the Verde Valley, but I believe the LDF 050 and 051 legislative maps proposed by the Coconino County Board of Supervisors and the CDF 010 congressional map proposed by the Navajo Nation remedy these failures and provide the Verde Valley with competitive districts that allow independent voters to impact and moderate our democracy. I ask that the Commission adopt these maps as they provide the competitive political environment that will help unite Arizonans by encouraging compromise and diplomacy. 

I’d like to thank the Commission for all their hard work as I can imagine the task of drawing these maps is difficult. I’d also like to thank them for giving me the opportunity to present my point of view.

The addition of all of Yavapai County to CD2 dilutes the voting power of Native Americans. We must honor the Voting Rights Act and protect communities of color. Native Americans deserve to elect representatives of their choosing. Please redraw CD2. 
There is an alternative to draft map CD2. CDF010 has been proposed by the Navajo Nation and we want to support it.
The draft map has taken a highly competitive district and made it solidly Republican by adding all of Yavapai County.
It is highly competitive with less than a 1% voter spread. Current draft map CD2 has a voter spread of 7.6% which violates the Commission standards of competitiveness at under 7%.

column5: Legislative Map
column6:
When the voters passed Prop 106 in 2000 and created the IRC, we canonized in our state constitution specific priorities to achieve fair, competitive and equitable maps. Maps must favor competitive districts to encourage high participation in elections, and guard against extremism. 

We must also respect the voice of Independent Voters and not diminish their voting rights by minimizing excessively partisan districts where the election outcome is decided in the primary. Independents already have an extra step in primary elections by having to request a ballot of a political party in order to cast a vote. Many Independents don’t realize they can vote in primary elections and fail to participate. 
None of our three Northern AZ LD’s, 5,6,7 are competitive in the proposed draft maps. We have an opportunity to create one competitive district, LD7 submitted to the IRC as LDF050. LDF050 includes Flagstaff, Verde Valley, Sedona, parts of Gina and Pinal Counties.

column5: Redistricting Northern Arizona
column6:

Wishing you a Thanksgiving filled with gratitude.
Speaking of which, the thing I would be most grateful for, now and for years to come, is living in a competitive voting district for state and federal elections. Since current proposed maps place me in LD 7, a district in which you have given a 28 point advantage to one political party over the other, Likewise, my proposed congressional district is noncompetitive, and the same is true of most districts proposed for my area.

Fairness is your ultimate objective, both legally and morally, so I urge you to listen to those of us who live in Northern AZ.

column5: Keep Greater  Scottsdale Together/Meaning of Community of Interest
column6:
I live in the McCormick Ranch neighborhood in Scottsdale, zip code 85258.  I advocate that  you adopt a map that keeps Greater Scottsdale together in one legislative district, as proposed in Map # LDF049, previously submitted by my fellow Scottsdale resident Emily Wilson.  Adopting this map would serve the constitutional mandate to respect communities of interest.
  
I have been a resident of the community of Scottsdale for almost all of the past 28 years.   My children attended Tavan Elementary, Ingleside Middle School, and Arcadia High School.  I helped to coach Odyssey of the Mind, attended PTO meetings, and supported the SUSD and its bond elections.   I currently serve on the City of Scottsdale Industrial Development Authority Board.  I use the Scottsdale public library.  I have held or participated in volunteer events a the library, in my home, and in various Scottsdale parks.   All of these activities involved interaction with other people also connected to Scottsdale.

Proposition 106, sections 14(A) through (F)  establish six goals that guide adjustments to the creation of districts of equal size in a grid-like pattern, which is the basic direction of the proposition and the presumptive starting point.   Keeping Greater Scottsdale Together  would serve the goals stated in section 14(D) of Proposition 106, which provides that “District boundaries shall respect communities of interest to the extent practicable.”

You must decide what is meant by “community of interest” as used in Proposition 106.  Community is broadly defined as a group of people living in the same place or having a particular characteristic in common, and joint actions that bring people together for some common objective.  Communities have a name.  Communities balance group interests against the interests of individuals.  

For purposes of Proposition 106 the definition of community must include a geographical component because Proposition 106 involves drawing  boundaries.  It also should include residents who share some purpose, interest or goal beyond the individual family level, frequently interact with one another, and  support one another and their shared purpose.  The fact that people individually conduct an activity in a particular location is not important.  The question is what they do together with others to advocate or support a shared goal that relates to common interests that are tied to a particular location.  The examples of communities of interest provided by this Commission, such as a group advocating preservation of a physical building in a specific location, is consistent with this view.  

Municipalities such as the City of Scottsdale are quintessential examples of communities.  Their boundaries were established under Arizona law by people who wanted shared local governance.  Residents share concerns about the quality of their public schools, municipal infrastructure, municipal services such as water and trash, police and fire, public amenities such as parks and libraries,  their neighborhoods, zoning, community character and historic preservation, taxation and spending.  They encompass similarly numbered census tracts, by which funds are allocated and data is tracked. They also share concerns about municipal governance and elections.  All of these factors affect groups of people residing in the community, not just isolated individuals.  Municipalities also seek advantages for their residents, such as state and federal grant funding, economic development activities, affordable housing and workforce development.  

In contrast,  although membership in an international  society of video gamers is arguably a community of interest, the interest is not affected by the physical location of the activity.  It would thus not be a community of  interest for purposes of Proposition 106.

Furthermore, since the independent redistricting process was created to redress a history of highly partisan districting, partisan preference should not be considered a community of interest.  

Some members of the public have argued that boundaries should be drawn based on the fact that they, as individuals, chose to live in a particular type of home, and patronize establishments near their homes.    Some argued that because they personally had never been to a particular location within a proposed district it could not be considered as part of their community. Others  claimed they have “nothing in common” with persons living in more or less densely populated areas, who are younger, or who live in multifamily housing.  In other words, they advocate segregating people into like-minded groups that avoid people who are not just like them.  Adopting individual characteristics and preferences as the standard for identifying communities of interest would contribute to polarization and animosity between different groups and views within our society.  Dividing people into groups based on their wealth, their age, the size or type of their homes, the make of their car, or where they went to college focuses on individual attributes and preferences, not shared goals or activities.  It would be unwise and contrary to the intent of the voters who adopted Proposition 106 to use this as the standard by which you evaluate Goal D.  

The City of Scottsdale should be kept intact in any legislative or congressional redistricting, because it is a community of interest that meets all the appropriate tests.  Splitting Scottsdale into multiple legislative districts is confusing to voters and makes advocacy for jurisdiction-wide priorities more difficult.  Keeping Scottsdale together would also tend to induce residents to engage and deal civilly with a broader range of individuals, thus reducing the tendency toward conflict and polarization.  

While Salt River Pima Maricopa Indian Community  is a community of interest distinct and separate from the City of Scottsdale, the two jurisdictions are physically adjacent and share many interests.  In addition, combining those two jurisdictions into a single legislative district would allow the Commission to balance the populations and create a competitive district, both considerations under Proposition 106.

Thank you for your time, service, and consideration of these comments. 

Mary Grier
Scottsdale Resident

Thank you for this opportunity to comment.  I have lived in Arizona all my life and moved to Cottonwood 15 years ago.

The draft map does not promote competitiveness for northern Arizona and does not preserve communities of interest. D7 in the draft map is not compact.  

Please keep the Verde Valley whole in one legislative district that includes all of Sedona and also includes Flagstaff. 

I go to much more frequently to Flagstaff than to Prescott, to shop at Sprouts, for medical appointments, and to hike in the summer. Flagstaff Medical Center is part of Northern Arizona Healthcare. I have never been referred to a doctor in Prescott. The drive times are about the same and I find the drive to Flagstaff less taxing.

I am a hydrologist and have worked for decades on sound water management for Arizona. The Verde River and Oak Creek flow through our communities and unite our communities. The snow and rain that fall in the Flagstaff to Williams area replenish our aquifers in the Verde Valley and keep our rivers flowing. Oak Creek provides more flow to the Verde River as does the upper Verde River at Paulden. The water in Oak Creek originates above the Mogollon Rim, in the Flagstaff and Williams area.  Integrated and collaborative water management across the Verde Valley, including Sedona, and on up to Flagstaff is essential. This is a very important community of interest that has shown much collaboration through the years. We need representation that works for the interests of the Verde Valley, rather than putting all focus on Prescott and Prescott Valley.

column5: Scottsdale Redistricting Plan
column6:
As an Arizona native and Scottsdale resident, I understand the critical importance of redistricting.  Our hope is that we can create a district that keeps greater Scottsdale together, and Map #LDF049 does exactly that. 

The district proposed by Map #LDF049 meets all six criteria established by the IRC for drawing a district.  It is within the margin of error for population.  It is compact and contiguous.  It is in compliance with the US Constitution and Voting Rights Act.  It encompases urban, suburban and rural areas.  It would be a politically balanced district. And most importantly, it recognises the shared interests of Scottsdale and the Salt River Pima-Maricopa Indian community.

My office is located in the Salt River Pima-Maricopa Indian community.  Scottsdale Community College, several schools, baseball fields and a thriving business community are located there as well - our two communities are interdependent and have a strong common interest.  We support Map LDF049 because it keeps these two communities of shared interests together.  Our communities deserve a legislator that understands the interdependence of these communities, and represents them both. 

The current draft maps split Scottsdale into three LDs.  It splits many of our precincts and divides our community.  We hope the IRC will consider our request to keep greater Scottsdale together.  Please refer to Map #LDF049 for an excellent way to achieve all the goals set by the IRC.

Thank you for your time and attention.
Robert Kelly

column5: Keep Greatrer Scottsdale Together - A True Community of Interest
column6:
I live in the McCormick Ranch neighborhood in Scottsdale, zip code 85258.  I advocate that  you adopt a map that keeps Greater Scottsdale and the Salt River Pima Maricopa Indian Community (SRPMIC) together in one legislative district, as proposed in Map # LDF049, previously submitted by my fellow Scottsdale resident Emily Wilson.  Adopting a map that Keeps Greater Scottsdale Together would serve the constitutional mandate to respect communities of interest.

My family moved to Scottsdale from Illinois back in 1958, and I attended kindergarten here.  There were still hitching posts downtown, many acres of orange groves, dirt roads with western names such as Cattletrack, and the land occupied by Scottsdale Fashion Square was used to grow table grapes.  We loved the western character and small town feel of the town.  Although we moved to Tucson and then Phoenix, I returned to Scottsdale in 1994 and except for one year have lived in the city for the past 28 years.   My children attended Tavan Elementary, Ingleside Middle School, and Arcadia High School.  I helped to coach Odyssey of the Mind, attended PTO meetings, and supported the SUSD.   I currently serve on the City of Scottsdale Industrial Development Authority Board.  I am an active community volunteer with Free Arts for Abused Children of Arizona (included a season mentoring in Scottsdale), and Arizona Town Hall (including events in Scottsdale).  I am a member of Soroptimist International of Phoenix (which founded Girls Ranch), and am on the board of Musician Enrichment  Foundation both of which have held multiple events in Scottsdale.

During my professional life as an attorney I worked in the Arizona Attorney General’s Office representing the Arizona State Land Department, and in the office of the City Attorney for the City of Phoenix, supporting the housing, real estate and economic development departments.  As an Arizona Town Hall volunteer I facilitated discussions in Scottsdale pertaining to economic development and Old Town  I mention these facts to establish my  ties to the community and my familiarity with economic development issues.

Proposition 106 identifies six goals that guide adjustments to the creation of districts of equal size in a grid-like pattern, which is the basic direction of the proposition and the presumptive starting point.  These goals are set forth in sections 14(A) through (F).  Keeping Greater Scottsdale Together  would serve all of these the goals, but particularly those stated in sections 14(D) and ( E) of Proposition 106.  Goal D provides that “District boundaries shall respect communities of interest to the extent practicable.”  Goal E provides that “To the extent practicable, district lines shall use visible geographic features, city, town, and county boundaries, and undivided census tracts.”  Keeping Greater Scottsdale Together would use city boundaries and include a geographic area with distinctive features, including the McDowell Mountains and preserve.  It would also respect the joint economic and other community interests of Scottsdale and SRPMIC.

Scottsdale and SRPMIC are jurisdictions of the type specifically  referenced in section 14(E) of Proposition 106.   Their combined populations would create a district within the population size range established by the Commission.  Each is also a community of interest within the meaning of proposition 106, section 14(D).   

Adopting the Keeping Greater Scottsdale Together map would allow Scottsdale and SRPMIC to more effectively advance and advocate for their shared community interests and concerns, which include:

•	Economic development interests such as the Loop 101commercial-industrial corridor, and the burgeoning regional industries such as medical research and treatment, and tourism.
•	The success and collateral impacts of casinos (there are two large casinos adjacent to the Loop 101 North).
•	Respect for the individual character of diverse and distinct neighborhoods
•	Scottsdale Community College, which is situated on SRPMIC lands but which serves Scottsdale residents
•	Transportation concerns, which impact both communities due to their proximity and sharing of a significant stretch of the Loop 101
•	Water use issues, including management of CAP and surface waters
•	Waste management issues
•	Maintaining the environmental health of lands and preserves
•	Cultures that value environmental stewardship, open space preservation, and citizen involvement 

Economic development is fiercely competitive and is tied to specific geographic locations.  A project will be built in a specific location within a specific jurisdiction that will exercise greater control and reap greater benefits from it than other jurisdictions.  Some communities want to attract sales-tax paying businesses to fund their operations.  Others want to attract major employers to provide well-paid job opportunities for their residents.  Municipalities are generally the entities that control issues such as zoning, infrastructure development, sales tax rebates and other incentives.   Scottsdale and SRPMIC  have significant mutual economic development interests, including the Loop 101 corridor.  

Municipalities not only compete for development projects and opportunities, they also compete for state and federal funding, status, favorable laws and regulation, and policies that advance their particular agendas.  

Scottsdale and SRPMIC should be kept intact in any legislative or congressional redistricting, because they are  separate taxing jurisdictions.  The people of Scottsdale voted to tax themselves to create the McDowell Mountain Preserve.  They conduct elections within their jurisdictional boundaries—splitting up those jurisdictions into multiple legislative districts is confusing to voters and makes advocacy for jurisdiction-wide priorities more difficult.  It would also induce residents to engage and deal civilly with a broader range of individuals, thus reducing the tendency toward conflict and polarization.  

The proposed Keep Greater Scottsdale Together map (#LDF049) would keep Scottsdale and SRPMIC precincts and census tracts together.  It is compact and contiguous.  It incorporates the political and geographic features (city and community boundaries, mountains and preserve areas) that represent a shared interest of the communities.  It would elevate, rather than diminish, the weight and significance of SRPMIC voters as a constituency within the district.  And it would result in a close to even split between the two major parties.

The maps currently proposed by the commission appear to include parts of Scottsdale in three different legislative districts, including one that extends all the way from the eastern county line to I-17.  It splits precincts and dilutes the power of Scottsdale and SRPMIC voters by lumping them together with Phoenix and Tempe voters.  It would force  the City to deal with 6 house representatives and 3 senators, each of whom would have other constituencies to represent and balance against the interests of these communities.  It also creates non-competitive districts.  For all these reasons it should be abandoned in favor of the Keep Greater Scottsdale Together map.

Thank you for your time, service, and consideration of these comments.  

Mary Grier
Scottsdale Resident

column5: Redistricting - Scottsdale Community
column6:
2021 Arizona Redistricting


My name is Douglass Ebstyne, I live in northern Scottsdale. My wife and I moved here nearly 6 years ago because we thought Scottsdale was a great community to live in. 

From my perspective the key issue in re-districting is community of interest.  All other criteria are anchored to community of interest. For example, adherence to city, town and county boundaries and undivided census tracts, districts being compact and contiguous as much as practical all tie into community of interest. 

Our Scottsdale home is north of Cave Creek Parkway in the proposed LD3. We live way north of 101, yet we shop in both Scottsdale Quarters and Fashion Square and everywhere in between. Our Church, which we love, is on Shea. We buy our cars and have them serviced in Scottsdale south of 101.  We grocery shop at Sprouts, Trader Joes and Whole Foods.  Costco is an integral part of our weekly routine. All our medical services are in Scottsdale. We eat in restaurants all over in Scottsdale. 

Please do not split up Scottsdale - or include it with Desert Ridge and the I-17 area, since those are not in our community of interest, going to either of them is a “road trip.” That is nonsensical. Scottsdale’s western boundary should define the western edge of our district. If you have to make a change, Camelback south should go to D8. And remove central Phoenix from CD1 – that is a non-starter. It is blatant jerrymandering!

Between sitting for 3 ½ hours at the redistricting meeting Tuesday evening (11/16) and another 2 ½ hours Thursday evening (11/18) I’ve heard a few people say that they want to have competitive districts. They suggest that people will be “more engaged” in the political process if everything is balanced. I find that to be a thin, weak and incorrect rationalization. 

To suggest that a detached, governmental body should be empowered to create unwanted and unnatural boundaries to neutralize one mind thought for the benefit of another is nothing short of ridiculous and unacceptable. This is a God-like task. 

Why should any government entity be allowed to determine voting lines that fragment existing communities of interest?  That is a process built upon prejudice! The government does not know better than a community that has developed over generations what its community of interest is. Nor is the government able to determine that one arbitrary voting configuration is “more fair” than what already exists within a natural community. To suggest otherwise is to say that we do not merit being treated as a free and independent people. 

Arizona has been a state for 109 years and today it is exactly the way “we the people” have made it. If that is unsatisfactory or repugnant to some, those individuals are free to either engage in the political process or opt for one of the other 49 states that more fully aligns with their expectations. Thank you.

column5: Keeping Greater Scottsdale Together
column6:
Please Keep Greater Scottsdale Together 
I have lived in Scottsdale for five years and have been a property owner here for 11. Since becoming a full-time resident, I have been active in my community and am currently president of my HOA board. I have been following the redistricting process closely and have a strong interest in keeping greater Scottsdale together, as do my neighbors. 
Since the IRC began its map-making, communities of interest have been a key consideration for each commissioner. I live within the footprint of the final draft map, D3. From my standpoint, D3 lacks a recognizable community of interest. It combines clearly rural and clearly urban areas that have little in common. This map is neither fair nor competitive. 
Please see map #LDF049 which fixes the flaws in D3. This map meets all six criteria laid out in the Arizona Constitution. Its particular strength is the economic communities of interest shared by the city of Scottsdale and the Salt River Pima-Maricopa Indian Community (SRPMIC). 
These economic communities of interest are evident in the 101 transportation corridor beginning at about 90th Street and extending roughly to McDowell Road. The city and SRPMIC also share many mutual interests - in protecting desert lands, valuing diverse neighborhoods and valuing a culture of citizen involvement, to name a few. 
I respectfully request the IRC to consider the shared communities of interest between Scottsdale and SRPMIC and keep greater Scottsdale together. I urge you to adopt map #LDF049.

column5: IRC Draft Map Irregularities
column6:
Thank you for the work you are doing.  I know this is close to the end of the service you are performing but please let it weigh heavy on the team you have formed- these maps matter for 10yrs and are to do a service to ALL AZ not just the political parties.  Independents should have a chance to be heard as well as those in the middle - not just the 2 extremes.

Inline with my concern on moderates and Independent voters and ALL of AZ for years to come, I would like to state my concern today regarding the constitutional bound objectives of the commission.  I believe the current team, while attempting to 'even the districts' between parties has incorrectly applied the objectives to the draft map for Southern AZ specific to the LD17 creation at the bidding of a partisan map submittal illegally disguised as a public submittal.  The creation of this politically safe district for the party submitting the map unfairly impacted other districts (LD21, LD10, CD2)

The objectives of the drafts maps are as follows (in no particular order):
A. Districts shall comply with the United States Constitution and the United States voting rights act; 
B. Congressional districts shall have equal population to the extent practicable, and state legislative districts shall have equal population to the extent practicable; 
C. Districts shall be geographically compact and contiguous to the extent practicable; 
D. District boundaries shall respect communities of interest to the extent practicable; 
E. To the extent practicable, district lines shall use visible geographic features, city, town and county boundaries, and undivided census tracts; 
F. To the extent practicable, competitive districts should be favored where to do so would create no significant detriment to the other goals. 

These criteria absolutely all matter.  

Competitiveness as ruled by the AZ Supreme Court in 2008 is absolutely critical to the survival of AZ democratic practices and choice of leaders.  

The court rules that the competitiveness goal cannot be considered less mandatory than the other goals, ignored, or relegated to a secondary role, yet in shifting LD17 from a competitive to a non-competitive district in service of partisan outcomes, the commission is doing exactly this- drawing this district into a safe district for one party and creating 'party safe' district across southern AZ to accommodate this radical LD17 shaping.  The commission had now made LD21 a gerrymandered district that separates core Tucson neighborhoods from the rest of Tucson. It also shifts much of this area from a previously competitive district (LD10, CD2) into a safe Dem district and makes LD17 a safe Rep district.  

We need competitive districts that are drawn responsibly in accordance with the constitution - not across party lines. 
The best way to represent Independents, Non-Affiliated voters as well as right-leaning voters in left-leaning areas, or left-leaning voters in right-leaning areas, is to give them a competitive district where their voices might actually be heard.   The era of extremism has got to stop.  If it is not and AZ residents are not heard, our democracy will fail.  No district should be safe.  Politicians should have to reach out to ALL their voters so that we end up with better results and governorship in Washington and at the state level.

Creating 3 safe Democratic legislative districts and 1 safe Republican district in Pima County isn’t balance - it’s a disservice to voters. Rs, Ds, and independents all lose. We’re asking you to quit sidelining competition in Pima County and everywhere in the state.  

Help ALL Arizona voices be heard.  Move from the current draft map 9.2 to Legislative district draft map 9.0 and work with this map to make competitive districts for all of AZ.  

Please remember, 10yrs of silencing voters can impact the extremism we could see at the state capital and beyond.

These activities span  Santa Cruz County and are interwoven with each other as they support the livelihoods of so many of its residents.
I implore you to not divide this county into different legislative districts.  We need one representative who sees and understands the whole picture of Santa Cruz County and how all the parts are working together for the benefit of the entire county and its economy.  We have a strong ranching tradition. We are part of the Santa Cruz Valley National Heritage Area and have been designated a Global Diversity Hotspot. As a border community, we have a relationship with Mexico whose tourists and shoppers are important to the area as well as a considerable Hispanic population and culture. 
Dividing our county into different legislative districts breaks up the cultural heritage of our area, our  unique and important natural resources, and the economic relationships of our communities.  Santa Cruz County is unique in its diversity and common interests.  We need representation that keeps our county together.

column5: D3 Needs to Be Fixed
column6:
My name is Victoria Kauzlarich.  I have lived in Scottsdale for ten years and have been a property owner here for 20.

I’ve been following the IRC’s progress toward redistricting for months.  I have submitted several written comments and appeared before you publicly during hearings held in September and October.  I also attended the public hearing at Salt River.

I wish to comment on the D3 map.  I’m conversant with the 6 criteria for drawing a district.  Other than meeting the criteria of total population and compactness/contiguousness, I frankly don’t see how the D3 map meets the remaining criteria.

D3 has no discernible community of interest.  The only apparent geographic features are the county boundaries shared with Yavapai, Gila & Pinal. This map looks like what was left over from redistricting decisions made elsewhere in the state.

When looking at the criteria for competitiveness, there is none.  D3 has a 2016-2020 composite of 60(R) - 39(D).

The solution to this problem is NOT to keep LD23 intact as some have suggested.  The solution is to look at this entire region with a new set of eyes.

D3 has an east/west orientation - a footprint guaranteed to be deeply red.  In this region, the key to developing a competitive map is to run it north/south.  As the urban/suburban gives way to the rural, we find that Republicans dominate this landscape.  As we get closer to greater population density, there are more Democrats.  So, Republicans to the north.  Democrats to the south.  

I draw your attention to 3 maps which demonstrate how to create competitive districts in at least part of D3:  map #CDF011, #CDF012, (both of these are LD maps with CD numbers) and map #LDF049.  Each of these maps meet all 6 district criteria and go a long way to creating more fair and competitive maps.  I urge you to factor these three maps into your thinking when drawing final versions.

Thank you for your time and attention.  I’m grateful for your consideration.

Victoria Kauzlarich
Scottsdale Resident

column5: Keep Greater Scottsdale Together
column6:
I am a 31 year resident of Scottsdale of LD23, having spent the last 29 years in the same house near 93rd St and Cactus.  I have watched the evolution of the city over this time, as the population has increased and the tensions between the old and new have waxed and waned over the years.  Happily, however, the sense of a unified city identity has still prevailed, as the city’s residents pride themselves on maintaining Scottsdale as an attractive, diverse and safe place to put down roots.   The is part of why keeping greater Scottsdale together in the redistricting process is so important.

In reviewing the IRC’s proposed legislative district map #3, I am concerned with the way it breaks up Scottsdale by dividing it into 3 districts, which will be much harder to manage as a unified entity, equally serving all of its residents.   The proposed western boundary of Hayden Road would be an artificial division, when Scottsdale Road has long been symbolic of a western boundary and is considered the key north/south artery for the city.  Creating a map that keeps greater Scottsdale together, such as the newly proposed map LDF049, would better serve the residents of Scottsdale.

The IRC proposed map #3 also breaks up nine existing precincts in Scottsdale’s current LD23. This means residents who have been politically active in those areas over the years through reaching out to their neighbors will now have to begin that awareness process anew.   Encouraging strong neighborhoods with people who know each other and have shared interests enhances a city’s strength.  Precincts are one of the structures that enable the development of this unity and keep greater Scottsdale together.
 
In comparing the IRC map #3 with the proposed improved map LDF049, I find the inclusion of the Salt River Pima-Maricopa tribal community in the new proposal to be a major improvement when considering shared communities of interest, contiguous geographic boundaries, and a commitment to both the Voting Rights Act and the creation of competitive districts.   Both the city of Scottsdale and the Salt River tribal community are aligned in their development of land on each side of the #101 freeway all the way to McDowell Rd.   The economic success of both entities is linked through much of this development.  The inclusion of this community in the LDF049 map balances the representation between political parties more evenly than the current IRC map #3, which is skewed 60/40 towards the Republican party. A more even representation between voting blocs and communities of interest should result in better outcomes for all, given more voices will be heard.

My hope is these comments will help you keep greater Scottsdale together as you continue your work on the final version of the new legislative districts.   Thank you for the work you’ve done to date and please refer to the proposed map LDF049 in your final deliberations.
 
Respectfully,
Barbara Carpenter
Scottsdale Resident and HOA Board Member

column6:
As a Wildlife Biologist, Naturalist, and co-owner of an Ecotourism business in Santa Cruz County, I firmly believe that for voting purposes Santa Cruz County should remain one district rather than divide it in two and assign it to other districts. The residents of Santa Cruz should have the right to determine via their vote what happens in terms of Conservation, Ecotourism, and the economy in general within their Reflecting the biological reality of the Patagonia Mountains, Santa Cruz River, San Rafael Grasslands, Canelo Hills, and other conservation units centered in the county. Please keep these like-minded Sky Islands Communities of Interest grouped together, as we share critical environmental and policy concerns and would greatly benefit from being maintained in a single, compact, contiguous, and competitive district. 
Eco-tourism and Birding constitute a vital economic and environmental link throughout this area - interests not shared by the towns in Cochise County. Therefore as a Santa Cruz County business owner for the past 15 years, I urge you not to separate and disperse our communities, as that will certainly negatively impact the financially and environmentally beneficial efforts that we have collectively established here over many years. 
The Santa Cruz Valley contains several stretches of natural river flow, important riparian and grassland habitats, unfragmented wildlife migration corridors, and diverse plant and animal communities - including numerous endangered species. Given global warming and an ongoing 20+ year drought, preserving and protecting our watershed is more crucial than ever. The headwaters of the Santa Cruz River are in San Rafael Valley and the Sonoita Creek Watershed is a major tributary to the Santa Cruz River. Both the Santa Cruz River and Sonoita Creek, remarkably, still hold perennial stretches of water - something that is now vanishingly rare in all of Arizona. Hence, they play a key role in drawing in Ecotourism revenue.
Furthermore, significant parts of Santa Cruz County are identified as Global Biodiversity Hotspots - recognized by many scientists as top regions in the world most in need of protection to ensure the survival of a broad spectrum of flora and fauna.  These areas include: The Santa Rita Mountains, the Patagonia Mountains, Las Cienagas National Conservation Area, the San Rafael Grasslands, and a number of other biodiversity hotspots. A large percentage of residents in Santa Cruz County value such areas not only for recreation, but also for their inherent conservation values.
The critical issues facing the communities along the Santa Cruz River corridor are best served by working together to choose legislative and congressional representatives.

We share the same transportation corridors, schools, parks and shopping centers. The many Independents are swing voters who support candidates who reflect moderation, something Arizona could use, particularly as we face difficult decisions about how to grow our state in the face of climate change - water issues and mountain fires - all require moderate voices that will keep our state habitable long into the future. Education funding and road conditions are other big concerns here, too. : I ask the IRC to live up to the expectations set by voters who established the IRC in 2000: create legislative districts that reflect the Arizona electorate. Given that 1/3 of voters are Independents, recognize that Arizona is a moderate state.
Independent registration has grown by 52,941voters since Nov. 2020, while Republican registration has dropped 8,916 and Democrats are down 3,784. Every year after the legislature adjourns, voters run petition drives to get initiatives on the ballot to overturn radical legislation that voters didn't want. Currently we have 3 petitions to overturn legislation on voting rights and 3 dealing with education funding. We have irresponsible laws that hinder public health policies during a deadly pandemic. We need legislative districts that will elect moderate leaders who reflect Arizona and provide a more efficient, competitive, diverse way of governing. Lastly, ensure communities of color have adequate representation.
