column5: LD6 and LD7 - Navajo Nation IMPORTANT
column6:
Below is some data disputing the discussion of the loss of citizens on the Navajo Nation being used as verification to delete Flagstaff and retrogress small communities in the White Mountains. The alleged 40,000, the number I heard mentioned, did not affect voting in 2020. This argument is a moot point. 

For the Presidential Election of 2020, Democrats turned out 91,374 voters. 25,428 more in 2020 than 2016. 9,202 more Democrat voters turned out than Republicans in the three counties of Apache, Coconino and Navajo where the Navajo Nation rests. The alleged 'loss' of 40,000 should not be a factor in the drawing of LD6 and LD7. Period. Voter stats show that Democrat voters on reservation lands outnumber Democrats in Flagstaff. Will follow up with as close to exact numbers tomorrow.

It's time for Arizona to do right by the citizens of the White Mountains, and keep them together to work on issues that unify them as communities. If you look at representation from past representatives in the current LD7, approximately 80% (possibly higher) of bills written were for the Native populations. The southern side of the current LD7 have rarely, if ever, seen their representatives, received a return phone call or assistance with issues. Personally, I don't like the segregative tone of discussions and requests in your meetings nor providing preference to one one race over another. I thought that was what all this hatred, fighting and white supremacy accusations has been about. The hypocrisy is startling. Everyone I know and every white candidate or representative that I personally know has a great love and concern for our friends and fellow Americans in the Navajo, Hopi and Apache communities. That is not reciprocated from Native representatives. It is egregious some of their people, elderly and Veterans still live without power and water, don't fund programs to protect victims and prosecute offenders of violence against missing and murdered indigenous women and children, don't have adequate healthcare, schools, emergency services, roads, etc. with the amount of federal dollars received over the last five decades under Democrat control. But... the Navajo Nation just purchased a 5 million dollar office space in Washington D.C. 

During Covid in 2020, many spent time and money of our own delivering food and supplies to tribal communities in need (despite receiving over 714 million in CARES Act funding). LD6 Representatives went into both LD6 and LD7 and two candidates running in LD7 went into both districts as well all year delivering food and supplies. But, your Mission Statement and Constitution calls for communities of interest. Flagstaff is currently intertwined with the Nation, and it is better aligned as a community of interest than the small towns in the White Mountains of rural Arizona where there are no commonalities. The way Snowflake, Taylor, White Mountain Lakes and Show Low was plucked into the newly proposed LD6 has the distinct appearance of an ill-intended motive or direct request. 

I emailed documents showing requirements established by the Navajo Nation to register and vote, along with their rules regarding cancellation of voter registration for not voting in "every major tribal election". I suspect voter suppression could be the next issue to come up if Native Democrats don't get exactly what they want. Arizona legislation and laws are less restrictive than the Navajo Nation voter requirements. In Apache County ALL early voting sites are on the reservation with the exception of the county seat building. There are ZERO early voting sites off the reservation, which is suppressive of voters off the reservation, not on. Our voices matter just as much as anyone else's voice does. Keep our communities of interest together, ours and theirs; that's what they've asked for. Flagstaff is without argument, better aligned and a large employer of the Native people. It does not align with your 'Legal Overview' to place a burden on communities that have, in the past and present, good representation, working relationships, similar needs and lifestyle, to create a minority, and strip the good away because Native Democrats want to be sure their candidate wins the Primary. That is gerrymandering, discriminatory and retrogressive. Your own legal overview does not support the current map, nor the reasons for it. While I don't believe those in your ear speak for all Americans on tribal lands, if they are demanding to stay together, so are we; for representation's sake. The current map will leave thousands of individuals worse off than they were. Please put White Mountain communities together. It is time to get this right. Thank you for your time and efforts.

column5: CD6/CD7
column6:
Re CD6/CD7 The commission should honor Mayor Romero’s request that the eastern boundary of CD7 be Campbell Ave. East of  Campbell, the UA “community of interest” (COI) extends randomly into Tucson and the unincorporated areas of Pima County. For example my husband and I are both UA employees and live in Catalina Foothills. Most of my work friends live in the Foothills or other unincorporated areas around Tucson. There is no boundary within Tucson or Pima County that effectively delineates the UA COI. 
I have heard the commission give decision-making weight to the opinions of multiple mayors all over the state, to one City Councilwoman in Phoenix, even to private citizens who happen to have a direct line to commissioners. (I would gladly send my comments by phone or text if I had such contact information although I thought all comments were to go via this public comment mechanism). Why not give that same weight to the comments of the Mayor of one of the largest cities in Arizona? Put the eastern boundary of CD7 at Campbell. 
The construct of communities of interest can be very nebulous and hard to prove. In the case of the CD6/CD7 boundary discussion the UA COI fits that description- hard to justify any particular line. So why not follow the Mayor’s request?  One fears that the attempt to move the boundary further east is actually partisan and an attempt to make CD6 less competitive. The majority of citizens speaking at the Listening Sessions favored competitive districts
Be fair to the citizens of Arizona who voted for this independent redistricting system precisely because they did not want districts based on partisan decisions.

column6:
To  the members of the IRC:

Your proposed draft map 15.0 separates the towns of Snowflake, Taylor, Show Low, Pinetop and Lakeside from their neighboring communities of interest in LD7 in the White Mountain area, and includes them in LD6 with the Native American communities.
I strongly disagree with this proposal and request that you return to the district boundaries shown in map 12.1.1, which unites these towns with their neighbors in LD7, and includes Flagstaff with the Reservation district in LD6.
As Commissioner Mehl has recommended, this more closely follows Arizona redistricting criteria of preserving communities of interest, being compact and contiguous, and following existing political subdivisions and natural boundaries.
Do not follow the path of drawing district boundaries to guarantee a particular electoral outcome based on race or political party.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment.

Jerry Hubbard
Overgaard, AZ

column5: Partisan gerrymandering
column6: I am well aware, as I am sure that all of you are aware, that Arizona was one of the first states to put into place an Independent Redistricting Commission, instead of state legislators, to redraw the district voting maps after each 10-year census. Arizona was held up as an example for the rest of the country as moving toward a more democratic and independent process that encouraged more open and honest debate, more candidate contact with all constituents in a wide-ranging arena, a process that made it necessary for each candidate to explain their policies and to have to answer questions from the public. This does not happen now because we have "protected" districts, where a candidate does not have to answer to the public as a whole, but can expect to rely on his or her very narrow base. This was not the intent of the first Independent Redistricting Commission, and should not be so now. Although equal population, minority groups, and communities of interest are important considerations, the over-riding consideration should be districts that are as diverse and independent as possible. Without that particular consideration, we will always have extreme partisan candidates and extreme partisan policies that do not reflect the concerns and needs of the majority of the public. Please do not undo the reputation of a fair Arizona Redistricting Commission! Every single candidate should have to work honestly for their share of voters!!

column5: Princeton Gerrymandering Project Analysis of current maps vs. draft maps
column6:
One of the three national experts who presented to the Arizona Independent Redistricting Committee regarding measures of competitiveness was Dr. Samuel Wang of Princeton University. Dr. Wang created the Princeton Gerrymandering Project which, among other things, has developed a well-respected method to score proposed redistricting maps for their fairness, competitiveness and partisan bias. 

	Princeton scored the draft maps that the IRC published October 28th before the 30 public comment period. The scores were published the day after the draft maps were finalized. Both the congressional and legislative draft maps received an “A” for partisan fairness. The Congressional map, 7.1, was scored to have a 5.6% partisan bias towards republicans. See: https://gerrymander.princeton.edu/redistricting-report-card?planId=recSdMbhcDC0NV6UO

The LD map, 10.0, had a 3.3% partisan bias towards republicans. See: https://gerrymander.princeton.edu/redistricting-report-card?planId=recwc9wLzOGzNpLud 

Both of the draft maps received the grade of “C” for competitiveness with the congressional map having only three of nine competitive districts and the legislative map having only five of thirty competitive districts. 

	The IRC then had 30 days of hearings to receive public input on their draft maps. Hundreds of concerned citizens testified in favor of increasing the number of fair and competitive districts in both the congressional map and the legislative map. The number of witnesses supporting fair and competitive maps were roughly six times those who disfavored competitive districts. Voters who supported Proposition 106 (which created the IRC) expect the Commission to honor their charge to create fair and competitive districts, not a super majority of safe seats or a partisan map. 

Chair Neuberg said that she heard the public’s call for competitive districts but she announced to the public that she is constrained by the Voting Rights Act which makes it impossible to draw competitive districts. She has used this justification (which is incorrect, of course) to give license to her republican colleagues to take advantage of the final map drafting process. 

	Instead of heeding the overwhelming public call for fair and competitive maps, the IRC is currently engaged in a partisan exercise to create unfair and non-competitive maps. The two republican members of the IRC openly acknowledge that they are receiving private communications from partisan actors over their lunch break which are framing their suggestions for changes to achieve partisan advantage. (Jeremy Duda, a reporter for the Arizona Mirror, noted that they changed district lines to accommodate a republican legislator, Sine Kerr, who was about to be stuck in a democratic district but they changed the lines to accommodate her). Their changes to the draft maps have not focused on fairness but have been designed to create the maximum amount of partisan bias in favor of the republican party. 

	The Princeton Gerrymandering Project has scored their most recent maps as of today, December 20, 2021. Specifically, they scored two maps, CD 11.1 and LD 15.0. Both maps have gone backwards from the draft maps according to Princeton’s scoring. The republican bias on the legislative map has more than doubled to 6.7%. Not surprisingly, the partisan bias grade has been lowered to a “B” from an “A”. There are fewer competitive districts (down to four from five out of thirty on the LD side). The number of county splits has increased and the compactness scores have gone down. This is a worse map according to nearly every criteria Princeton employs. The congressional map now has only two districts that are rated competitive under Princeton’s scoring. I requested Princeton score CD map 12.1 which was adopted by the IRC late today. Based on Timmons’ competitive data analysis, I am sure map 12.1 is a step in the wrong direction. 

Princeton Gerrymandering Project’s scoring of the recent maps can be found here: 

AZ cong map 11.1 (RC): https://gerrymander.princeton.edu/redistricting-report-card/?planId=rectm7R9VDddge6nf

AZ SL map 15.0 (RC): https://gerrymander.princeton.edu/redistricting-report-card/?planId=recYW2ZCwhirMcFw0

	Frankly, it is shocking that the IRC would willfully ignore the input of the public during the constitutionally required 30 day comment period. It is even more shocking that the draft maps, which were clearly biased towards republicans, should become even more biased during the final two weeks of mapping deliberations. This is not the fault of the public or the Voting Rights Act. It is plainly a failure of leadership. Chair Neuberg’s legacy shall be forever tarnished based on her actions and inactions over the last 45 days.

column5: IRC-Blessed Gerrymandering
column6:
I’ve been following the redistricting progress, and map after map, it has boggled my mind how fair and balanced maps with more moderately drawn districts are abandoned in favor of one’s that overwhelmingly favor Republicans — some of these new districts explicitly drawn to create new safe districts for Republicans (LD17 in particular, which goes against the very rules that the committee adopted to ensure balanced districts). When Arizonans voted to create the IRC, it was done in an attempt to remove politics from our once-in-a-decade redistricting process so that both parties have a fair shot and so that Arizonans continue to have a fair say in their representation. Unless serious steps are taken to ensure a balanced process by the supposedly independent Chair of the IRC, Republicans will have unfairly secured a an unbalanced map in their favor for the next 10 years despite a clear minority of voters supporting them — the very antithesis on the democratic process — and very little faith will be left in the IRC and Arizona’s democracy. 

Given how vocal opponents have been with regards to the blatant partisanship of this commission’s members and how their voices have continued to be ignored, I’m not sure you’ll even read this, but I’d love to hear any sort of rational for forcing a Republican district into Tucson and for fracturing Flagstaff to raise Republicans’ standing there.

column5: Reject the GOP gerrymander
column6:
As the Arizona GOP has become a proving ground for far-right extremist politicians, Independent Redistricting Commission Chair Erika Neuberg has delivered them the gift of the most imbalanced, gerrymandered congressional map that Arizona has seen in a generation.

Democratic Commissioners Shereen Lerner and Derrick Watchman have negotiated in good faith, taking Neuberg at her word that as Chair, she would give voice to Democrats, Independents, and Republicans. However, the past weeks have revealed that she was never interested in upholding the criteria for fair and competitive maps clearly outlined in our constitution, choosing instead to undermine the voting power of Arizonans and drawing a 6-3 congressional map in favor of an increasingly radicalized Republican Party.

Despite changing her registration from Republican to Independent in 2016, it is now all too clear that Chair Neuberg is a partisan in sheep's clothing. After two decades of the IRC successfully fulfilling its mission to take power to draw districts away from politicians, Chair Neuberg has abandoned her role as nonpartisan arbiter and negated the voting strength of Independents and Democrats throughout the state. She has been an active participant in the Republican Commissioners' efforts to achieve a warped congressional map so gerrymandered. A Republican legislature might have as well-drawn it.

Suppose this congressional map, or a map resembling it, is passed. In that case, the legacy of Chair Neuberg and the 2021 IRC will be one of rank partisanship that enabled the rising extremism in the Arizona Republican Party, prioritizing it above the needs of Arizonans.

Reject the GOP gerrymander.

In a state that is almost evenly split between Republicans, Independents and Democrats (about 1/3rd each), it appears obvious that AZ's voters want choices!!! More importantly, primary voters are not reflective of all the registered voters in a district (whether congressional or legislative).  This leads to candidates with more extreme views (on both sides) being elected, which further discourages so many from having faith in the political process, thus weakening our democracy.   

In addition, and perhaps of greater significance, the law that created the IRC specifically included competitiveness as a criteria, which unlike 'community of interest,' is an objective term & the IRC itself adopted a clear & objective definition of such.   Therefore, I am very distressed to read that so close to the December 22, 2021 deadline the IRC adopted for final maps, the number of truly competitive districts remains so low.  I am also very distressed that in an evenly divided state, the current maps provide such an advantage to Republicans.  

Please IRC Commissioners, even if you have to extent your deadline, go back to the maps and focus on competitiveness; and for the non competitive districts, strive to have an equal number that lean Democratic as Republican.

Thank you for your service to AZ.

They offer no incentives for the winning candidate to address the concerns of their constituents or to cooperate with members of the opposing party.  They are the antithesis of democratic process.

That is why voters amended the constitution to require that the redistricting process make districts competitive unless to do so would harm or undermine one of the other goals stated in the constitution. Moving the boundaries south to pick up parts of the overpopulated LD 4 and LD 8 and remove parts of the underpopulated rural areas in the north would preserve communities of interest (the more urban parts of Scottsdale along the Loop 101 corridor) and would make the district more compact and closer to the population target, and more regular in shape.  For these reasons it is constitutionally required that the Commission make LD 3 more competitive.

column5: reject the gerrymander

Arizona voters created a way to make elections more fair. Arizona Proposition 106, also known as the Constitutional Amendment Relating to Creation of a Redistricting Commission, was on the November 7, 2000, ballot in Arizona as an initiated constitutional amendment. It was approved by 56 percent of voters. 
Proposition 106 amended the Arizona Constitution to create an independent redistricting commission to re-draw the state's legislative and congressional district lines after every census. The measure was actively opposed by political conservatives.
Later the constitutionality of Prop. 106 was challenged in the courts; that effort failed. In 2015 the U.S. Supreme Court ruled the measure constitutional writing,
“The people of Arizona turned to the initiative to curb the practice of gerrymandering and, thereby, to ensure that Members of Congress would have “an habitual recollection of their dependence on the people.” The Federalist No. 57, at 350 (J. Madison). In so acting, Arizona voters sought to restore “the core principle of republican government,” namely, “that the voters should choose their representatives, not the other way around.” Berman, Managing Gerrymandering, 83 Texas L. Rev. 781 (2005). The Elections Clause does not hinder that endeavor.” 

Clearly, the opponents of Prop. 106 and the IRC it created, decided to defeat the will of the voters with another effort. This time they packed the 2021 commission by adding a pro-Republican “Independent”, Ms. Neuberg. This third conservative in the five member commission was never interested in upholding the criteria for fair and competitive maps clearly outlined in Arizona’s constitution, choosing instead to undermine the voting power of Arizonans and drawing a 6-3 draft congressional map in favor of an extremist anti-democracy party. Another black mark for Arizona!

column5: Santa Cruz County
column6:
Chairwoman Schupak Neuberg and Members of the Arizona Redistricting Commission,
My name is Bruce Bracker, I was born and raised in Nogales Arizona where my family has been involved in local government, supported local charities and owned and operated small businesses for close to 100 years.
I am currently serve on the Santa Cruz County Board of Supervisors representing District #3 which encompasses Tubac, East Rio Rico and all of eastern Santa Cruz County which includes Patagonia, Sonoita and Elgin.
When I addressed this commission at the meeting in Nogales in early August, I emphasized that it was very important to keep Santa Cruz County whole, something that I reaffirmed in my previous letters submitted in October and November of this year.
At your meeting on December 17th you once again adopted a position where you are dividing Santa Cruz County into two Legislative Districts and gerrymandering the entire southeastern border of the state into one district, map 10.0 and 10.2. This does not align with your “community of interest” mandate.
It is critical that all of Santa Cruz County be kept as one legislative district. From our perspective, as a community of interest, we deem it essential that we remain as a part of the same district that includes University of Arizona and Pima Community College. Pima Community College is our partner for our community college district and our partner for our high school JETD programs. The University of Arizona has had a satellite campus in Santa Cruz County for many years and we benefit from their economic research of our community.
Dividing our county and, by redrawing the district lines to include the eastern portions of the county in a district that includes Cochise County, you are actually combining two portions of Arizona that have very little in common. There is little in the way of familiar, educational, or economic ties between these two areas thus I am puzzled and cannot find a rationale for this action. In fact, the realignment in this instance is counter to the best interests of the eastern portions of my County. It will weaken our political significance; it will further entrench the economic disadvantages and alienate our residents from each other by forcing them to find new economic and political alliances to be recognized and considered.
In closing, I also mentioned at your meeting in Nogales that it is very important to have two congressional districts that represent the communities on the US-Mexico border. This reasoning also applies to State legislative Districts. Though rural, our proximity to
Board of Supervisors

the US – Mexico Border means that we are dealing with issues that require the attention of the State Legislature and the Governor. By creating a disjointed border district, you dilute the representation for the region. I urge your reconsideration of this proposal and stress the importance of keeping all of Santa Cruz County within one legislative district. Our economic, social, and political future depends on it.
I thank you for the attention you give to this urgent petition.
Sincerely,
Bruce Bracker

column5: Prop 106 Violation
column6:
To: Arizona Independent Redistricting Commission
ATTN: Chairwoman Neuberg, Vice-Chair Watchman, Commissioner Mehl, Commissioner Lener, and Commissioner York,
Brett Johnson, Snell and Wilmer
Roy Herrera, Ballard Spahr
 
Dear Commissioners,
 
My name is Alex Smith, a resident and voter of Maricopa County. I am writing to the Commission to express my concern that the Independent Redistricting Commission is not in compliance with the residency requirements.  Commissioner Watchman was appointed as a representative from Apache County, however, according to the Maricopa County Accessor’s records, Commissioner Watchman owns a home in Maricopa County. While this is not determinative that the Commission is acting in contradiction of the law, it is concerning that the IRC appears to not be honoring the intent and is not honoring the language of Prop 106. This is important to voters like me because Prop 106 (enacted by the voters) established what is supposed to be a transparent, fair, and representative independent redistricting commission.
 
I understand that Commissioner Watchman might “reside” in Apache County, but it is possible that he actually resides in Maricopa County. Arizonans deserve transparency in our democracy, and the map drawing process is no exception, which is why the Commission should address this residency question immediately.
 
The diligent work of the Commission so far gives me hope that the Commission and the commission’s attorneys Chairwoman will do the right thing by giving this issue the serious consideration it deserves. Ultimately, the Commission should investigate this and provide an answer to the public prior to voting on any maps.
 
 
Sincerely,
 
Alex Smith

column5: IRC Process going forward
column6:
IRC Meeting Comment 12/21/21

All members of the 2021 IRC deserve our gratitude, but I want to extend my special thanks to Shareen Lerner.  She is blessed (some might argue cursed) with incredible patience and remarkable anticipatory problem skills.  When selecting starting points for both CD and LD maps, she shared her best hypotheses, but never imposed her view on her colleagues. Instead she listened respectfully, offered counterproposals that referenced specific Constitutional criteria, and only then alerted her colleagues to potential pitfalls that going down other paths might lead to. Time after time she was outvoted, and time after time those of us who followed the IRC proceedings witnessed the results of ignoring her foresight—dead ends, tradeoffs, fits and starts--and restarts. That’s how we left things yesterday.

Today we learned what being taken seriously by Commission colleagues requires. Playing well with others is insufficient.  No one should be surprised that Commissioner Lerner’s righteous indignation erupted this morning.  Her message was not new, she just repeated it more forcefully.  Drawing her own red line was a game changer. Her colleagues became more willing to compromise, and the process moved noticeably forward.  Perhaps if she had done that when the shenanigans started, all of us might have been saved a lot of time and anguish.  Lesson learned.

If maps are approved tomorrow as anticipated, we are likely to end up where we expected we would—with some people happy and others disappointed and/or angry.  But only time will tell if the process actually ends there.  We know the previous Arizona IRC was involved in court proceedings.  

A few days ago, the Commission’s legal team reviewed a current court case regarding the Texas redistricting process.  Their summary foreshadowed what might await Arizona.  The Texas case demonstrates that courts will hear meritorious lawsuits even in the absence of pre-clearance.  One thing the lawyers mentioned that could trigger a case in Arizona is evidence that better and fairer maps than those chosen were suggested and available.  (This seems possible.) Another potential trigger is evidence that the Constitution was violated.  (This, too, seems possible, as evidenced by facts uncovered and published by area investigative reporters.)   Another possible source of evidence is the written record of changes made to approved draft maps, which arguably provides a roadmap documenting bias. 

I know current commissioners are likely to be called upon to provide guidance to the 2031 commission.  I learned many things following this commission’s work that I would like to make part of the public record. At the beginning of the process, it is important to have public discussions about all the criteria. What do the individual criteria mean and how will they be used to arrive at specific decisions--especially when they are in conflict and must be weighed.  Here is an example:  Consultants helped the current commissioners develop a common metric for competitiveness, but they never came to a common understanding of the role competitiveness can and should play in the redistricting process. I don’t believe they did this for COIs either, which created problems throughout the process.  (Many Arizonans continued to believe that a COI is defined by where you shop, dine, and worship.)  Likewise, commissioners did not develop a common understanding of terms like “to the extent practicable” or “significant detriment to other criteria.”  This lack of clarity then spilled over into a large portion of the public.  Having said that, some IRC followers were incredibly well informed and thoughtful. They contributed maps, documents, and public comments.  I was amazed at the investment so many Arizonans put into following the Commission’s work, attending public meetings, and providing thoughtful feedback.  

I want to end by thanking all the commissioners, staff, lawyers, mappers and consultants for their work.  Democracy can be slow, messy, and imperfect, but I continue to believe it is worth the time and the effort.

column5: Map 16
column6:
Oops! it appears from map 16 that the commissioners have lost the Forrest for the trees.  With our population almost evenly divided between the three parties, each group should be given a third of the  seats in a map of the state's voting districts: 1/3 Republican,1/3 Democrat, and1/3 Independent. We should see equal representation by each party in the final maps for both the legislative and Congressional districts. That means, out of the 30 legislative seats  posted Tuesday night;10 should lean Republican; 10 should lean Democrat, and 10 should lean competitive for Independents.  In the same  way, tomorrow, when finalizing the Congressional Districts: 3 would lean Republican, 3 would lean Democrat, and 3 would lean competitive for Independents.
    Unfortunately for the the details hammered out on Tuesday's LD map, the commissioners were very patient in wading through many compromises but they somehow became unmoored from the big picture. They will still need some major adjustments on Wednesday if the maps are going to represent the state of Arizona fairly. The 'final' legislative districts  on map 16 should have even 10:10:10 ratios and  instead have the ratio of 14:12: 4: 14 Republican leaning;12 Democrat leaning; and 4 Competitive leaning. Where's the fairness in giving Republicans a two seat advantage over the Democrats?  Where's the fairness in telling Independents that there is a 'real' race where everyone's vote counts in only four seats out of the entries House of Representatives The commissioners spent hours changing details about districts without checking on the big picture and now there will need to be some major adjustments if the map is going to be an equitable arrangement for Arizona's voters to to be saddled to for the next ten years!  It is obvious that no members of the IRC would even think of gerrymandering their final map in this way yet too much attention to details (and, really, a pretty unwieldly mapping app) have has allowed this to happen. Hopefully, when the commissioners begins the CD on Wednesday they will be able to keep their eye on the big picture and create a genuinely representative (3:3:3) proportion on the CD map and  won't have to return to the drawing board on that one as as well.
     As hard as our commissioners have been working, it is unlikely they will be able to totally  repair the LDs and finish the CDs tomorrow.  There is not enough time in one day to adequately give careful attention to quality and integrity to the big picture that is needed. Maybe it is best for everyone to take a few days to rest and clear their heads before coming  back on the 26th or 27th to complete the work. It is really no big surprise they the commission will not be finished with their weighty task on the 22nd as  tentative goals for big projects such as this never finish early. Still,  it must be discouraging for members of the commission who must  certainly be growing very weary of compromising on irrelevant details while everyone ignores the white elephant of equal ratios at the state level.(Even the two hundred plus volunteers that applied for the honor of representing Arizona as one of  the five redistricting commissioners are probably thanking their lucky stars that they didn't make it at this point!).
     No one can get our exhausted  commissioners across the finish line; only their own continued work ethic and commitment to fairness can do this.* Hopefully they will find strength in knowing that their grand children will hear about what they did. Hopefully they will be proud to know their state will again lead the nation in pioneering the best practices for supporting and strengthening its democracy with fair voting districts. It may not always seem so but many of us who are not on the hot seat  for accomplishing such a commendable task truly do appreciate their patience and perseverance   in succeeding at the task.  The public also has seen the  respect they  have modelled for the differing opinions of their colleagues and members of the public! Thank you to all of them!  Have a restful holiday and everyone come back refreshed!  
* The regrettable decision to 'borrow' tech people from the current state's administration (it to save the state money?!) which came about halfway into the redistricting year is not too late to change.  The commission as well as the public have definitely been hindered by a mapping and feedback app that is pretty user-unfriendly. Even Zillow has a user-friendly app that allows anyone to outline a territory on a map, select one of about five filters, and get immediate feedback.  Customers can do this immediately without any tutorial and without filtering every question through their app crew. The support staff which the IRC has borrowed from the state ,especially the map people would probably be very grateful if the commission spent the balance of the 6 million budget they were allowed to hire a expert from silicon Valley to mentor them and get the app up to modern snuff.  if not enough money remains, there would certainly be justification for adding the 22% inflation that has occurred since this amount was allotted for the fist IRC ten years ago.  About1.3 more billion dollars added would definitely be pretty enticing for a 'temp job" by one of the best programmers in the world. Additionally
the state would benefit for decades to come by securing a powerful user-friendly app to build on.  This time, it needs to be the Chairman and perhaps another member of the council ( maybe the other PhD who is also skilled at research) who locates and acquires the outside help for the commission.  I would suggest starting with a local Zillow Realtor and working their way to the top of the company; the process would most likely go VERY QUICKLY and, if they don't get to the CEOs desk in an hour (Rich Barton) is one of the top programmers in the world), they may at least reach his executive assistant, Kristen Fowler who could give them other recommendations for the another top -rated -tech -guru who can advice our Arizona people for a few days. 
    Those of the IRC team who have paid such admirable attention to the state's budget and chosen to use our government's support staff inn order to help do this might not understand at first, but it is the right of the commissioners to do this and, it would be crazy  to be penny wise and foolish at a time like this.  The most import decision that can be made for our state is happening right now and we need to do the right thing' get the best help there is.  Arizona can do this!

column5: AZ redistricting
column6: Speaking as a citizen of these Unites States of America, a democracy, we want a governing system in place that represents its citizens - ALL of its citizens.  In the state of Arizona, also a democracy last time I checked, we want fair, competitive, compact maps that consistently (not selectively) respect communities of interest and comply with Voting Rights Act requirements.  What is being proposed is turning out to be a far cry from the compact, geographically rational, competitive districts called for in the AZ constitution.  When we have a system that is set up so one party always wins, that’s not democracy and we will end up with skewed representation where only a select few citizens are heard.  How is that democracy?  The purpose of the AIRC is to ensure that bias does not corrupt the decisions of the redistricting maps, but that it exactly what is happening.  The commission is not achieving the purpose of their duties to meet the six constitutional criteria - particularly compactness and competitiveness.  Gerrymandering LD17 and LD21 achieves the exact opposite of these criteria. These districts are neither compact nor competitive and it is quite remarkable how something like this could even be considered by an “independent” commission.  I implore the commission to go back to map 9.0 which is the closest thing to representing a democratic state.

column5: Redistricting Santa Cruz County
column6:
I have not only resided in Santa Cruz County for 26 years; I have lived an actively involved life in working with many people across the county who are focused on protecting and enhancing the true wealth of this county:  our public lands, our diversity, and our cultural history.  As the co-owner of a retail business for 15 years in Patagonia, I know first hand that this area is a world-wide destination for nature based activities.

Santa Cruz County is the smallest county in Arizona based on geographic size and is one of the smallest based on population and per capita income.  It is also reported that Santa Cruz County has the highest quality of life.  I believe that quality of life reflects the residents being actively engaged in co-creating a thriving community for all.  

Based on my experience, I implore you not to divide Santa Cruz County into different legislative districts.  All of Santa Cruz County is a community of interest with visible geographic features: the headwaters of the Santa Cruz River are in San Rafael Valley and the Sonoita Creek Watershed is a major tributary to the Santa Cruz River.  A significant part of Santa Cruz County is identified as a Global Biodiversity Hotspot recognized by many scientists as one of the top regions in the world most in need of protection for species survival.  The Patagonia Mountains on the southeastern Santa Cruz County border are key to Santa Cruz County’s future well being.  

In order to best protect this CommUNITY of interest, it is critical that all of Santa Cruz County continue as one district rather than being divided in two and assigned to other districts.

DO NOT divide up the Santa Cruz Valley Watershed which includes the Patagonia Mountains and the Town of Patagonia.  A 6:30 congressional map, in favor of Republicans, is not a map that reflects AZ in 2021.  AZ is no longer a Republican dominant state.  AZ's US Senators are both Democrats.  AZ went blue in the 2020 presidential election.  A majority of our members of Congress are Democrats and Democrats hold nearly half of all of the state legislative seats.  DO NO ignore the will of the AZ voters!  The IRC was created by voters to prevent gerrymandering:  the proposed level of partisan imbalance is a clear indicator of pending partisan gerrymandering!

This seems like the right comment to start this dialogue.  I have watched and listened and heard the commission. I ask, given the proceedings, has the commission truly acted as independent or has it sides with one participant who has made aggression comments and surreptitious submittals of maps?

The current maps and the maps like LD v10 have shown this process is not independent.  It has not been since inception.  As a man who has faith leaders should do the right thing and hold themselves to the truth and have the purest of motives, I see this has not occurred.  

Please review the current maps.  Ask for outside counsel to review the maps.  They are tainted especially the current CD12.1.  This is a horrible map with leanings to appease a party not the people.  Consider the voices of the communities of interest and the goals of the commission.  NO- Native Voices are not going to be 'heard' in DEM primaries if the district is gerrymandered?  This  comment by a committee member should have stricken this member from a vote.  This would assume the GOP is not out to represent this minority in any shape and should be considered only for a homogeneous few.  This is not fair representation then if the majority of districts lean to the GOP. 

To fix this- considered looking at the comments of those asking for competitive districts and review the tenants of the IRC and avoid gerrymandering tests with these three statistical steps taken directly from Stanford law review article 'Three Tests for Practical Evaluation of Partisan Gerrymandering' by Samuel S.-H. Wang:
(1) an unrepresentative distortion in the number of seats won based on expectations from nationwide district characteristics
(2) a discrepancy in winning vote margins between the two parties
(3) the construction of reliable wins for the party in charge of redistricting, as measured by either the difference between mean and median vote share, or an unusually even distribution of votes across districts. 

The first test relies on computer simulation to estimate appropriate levels of representation for a given level of popular vote and provides a way to measure the effects of a gerrymander. The second and third tests, which can be used to help evaluate redistricting intent, rely on well-established statistical principles and can be carried out using a hand calculator without examination of maps or redistricting procedures.  We should not need #3 but unfortunately commission vote have been heavily one sides as if run by a partisan group.

Currently the maps fail, lean GOP and the only hope is you look deep in yourselves as as INDEPENDENT commission and redo the decisions and votes made that impact the INDEPENDENT effort.  You have the power.

column5: Postmortem Notes for the Independent Redistricting Commission
column6:
I took some time to do a postmortem from my perspective as an Independent voter on what I felt went right and what could be improved about the commission’s work during the past year.

What went right:
1.	The experts who were brought in to analyze the polarization data and to provide discussions of other topics like measuring competitiveness were all very good.
2.	Executive Assistant Valerie Neumann provided excellent and (usually) timely help responding to ad hoc requests from the public.
3.	The IRC stuck to its schedule.

What could be improved:
1.	The IRC stuck to its schedule, whether or not that was _enough_ time to spend on their task and get it right is a different question.
2.	The method for selecting commissioners was politically manipulated by the governor, so the process as designed was subverted from the start.
3.	The commissioners failed to see their role as representing _all_ Arizonans and instead frequently stated that they represented their political party and/or the people of their county or the place of residence.  That immediately set up an adversarial relationship among the commissioners and injected political partisanship into every discussion.  There was never an opportunity for impartiality.
4.	The mission of the commission was never clearly stated and agreed upon.  That meant the process had no clear guidance.  From the outcome, it’s clear that, for the majority of commissioners, creating (as stated in Proposition 106) “fair and competitive” districts was NOT their mission or even _a_ goal, when it should have been driving the entire process.
5.	The commissioners failed to comprehend the opposing forces that were intentionally set up by Proposition 106.  It pits the tendency to want to be in homogeneous districts with the need to be in diverse districts.  It’s the job of the commission to balance those forces to find their equilibrium when drawing the boundaries.  That process was meant to be difficult, and the only way to achieve it is by having a healthy debate of the issues that arise because of it.  That was the mechanism Proposition 106 set up with the aim of bolstering democracy, and it was disregarded by the commission at every step.
6.	The commission failed to define the six criteria and the importance of each one to the overall outcome was never made clear.  That allowed commissioner Neuberg to elevate the Communities of Interest criteria to the level of an 'organizing force' over the rest.  Even where the commissioners did agree on measurements and criteria, they did not decide in advance how they would be applied.
7.	Because the first Listening Tour focused on getting people to talk about their Communities of Interest, it set the stage for people to believe that they could have districts that would reflect those communities – and only those communities – that their voices, and only their voices, would be heard.  That was unrealistic, but the commission did nothing to set expectations otherwise.  That also set the tone and direction for all future discussions and considerations, even after the point where the communities that arose from those tours were no longer referred to or used as discussion points.
8.	The commission never tried to resolve the points of difference between the various Communities of Interest, or even made clear where the points of contention lay.
9.	The acceptance of the idea that the commission had to build everything from scratch worked against it from the start.  It was unable to hit the ground running in ways that could easily have been avoided (e.g., assembling the IT team and resources and getting an effective website up and running, understanding its obligations under the Open Meetings law, establishing a team and process for handling Public Records Requests, and it never really established a coherent strategy for outreach or the gathering of public input much less outbound messaging) by using experienced and highly-qualified personnel and consultants.  It also resulted in it making a bad choice for Executive Director and delayed selection of an Outreach Coordinator to the point of making that position meaningless.
10.	The public hearings were insufficient to gather testimony that reflected the general will of the people.  They did not occur at the times and places that allowed members of the general public to take part in them.  As such the views presented were skewed away from minorities.  It was no doubt expensive to conduct these but in the end that might not have mattered much, since the testimony was disregarded in large part anyway.  They served to give the commission the impression it was listening to the public and provided a talking point they could bring up to reassure themselves that they had done their best.
11.	Polarization analysis should have been conducted on all districts.
12.	A report of the outcome or gist of all Executive Sessions should have been shared with the public, including
  a.	Reports (at least their executive summaries) received and reviewed.
  b.	A summary of the legal advice provided to the commissioners.
13.	Although I did not submit any myself, I have heard from more than a few people that the Public Records Requests they made were not follow-up in a timely manner, often for many months if at all.  This made it difficult for the public to perform its role in the process, and is probably a violation of several statutes.  Certainly it undermines the credibility of the commission and makes it harder for the public to have any confidence in the process or outcome of the IRC’s work.
14.	The Executive Director was not up to the level expected from someone in that role serving a commission of such crucial importance.  His reports, when they weren’t late or skipped entirely, were wholly inadequate and amateur.  The public was never able to see any detail around the expenditures for the various consultants or other items being paid for with our tax dollars.  We never did see the budget report he kept saying for months would be forthcoming.  He was poorly prepared for meetings and frequently failed to follow through on requests from the commissioners or other action items.  It’s difficult to know whether this was due to ineptness or if it was by design, but every time the chair publicly commended him during meetings it was painful to believe she could not see how poorly he was performing and what a disservice he did to the commission and to the citizens of Arizona as well.  It’s further evidence of the low level of her quality standards, something we saw demonstrated too often during the year.  We all deserved so much more.
15.	The mapping consultants should have been tasked with delivering a version of the draft maps that optimized the criteria.  This was a simple and obvious request and, given the expertise the chair so often championed, they had (or should have had) the skills and resources to carry it out.  But no one on the commission asked, so they did not.


William Bowlus-Root
A very concerned citizen
